A US federal judge has ordered the Donald Trump administration to restore White House access to journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico, ruling that the ban was likely unconstitutional, Reuters reported. US District Judge Timothy Kelly issued the order in a lawsuit filed by the three news organisations challenging the administration’s decision to bar them from White House access. Trump had accused the three organisations of repeatedly publishing what he described as “FICTION and LIES”. The president made the remarks in a social media post while defending the decision to restrict their access. The US Department of Justice had argued that the administration’s decision was justified on national-security grounds. According to CNBC, DOJ lawyers told the court that “access to the White House is a privilege — not a right”. The department also said Trump had determined that the outlets had reported classified or sensitive information related to national security. The three organisations filed a lawsuit in federal court in Washington, DC, arguing that the restrictions amounted to unlawful retaliation for constitutionally protected speech, Reuters reported. They also accused the administration of violating their due-process rights. “This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the organisations said. The White House has maintained that the affected organisations can continue covering the administration without having direct access to the Oval Office or other White House spaces. It argued that journalists from the outlets could report from outside the White House and said they should not be able to demand access to the president’s office. “The Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President’s Oval Office,” the White House said in a statement, accusing the outlets of spreading what it called lies and saying their reporting harmed the American public. The court proceedings will now focus on the administration’s national-security justification for the restrictions and the media organisations’ First Amendment claims. Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Trump, is overseeing the case and has ordered the restoration of access while the legal challenge proceeds. Independent Talent Group (ITG) has bought into UK sport talent agency Tongue Tied Management (TTM).
The deal comes as ITG seeks growth following Sienna Private Equity last December buying a major stake in Duncan Heath’s agency, which represents the likes of Daniel Craig and Gillian Anderson.
TTM represents athletes, coaches, broadcasters, and creators, including Jill Scott, Manchester United coach Michael Carrick, Dion Dublin and Hayley McQueen. FIFA-registered intermediary and Women in Football board member Jo Tongue founded and leads the agency.
“This strategic investment is an important step in Independent Talent Group’s ambition to build Europe’s leading entertainment and sport talent group,” said Sally Long-Innes, CEO of ITG. “Tongue Tied Management is an exceptional founder-led business, built on outstanding expertise, and deep client relationships – leading in growth areas like women’s sport.”
Watch on Deadline
Tongue said ITG’s investment would allow TTM’s team and clients “access to a broader network across entertainment and global commercial partnerships, while preserving the spirit, culture, and personal approach our clients value.”
The news also comes soon after ITM set up a studio with former BBC News boss Deborah Turness.
“Our ambition is to build a business that has broader capabilities and expertise at the intersection of culture, entertainment and sport whilst keeping a focus on what matters most: outstanding people, exceptional talent and long-term relationships,” said ITG founder and chairman Heath today.
“This investment reflects how we intend to grow in the sport and entertainment sectors – backing exceptional founders and investing in great businesses to strengthen our collective platform and give both partners more opportunities to grow.”

Meta announced a slate of new wearables during its annual Meta Connect showcase on Wednesday. The star of the event was the new Meta VR Glasses, which pack virtual reality tech into a lightweight smart glasses-style frame with a tethered puck. Meta also announced new pairs of screen-free smart glasses, along with some new AI features and style and frame options.
Meta Connect 2026: The 7 biggest announcements
This year’s Meta Connect featured a new lightweight VR wearable and camera-free Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses.
You can catch up on all the highlights from this year’s Meta Connect below.
Meta’s latest wearable offers full virtual reality in a smart glasses-style form factor. Unlike a typical VR headset, the VR Glasses don’t have any straps, and Meta says they’re “five times lighter than Meta Quest 3” at just 100g. Similar to Google’s Project Aura, the glasses are tethered to a pocket-sized puck with the compute hardware, battery, and storage, including a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite, 128GB of storage, and 12GB of RAM. The 5K micro OLED “Infinite Display” has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye, with a refresh rate of up to 120Hz.
The Meta VR Glasses are launching in spring 2027 for $1,299, pricier than the Meta Ray-Ban Display but less expensive than the Apple Vision Pro, while offering similar features. Users can connect the glasses to a Mac or Windows laptop for use as a virtual external display, with an option for a virtual surface keyboard and touchpad.
The VR Glasses also have access to the full Meta Quest catalog of apps and games and support for Xbox Cloud Gaming. Meta says the glasses are “the first IMAX Enhanced certified VR device ever,” and users will be able to watch “immersive live sports” with them as well as 3D movies. They even have a “hologram” feature that creates a “photorealistic digital version of your face” for using in calls while wearing the glasses, reminiscent of the “personas” on the Apple Vision Pro.
Meta is launching camera-free smart glasses
The highlight of the Ray-Ban Meta Audio is the feature they don’t have: built-in cameras. You can use them for things like listening to music, taking calls, or chatting with an AI assistant, but they can’t take pictures or record video — features that have sparked privacy and harassment concerns around Meta’s other glasses.
Meta says the new audio-only glasses are also its “lightest, slimmest AI glasses yet,” weighing just 43g. They offer up to 12 hours of battery life per charge, or 48 hours with the charging case. The Ray-Ban Meta Audio will launch on October 13th starting at $349 with 23 different color and lens combinations.
Refreshed Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 arrive with battery and design upgrades
Meta launched an updated version of its main Ray-Ban Meta glasses, starting at $449. The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 offer up to nine hours of battery life, one hour more than the Gen 2. They also have “a new customizable action button for instant access to Meta AI” and a new six-mic array that Meta says “cuts more than 90% of background noise.”
The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 has a slimmer design than the Gen 2 as well, with 27 color and lens combinations, including new Zena and Aviator frame styles. Notably, one thing that hasn’t changed is the built-in LED light that indicates when the glasses are recording, which Meta rolled out a privacy fix for last month.
Budget glasses launch along with new glasses styles
Alongside its pricier Ray-Ban glasses, Meta also announced some updates to its in-house line of glasses. It’s launching a new lower-cost version of the Meta Adventurer, which will start at $249 for a basic design with black frames and gray lenses, launching October 23rd.
Meta is also introducing a new “Mix & Match” program for customizing its glasses with different frames, lenses, and case colors. Plus, its EssilorLuxottica collection is getting two new styles, Capri and Nova, and the Kylie Jenner Starfire frames are getting a new ivory colorway. Meta’s also launching a new collaboration collection with Lisa of Blackpink.
Meta Glasses are expanding to more countries starting today, too, including Singapore, South Korea, Mexico, and the United Arab Emirates, with availability in Brazil “coming soon.”
Meta Ray-Ban Display is coming to more regions with some new features
A year after they originally launched, the Meta Ray-Ban Display are coming to more regions. The glasses are on sale in the UK and Canada starting today, and they’ll be available in France, Italy, and Germany starting on October 13th. Meta’s also introducing online ordering for customers in those regions and the US.
Meta’s launching a new Explore app for Display glasses where users will be able to “browse and use a growing selection of experiences built for your glasses.” The Meta Ray-Ban Display is also getting photo editing, an improved calendar, and mirrored phone notifications. Plus, Meta says the “hologram” feature launching on its VR Glasses is rolling out on the Meta Ray-Ban Display “in Early Access on WhatsApp to Meta Ray-Ban Display users in the US later this fall.”
After launching its new Muse assistant earlier this month, Meta says it’s “working on” bringing the AI to its smart glasses. When it arrives on the glasses, Muse will be able to do things like guide your workouts, log meals, book appointments, and “help buy products you see.”
Meta also announced some new features for Muse, including video calls with a customizable live avatar of the AI. Plus, Muse agents are getting their own email addresses for completing tasks and communicating with users.
Meta is making an AI ‘charm’
Mark Zuckerberg teased one last device, Muse Charm, a small AI gadget that houses the Muse agent and looks a little bit like a supersized Tamagotchi. More details will be shared “soon,” he said, but the product is supposed to ship in time for the holiday season.

MP Materials mines and processes rare earth minerals in California, including neodymium-praseodymium oxide used in high-performance magnets.
Credit:
David McNew/Getty Images
MP Materials mines and processes rare earth minerals in California, including neodymium-praseodymium oxide used in high-performance magnets.
Credit:
David McNew/Getty Images
All of these devices function because of 17 metals collectively known as rare earth elements. The scientists who gave the group that name in 1794 created a misnomer. Cerium alone is about as common in the Earth’s crust as copper.
However, separating rare earth minerals from one another and from raw ore is intensely difficult. As a result, countries that control the processing of rare earth minerals have a lot of political leverage.
China processes most of the rare earth minerals used around the world, and it isn’t just consumer electronics that depend on Chinese exports. The US military’s F-35 fighter jets and Virginia-class submarines need rare earths too.
I spent years adjudicating war games for the US Navy. War games force players to identify the hidden constraints that render a beautiful plan untenable. Rare earth processing is exactly such a constraint.
China showcased the power of its rare earths leverage with a series of export controls issued in 2025 that it agreed to suspend—at least until Nov. 10, 2026. Controlling the supply enables a government to slow a rival’s growth, or halt it. China’s ability to extend the suspension of its export controls or let them go into effect gives it leverage on the geopolitical stage. In the parlance of Theodore Roosevelt, it’s a very big stick.
The US has rare earth minerals, but few mines. For years, it shipped much of what it does mine overseas for processing. MP Materials’ Mountain Pass mine and processing facility restarted in California in 2017.
The US has rare earth minerals, but few mines. For years, it shipped much of what it does mine overseas for processing. MP Materials’ Mountain Pass mine and processing facility restarted in California in 2017.
Credit:
Tmy350/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA
China, which mined about 60 percent of the world’s rare earth elements used in magnets in 2024, handled about 91 percent of separation and refining.
Buyers using processing in China got material below the cost of making it themselves, and none of the cleanup bills or the bad press. But they ceded leverage to the processor in exchange. The trade was understood. It just didn’t look as threatening at first from a China that was still rising.
Why rebuilding is slow
The US Government Accountability Office cited estimates in 2010 that rebuilding a domestic supply chain including mining, separation, and magnet manufacturing would take as long as 15 years. Actually rebuilding that supply chain has been slow for several reasons.
China runs its plants with thousands of experienced engineers; the US has far fewer experts. Today’s industrial-scale cutting-edge technologies were developed in China, and the government there has no reason to share. Beijing also banned exports of the separation technology itself in December 2023.
The US has rare earth deposits, but little mining. The pink areas in this US Geological Survey map are believed to have potential for rare earth deposits.
Credit:
USGS
The US has rare earth deposits, but little mining. The pink areas in this US Geological Survey map are believed to have potential for rare earth deposits.
Credit:
USGS
The US government has committed more than $7 billion since April 2025 to try to rebuild US rare earth production capacity. The Pentagon bought $400 million of preferred stock in rare earth producer MP Materials in 2025, giving it 15 percent ownership of the company. MP Materials expects its next magnet plant to begin testing the equipment in 2028.
The Commerce Department also signed a letter of intent in 2026 to give a magnet maker, USA Rare Earth, $277 million in direct funding and a $1.3 billion loan, both aimed at developing facilities in Texas and Oklahoma.
But export roadblocks put up by China are making rebuilding that supply chain more difficult.
What happens on November 10
On Oct. 9, 2025, China’s Ministry of Commerce announced six wide-ranging export control measures. One, Announcement No. 61, affects what even factories abroad can export. A factory in Germany or Japan would need a Chinese license to export a product if Chinese-origin rare earths made up 0.1 percent or more of its value, or if it used Chinese rare earth technology.
Both controls snap back into place automatically unless both governments extend their pauses.
What stays in place
Some of the export rules were never suspended, including licensing imposed by China in April 2025 on exports of seven of the heavier rare earths.
Automaker Ford saw how the export controls can affect a company when it had to idle its Chicago assembly plant for a week in May 2025 for want of magnets—critical to speakers and electrical motors—because of the export rules. Ford CEO Jim Farley described his supply as “day to day” because he had no alternate source. Ford was able to resume production only with Beijing’s approval.
On June 22, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce put 10 US companies on its export control list. Neither Chinese nor foreign firms can sell those companies any goods that have both civilian and military uses. Most of them build drones, radar, aerospace systems, and military vehicles. Two of them—MP Materials and USA Rare Earth—are the federally backed American companies furthest along in building a mine-to-magnet chain.
Beijing said its move was a response to a similar move by the Pentagon. My interpretation is that China picked MP Materials and USA Rare Earth because they are best placed to reduce America’s need for Chinese processing.
An extension of the pause on Nov. 10 would honor the truce, but the heavy rare earth licenses and the June 22 ban on the targeted firms would still apply. The truce means both parties get to play nice. It doesn’t mean they are being nice.
Rebuilding a US rare earths supply chain would remove most US dependence on China for rare earths and the political leverage it implies. But it would take longer, startup costs run to the billions of dollars, and separation produces acidic, and sometimes radioactive, residues.
Building a supply chain with allies such as Australia or Japan, both of which have started to build capacity, would lower the risk of the US being cut off unilaterally. Japan has run this play with some success, but the suspended Chinese rules affect any use of their technology abroad.
President Xi’s Sept. 24, 2026, meeting with Trump may help determine the status of the Nov. 10 restrictions, but the larger conflict over leverage will continue.

Rogers has directly received campaign donations from people who appeared in the Epstein files.
Contrary to the claim's implication, Rogers received much of these funds during his 2024 Senate campaign, not his 2026 campaign. Furthermore, these donors sent most of the funds to independent PACs supporting Rogers, not directly to Rogers' campaign.
Being named in the Epstein files is not necessarily evidence of wrongdoing. It's unclear whether any of these donors knew of or were complicit in Epstein's crimes, and there's no evidence they were.
In September 2026, a claim spread online that Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate for a U.S. Senate seat to represent Michigan, had received nearly $4.7 million from donors who appeared in files related to the federal investigation of the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The rumor spread on X, Threads and Facebook (screenshot). Some posts also claimed at least seven of Rogers' donors had ties to Epstein. Rogers' Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, also shared the rumor.
This claim is mostly true at face value, but it needs significant context.
It originated with a report in the Detroit Metro Times, a progressive news outlet, titled, accurately, "Donors named in Epstein files gave nearly $4.7 million to Mike Rogers and groups backing him."
The story explains that Stephen Schwarzman, co-founder and CEO of investment management company Blackstone, donated $4.5 million in 2024 to a super PAC that supported Rogers. By law, super PACs, which are allowed to raise unlimited money, can't coordinate their spending with the actual campaign. Schwarzman also donated a much-smaller amount directly to Rogers' Senate campaigns from 2023 to 2025.
Snopes independently verified the amount Schwarzman donated and that he appears in the Epstein files. However, as the Metro Times story states, there's no evidence Schwarzman and Epstein directly interacted. No one, including federal prosecutors, has publicly accused Schwarzman of wrongdoing connected to Epstein.
The other six donors who donated the remaining money had varying degrees of closeness to Epstein — but there's no evidence any of them knew of or assisted in his criminal activities.
As for El-Sayed, we found no evidence any people named in the Epstein files donated directly to his campaign. Two people with passing mentions in the Epstein files sent money to a super PAC supporting El-Sayed.
Rogers' campaign spokeswoman, Alyssa Brouillet, pointed to Rogers' time in the FBI "busting human traffickers" and said in an emailed statement that "any attempt at associating him with criminals is insulting and patently false."
Federal Election Commission data indicates Schwarzman sent "GLCF, INC" three donations totaling $4.5 million: $2 million in June 2024, $1 million in August 2024 and $1.5 million in September 2024.
GLCF stands for Great Lakes Conservatives Fund — a super PAC that solely supports Rogers, according to OpenSecrets, a nonprofit group that tracks campaign finances.
A Federal Election Commission search for donations from Stephen Schwarzman sent to Rogers' campaign committees shows the billionaire businessman also sent at least $13,600 to "Rogers for Senate," the committee name for Rogers' actual campaign, and $7,000 in 2025 to "Team Rogers," a joint-fundraising operation for Rogers. Schwarzman also sent $5,000 to "MR PAC," which stands for Michigan's Resurgence PAC — which Rogers used to raise money to support other politicians.
(Federal Election Commission)
Schwarzman in the Epstein files
Schwarzman's last name appears frequently in the Epstein files. For example, one document shows Epstein was emailed an invitation to a 2015 cocktail party to celebrate the release of the film "The Imitation Game" on behalf of Schwarzman and others. In another email, Epstein appears to call Schwarzman "terrific" after suggesting to someone that "attaching to Blackstone might be a good idea."
However, none of these emails indicates Schwarzman and Epstein ever met in person. There also aren't any publicly available pictures of Schwarzman with Epstein, although there is an authentic picture of the Blackstone CEO in conversation with Epstein's associate Ghislaine Maxwell at a New York gala.
In an emailed statement, a spokesperson for Schwarzman told Snopes it would be "categorically false and grossly irresponsible to claim or imply that Steve had any relationship with this despicable individual."
The spokesperson said Epstein did not attend the 2015 cocktail party, and the invitation was extended through a PR firm that worked with the film's distributors, not Schwarzman.
The same PR firm, the spokesperson said, invited Epstein to another 
Other donors' connections to Epstein files
Here's a list of other people in the Epstein files who donated to Rogers from 2023 to 2025, per Metro Times reporting and Snopes' independent verification using FEC data:
- Marc Rowan, Apollo Global Management CEO: $25,000 to GLCF, $14,000 to Rogers' campaigns and $7,000 to Team Rogers
- Ronald Lauder, Estée Lauder heir: $3,300 to Rogers' 2024 Senate campaign
- John Catsimatidis, grocery chain billionaire businessman: $13,600 to Rogers for Senate
- Joseph Baratta, Blackstone executive: $10,300 to Rogers for Senate
- Howard Lorber, real estate executive: $5,693 to Rogers for Senate
- John W. Childs, private equity investor: $8,530 to Rogers for Senate, $60,000 to GLCF and $12,000 to Team Rogers
Of the list above, Rowan and Lauder have the most documented interaction with Epstein.
Rowan planned a breakfast at Epstein's house and kept regular correspondence with him from 2013 to 2016. The files show Lauder and Epstein planned meetups in 2017, including luncheons and a museum tour. Lauder's signature also appears in the files on joint purchase agreements for artwork, which Epstein appeared to help with.
In an email, Apollo Global Management spokesperson Giovanna Falbo directed us to a Feb. 18, 2026, news release where the company referred to its investigation into Apollo's ties to Epstein and denied that Rowan had "either a business or personal relationship with Jeffrey Epstein."
Business Insider reported that Catsimatidis was in one of Epstein's 1997 address books. Catsimatidis told Business Insider he met Epstein once in the 1990s through a friend and never saw him again, although Epstein called the billionaire "once or twice, I don't know about what."
Epstein said in a 2016 email that 
Most mentions of a "Joseph Baratta" in the DOJ's Epstein files appear to actually reference an attorney — Joseph P. Baratta — not the Blackstone executive, Joseph A. Baratta. There are a couple of mentions of the executive, but nothing that suggests an actual relationship.
"Joe has absolutely no relationship with him, and it would be outrageous and patently false to suggest otherwise," said a spokesperson for Baratta, who also represents Schwarzman.
Lorber is referenced in relation to some real estate deals Epstein contemplated, as well as a suggested "war council" to help Trump respond to the aftermath of the Russia collusion investigation. There's no evidence such a "war council" ever materialized.
Similarly, the DOJ files include financial transactions connected to Childs, but there's no documented correspondence between Childs and Epstein.
In February 2019, Childs was charged with soliciting prostitution in a human trafficking sting. He denied the allegations. The charges were reportedly dropped in 2020 and his record expunged after the courts determined prosecutors brought the case in violation of his Fourth Amendment privacy rights.
We attempted to reach Lauder and Lorber to clarify the extent of their relationships to Epstein and await responses. We were unable to reach Childs.
The bottom line
Rogers and PACs supporting him did, in fact, receive millions from donors who appear in the Epstein files, largely from Blackstone co-founder Stephen Schwarzman. However, simply being named in the files doesn't mean a person knew of or assisted in Epstein's criminal activities. For example, the Epstein files release contained dubious allegations, newsletters Epstein subscribed to and what appear to be mundane business transactions, like for facility maintenance.

Why India's Election Commission is in the eye of a storm - again
- Published
India's Election Commission (ECI) is facing yet another crisis of credibility after a series of fresh allegations of irregularities against its chief.
One of the most trusted public institutions in the world's largest democracy, the three-member commission is headed by the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and includes Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi as commissioners.
The latest row broke out after a report in the Indian Express newspaper, external said that in the past few months, CEC Kumar had been repeatedly questioned by his two colleagues over the integrity of the voter database, changes to the way new voters are enrolled and the security of the electoral rolls itself.
The report said that Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi objected to several decisions which were taken without their knowledge. There were at least 14 times in the past 10 months when Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi were kept in the dark, it added.
In one instance, the report says, the two commissioners even wrote a letter complaining to the chief secretary, the top bureaucrat in the Indian government.
The revelations have created a furore, with opposition leaders demanding Kumar's resignation. Sandhu and Joshi have not publicly commented on the report but the ECI said in a statement that "differing views" were part of the "decision-making process".
The report comes at a time when the commission is carrying out a controversial country-wide revision of the electoral database.
The Election Commission says the aim of this Special Intensive Revision - better known by its acronym SIR - is to ensure that no ineligible name remains on the rolls.
It says the last revision was done nearly a quarter of a century ago and the voters' list needs to be updated to account for those who have died, left the country or are registered in more than one place as they've moved to a new address.
But the exercise has been mired in controversy from the start with the opposition parties accusing CEC Kumar of manipulating voters' list to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.
But the latest revelations are being seen as much more serious as they are about questions being raised from within the Election Commission about the way its chief is functioning.
From the start, questions have lingered over the robustness of the revision, which has seen 130 million names from across India struck off the voters' list.
Millions of voters have also complained to the authorities that their names are missing, saying the new process set by SIR to register as voters is too cumbersome and involves furnishing documents that many don't have.
Former CEC SY Quraishi, who says he has "been a critic of the SIR from the beginning", told news agency PTI that he always wondered why Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi had been "keeping quiet".
"[Now] I realised that very silently and quietly they were protesting, they were writing notes. That is a good thing, they have gone up in my esteem," he said.
The revelations have also provided fresh ammunition to the opposition parties and critics who have repeatedly claimed that SIR is being used to exclude their voters for the BJP's benefit and that elections in India are no longer free and fair.
On Wednesday, angry opposition politicians once again questioned the sanctity of India's election process and demanded that CEC Kumar resign, saying he had no right to continue in office, with some even calling for his arrest.
The charge was led by MP and senior Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi who has repeatedly accused the Commission of "stealing votes from the opposition". On Wednesday, he also accused the Commission and its officers of "treason".
"Vote chori [theft] is a crime against the Indian people and a direct attack on our constitution. The BJP, RSS [Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh] and EC who organised it have committed an act of treason. Justice will be served," he posted on X, external. He also shared a 15-second video telling the commission and its officers that "your time will come. You cannot get away".
Mamata Banerjee, leader of the regional Mamata All India Trinamool Congress, called for Kumar's arrest and demanded fresh polls with the pre-SIR voters' list in the state of West Bengal which she lost to the BJP in the recent elections. At least 2.7million voters were removed in the state during SIR - Banerjee and her supporters say that cost them dozens of seats and the election win.
Within hours of the Indian Express report and statements from opposition leaders, the Election Commission put out a statement, external defending its way of working.
"Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution. They are a part of the decision-making process before a final decision is taken.
"Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorised to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system," the statement said.
The note said that highlighting "certain specific internal notes and observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives" give only part of the picture.
And that in recent months, the commission has "introduced around 40 new initiatives and undertaken many electoral reforms including the conduct of electoral roll revision (including SIR) across the country. All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full commission in the past one year".
The BJP has also defended CEC Kumar, calling the opposition criticism a "smear campaign" and that dissent was "a sign of a vibrant democracy".
Party spokesperson Sambit Patra told a press conference that "ever since the Modi government came to power in 2014, opposition parties have been collapsing one after the other". And because they cannot win elections, they are trying to "undermine the institutions of the country", he said.
But the row over the election database is likely to intensify. Banerjee has already said opposition parties will hold protests until Kumar remains CEC.
And India's influential Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which recently forced the education minister to resign, has also said it will protest against the "hijacking of India's democracy".
Analysts say the defence of the Election Commission is unlikely to satisfy many, with some pointing out that its statement doesn't address all the issues raised in the newspaper report and that "CEC Kumar needs to clear the air, external if we are to view the Commission as an impartial body".

Will FDA advisers recommend a multi-cancer blood test for approval? They'll vote
A key advisory committee that reviews medical devices for the Food and Drug Administration will meet today to vote on whether the agency should approve the first multi-cancer blood test. Grail, the company that makes the Galleri blood test under review, says it can detect up to 50 forms of cancer, many of which are not routinely screened for today.
The panel of independent experts will hear from Grail, FDA officials and the public before voting on a recommendation. The FDA often follows the advice from its panels, but does not have to. Ultimate approval by the agency could mean insurance reimbursement for the test, which costs $949.
There are hundreds of companies chasing the promise of blood tests to detect cancer, which is done with a simple blood draw and could help detect disease earlier by looking for genetic material or other cancer markers shed in blood or saliva. Grail says its Galleri test should be additive to standardized cancer screenings, like colonoscopies and mammograms, and not be used as a replacement.
While blood tests for cancer already exist in the market, none that screen for multiple cancers has undergone safety and accuracy reviews to win FDA approval so far. Many doctors and patients hope such technology will ultimately help detect disease earlier, when more treatment options could be possible.
The financial incentives to win FDA approval also became far more powerful after Congress approved Medicare to cover multi-cancer detection tests that are greenlighted by the agency. Based on its promise, the FDA expedited its review of Galleri, which is the furthest along in that approval process.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
As such, Galleri is seen as a kind of bellwether for the whole industry — and for the potential use of a blood test to screen for cancers in general.
"It's a new era for early cancer detection, and if the FDA approves it, it validates the overall concept," says Cristian Tomasetti, director of City of Hope cancer center's early detection and monitoring division. In 2018, Tomasetti was part of a team that developed a competing blood test technology that is the basis of a test made by Exact Sciences (since purchased by Abbott), which is also pursuing FDA approval. (Tomasetti is no longer involved with that company.)
The questions to answer
The FDA laid out key questions for the committee to answer about Galleri, centered on whether the clinical data show the test detects cancers reliably and early enough to justify use of such terms in its marketing. The agency also wants to consider harm from false results, and potentially require the company to include caveats in its marketing, such as warnings that a false negative does not rule out the presence of cancer, nor a positive detection signifying cancer.
The advisory committee will review two major clinical studies conducted by Grail, including one involving more than 140,000 patients in the U.K.'s National Health System, and another of over 35,000 North American patients, all over the age of 50. The interpretation of those studies has been somewhat controversial. On the one hand, the Galleri tests did not meet their primary end point of reducing mortality overall, nor did it reduce the combined number of Stage III and IV cancers. But in subsequent updates to its NHS study, Grail clarified that Stage IV cancer diagnoses (not combined with Stage III) decreased over its three-year study period, suggesting tests may have shifted cancer diagnosis to earlier stages.
While the trials have not fully proven the test's benefit, the key underlying question to the inquiry — not just for the FDA, but also for patients and doctors — is whether the Galleri test is accurate enough and can reliably catch cancers early enough to reduce deaths from cancer.
Tomasetti acknowledges that Galleri's tests did not meet their end points in their clinical studies. But he says that's in large part because the study specified very ambitious goals, such as showing reductions in mortality within a short period of three years. Mortality reductions are typically measured over the long term. Tomasetti says there are other problems that arise from the short duration of the studies; namely, in the initial years of testing, one would expect to detect more late-stage cancers that already existed in the population.
"This is kind of a technicality," that the study didn't meet its initial endpoint, Tomasetti says. "To me, it doesn't mean that the study — in terms of substance — failed to show evidence of what [multi-cancer detection tests] can actually do." He says longer-term studies are needed to confirm that using the tests regularly will help shift diagnoses from Stage IV to earlier stage diagnoses. Based on the totality of data, Tomasetti says he thinks the FDA appears poised to approve Galleri's test.
Oncologist Tom Beer agrees. Beer is chief medical officer for Abbott Cancer Diagnostics, working on a multi-cancer test called CancerGuard, which is also seeking FDA approval. Beer also sees patients in his clinical practice in Oregon, and says 70% of cancer diagnoses and deaths are from diseases like pancreatic cancer, for which no screening exists.
"I'm keenly aware every week when I'm in the clinic, of how many patients are diagnosed with cancers that we don't screen for," he says.

US State Secretary Marco Rubio says global system ‘broken’: ‘Can’t address potential conflicts like India-Pakistan’
Marco Rubio also pointed to US President Donald Trump's remarks stating the United Nations was “not living up to its potential”.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday said the international system which exists is “broken”, and therefore could fail to address potential conflicts, citing India and Pakistan in this context.
He pointed to US President Donald Trump's remarks of the United Nations “not living up to its potential”, while adding that it “would be great” if there was a “functional international system” to deal with conflicts, news agency PTI reported.
“It would be great if we had a functional international system, for example, that could deal with a war between Thailand and Cambodia that occurred, or a potential conflict between India and Pakistan...Right now, we don't seem to have a functional international system that can address it,” the top US diplomat said.
Rubio's remarks come a day after Trump repeated his claim that he stopped India and Pakistan from going into a full-fledged war in May 2025, something which has consistently been rejected by New Delhi.
‘International system failing because it has grown beyond its mandate’: Rubio
Rubio spoke about the “utility” of the international system at present, saying it was visible to all. “We're here...I think the President has said that the United Nations, for example, has tremendous potential, but it's not living up to it…” Rubio told reporters in New York.
“I think multiple leaders...pointed to the fact that the international system is failing, and it's failing because it has grown beyond its mandate,” the US Secretary of State said, according to PTI. Rubio further said the system had “grown beyond its intent.”
“It's involved in all kinds of things that shouldn't be involved in, and it's unable to solve virtually any major conflict in the world,” Rubio added. He said there was consensus at the UN General Assembly on the point of view that the international system was “broken.” “But it's broken because it broke itself. It needs to be brought back to its proper focus and its proper role,” Rubio stated.
Rubio also said that the US would eventually “always act in the national interest of our country, not in the interest of the international order.”
What did Trump say at the UNGA?
Trump on Tuesday reiterated his claim that he stopped the conflict between India and Pakistan last year. He made the remarks at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, where he defended the war with Iran and repeated his claim that he ended eight wars in his second term as US President.
“The Prime Minister of Pakistan, a terrific man, said that Donald Trump was responsible for saving 30 million lives, and probably many more than that,” Trump said at UNGA. The US President further claimed that leaders of the countries, where he intervened to end conflicts, wrote him a letter to express gratitude.

The military escalation between India and Pakistan came after the Pahalgam terror attack in April, 2025, in which 26 civilians were killed. Following this, India had launched strikes against terror bases in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir under ‘Operation Sindoor.’
Trump has, several times in the past, claimed that he brokered the ceasefire between India and Pakistan after the military escalation in May 2025. India has consistently denied the claim and maintained that the ceasefire was agreed upon mutually between India and Pakistan, and rejected claims of any third-party intervention in the matter.

As the sun sets at Kannanthura Beach in Thiruvananthapuram, the crash of waves is interrupted by the rising hum of two-stroke engines. A contingent of vintage scooters, painted in bright metallic shades, heads towards the sandy coastline, leaving behind a cloud of dust that disappears within seconds.
The 10 scooters, ranging from a sleek silver 1982 Vijay Super Mark 2 to a blue 2000 LML Vespa, belong to members of the Vintage & Classic Scooters Club (VCSC), Thiruvananthapuram chapter. Founded in 2017, the club is among several city-based two-wheeler communities that bring automobile enthusiasts together, promote safe riding and encourage proper vehicle maintenance.
Clubs such as VCSC, Travancore Royal Enfield Club (TREC), Voyagers Brotherhood, Riders of Technopark, Royal Enfield Retro Riders Trivandrum and Trivandrum RX organise short and long rides, help members source spare parts and connect them with mechanics and other resources.
For many owners, these communities are also a way to share a personal passion with a larger group. Akshay AS, admin of VCSC Thiruvananthapuram, which has more than 40 members, says his love for scooters and two-stroke engines began with the vintage Bajaj Chetak. “Before I joined VCSC, I used to believe that old people rode scooters and they couldn’t survive long distances. But then I found like-minded people who love them. We have made so many friends in the group and across south India through our rides.”
“Not all scooters are suited for long rides, but we still do it. When problems arise, we help each other out,” adds Akshay, who owns a vintage LML Vespa.
ALSO WATCH Watch: How to restore a vintage car?
TREC, founded by Arun S Kumar in 2020, has more than 400 members and organises over 12 long rides a year. Its recent ride was to Ilaveezhapoonchira in Kottayam. “A few years ago, I used to have a vintage Bullet. Back then, there weren’t many active groups organising rides. Those using old bikes face certain difficulties, such as identifying the right parts and finding the right mechanic. So, I began enquiring and started a support group for old Bullet riders. That evolved into TREC, which now has both vintage and new bike riders,” he says.
Riders of Technopark, founded in March 2025, started with four riders. “We used to go on long rides, travelling individually or with other groups. We also attended and organised events for other communities. So, we thought, why not do the same for techie riders in the city? It is solely built on brotherhood,” says Kiran MR, founder of the club, which now has more than 500 members.
The club participated in India Bike Week, billed as India’s biggest motorcycling festival, in 2025. “We were only a few months old when we attended the festival. From a club’s perspective, that would have been impossible for a new club to achieve. We needed 35 riders. It tested our endurance and our ability to adjust to people riding at different paces. It brought together people of different ages,” Kiran says.
Voyagers Brotherhood organises rides across the country. Its nearly 150 members ride Harley-Davidson, BMW, vintage Jawa and Yezdi bikes, as well as Ola scooters. Lakshmi S Nair, the club’s president, says, “We plan rallies on February 14 to commemorate the Pulwama attack and on Kargil Vijay Diwas, among others. We also organise interactive sessions at colleges and road safety awareness programmes.” Last year, the club earned a world record for creating the largest bike image forming the words “Say No to Drugs”.
Women are also active members of these communities. Dauntless Royal Explorers, billed as Kerala’s first women’s only rider’s club founded in 2016, by Shyni Rajkumar, currently has 40 members. While more than 20 women are part of Riders of Technopark, Voyagers Brotherhood has around 25 women members. “We organise workshops for women. We even have those riding Activa scooters approach us. Even though some of them are concerned about what others might say, people are still coming forward,” says Lakshmi. The vintage vehicle groups have fewer direct women members, though women associated with members regularly attend their events, organisers say.
The communities also offer practical support, from servicing and repairs to sourcing spare parts. “We suggest mechanics in their area. With our members spread across the district, we help them irrespective of their age,” says Vineeth VS, a member of Royal Enfield Retro Riders Trivandrum, a vintage bike community. “Our club collaborates with vendors who can provide riding gear at cheaper rates. We even support our peers with insurance claims if they meet with an accident.”
For Aneesh Kumar, a member of Trivandrum RX Club, the appeal lies in restoring the machines themselves. “We find the act of building and restoring a vehicle more exhilarating, especially when you work with a mechanic, finding parts from Bengaluru and Delhi. It is a great joy to build a vehicle like that.”
Vineeth points out that Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) are also an important part of the communities. “When they return to the city for their vacations, we organise rides with them too. A few of them have left their vehicles here. It is our duty to take care of them and help with repairs if needed. Whenever they come, we meet, ride and eat food together. It gives them great joy to be part of the collective.”
He adds, “When we build communities like these, we bring together people of different age groups. Youngsters reach out to us to improve their bikes. Many of them enjoy preserving vehicles, which gives us happiness that even after our time, this hobby might go on.”

Some Samsung smart fridges stopped working on Tuesday due to a firmware update.
Korean outlets were the first to report the problems, which affect Samsung’s Bespoke AI line of fridges. Star News Korea, per a Google-provided translation, said that most of the affected devices were four-door fridges from 2024 or later.
Affected fridges “suddenly lost power and stopped functioning immediately after” trying to issue a firmware update through SmartThings, Samsung’s smart home platform, per Star News Korea. The SmartThings app then showed the devices as offline. Some users said that their fridge’s internal display was stuck showing the message “Checking SmartThings app during update.”
There are numerous reports on Samsung’s Korean community forum detailing the problem. Some users claim that they have owned their affected fridge for just a year or less.
“[T]he refrigeration and refrigeration functions themselves did not work normally, so all the food in the refrigerator had to be disposed of,” one user wrote, per a translation.
Samsung didn’t respond to Ars’ questions about what it will do to prevent this from happening in the future or how many units are affected and in which countries. SBS Korea reported that customers have filed hundreds of cases.
The complaints seem to originate only from Korea, where the problem has been made worse because it’s happening during a major Korean holiday, Chuseok, which celebrates the autumn harvest and starts Thursday.
“Customers only trusted Samsung Electronics and made an official update, but it is so absurd and embarrassing that they can’t even use refrigeration and refrigeration functions before the Chuseok,” a forum user wrote, per a Google-provided translation.

Nigerian football enduring 'worst time in history' - Odegbami
- Published
As Nigeria begin their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifying campaign, former international Segun Odegbami, who won the tournament on home soil in 1980, says the country is experiencing the "worst time" in its football history.
Over the past 12 months both the Super Eagles and Super Falcons failed to qualify for their respective Fifa World Cups.
But beyond the failure of the senior national teams, Nigeria has also endured disappointing results at age-group level and in African club competitions - although the West Africans recently reached the quarter-finals of the Under-20 Women's World Cup.
Odegbami says the diminishing returns represent a "tectonic shift" for one of the continent's traditional powers.
"It has never been this bad in our entire history that we didn't qualify for the World Cup," the 74-year-old told BBC Sport Africa.
"Our girls (the Super Falcons), who were African champions, failed to win a competition (the 2025 Women's Afcon) that was just there for their taking. All our junior teams are not doing well.
"Our local league is not bringing in money. Something is definitely wrong."
The crisis has already triggered major changes within the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF).
Its president Ibrahim Gusau, general secretary Mohammed Sanusi and multiple members of the federation's executive committee resigned last month following mounting criticism.
Odegbami says Nigerian football had not been represented by its "first XI administrators" and has called for a restructure to create the conditions for long-term development.
"The outcry by Nigerians was total. Everybody wanted them out, to the extent that the President of the country himself (Bola Tinubu) made the pronouncement that he wanted reforms," he said.
"Everything came together like a jigsaw puzzle and is working now for us to produce a blueprint that will cover every aspect of our football development."
- 'Motherhood should not be the end of anyone's story' 
  - Published23 July
Sweeping changes at the NFF
A joint delegation from world governing body Fifa and the Confederation of African Football (Caf) has been involved in discussions with the National Sports Commission (NSC) over the future structure of Nigerian football.
The parties are working towards a roadmap for comprehensive reforms but NFF elections, scheduled for 27 September, have been suspended.
President Tinubu stated his desire for reform to overcome what he called "repeated failures".
Emmanuel Ikpeme has been appointed NFF interim general secretary, with Ademola Olajire the interim deputy general secretary.
The changes have prompted renewed debate among stakeholders over whether the country needs a deeper restructuring.
Nigerian sports journalist Fisayo Dairo believes any reform must extend beyond a change in leadership.
"The reform should be the setting up of a proper framework and structure that our football can thrive on," Dairo told BBC Sport Africa.
"[We need to] develop national teams, harness talent from the grassroots and have governance that incorporates all forms of stakeholders.
"The corporate world has to be fully represented so that the administration is able to generate funds."
'What is Nigeria's football style?'
For Odegbami, the current situation is a stark contrast to the era in which he helped transform the Nigerian game.
Nicknamed 'Mathematical' for his precision and skill on the ball, the forward was part of the Super Eagles side that won the country's first continental title in 1980, beating Algeria 3-0 in the final in Lagos.
"We had unprecedented support and fortunately the stars aligned with us," he said.
"It was an indescribable atmosphere during that period.
"That experience you can't even describe and compare. [It remains] indelible in our minds."
Nigeria lifted the Afcon trophy again in 1994 and 2013, and finished as runners-up at the 2023 edition.
The team also finished third in 2019 and at this year's finals in Morocco.
However, Odegbami argues sport has "not been a priority" of successive governments and believes his nation has been failed by football administrators since the mid 1990s.
"The pilots are not guiding us well, they haven't guided us well," he said.
"And that has affected every aspect of our football development: the grassroots, the discovery of players, the development of the players, the establishment of the institutions that will take care of them, the academies, the clubs that they will go into both locally and internationally.
"What is the coaching methodology? What is the philosophy of our football in the country?
"What is our culture, what is our style?"
Decaying infrastructure
Yet, alongside the failure to reach the past two men's World Cups, concerns over deteriorating infrastructure and inadequate investment have become recurring themes in discussions about the state of the Nigerian game.
Across Africa, meanwhile, other nations have continued to invest in hosting major competitions.
Senegal will be the venue for the Youth Olympic Games next month, South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia are holding next year's men's Cricket World Cup, Kenya will stage the 2029 World Athletics Championship, and Morocco will co-host the 2030 World Cup with Spain and Portugal.
Odegbami has bemoaned the fact that top-class stadiums which Nigeria used to possess have fallen into disrepair after being neglected.
He name-checked the National Stadium in Surulere, Lagos, which hosted games during the 1980 and 2000 Afcons, the Liberty Stadium (now Obafemi Awolowo Stadium) in Ibadan, Kaduna's Ahmadu Bello Stadium and the UJ Esuene Stadium in Calabar.
"I weep when I think of the amount of damage they have done to Nigerian football - the infrastructure that we had in the country, some of the historic monuments that were facilities for football in this country," he said.
"Whether it was wilful, whether it was ignorance, they did irreparable damage to what was Nigeria's heritage.
"Uyo is the best we have in Nigeria, but it is not half as good as what we had from the 1960s to the 90s."
The Super Eagles will begin their Afcon 2027 qualifying campaign against Madagascar at the Godswill Akpabio Stadium in Uyo on Friday (16:00 GMT) before travelling to Guinea-Bissau on 29 September.

Fury v Joshua announced for 11 December in Cardiff
- Published
Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will contest their long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.
The bout, more than a decade in the making, will be broadcast globally on Netflix.
BBC Sport understands the main event could take place in the early hours of Saturday morning in the UK, with organisers considering a late start to cater for audiences in the United States.
Joshua and Fury will come face-to-face at a news conference in London on Wednesday, 30 September, as the build-up begins to one of the most anticipated fights in British boxing history.
"I am inspiring a generation," Joshua, 36, posted on Instagram. Fury is yet to comment on the announcement.
The event is being promoted as a collaboration between Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's The Ring and UFC chief Dana White.
"Two of the best heavyweights of this generation, finally in the ring together," Alalshikh said.
"This will be one of the biggest fights in boxing history. I am very happy to make this fight happen for the fans."
The former two-time world champions had already signed contracts for the bout earlier this year, but the date and venue had yet to be confirmed.
London's Wembley Stadium and New York's Madison Square Garden were the frontrunners to stage the fight, but both presented issues before Cardiff recently emerged as an alternative.

"Forever indebted to the UK public for their support of Anthony Joshua. We couldn't have got this over the line without you," his promoter Eddie Hearn said.
It is notable that White, who fronts Zuffa Boxing, is involved in the promotion.
"For more than a decade, boxing fans have been clamouring for the heavyweight showdown between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua. Together, they bring 66 wins, 52 knockouts and multiple heavyweight world titles into the ring," White said.

There was no official statement from Hearn or Fury's promoter Frank Warren in the official news release sent by Netflix. Hearn had previously said he did not want White to be involved in promoting the fight.

CHOYR, MONGOLIA – When Mongolian herder Ganchimeg’s sheep strayed dangerously near a salt lake this summer, driven by hunger as nearby vegetation was poor, she was in a “total panic.”
“If they drank or stepped into it, the whole flock would be destroyed,” she said outside her traditional ger, the tent’s shape silhouetted on the vast horizon of the Gobi Desert.
But thanks to an app helping herders navigate the risks that climate change is bringing to Mongolia, her husband was able to reach the sheep before they drank the brackish water.
“He immediately rushed over at top speed and intercepted them,” said Ganchimeg, a mother of four who, like many Mongolians, goes by just one name.
“If we hadn’t used that GPS tracker, we might have lost our entire flock.”
Herders are on the front line of both climate change and desertification impacts — climate change is bringing extreme weather, including deadly cold snaps and droughts, which compound desertification caused by overgrazing.
Huge and sparsely populated, Mongolia is disproportionately affected by human-driven climate change, threatening the country’s nomadic population and livestock.
Bilgudei Gankhulug, the 26-year-old founder of the Hunu app used by Ganchimeg, said he was inspired to help herders after a 2024 dzud — an extreme weather event that brought temperatures as low as minus 45 degrees Celsius.
“Over 8 million livestock died. I saw a lot of herders losing their income, losing their livelihoods in just the span of a few months,” said Bilgudei.
Meaning “strong nomad,” the name Hunu “embodies our mission of empowering nomadic herders with the help of technology,” he said.
The app allows nomads to track their livestock with a solar-charging GPS device attached to one animal per group — sufficient for herds that tend to stick together on the spacious steppe.
It has an artificial intelligence-powered weather feature with updates on the deadly dust storms and blizzards made more common in recent years by climate change, which scientists say is intensifying globally.
The app also compiles useful information on maps showing snow depth, wind direction, soil moisture and drought, assisting nomads in crucial decisions on where to move next.
Mongolia hosted talks on a global desertification treaty, known as COP17, last month.
Countries agreed on financing for land restoration and tackling drought resilience, but concerns remain over a massive funding shortfall to the growing problem.
Bilgudei said he hopes to expand Hunu to central Asian countries, and met with pastoralists from Tanzania and Uruguay at COP17 interested too.
“Our problems are pretty similar,” he said.
About 80% of Mongolia is rangelands, large tracts of unfarmed land covered by native grasses and shrubs, according to Chimeddorj Buyanaa, Mongolia conservation director at the World Wildlife Fund.
“Rangelands are critically important for the local communities and also for the livelihoods of all of the Mongolian people,” he said.
Compounding the issue of climate change is rampant overgrazing that also endangers the region’s wildlife, including snow leopards and saiga antelope, Chimeddorj said.
Around one in four Mongolians are nomadic herders.
Nearly 82% of the country’s territory is affected by desertification and land degradation, authorities said in August.
Many herder families have simply decided to pack up and seek new lives in the city.
“Dundgovi province’s population has been declining continuously in recent years,” the southern region’s governor, Munkhchuluun Samdannyam, said at COP17.
The worsening climate is a major problem for the province — three-fifths of its economy depends on livestock husbandry, Munkhchuluun said — but consequences are felt further afield.
“Dust storms can begin here and travel south to China, Korea, Japan and even as far as the United States,” Munkhchuluun said.
“(It) is not only Mongolia’s problem.
“It is also a global problem.”
Speaking before heading to milk several camels tethered nearby, 49-year-old herder Bolormaa Erdenee said she was skeptical of forums such as COP17.
“I often question whether the true voice of our herders is actually reaching decision-makers or not,” she said.
Bolormaa and her husband raise about 400 livestock.
In their usual summer grazing area, she said roads for heavy mining trucks now crisscross the steppe, kicking up dust and disrupting her animals.
Several nomadic households nearby have already relocated nearly 200 kilometers away in search of greener pastures.
Hunu app founder Bilgudei — whose ancestors were nomadic herders — said traditional migration itself is a form of environmental protection.
Bilgudei said it’s important to “learn from the traditions ... and combine it with the science and technology.”

Judge orders Trump administration to restore journalists' access to White House
WASHINGTON — A federal judge ordered the Trump administration on Thursday to temporarily restore access to the three media organizations banned from covering White House events last week by President Trump.
In a ruling issued shortly after midnight, Judge Timothy Kelly granted a 14-day temporary restraining order to CNN, MS NOW and Politico, which had press credentials of their journalists covering the White House revoked on Saturday at the request of President Trump.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a joint lawsuit against Trump to challenge that decision on Monday, on the grounds that their constitutional rights had been violated.
Trump told reporters on Friday that his decision to ban the three media outlets from White House grounds had not been sparked by any specific reporting but the accumulation of what he called "two years of unfair and negative coverage."
However, a court filing by the Department of Justice on Wednesday argued that the three news organizations were barred because their reporting jeopardized national security and spread falsehoods.
In his ruling, Kelly said "the court is skeptical — at least on this record — that Defendants' interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes."
He also argued that the defendants offered no evidence to explain how "any of the reporting they identified in their letters to Plaintiffs damaged national security." Adding that the reporters who authored the stories that the DOJ lawyers identified in their letters to the three media "did not even hold hard passes."

Some people sharing the quote claimed Trump was specifically referring to the deaths of 18 service members during the conflict. He was in fact referring to the conflict itself.
A rumor circulated online in September 2026 that U.S. President Donald Trump had called the Iran war, initiated by the United States and Israel in February 2026, "small potatoes."
Users shared the claim on social media and Reddit. Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., shared the purported quote and added, "Tell that to the families of the 18 troops we've lost, the hundreds of wounded servicemembers, and the Americans suffering every single day from record high prices."
The quote was correctly attributed to Trump.
Trump made the statement during a news conference in the Oval Office on Sept. 4, during which he signed executive orders related to the cattle industry.
The news conference was available to view on the White House's official YouTube channel. The comment in question begins around the 25-minute mark after a reporter referred to Vice President J.D. Vance's statement that he did not consider the conflict in Iran a war and asked, "Can you explain to the American people if this is not a war, what exactly is it?"
Trump responded (emphasis ours):
A lot of people don't call it a war. I call it a military conflict. Because it's small potatoes for us. It's not a big thing. We did Venezuela and we did this. In Venezuela we lost nobody, in this we lost 18 people. And in Vietnam we lost 100,000 people, and in other conflicts you lost tens of thousands of people.
Trump continued by elaborating on some of the military operations the United States has enacted since the start of the conflict. He said, "It's a military conflict, but it's very intermittent. I could see somebody not calling it a war."
Asked directly by the same reporter whether he considered the deaths of 18 service members to also be "small potatoes," Trump said he'd met their families and had gotten "very friendly" with some and again mentioned the number of deceased from past conflicts to compare the size of the numbers.
The White House press office told Snopes via email:
President Trump cares deeply about our men and women in uniform, which is why he approved a historic pay increase for our military servicemembers and restored a focus on our warfighters at the Pentagon. Every loss of life within our armed forces is a tragedy and one loss too many, and the President honors and remembers the sacrifice of every hero who has fallen in the line of duty. The President was recognizing the importance of ensuring that Iran, a country that for 47 years has chanted "Death to America" and killed our troops overseas, can never possess a nuclear weapon.
Media outlets widely reported Trump's quote, including CNN, The Associated Press and USA Today.
Some social media posts called out Trump's comment and claimed he specifically called the number of deceased service members "small potatoes." In truth, he made the comment about the conflict itself, not specifically the number of service members killed.

At Area Hospital, Bhadrachalam, in Telangana’s Bhadradri Kothagudem district, a single specialist has helped bring specialised eye surgery to patients from remote tribal areas and even neighbouring States.
The Ophthalmology Unit of the hospital has completed 400 cataract surgeries since its dedicated ophthalmic operation theatre was established in December 2023. Patients have travelled to Bhadrachalam not only from Bhadradri Kothagudem district but also from Warangal, Karimnagar, Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Odisha.

Rahul. “Their support included intraocular lenses, surgical consumables and other requirements, enabling the unit to provide cataract surgery services consistently,” said Dr. Ravi Babu.

He appreciated ophthalmologist Dr. Santosh as well as the entire ophthalmology nursing, operation theatre and support teams for their sustained commitment. According to Dr. Ravi Babu, the ophthalmic operation theatre was established using district funds and, so far, has not received State funds.

Italy's parliament paves the way for a return to nuclear energy
Italy’s Senate has given final approval to legislation paving the way for a return to nuclear power
ROME -- Italy’s Senate on Wednesday gave final approval to legislation paving the way for a return to nuclear power nearly four decades after the Chernobyl disaster prompted the country to abandon atomic energy.
The measure cleared the upper house 81-51 with seven abstentions. It marks a major step in Premier Giorgia Meloni’s drive to bolster energy security and meet climate goals, even though the construction of possible new reactors is still years away.
The bill, which earlier passed the lower Chamber of Deputies, establishes a legal framework for next-generation nuclear technologies. It authorizes the government to draft implementing decrees over the next 12 months covering reactor licensing, safety standards, waste management and criteria for future sites.
The vote puts Italy on a path toward reintroducing nuclear power after voters twice rejected it in national referendums, first in the aftermath of the 1986 Chernobyl disaster and again following Japan’s Fukushima accident in 2011.
Meloni’s government argues that rising electricity demand, climate targets and energy security concerns exposed by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine justify bringing nuclear energy back into the country’s power mix.
Rather than reviving the large reactors of the past, the government is focusing on small modular reactors, or SMRs, and other advanced technologies that supporters say could be safer, more flexible and quicker to build.
The legislation does not authorize the construction of any reactors. Instead, it creates the regulatory foundation needed before future projects can be proposed, assessed and approved.
Italy was once among Europe’s nuclear pioneers, operating four reactors before a 1987 referendum effectively ended the program. Since then, the country has relied heavily on imported energy and has become one of Europe’s largest consumers of electricity generated by nuclear plants in neighboring countries.
The government says electricity demand could rise substantially in coming years as homes, businesses and transportation become increasingly electrified and as data centers and other energy-intensive technologies expand.
Italy’s move comes amid a broader European debate over nuclear power’s role in cutting carbon emissions and reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels. Countries including France and Poland are investing in new nuclear projects or planning major expansions.
Public attitudes in Italy appear to have shifted. A June 2026 survey by research firm Only Numbers found that about 55% of Italians support next-generation nuclear plants, with backing strongest among younger generations who have no direct memory of Chernobyl.
Even so, significant obstacles remain before any reactors could be built.
Italy still lacks a permanent national repository for radioactive waste from its previous nuclear program, with waste continuing to be stored at temporary facilities around the country. Future reactor projects and waste storage sites are also expected to face opposition from local communities.
Energy analysts have questioned the economics of nuclear power, pointing to high construction costs and the lack of commercially proven SMR projects operating at scale in Europe. Industry estimates place the cost of a single 300-megawatt SMR at between 3 billion and 6 billion euros ($3.5 billion and $7 billion), excluding additional infrastructure and grid expenses.
Michele Governatori, a senior energy adviser at climate and energy think tank ECCO, welcomed the creation of a regulatory framework but said it would likely expose limited private-sector appetite for new nuclear projects.
“Having a regulatory framework in place is positive, but it will also make clear the limited interest of private investors in technologies that are either not competitive today or not yet ready, such as SMRs,” he said.
Governatori added Italy should focus on measures already available to cut energy costs and reduce reliance on fossil fuels, including electrification, energy efficiency, renewable energy, storage capacity and power-grid upgrades.
Environmental groups and opposition parties have already signaled resistance to the government’s plans and could challenge future projects once specific reactor and waste-storage sites are proposed.

A disturbing video of a man assaulting a Bhelpuri vendor is going viral on social media (here, here, and here). The video shows the man approaching the vendor, eating Bhelpuri from his basket, spitting on him, and assaulting him. The video is being shared with claims that it shows a real incident in Patna, with users demanding action against the man. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows a real incident of a man assaulting a Bhelpuri vendor in Patna.
Fact: The video is scripted and does not show a real incident in Patna. The men seen in the video clarified that it was made for entertainment and that both are part of the same team. Several other videos on their social media accounts also show them acting together in different situations. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to a YouTube channel named Sonu Paswan. The man seen allegedly assaulting the vendor in the viral video posted a clarification video (archived) on the channel, stating that the video was made for entertainment purposes and does not depict a real incident. He said he regularly makes such emotional videos and appealed to viewers not to share the video with false claims. He also urged viewers to stop mocking or roasting his work.
We also found a clarification video (archived) by the vendor on the same channel. He stated that he creates emotional videos centred around poverty and that the man seen assaulting him in the video is also a member of their team. He clarified that the video does not depict a real incident.
We also found several other videos on Sonu Paswan’s Facebook account, in which both men seen in the viral video appear together, acting in different situations.
To sum up, this viral video of a man assaulting a Bhelpuri vendor in Patna is scripted, not a real incident.

Osteoporosis, a condition affecting older adults that causes bones to become thin and fragile, used to be a top priority for pharmaceutical companies. Eli Lilly, Merck, Novartis, and GSK each had their own treatment designed to stop bones from weakening. But the cumbersome requirements for taking the drugs, as well as a series of safety concerns, stifled their use. Many patients who are eligible for osteoporosis therapies don’t take any of the drugs available today.
Several companies hope to fill that void. Eli Lilly is recruiting scientists to work on osteoporosis therapies, according to Bloomberg. Other pharmaceutical companies are rumored to be following suit. Venture capitalists, having taken notice, are now making bone health one of their priorities.

Sofia Coppola says she still feels nervous whenever she begins a new movie, but considers that fear part of what makes the work meaningful.
During an appearance on the "Happy Hour with Ina Garten" podcast on Wednesday, the Academy Award-winning filmmaker said she has "no idea" how a new movie will come together when she first starts working on it.
"It's always scary — and someone told me it's not worthwhile unless it's scary, because you're invested in it," Coppola told host Ina Garten.
"It's a thrill," Coppola added.
Garten said she, too, sees discomfort as a sign a project is worth taking on: "If it doesn't keep me up at night, I don't want to do it."
Coppola said she sees no point in doing something that doesn't challenge her, even if starting a new film can leave her feeling like she has to find her footing all over again.
The uncertainty never really goes away, she said: "You're always like, 'What if it's a disaster?'"
However, once production begins, Coppola said she becomes absorbed in bringing her vision to life with the crew.
"But then I'm so fixated on what I have in my mind and seeing that come together, the fun of making it and getting together with the crew to make it," she said. "It's so collaborative."
Coppola also said she avoids reading bad reviews, though she recently came across a box of negative reviews of her 2006 film "Marie Antoinette."
"It's so fun that it survived and found a new audience that likes it," she said.
Coppola has previously spoken about dealing with self-doubt.
In a March NPR interview about her documentary on fashion designer Marc Jacobs, Coppola said she could relate to his worries as he prepared for a runway show because she was "going through the same exact thing" while making the film.
However, she said having some self-doubt can be useful: "I don't trust anyone that doesn't have a little self-doubt. I think you need a little to keep you on your toes."
Other high-profile figures have similarly said they see uncertainty as an opportunity to grow.
In January 2024, Barbara Corcoran said that feeling like an impostor had fueled her success, since it pushed her to work harder and, in the process, build confidence.
"My success is entirely due to my insecurity," she said.
In October 2024, Anna Kendrick said she felt similarly out of her depth when she pitched to direct Netflix's true-crime film "Woman of the Hour." After her first pitch, the producers asked her to try again the next day with more confidence.
"They knew that I was faking it. They have told me to fake it, and they still were like, 'Well, that lady seems like a leader. Let's hire her,'" Kendrick said.

The Linux operating system will run on just about any computer. I mean that literally. Remember the Intel Pentium 4 processor? It came out in 2000, and it’s still supported by Debian Linux. But once upon a time, getting Linux working meant jumping through all sorts of hoops and dealing with frustrating experiences trying to get everything to work on hardware designed for Windows or macOS. Thankfully, those days are mostly behind us. I’ve installed Linux on every laptop I’ve tested since 2020. Almost all of them worked great, but some were easier to get running than others.
Beyond supporting older hardware, Linux offers other user benefits, like greater control over operating systems that run on the Linux kernel, better security and malware protection, no unwanted software (bloatware), and faster performance. It’s not just for developers; it’s for casual users too.
For most people, a laptop preinstalled with Linux is your best bet. Plenty of hardware makers now ship laptops running Linux right out of the box. This guide recommends the best of these.
