Best for Most People
System76 recently updated its Lemur Pro with a new chip and a few other tweaks. I’ll be testing it very soon, but I don’t expect to change my recommendation here. The Lemur Pro has long been my favorite Linux laptop, and the latest model will likely continue that. It strikes the best balance between size, weight, power, and price, even with the price hike on the latest model.
At just over 12 inches wide and weighing 2.5 pounds, the 14-inch model is plenty portable. The 16-inch version is 14.1 inches by just under 10 inches. The 14-inch base model gets an Intel Core Ultra 5 325, with the option to upgrade to a Core Ultra X7 358H. The latter chip is the default for the 1-inch model. My one gripe with the new model is that the RAM is fixed at 32 GB. You can still cram up to 8 TB of storage into each of the two SSD slots.
The Lemur Pro offers very solid performance that’s plenty for all the things most people do every day. It can even handle light video editing and other intensive tasks, though it has no dedicated graphics card; for that, you’ll want the Pangolin Pro (see below). That said, I’ve been impressed with the Arc B390 iGPU in the Ultra X7 model. I’ll add more performance details after I’ve had a chance to test more.
The port selection is good, with two USB 3.2 Type-C ports—one of which is a Thunderbolt 4 port—a USB-A port, a 3.5-mm headphone/microphone combo jack, a MicroSD card reader, and an HDMI 2.0 port. Battery life is also fantastic, lasting all day in most use cases. The keyboard, while not my favorite, is pleasant enough to type on.
As with all System76 laptops, it ships with the company’s Pop!_OS Linux distribution preinstalled (you can also opt for Ubuntu, but I highly suggest trying Pop!_OS). Pop!_OS’s Cosmic desktop is based on Gnome, but unlike Gnome, Pop!_OS is very customizable and can be tweaked to your liking. Aside from Arch Linux, Pop!_OS is my favorite distro.
Best MacBook Replacement
Tuxedo’s InfinityBook Pro 14 (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is a svelte, lightweight laptop that’s dedicated to the open-source world. Tuxedo is based in Germany (which is why the price is in euros), and like System76, it has a long history of providing excellent Linux support.
The InfinityBook Pro is Tuxedo’s everyday laptop, powered by an AMD Ryzen 7 H 255 chip. I haven’t tested Tuxedo’s AMD model, but I have tested the same chip in other Linux laptops and found performance very good. Note that the H 255 has no active NPU, so it’s not ideal for local AI, but it’s plenty for average to demanding workloads. I had no trouble playing back 8K video out of a GoPro, for example. The InfinityBook can be configured with up to 96 GB of RAM and 8 TB of storage per drive slot (there are two SSD card slots), though of course, with the price of memory and storage where it is, it will cost you.
The performance specs are solid, but the real highlight of the InfinityBook is the gorgeous 2,880 x 1,800-pixel-resolution matte screen. At 400 nits, it’s plenty bright enough to work anywhere, and the anti-glare matte finish means you can see it under bright sunlight. In my testing of the Intel model, the InfinityBook Pro had plenty of power for most tasks, and I expect the AMD chip to deliver the same. The battery life is solid and lasts all day, and the custom tools for fine-tuning the power settings are the best I’ve used. Tuxedo’s custom OS (based on Kubuntu) is a great Linux experience, and the website offers extensive documentation and help for new users.
Best DIY Linux Laptop
Framework’s Laptop 13 is my personal favorite. It’s not my top pick because it won’t be right for everyone (it’s lacking in ports and doesn’t have the premium feel of the Lemur Pro), but it does everything I need, has great battery life, and I happen to love the ability to swap the ports around in different configurations. I’m typing this on a Framework laptop running Arch Linux.
There are a few flavors of the Laptop 13. I tested the second release of the 13-inch model (8/10, WIRED Recommends) and loved it, but since then we’ve reviewed the newer 13-inch AMD Framework, the 16-inch Framework, and the smaller Framework 12. All of them make great Linux laptops because Framework officially supports Ubuntu and Fedora Linux, and also has a helpful forum of users who’ve made just about every Linux distro you can think of work on their Framework Laptops.
The current line of DIY Framework Laptop 13 can be configured with either an AMD or Intel processor (though Intel seems to be frequently out of stock). The AMD Ryzen model ships with AI 300 Series chips, starting with the Ryzen 5, with several upgrade options to the Ryzen AI 7 and even the Ryzen AI 9 HX 370. An Intel configuration starts with the Core Ultra 5 125H, with upgrades to the Core Ultra 7 155 or even 165H available. Whichever processor you pick, you can upgrade to up to 96 GB of DDR5-5600 RAM and choose a drive up to 8 TB.
I’ve tested Framework laptops with Ubuntu, which Framework supports, and Arch Linux, which is community-supported, and both worked great. My only gripe with Framework is the same as with many Linux laptops: battery life could be better. I get about seven to eight hours with casual use, and much less when editing video or doing other intensive tasks.
My other complaint is that the Framework’s build quality isn’t as nice as System76 or Tuxedo’s offerings, but that may change with the new Framework 13 Pro, which will be shipping soon; we’ll update this guide as soon as we get our hands on one.
A Sysadmin Favorite
System76’s Pangolin Pro is a 16-inch, AMD-powered laptop with enough ports to leave the dongle at home. The Ryzen 7 chip has plenty of power for most tasks; it didn’t even break a sweat playing back 8K video, though it did spin up the fans when it came time to export that video down to 4K. As you would expect, benchmarks on graphics-intensive tasks are behind any machine with a dedicated card—though you can plug in an eGPU via the OcuLink port—but the Ryzen AI 7’s overall performance is quite good.
You can configure your Pangolin Pro with up to 96 GB of RAM and 16 TB of storage should you have recently won the lottery, but the base model comes with a more affordable 16 GB of RAM and 500 GB of storage.
The battery life is good for the size—it lasted all day in most of my testing. The keyboard is quite nice to type on. The oversized trackpad sometimes got in my way, but it wasn’t a deal-breaker; you just have to watch where you rest your palms, or you might right-click by accident.
This laptop has plenty of ports, including two USB-C (one 4.0, one 3.2 Gen 2), three USB-A, a microSD card reader, an Ethernet port, an HDMI port, and the aforementioned OcuLink port for docking or external graphics if you have an eGPU lying about. It’s hard to complain about that list, especially with the ability to plug in a graphics card when you need it, though I do wish the two USB-C ports were on opposite sides of the laptop.
System76’s Pop!_OS Linux has long provided what I consider one of the best Linux experiences out there. The Cosmic Desktop and the custom apps System76 ships with it provide that "just works" stability you need to use Linux daily without even noticing you’re using Linux.
Best for Performance
The Kubuntu Focus Zr 1 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) is a powerhouse, but at 15 inches by 12 inches, over an inch thick, and weighing in at 8 pounds, it’s not a laptop you casually cart around. But if your work requires serious computing power, be it machine learning (running TensorFlow), local LLMs, big data crunching workflows, or high-end video editing, the Zr Gen 1 delivers power in spades.
Inside, the Zr Gen 1 features an Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX with 24 cores, an RTX 5090 graphics card, 24 GB GDDR7 RAM (expandable up to 192 GB), and two SSDs (one 1 TB and one 2 TB; you can have up to four drives, one of them being a PCIe Gen 5x4 NVMe). Along with the discrete GPU, it has an integrated one as well, so you can turn off the discrete card to maximize battery life. I spent about 90 percent of the time with the discrete card off and just turned it on when editing photos and video.
The screen is a gloriously large 18-inch LCD display (2560 x 1600 pixels, 168-dpi density) with a max brightness of over 500 nits and a matte finish that makes it easy to use even in bright light. It’s one of the better LCD panels I’ve used lately, and gamers will appreciate the 240 Hz refresh rate. You can also plug in up to four external displays. Thanks to the size, the Zr has plenty of room for a full-size keyboard with a numeric pad. The keyboard is user-configurable and features a 65,536-color LED backlight system that you can tweak to your liking.
Kubuntu Focus delivers a very stable Linux experience. Every update is tested and validated on the hardware before it ships. Kubuntu Focus hardware is tested for at least three years, and if a problem is found, the company works with the developers of the core components to fix it before it ever reaches a customer. The last known stable version of software remains unchanged until the next version passes all tests and has no issues. Kubuntu Focus does this even at the application level, testing everything from dev tools like JetBrains, to consumer software like Dropbox, Steam, Zoom, Slack, and more to ensure everything works before it ships out to you. The result is a level of Linux stability you’re not likely to achieve on your own.
If Your Budget Is Tight
One of the beauties of Linux is that it requires fewer resources and maintains support for older hardware for far longer than Windows or macOS. That means you don’t need to spend a fortune on a new laptop; you can breathe life into an old one or grab a used laptop off eBay. I have, in fact, never purchased a new laptop for Linux. I have been buying used hardware for years, working my way through Lenovo’s X-series laptops (starting with an X220, up through a T14 at which point I jumped ship for the Framework), but old Dell XPS and some Asus laptops are also great for Linux. If you opt to buy used, check out our guide to buying used on eBay to make sure you get a good deal.
The specs you need depend on what you’ll be doing. If you’re editing video or gaming, you should probably stick with one of our picks above. If you just need to do typical office work, edit some photos, and watch 4K video, you can get by with a 12th-generation Intel i5 or newer processor, 8 GB of RAM (the more, the merrier), and an SSD large enough to store your data. If you want an AMD system, stick with a Ryzen 5 9000 series or Ryzen 200 series.
If you’d like some more help speccing out a solid Linux system, see our step-by-step guide to choosing the right laptop.
What to Look For in a Linux Laptop
Buying a Linux laptop involves a little more research than Windows or macOS. In addition to the specs, you need to make sure the hardware in question works with Linux. These days almost everything works pretty well with Linux, but there are some exceptions.
Expect to wrestle with Nvidia graphics cards. The company has never been supportive of Linux and probably never will be. I’ve always steered clear, but if you want a dedicated GPU from Nvidia, do your research. The Arch Linux Wiki is a good place to start.
On the processor front, Intel generally has better Linux support than AMD, though that is changing, judging from our AMD-powered recommendations above. I have used Linux on AMD for quite a while without any issues (though I do have a slightly older system, which helps).
The other thing to consider is which Linux distro you’ll use. A distro is essentially the operating system that’s built on top of the Linux kernel, and there are many distros to choose from. If you don’t already have a favorite or don’t even know what a distro is, I suggest Pop_OS! by System76, a company that also makes many of the laptops in this guide. Pop_OS! provides (by far) the best user experience I’ve seen on a Linux laptop. It strikes a great balance between being easy to use for Linux newcomers and well-stocked with power-user features. It has great documentation and should have you up and running without any trouble. I’ve used it on every laptop in this guide.

Lourdes: What to know about one of Catholicism’s most famous pilgrimage sites
Pope Leo XIV plans to visit the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes in southern France on Sunday
PARIS -- PARIS (AP) — Pope Leo XIV will visit the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes this weekend as part of his four-day apostolic journey to France, which is the first official papal state visit to the country in 18 years.
The site near the Spanish border draws millions of pilgrims annually, including sick and disabled believers hoping for a cure from the famed spring water in the Lourdes grotto. Here is what to know about Lourdes, one of Catholicism’s most important pilgrimage sites.
The popularity of Lourdes is intrinsically linked to Bernadette Soubirous. A young girl who came from a modest background, she was uneducated, with no knowledge of religion, and suffered from asthma when she reported 18 visions of a lady dressed in white in the Grotto of Massabielle near Lourdes, between February and July 1858. The Catholic Church later accepted that the visions were of the Virgin Mary.
Bernadette’s visions, and the subsequent discovery of allegedly healing spring waters, led the church to build a sanctuary there.
In 1866, Bernadette left Lourdes to join the convent of the Sisters of Charity in Nevers, where she lived until her death at age 35. She was canonized in 1933 by Pope Pius XI to become Saint Bernadette.
Believers say that during the ninth apparition of the lady dressed in white, Bernadette heard her say: “Go and drink at the spring and wash yourself there.”
Millions of pilgrims and visitors have since journeyed to Lourdes to drink and wash in this water, which has no therapeutic or specific properties. Lourdes water is free to access from the sanctuary’s taps and drinking fountains. Many pilgrims take some back home.
Lourdes became a major pilgrimage destination after the Catholic Church officially recognized Bernadette's visions as Apparitions in 1862. From then on, millions of pilgrims from all over the world began flocking to the Grotto of Massabielle.
As well as being a holy site, Lourdes attracts around 3 million pilgrims a year, including approximately 60,000 sick and disabled pilgrims. According to the town hall, it's the fourth most visited Catholic pilgrimage site in the world, after the Vatican, the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Mexico City, and the Basilica of Our Lady of Aparecida in Brazil.
The Grotto of Massabielle is one of the 22 sites making up the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes. The sanctuary is home to numerous places of worship, including three basilicas: the Basilica of the Immaculate Conception, which is the oldest, the Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary, and the underground Basilica of Saint Pius X.
Pilgrims can also follow one of the two Stations of the Cross, featuring cast-iron or marble statues, before taking a dip in the sanctuary’s baths. There, they can immerse themselves in the 12 degrees Celsius (53.6 degrees Fahrenheit) water from the spring discovered in the Grotto of the Apparitions.
Among the millions traveling to Lourdes, many seek physical and spiritual healing, hoping for a miracle. The Catholic Church has officially recognized 72 healings as miraculous at Lourdes, out of more than 7,000 cases examined since 1858.
Less than 15,000 people actually live in Lourdes. But with nearly 10,000 hotel rooms and around 21,200 beds, it has the second-largest hotel capacity in France, after Paris.
Finding an affordable roof over your head during Leo's visit is, however, a tall order.
The pope's visit to the city will draw hundreds of thousands of visitors, sending accommodation prices skyrocketing. Some hoteliers are charging extremely high rates, sometimes reaching more than 2,000 euros ($2,300) per night.
Even though most pilgrims traveling to Lourdes each year come from France — 42%, according to the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes — many visitors from Eastern Europe are expected to come and greet Leo.
Following the end of the Cold War, Catholics from Central and Eastern Europe gained the freedom to go west, sharply increasing the number of pilgrims from former Communist countries visiting Lourdes. This trend has continued to the present day. Poland ranks sixth among the more than 160 nations sending pilgrims to Lourdes each year.
Leo won't get a glimpse of the mosaics by an ex-Jesuit artist accused of abusing women adorning the façade of the Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary. They will all be covered during Leo's visit.
The artwork was made by Rev. Marko Ivan Rupnik, a Slovenian artist whose mosaic designs decorate Vatican chapels and churches and basilicas around the world. The Vatican confirmed this summer that a church trial against Rupnik is ongoing.
Lourdes Bishop Jean-Marc Micas announced the move last month, following a decision two years ago that the mosaics would no longer be lit up during the evening prayer. In March 2025, the mosaics on the basilica's entrance doors had already been covered.
The Rupnik scandal exploded publicly in late 2022, when Italian blogs first reported claims by women and nuns of sexual, spiritual and psychological abuse by Rupnik dating back to the 1990s that had been consistently dismissed by the Catholic hierarchy.
Leo will meet seven survivors of sexual abuse who were assaulted as children or adults, according to the Bishops’ Conference of France. A 2021 report estimated that 330,000 children had been sexually abused over 70 years by church personnel in France.
The Lourdes sanctuary said the pope will land at the Tarbes airport on Saturday and begin his pilgrimage with a prayer at the Grotto of the Apparitions. On Sunday morning, Leo will meet with the bishops at the French Bishops’ Conference, then celebrate Mass on the Prairie, followed by the Angelus prayer.
In the afternoon, he will meet the staff and sick people of the Accueil Notre-Dame. He closes the visit with one of Lourdes’ signature rites: the Rosary and torchlight procession through the sanctuary.

Good morning. Yesterday was the first official day of autumn. “Fall, leaves, fall; die, flowers, away,” Brontë wrote for those of you who have been thinking about pumpkin spice lattes since July.
HHS unveils new initiatives on animal testing
HHS laid out its latest strategies to speed the shift away from using animals in medical testing. Beginning next February, research methods other than animal testing can be used when “appropriate” for determining the safety of drugs and biologics, according to a final FDA rule issued yesterday. At the same time, the NIH unveiled several initiatives designed to encourage the use of non-animal approaches such as cell-based assays, organs-on-a-chip, and computer models.
STAT’s Ed Silverman wrote about the new policies and spoke with advocates on both sides of the long-running debate. Read more.
700,000
That’s how many seniors have started taking GLP-1s since July, when Medicare began covering the drugs, Eli Lilly CEO Dave Ricks told CNBC on Monday.
Medicare is technically prohibited from paying for weight loss drugs, but the Trump administration circumvented the law by making the drugs available through a demonstration program, sort of like an experimental pilot. But as John Wilkerson reported over the summer, this theoretically temporary program may prove difficult to actually end.
Drugmakers look to bolster brittle bones again
Osteoporosis used to be a top priority for pharmaceutical companies. Big players like Eli Lilly, Merck, and Novartis each had their own treatments designed to stop bones from weakening. But a lot of eligible patients don’t take the existing medications, likely due to a long list of side effects, along with the simple fact that they can be annoying to take. Patients are often required to stay upright for 30 minutes and avoid eating for up to an hour.
But late last year, drug developers were handed a fresh incentive to address those concerns: The FDA said in December that it would allow companies to use a new clinical endpoint that could shave years off of development timelines. And several companies already seem to be jumping at the chance. Read more from STAT’s Allison DeAngelis.
A private equity-owned hospital chain goes nonprofit
It’s unheard of: Quorum Health, a private equity-owned hospital system, is in the process of converting to a nonprofit organization. While individual institutions have made the change before, Quorum will transition all 11 of its hospitals, most of which serve rural areas.
There are concrete benefits to the nonprofit structure, including tax advantages, discounted drugs, and the ability to apply for grants. But some are concerned that the deal is structured to benefit Quorum’s current investors to the detriment of the hospitals and their patients. “The question is, are the creditors taking enough of a discount to leave a hospital company that is viable?” said Jim Baker, executive director of the Private Equity Stakeholder Project, a nonprofit watchdog group. Read more from STAT’s Tara Bannow on the high stakes transition.
The state of youth gender-affirming care
Last Friday, the Justice Department announced that it had reached settlement deals with NYU Langone and the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center over the provision of gender-affirming care to young people. Both hospitals agreed to stop providing puberty blockers, hormones, and rare surgical procedures to minors. At least six institutions have made such deals, though none have admitted to or been convicted of any wrongdoing. For the Trump administration, ending the services is the point, as health officials have repeatedly asserted their desire to stop what they call “sex-rejecting procedures.”
The chilling effect of the government’s dogged offensive against transgender health care has been swift. Dozens of hospitals have stopped providing care, even if they haven’t directly been targeted by legal action. NYU Langone said in a statement that the settlement protects patients from the threat of extensive government subpoenas that had been directed at the institution. The AP has more on the agreements.
How to support mentally ill pregnant people
A decade before she began pursuing pregnancy, Meg LeDuc had a harrowing break with reality. She stopped taking her antipsychotic medication, leading to multiple overdoses, including twice within two weeks. Even with years of stability separating her from that experience, LeDuc worried that, if she became a mother, she would be a danger to her own child.
She and her husband were cautious, seeking prenatal counseling on the safety of her medication regimen in pregnancy and her potential for relapse. But as LeDuc notes in a new First Opinion essay, this sort of care remains out of reach for many women with serious mental illness, 20% of whom are uninsured.
“People experiencing such devastating delusions deserve humane, quality care. With such care, we are capable of leading rich, fulfilling lives,” she writes. “And even being good parents.” Read more about the limits of reproductive psychiatry.

One of South Africa’s most senior police officers has been charged with raping an 18-year-old woman and grooming a 16-year-old girl, as the country’s police face allegations of corruption and failing to tackle violence against women and girls.
Shadrack Sibiya, who was already suspended from his role as deputy national police commissioner over allegations he interfered with political killings investigations, was arrested on Monday. He is facing charges of rape, people trafficking, promoting the sexual grooming of a child and two counts of grooming a child.
Sibiya appeared briefly in a Johannesburg court on Tuesday. He was then taken to prison in the capital, Pretoria, before a bail hearing on 29 September, as prosecutors had argued he was an escape risk.
South Africa is reeling after the discovery of nine women’s bodies across Ekurhuleni, the municipality east of Johannesburg, in September. Meanwhile, the Madlanga Commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police for the last year.
Puleng Dimpane, the acting national police commissioner, said: “Police officers are entrusted with protecting women and children. They cannot themselves be implicated in conduct that undermines this responsibility. As the country continues to confront the scourge of gender-based violence and femicide, there can be no room for anyone within the police service who is alleged to abuse their position or violate the rights of women and children.”
Sibiya is accused of raping an 18-year-old woman at a hotel in May in the Sandton business district of Johannesburg. The alleged rape took place “whilst she was passed out due to intoxication administered by the accused”, according to a copy of the charge sheet.
The alleged grooming of the 16-year-old girl took place over WhatsApp between 20 July and 3 August, according to the charge sheet. This allegedly included Sibiya sending the girl naked photos of herself, which she had not sent to him.
Sibiya did not enter a plea at the hearing on Tuesday. His lawyer told the court that they needed more time to consult with and get instructions from him, according to News24.
Firoz Cachalia, the acting police minister, said: “We strongly condemn the alleged conduct.
“Where allegations of sexual offences are made against a member of the service, they must be investigated without fear or favour.”
When Sibiya appeared before the Madlanga Commission in February he denied allegations that he had moved 121 political killings investigations from KwaZulu-Natal province to the national head office without explanation.
Sibiya also denied that he had received a gift of 20 impalas from Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala, a businessman who received an allegedly fraudulent 360m rand (£16.7m) police health services contract soon after the alleged gift.
Matlala, who has been charged with attempted murder, alongside several other charges including fraud and money laundering, declined to comment on the impalas when he appeared at the Madlanga Commission in August. He said he did not want to incriminate himself as the matter was under investigation.

Recently, I may have saved a woman’s life on the road. Somehow, this was something I had expected to happen.
On that day, I saw a truck leave a construction site with a tangled wire trailing behind. I frantically looked to see what the wire was attached to and spotted the scaffolding a few meters ahead. I shrieked and grabbed the hand of the woman walking in front of me just as the metal pipes came crashing down. We hugged for a brief second, and then walked our separate ways.
Mumbai (pictured top) is a city that is being made every day, and so much of the Bandra-Khar area that I inhabit is never not under construction. Since I moved here from Seoul earlier this year, I have learned to be hypervigilant every time I walk the streets.
I was reminded of that moment last week as news broke about the collapse of a five-storey building in Delhi, which killed seven people. Authorities had flagged safety concerns in the neighbourhood months earlier, the Hindustan Times reported, after 23 people died in a fire at another building.
As the world’s most populous country, India can feel like a place where life can be startlingly cheap, and people die every day in tragedies that could have been prevented. According to analysis of government data by the Times of India, between 2020 and 2004 nearly 33,000 deaths occurred due to building collapses, fires or people falling into pits and maintenance holes.
The collapse in Delhi has prompted questions, once again, about the state of urban infrastructure in India’s biggest cities. At a time when the country is undertaking a rapid infrastructure boom – new airports, high-speed expressways, luxury residential towers– daily life in cities like Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru appears to be deteriorating.
Indian cities are not walkable, they rank among the worst for air quality, construction is poorly regulated, seasonal flooding is common and waste management remains under pressure. These challenges are only going to increase; the World Bank expects India’s urban population to double, going up to 951 million, by 2050. More than half of the urban infrastructure the country will need by then has yet to be built, it said.
So, what would it take to make our cities better and safer? The experts I spoke to broadly agreed that Indian cities don’t lack rules as much as the political will and institutional machinery to enforce them.
For infrastructure veteran Vinayak Chatterjee, one solution lies in giving urban local bodies more power. He points to a constitutional amendment from 1992 that was meant to strengthen municipalities and give them greater responsibility over urban planning. “But it remains largely unimplemented – in spirit and will. It is a serious matter that affects the very fabric of our urban existence,” said Chatterjee, founder of the Infravision Foundation.
Rahul Goel, an expert on transportation safety and a professor at the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, believes the problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking. “People are using public space for personal use. Everything becomes better when you remove on-street parking,” he said, arguing that freeing up roads would make pedestrians and cyclists safer, reduce traffic jams and make walking easier.
In other cities in the global south, from Bangkok to Manila to Cape Town, one cannot just park their car on the road to run errands, Goel said. He described it as a governance failure, saying there is a need to create more parking spaces and perhaps have civil defense personnel or municipal workers enforce fines.
“Our streets are self-run,” Goel said. “That’s why they are in complete disarray.” He pointed to the Delhi Metro as an example of a space where people follow rules and things are orderly. “When rules are enforced, people follow them.”
The same gap between rules and enforcement is evident at construction sites.
India has detailed guidelines for construction approvals, including how traffic must be managed, what signage must be put up, and creating paths for pedestrians. But compliance remains a significant problem, says Geetam Tiwari, emeritus professor at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. In an audit of construction sites on highways, including bridges, Tiwari and her colleagues found widespread violations. Contractors had a financial incentive to complete projects quickly with payments being tied to the pace of construction, she said, adding that penalties for violations were low enough that it was cheaper to simply pay the fine than make fixes.
For unsafe buildings and unauthorised renovations, Tiwari said, the solution also requires bringing stakeholders together: resident associations, landlords, lessees and local authorities to conduct audits, raise awareness and penalise contractors who violate safety requirements. Actions, she said, that should not wait for the next tragedy.
In the aftermath of the Delhi case, the high court has directed authorities to inspect student accommodations for safety. Building owners have been arrested and several municipal officials in charge of the area have been suspended.
A similar governance deficit shows up when it comes to air pollution, another long-time challenge for Indian cities. Ronak Sutaria, founder and CEO of Respirer Living Sciences, has been working on one aspect of this issue: by developing affordable air-quality monitors for construction sites. Respirer’s air-quality monitors are now installed in 5,000 locations across 10 cities in India, helping authorities identify pollution hotspots. (Some cities, including Mumbai, require construction sites to monitor pollution levels.)
“A number of sites are getting alerts [from authorities] and are taking dust-suppression measures, for instance, to bring down [pollution] levels. So, the entire loop is sort of working,” Sutaria said.
Indian cities continue to grow, but the question is whether governance can keep pace. On that afternoon in Bandra, I recall thinking how lucky the woman and I were not to be grievously injured. But we shouldn’t have to rely on luck to survive.
What else we’re reading about
New Delhi declaration | The Brics summit held in New Delhi over the weekend adopted a declaration with Iran and the United Arab Emirates agreeing to a late-stage compromise on the language about the war in the Middle East. Chinese president, Xi Jinping, who visited India for the first time in almost seven years, announced that China would helm the group’s presidency for the next year.
Political donations | An investigation by the BBC’s Shubhangi Misra claimed that six unrecognised political parties registered in Gujarat received donations of £132m (Rs 1,700 crore) in 2023-24, higher than the income of national parties excluding the BJP. Despite fielding few candidates and evidence of little political activity, the high amounts expose glaring gaps in oversight of political finances.
Women’s health support | Two south Indian states, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, have recently announced policies aimed at supporting women through perimenopause and menopause. Karnataka plans to introduce a women’s health programme that will integrate menopause into the public health system. Tamil Nadu will assess the physical and mental health needs of perimenopausal women.
Calling all emerging writers | Applications are open for South Asia Speaks, a wonderful platform for emerging writers from the region offering free, year-long mentorship and resources to develop a book-length project. The deadline is 30 September – find out more and apply here.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
This week, writer and professor Amitava Kumar (@amitavawriter), whose latest book, The Social Life of Trains, explores how railways helped shape India’s national identity, suggests the work of a poet he discovered on Instagram:
“Can I begin with a confession? I have been a professor of literature for more than three decades, but I don’t often understand poems. How lovely it is, then, to discover a poet whose lines are as clear and beautiful as the dawn! Recently, I came across the poems of a young Hindi poet named Parag Pawan. They spoke to me and, more importantly, they spoke to our moment. I immediately sat down to translate them into English.
A series of his poems could be translated as Poems for the Unemployed. One of the poems, sharp and precise, begins with the funny, acerbic lines: ‘On the topic of our unemployment / the prime minister gives speeches / but he doesn’t give us jobs. / He works for eighteen hours / while we believe that asking anyone to work / for more than eight hours / is exploitation.’”
Count it
A number worth knowing
2,192
That’s the number of days Umar Khalid has spent in jail since his arrest on 13 September 2020 – without trial. Last week, the student activist wrote a searing account describing the daily drudgery of life in prison, published in The Quint. Earlier this year, in his first interview since being jailed, Khalid told the Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Peterson: “Humanity is a privilege that is not granted to people like me.”
Vibe check
As more people read news online, watching Ayan Shaikh (@paperboy_ayan) delivering newspapers with serious swag gave me great joy and some hope. The 22-year-old from Ahmedabad posts videos of it on Instagram, and it’s a feat to watch. Watch his papers swerve, reach gravity-defying heights and land with pinpoint accuracy and tell me his deliveries don’t rival Jasprit Bumrah.
Delivering papers was Shaikh’s first job after he dropped out of school. He spent four years mastering the techniques that would allow him to make faster deliveries to earn more money. The first video, filmed by his friend, had 20m views and a recent one has crossed 128m, more views than many Bollywood stars might command. He starts his day at 4:30am, making 300 deliveries in two hours, before he begins a second shift as a gig worker for quick commerce apps.
“I think people love [the videos] because I do it passionately … from my heart,” he said. “If you do things dedicatedly, anything is possible. It won’t work out once, twice, thrice, but it might on the fourth attempt.”
Get in touch
Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

Meta knows you probably have some privacy concerns about its smart glasses.
At its annual Meta Connect event today in Menlo Park, California, the company announced plans to incorporate its siloed AI processing scheme known as Private Processing into its Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses. The feature, designed for WhatsApp last year, allows the glasses’ AI assistant to get to know you and fulfill your requests without Meta accessing any of your data.
“Most of the time, glasses are helping you see well, protecting your eyes and complementing your look, and that’s it,” Meta wrote in its press release, perhaps somewhat underselling the monumental historic significance of vision-correcting lenses as a technology. “But AI glasses have the capacity to provide superpowers like translating a conversation or summarizing notes or a conversation.” So the company says it sought to answer the question: “How do you build a hyper-personalized AI that knows your world deeply with enhanced privacy?”
Private Processing is designed to enable AI cloud processing that protects data from all outside parties, including Meta itself. For its smart glasses, Private Processing could theoretically enable chat interactions wearers have with Meta’s AI assistant through its smart glasses and commands, including private transcriptions and messages. However, the company has not yet said specifically which features it will support.
Meta introduced Private Processing into WhatsApp and its Meta AI app last year. The service helped enable WhatsApp’s Incognito Chat. The goal was to let customers use AI services without undermining WhatsApp’s flagship end-to-end encrypted secure messaging feature.
In a short conversation at Meta Connect, WIRED spoke with Meta’s Pritam Shah, director of engineering, on adding Private Processing to the glasses.
“What we are doing right now is sharing our excitement about this enhanced privacy platform,” Shah says. “We have the platform ready. We have it working. It's not just a white paper and a blog. The reason why we are announcing it right now, before putting more experiences on this platform, is so that we can start working with the security community and the privacy community and a third-party auditor.”
All of this comes at a moment of reckoning for Meta. The company has long been criticized for how it handles user privacy. This year alone, Meta has fielded months of controversy from people worried about its use of face-recognition technology and how its smart glasses could be used to arm sexual predators. Some people have dubbed them “pervert glasses,” confronted people wearing them, and even built apps like ZuckOff to detect Meta’s smart glasses nearby.
More broadly, Meta has been dogged by years of security and privacy gaffes that have eroded user trust, and its products have often seemed to be better at surveilling users than helping them. But at Meta Connect, the company tried to position its smart glasses as a tool that isn’t creepy
When the company launched its Muse AI agent earlier this month, it positioned the assistant as being geared toward security and privacy, specifically touting Muse’s cloud environment, known as Secure VM. It’s working on a version, dubbed Confidential VM, that will feature enhanced privacy guarantees, including a similar promise to make data inaccessible to Meta itself. Muse will also be coming to Meta’s glasses.
Private Processing isn’t available yet on Meta’s glasses, and Shah doesn’t have a timeline for when it will be added or which specific features will work with it.
“These are examples,” he says. “These are not concrete features coming, but these are some examples. And there will be even more powerful examples.”

Nikon's new Z5 IIC is a cheaper Z5 II without the electronic viewfinder
With RAW video and a flip-out screen, it should be a great vlogging camera.
Nikon's Z5 II is already one of the least expensive full-frame cameras available, but if you can do without an electronic viewfinder, there's now an even cheaper option. The company just announced the 24-megapixel Z5 IIC mirrorless camera without an EVF, but nearly all the other features of the Z5 II including RAW internal video. It's available at a very reasonable price, which is great news considering the steep inflation across the camera world of late.
Electronic viewfinders are expensive components and removing it allowed Nikon to not only lower the price but make the Z5 IIC lighter and smaller (the "C" is for "compact"). It weighs just 537 grams, nearly 25 percent lighter than the 700 gram Z5 II. And yet, it still has a full-sized grip and a good array of manual controls, though it's missing the Z5 II's joystick and a few other buttons. Most importantly, it has a fully articulating 3.2-inch 1040K dot touch display ideal for solo shooters. It also looks nice, especially the silver and black version.
The Z5 IIC is perhaps the best vlogging camera for debutants. It supports 4K video at 30 fps that supersamples from the full 6K sensor width, or 4K 60 fps video with a 1.5x crop (1080p at 120 fps). Moreover, you can capture that video in Nikon's N-RAW format with N-Log to maximize quality, something aspiring filmmakers will appreciate (H.265 is also supported). With the same video autofocus as the Z5 II, it should be fast and responsive. Nikon says it now supports fish(!) along with human, animal, bird and vehicle subject detection. It also offers in-body stabilization with 7.5 stops of shake reduction, a surprising feature for an inexpensive camera.
Other niceties for creators include scene modes for capturing 15 different types of scenes ranging from portraits to pets and food, or night landscape and twilight scenes. It has a REC light up front so your subject knows you're filming, a "product review" mode where the camera switches focus from presenter to objects and back again, "imaging recipes" (including some from the cinema camera company RED) to give you a filmic look, a waveform display to gauge video exposure and focus peaking/zebras. One drawback is the single SD UHS II card slot, rather than two as on the Z5 II.
The Z5 II will be nice for photographers as well, as long as they don't mind the lack of a viewfinder. It supports 14 fps burst speeds (RAW and JPEG) with continuous autofocus or 30 fps (JPEG only) in electronic shutter mode. Photo autofocus offers all the same subject detection features as video, including that weird fish mode. It should be a great low-light camera (like the Z5 II) as the expanded ISO range goes up to ISO 64,000.
The Nikon Z5 IIC is now on preorder for $1,400 (body only), a veritable bargain for a full-frame camera, especially considering the features like in-body stabilization and RAW video. You can also pick it up in a bundle with the Z 24-50mm f/4.3-5.3 kits lens for $1,700.

Siberian town ‘under siege’ by bears as at least six people killed in just a month
At least 14 people have been killed in bear attacks across Russia since January this year

At least six people have been killed in bear attacks in Russia’s Siberia over the past month, prompting prosecutors to investigate the reasons behind the attacks.
In the Siberian region of Krasnoyarsk, the investigation will now reportedly focus on whether local officials were negligent in failing to control the bear population or prevent the animals from entering populated areas.
Russia’s brown bear population has more than doubled since 1990, rising from about 130,000 to nearly 308,000 in 2026, according to the country’s natural resources ministry.
While the ministry has rejected that the number of bear attacks across Russia has increased and is in fact saying that it has remained relatively stable at around 20 to 30 a year, local officials and media have raised concerns, The Moscow Times reported.
At least 14 people have reportedly been killed in bear attacks across Russia since the beginning of this year.
Russia’s Investigative Committee said on its website that local officials had “failed to take measures to regulate the predator population or prevent them from appearing in areas inhabited by people”.
In the remote town of Podtyosovo, two people were found dead in a forest earlier this month, followed by the death of a 40-year-old factory worker who was walking through the forest on 6 September.
Earlier this month, two people were also killed while foraging for wild berries in a remote forest along the Lena River.
“One person managed to escape and report the incident,” the region’s interior ministry said.
In yet another recent incident, a 39-year-old was reportedly killed by a bear early on Wednesday.
In neighbouring Khakassia, deputy regional head Dmitry Buchenik said bears had surrounded the forest town of Abaza, which has about 10,000 residents, “on all sides”.
“It was an alarming night in Abaza. The taiga town is effectively under siege by bears,” he reportedly said. Some bears were chased away, while three were killed, including one that Mr Buchenik described was “huge”.
Authorities have reportedly killed more than 530 bears who were considered to be aggressive across Russia since spring.
According to Tass news agency, in August this year a high-profile attack took place in the village of Artybash in Altai Republic, where a bear tore into a tent at a tourist camp and dragged a 29-year-old woman from Novosibirsk into the forest.
The woman, who was reportedly an employee of the emergency situations ministry, was killed in the attack.
Earlier this month, a high-alert was declared in Krasnoyarsk, while a curfew was imposed in the Altai Republic. Tourist routes in Khakassia, Altai and Krasnoyarsk Krai were also reportedly closed.
Tatyana Pevneva, a senior researcher at the R A Shilo Novosibirsk Zoo told Tass that in autumn, bears are driven by hunger as they try to build enough fat reserves to survive the winter.
They can eat at least 10kg of food a day, mainly berries, mushrooms, nuts and carrion, according to Ms Pevneva.
The amount of fat they need depends on their size. A bear weighing around 200kg needs to build up 40-50kg of fat, while larger bears weighing 300-350kg may need up to 80kg, according to Dmitry Taranenko, a senior researcher at the Institute of Animal Systematics and Ecology of the Siberian Branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences.
Bears that fail to gain enough fat may be unable to hibernate properly or wake during winter. These bears, locally referred to as “shatun bears”, then roam in search of food, attacking livestock and sometimes approaching humans, Ms Pevneva said.

Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
- Published
"What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give."
"For us, for all the other women. How many other bodies will be found before something happens?"
Nokwanda is speaking to the BBC from the family home near South Africa's main city, Johannesburg, just two days after relatives identified Dineo's body.
The 38-year-old mother-of-two was last seen alive last Sunday. Her battered body, partly burned, found later in the residential region of Ekurhuleni.
Nokwanda weeps as she describes how the family will have to face, at some point, the grim task of telling Dineo's daughter of her death.
"How do you explain that your parent was brutally murdered, dumped in a field, and just left there, discarded like a piece of rubbish.
"There's no coming to peace with it," she adds. "It's something that you can never reconcile yourself with, that you can never get over."
Dineo's death this week has come amid a series of comparable incidents in Ekurhuleni – her body one of three discovered there this week. In total, nine bodies of murdered women have been found in similar circumstances in the region since July.
The problem has always been there but this spate of grim discoveries has once again sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country – which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.
Themba Kekana is also living in shock at the death of a loved one.
His sister, Itumeleng, was one of the first to disappear in Ekurhuleni.
The 32-year-old shopkeeper's body was found in July, 17 days after she was last seen alive. Her body was badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge.
"We are devastated with grief," says Themba, wet eyes shining.
"I look at my sister's young daughter and my eyes fill with tears, I know there is no way that I can ever take this pain away from her.
"No family should have to deal with what we are faced with."
Only one arrest has been made in connection with the murders – and that was two days after the first body was discovered on 15 July.
Nobody has been detained following the murders of Itumeleng or Dineo or the other six Ekurhuleni women.
Most of the victims were young, in their 20s or 30s, and almost all had suffered extreme violence before their deaths.
Police have said they are not sure if they are hunting a serial killer. It is possible the cases are not linked.
Either way, what has happened in this residential district east of South Africa's biggest city has traumatised the nation, shining a spotlight on a situation that many believe is a crisis.
South Africa's police issue detailed crime statistics every quarter, which show that during the last quarter – between April and June this year - 5,427 people were murdered.
The official data does not distinguish between the genders of the victims, but this week the country's Human Rights Commission released figures showing that 569 women had been killed in that period (six a day on average), with another 1,052 who faced attempted murder.
Many women - already feeling unsafe - have been left reeling by recent events.
And it has put pressure on the government, less than a year after ministers acknowledged the scale of the issue and declared gender-based violence a national disaster.
Announcing the move last November, Minister of Social Development Nokuzola Sisisi Tolashe said treating the issue as a national disaster would help the government tackle the crisis.
It followed weeks of protests, culminating in a "Women's Shut Down" march as South Africa hosted the G20 summit.
This week has seen a chorus of calls for things to go further.
Rights group Amnesty International said an important first step towards protecting South Africa's women was to recognise femicide as a separate crime.
"Every day that femicide remains unrecognised as a crime is a failure to confront the targeted killing of women," said Amnesty's country director Shenilla Mohamed in a statement. "It is time to call it what it is: Femicide.
"Femicide is a gender-motivated crime. It is the killing of a woman because she is a woman."
Amnesty says femicide is criminalised as a specific crime in 33 countries, including Gabon and Morocco in Africa.
It argues that making that change in South Africa could help focus on the scale of the issue.
"It would compel the state to confront their failure to protect women and girls from violence," says Mohamed. "You cannot fix what you are not tracking."
Almost everyone in South Africa agrees more needs to be done.
President Cyril Ramaphosa this week pledged to leave "no stone unturned" in investigating the crimes in Ekurhuleni, adding: "As a nation, we must stand up for the rights, safety and dignity of women and girls."
Lebogang Ramofoko, an advocate for gender and social justice, said the levels of violence against women in the country were symptomatic of a much bigger problem – a lack of regard for humanity.
"The bodies of black women have been treated as disposable in this country for time in memorial, passed down from colonisation through to apartheid," she tells the BBC, referring to the legalised system of racism that was in place until 1994.
"What we see happening to women is testimony to legacies of violence from those systems whose traumas were never addressed.
"This is not to say black men are inherently violent, but in systems where violence was meted out against them for decades, historically black women were the people that that violence would be taken out on - that cycle has not been broken."
In Kempton Park, a district of Ekurhuleni where five of the nine recent bodies were found, Lumka Maqhubela is part of the Girl2Woman Foundation group which has held protests to raise awareness of the crimes.
"We are grieved, we are scared," she says. "If the police cannot protect us any more the government should step in and do something.
"It's clear that we are not safe, we cannot be told by the police to be more vigilant. They should be doing more to make our communities safe – what else are we expected to do? We are not safe anywhere, not in our homes, not in the streets, it needs to stop."
"I feel uncomfortable," says Thulisile Sibande, 32. "When I go to a shop, I have to look around. I'm shocked and scared. So scared, it's a trauma."
Thembi Mabena, 60, tells the BBC she lived in the same neighbourhood as Dineo Motapane.
"She was laughing every day, with everybody," she remembers. "Now I'm worried.
"I know many children, girls, who tell me they are afraid to go to the shop alone. There is no safety, even for me too. I am old, but there is no safety."
"In South Africa," says Lerato Mzizi, 20, simply, "women are not safe any more."

In September 2026, social media users shared a video of an unusual animal encounter. The clip showed a rhino and a much smaller muntjac deer appearing to play together and butt heads in the snow.
"A tiny 13 kg Chinese muntjac deer playfully challenged a 1.7-ton rhino named Maruśka at the Wrocław Zoo in Poland," one Reddit post (archived) captioned the video.
Since January 2026, the clip has appeared in posts on X, Threads, Facebook and YouTube. Overlaid text in a YouTube video described (archived) the encounter as "David vs. Goliath," while some social media users wondered if the footage was generated using artificial-intelligence tools. For example, one Reddit user wrote (archived): "Saw this on another reddit post and many people were saying it's AI, but I'm really not sure it is."
However, the video was real. It showed Maruśka, a female Indian rhinoceros, and Tata (Polish for "Dad"), a male Chinese muntjac, a small deer species.
The footage originated from Zoo Wrocław in Poland. Managers of the zoo's official Facebook and Instagram pages posted the clip on Jan. 8, 2026. In the caption (translated from Polish), the zoo framed the scene as a humorous confidence mismatch and said the muntjac's bravado was driven by mating-season hormones:
Looks like someone forgot to look in the mirror this morning
Respect to Maruśka for her angelic patience!
Where does this bravado come from in the male Chinese muntjac?
It's nature calling! His partner is in heat, and testosterone is surging in the bachelor. He needs to burn off energy and show who's boss - even if his sparring partner weighs 1.7 tons. Who would have thought there was such a warrior in such a small body?
The clip was widely covered by national and local Polish news media outlets that cited the zoo as the source.
After the video went viral online, Zoo Wrocław published a follow-up article on Jan. 12, 2026, crediting the clip to employee Kamil Guzik, a foreman in the zoo's carnivorous mammals section.
Wrocław.pl — an online news portal in Wrocław, the city where the video was captured — spoke with Maciej Okupnik, a hooved-animal keeper at Zoo Wrocław, who explained why the two species shared a space.
The website quoted Okupnik as saying muntjacs and rhinos can live in proximity to one another both at the zoo and in the wild. He said muntjacs are territorial and mark areas with scent glands near their eyes, while rhinos typically tolerate other animals in their territory because "they're not afraid of anyone." He reportedly described the encounter as theatrical and said similar standoffs had occurred before but this was the first time staff had filmed one.
TVN24, a Polish news media channel, said Okupnik emphasized that the male muntjac's behavior was driven by a mix of territorial instinct and hormones because his partner was "in heat." He said the animal's priority was to defend his space and impress the female, not to challenge the rhino, and that Maruśka was not aggressive toward him in day-to-day interactions. Okupnik added that the rhino appeared to treat the lunges as an invitation to play, with no signs of real aggression. At one point, Maruśka snorted as if to signal she had enough and simply walked away.
Snopes has fact-checked several rhino-related rumors before. For example, in June 2025, we examined a claim that the northern white rhinoceros was extinct after the last such rhino died.

Quick Answer
The iPhone Duo hides several firsts and oddities: horizontal rear cameras, vertical UI elements, top-mounted volume buttons, Apple Pencil support, titanium construction, Smart Take, a circular status bar, unusual USB-C placement, and no Action button or Pro camera controls.
Apple launched many devices at its recent Surprise and Shine event, but there was no doubting the star of the show. It was the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, and the device that many are expecting to do for foldables what the iPhone did for smartphones almost two decades ago. Small wonder then that the past few days have seen everyone and their grandmother discussing the iPhone Duo.
Debates have been raging over its animations, its crease, its cameras, its apps, and of course, its price. Some are hailing it as the coolest thing since sliced bread, while others insist it is a spawn of Satan in smartphone shape. But in all this debate and discussion, some important aspects and features of the Duo have either escaped attention or have not been adequately covered.
Here are ten things you might have missed about Apple’s first foldable.
Table of Contents
The first iPhone with horizontally arranged cameras on the back…selfie cameras on the corners
iPhones have been coming with multiple cameras (two or three) on their backs for a while now. However, they have always been arranged vertically, one below the other, or in the case of some Pro devices, with two cameras one below the other and the third one placed between them but slightly to the side, forming a triangle of sorts. The iPhone Duo thus becomes the first iPhone to have cameras placed next to each other horizontally, in what some would term a very Pixel-like style. The selfie cameras also get new locations – moving to the right corner of the external display and close to the right corner of the internal display (when opened), where it actually lies under the display. Regular iPhone users are sure to notice a change in perspective.
The dock, navigation, and even the Dynamic Island just got radically right, and utterly vertical
The cameras on the iPhone Duo might have gone horizontal, but some elements of the UI have gone vertical! While everyone has been focusing on the crease in the middle of the iPhone Duo and its visibility (it’s not easy to spot, by all accounts). Apple moved many iOS elements to the right side and gave them a vertical orientation. Lock screen controls, navigation buttons, the home screen dock, and even the Dynamic Island are on the right side of the iPhone Duo, and what’s more, are arranged vertically.
The Dynamic Island even slides open vertically to show information and updates. Evidently, this was done because of the width of the iPhone Duo (it is also the widest iPhone ever), which would have made it difficult to reach these elements. They have therefore been placed on the same side as the display unlock/power button, which is also a fingerprint scanner. This is pretty right-wing in UI terms, literally.
Volume buttons on the top
The iPhone Duo comes with a rather different volume button placement from other foldables. While it is conventional for most foldables and indeed, most ‘normal’ phones, to have volume buttons on the right or left side, the iPhone Duo actually has volume buttons on the top, aligned slightly towards the right. This is a volume button placement we have seen on the newer iPad minis but not on any other iPhones or iPads. It is a rather odd location in our opinion, and if opened and rotated clockwise, it would place the buttons on the lower part of the right side, and on the top of the left side if rotated anti-clockwise.
Camera Control? Present! Action button? Er…
While the iPhone Duo comes with a Camera Control button like other recent iPhones, it, rather surprisingly, does not have an Action button, which is generally seen on the left side of most iPhones and can be customized to carry out a number of tasks. It used to toggle Silent mode on and off, before being changed to an action button. Clearly, it was either not good enough to make the cut for the Duo or perhaps there simply was not enough space for it.
Apple Pencil support exists, but only for the Type-C one
The iPhone Duo is the first iPhone to come with Apple Pencil support. What’s more, it supports the Apple Pencil on both its internal as well as external display. But there is a catch – it only supports the basic Apple Pencil (USB-C). This means that while one can scribble and sketch easily, there’s no pressure sensitivity and no support for double taps. One will also need a Type-C cable to charge it, as it cannot charge magnetically. Given the price and potential of the device, it would have been good to have Apple Pencil Pro support on it.
Only new iPhone with Titanium
Remember how Titanium was the coolest thing in premium phones a few years ago. Well, while it still remains a very premium material, it has largely disappeared from the smartphone scene, with even Apple seemingly moving on to other materials, with only the iPhone Air using Titanium last year. This time around, it is the iPhone Duo that carries the Titanium legacy forward. While the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max use “forged aluminum” and ceramic glass, the iPhone Duo comes with a main chassis made with grade 5 Titanium, and 3D-printed titanium is also used for the hinge cover.
The only iPhone camera with Smart Take
Although its cameras might not seem as formidable as those on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, the iPhone Duo has a slice of camera magic up its sleeve that no other iPhone has. This is Smart Take, which, with some AI magic, automatically works out when you are perfectly placed for a photograph and takes it without you needing to hit a capture button or prompt the device in any manner. It is supposed to work very well with individual and group selfies, and uses the rear cameras while showing you a preview on the cover display. While the feature is designed mainly for the fold form factor, it would be great to see it on “normal” iPhones too, although one might not be able to see previews!
A Type-C port placed under the cover display
In another case of rather unusual placement, the Type-C port of the iPhone Duo is actually placed on the base of the cover display or the upper panel. In many foldables, the charging port is placed on the lower panel, so that the phone can be opened without moving the charging cable. That is clearly not going to be possible on the iPhone Duo.
The status bar is closed…and is now a circle
The move to a foldable form factor has led to a redesign of some UI elements on the iPhone Duo. Perhaps the most surprising of these is the status bar. Until now seen in the top right corner, and displaying signal strength, Wi-Fi, and battery, it has now been changed to a circle, with the battery life and signal strength being on the circumference and Wi-Fi being at the center. It is not really as intuitive as its predecessor, but we guess users will get the hang of it.
No Pro controls in the camera
The iPhone Duo comes with two 48-megapixel cameras on the back – a new Fusion Main camera, and the same ultrawide that is on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. But while these pack in a lot of features such as three photographic styles, smart focus tracking, next-generation portraits, macro photography and more, the iPhone Duo’s camera app does not come with the Pro Controls seen on the 18 Pro and Pro Max, which let users play around with shutter speed, white balance, and aperture. This l is a bit of a pity, especially given the vast viewfinder the open Duo can serve up. But well, to be fair, this was never meant to be a camera phone.

Why this break has come at the worst time for De Zerbi & Spurs
- Published
Big spending always means big ambitions, but shelling out so much money on so many players the way Tottenham did this summer produces problems for any manager, and there is no quick fix.
If I was given a bundle of cash and asked to buy an outfit for a wedding, and I spent every penny of it on pink shoes, brown trousers, yellow shirt and orange tie, then I am sure you would all say that just doesn't work.
That is similar to what has happened at Spurs, where the board backed Roberto de Zerbi to the hilt with an outlay on new players of around £400m.
It was an almost unprecedented occurrence from a club that has always been renowned for being careful with investment in their team, and it sent expectations from many Spurs supporters through the roof.
The club had just avoided relegation two seasons running, finishing 17th twice in a row, but suddenly some fans were looking forward to a season competing for trophies and a top-four finish.
Their early results and performances have been disappointing, of course, but fans have to understand all the different factors that affect you when you are building a team - and it is ridiculous to suggest De Zerbi should be under pressure already, especially after he kept them up last season.
Let's give De Zerbi a chance
Finding a way for your club to win takes a manager in lots of different directions but they all involve time - on the grass or with social interaction with the players.
Not only has De Zerbi not been given that early time and opportunity, the majority of his players have now been taken away from him for another three weeks on international duty.
De Zerbi has many other issues to deal with, from Tottenham's poor home form to their inability to recover from conceding the first goal in games.
But his biggest challenge right now will be to fit those players who have just arrived in with the ones already at the club, into a unit that plays as a team and produces results so that the money the club has spent is justified.
All of this will take time, and patience, and all the kinds of little detail that supporters never see.
In my day, we were given time to create a team, and a family. For today's managers, time seems more limited than ever.
We are only five games into the season but there are already some Spurs fans who seem to think De Zerbi is the worst manager in the world, even though he has proved elsewhere how good he is.
I like De Zerbi's passion, and his approach. That will count for nothing if Spurs don't eventually produce, but let's give him a proper chance.
Combinations can take time to click
De Zerbi is a very passionate, straight-talking and ambitious manager who demands total commitment and backing from his board.
He has definitely had that at Spurs, which has left people wondering why he has made such a slow start.
But, before the season started, I thought his biggest challenge with so many different types of players arriving would be to put players together that fit as a team, not as a group of individuals.
I've been in that situation myself, for example in my early days at Stoke, when I signed Gerry Taggart and Michael Duberry to play together, two centre-halves who were complete opposites in relation to how they dealt with space on the pitch.
Gerry always wanted to drop off deeper because he wasn't overly quick, whereas Michael was fast and didn't ever worry about leaving space behind him.
I couldn't make Gerry any quicker, so common sense locked in and I had to convince Michael that he would have to take a step away from his main strengths of pace and power and work along Gerry's lines instead.
We spent a great deal of time on the grass in training until we finally got both working in unison. Both were different, but they understood the importance of working together as a pair for the benefit of the team. Even so, it still took time for it to click.
For any manager trying to build a successful team by developing combinations like that, the main thing you need is time with your players.
It can happen where a lot of new players settle in quickly at the same time and the team starts well - like Sunderland last season, or Brighton pretty much every year when they have lost several key players - but the difference is that while those clubs might also have changed their manager, they have not changed their identity.
Whether it is Sunderland and Brighton, or Brentford and Bournemouth, they all have a set identity so that when they look for a player to fit in a certain position, he has to have certain strengths.
When you don't have that solid base behind you, knowing exactly what is needed for certain positions, then bringing 10 new signings and all in one window like Spurs have just done, is going to create many issues for the coach.
Each player has a different personality and needs different amount of time to settle in, not only to a new environment but also to adjust to the demands of a very single-minded and demanding coach like De Zerbi is.
This settling-in period would have been covered if all the players had had a pre-season together, to get up to speed with their team-mates and what De Zerbi is asking of them, with his front-foot style of play.
That did not happen, and then even after the season started, Spurs were still adding to their squad.
Finding out who understands importance of teamwork
Coaching a team to be a team takes time, patience and a sound idea of the strengths of all your players.
Even when you have got that, trying to knit every player together takes time, and that is still De Zerbi's issue now.
For starters, he was always playing catch-up. Because all of his players were not in place when the season began, he missed the opportunity to assess his squad and impose his own principles on his top group of players.
He is a coach at heart and will want to be out on the training pitch conducting a system of work for the team, in and out of possession, that he believes will bring success to the club. This international break means he cannot do that with all his players.
Another issue De Zerbi has is that he has only been in the job a few months and he is still getting to know the existing players, not just the new ones, on and off the grass.
On it, you need to find out who understands the importance of teamwork and who doesn't, to iron out shortcomings and and see what works and what doesn't.
An example of when you realise something doesn't work was my experience at a club who had just bought a right-back from a top Premier League team, for more than £1m which was big money at the time.
We were struggling at the bottom of the league when I came in and needed a direction on the pitch that would bring better results.
During the defensive work we were doing in training, the full-back kept picking up what were, in my opinion, poor positions while covering from the opposite side to where the ball was.
I must have stopped the session on at least four occasions to remonstrate with him and give my view, but in the end the lad told me that this is not what he believed was right.
I immediately replaced him with a young full-back from the reserves who had been playing for the opposition in the drill, who understood his role was for the team, and not for himself.
Getting to know your players' characters too
Getting things right off the pitch is so important too, and that involves getting to know what your players' characters are like, finding out what they are like as individuals, and understanding their lifestyles.
I had three South American players at West Brom who were fantastic lads but we still had to look after them.
I spoke to my assistant, David Kemp, about taking them and their families out for dinner, and by spending time with them and their children and their wives I believe we won a degree of respect and trust that we would never have had if we had not bothered to meet them all together as a family.
You have to realise that players from different cultures can be used to living a different lifestyle, and this can make a difference to how quickly or how well they fit in.
I had one player in the Premier League whose routine I just could not believe, yet he became such an integral part of keeping a struggling club up.
His 24 hours typically played out like this - training from 8.30am to 1pm, home and bed until 9 or 10pm and then up and out again for dinner and then a casino or whatever, until the early hours.
Then he would be up for training, and he would go again.
It took me a few weeks to get to the bottom of this but, once I confronted him, he was adamant that his routine suited his lifestyle. He certainly knew the best restaurants around town, but his performances were always of the highest quality on the pitch.
Did he heed my advice? I think he did, but he was such a great lad, top player and a great team member that he wasn't a problem anyway.
He had been a bit isolated from the rest of the squad at first, but it just took him some time to integrate.
Again, finding out about him as an individual and making personal contact with him, was important, and it was something I always saw as vital with all my players.
Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

Alcaraz on late finishes, missing Sinner and Laver Cup return
- Published
Most players, after seeing their US Open title defence end at 3.34am after five intense sets, would not walk away smiling.
Carlos Alcaraz is not most players.
After his loss to Ben Shelton - a match that played out over a gruelling four hours and 28 minutes - the Spaniard was filmed walking down the Arthur Ashe tunnel with a huge grin on his face.
Alcaraz had been competing in his first tournament for over five months after suffering a wrist injury that left him in pain every day.
He did not defend his French Open title or compete at Wimbledon, and did not know if he would play in New York until a week before.
"The quarter-final was great - it was a gift for me," Alcaraz told BBC Sport before this week's Laver Cup in London.
"I suffered, but I enjoyed and that's why I smiled when I walked out of the court because I missed that feeling."
The match against Shelton was the latest finish in the tournament's history, and was one of several matches at Flushing Meadows to finish in the early hours.
Eventual champion Alexander Zverev finished past 1am in three of his first five matches, while Venus Williams finished her first-round match at 2am.
"I think it's too much," Alcaraz said of playing so late.
"The last match people stayed but if that match was played earlier, the court could have been packed.
"I would like to change the schedule a little with a maximum finish at 11pm or whatever would be better."
Alcaraz, 23, is one of a number of players to have missed large chunks of the season with injury.
Britain's Jack Draper has had a lengthy struggle with an arm injury, ultimately ending his season early to recover, while Alcaraz's rival Jannik Sinner missed the US Open with a knee injury.
The Spaniard said at the US Open that he will miss some tournaments in the future to allow himself to be "mentally and physically healthy".
He will compete for Team Europe in the Laver Cup at The O2 in London this week, between 25-27 September.
The team tournament pits Europe - captained by Yannick Noah - against a United States team overseen by Andre Agassi.
"When you have your team-mates, the best in the world, by your side, it's a weird feeling but it's beautiful," Alcaraz said.
"We played like our lives depend on it. That's why the Laver Cup is so good to watch as well."
Alcaraz and Italy's Sinner split eight Grand Slam titles between them from 2024 and 2025, establishing a generational rivalry in the process.
They have only met once this year because of injuries, with Sinner winning their sole meeting in the Monte Carlo Masters final to become world number one.
"I have text him not too much, but a few times when he has been winning everything, mostly at the beginning of the year," Alcaraz added.
"I miss him, I miss seeing him around, playing against him. He pushes me to be a better player.
"People will be waiting for those matches, so I think it's going to be better."
