By 2007, three sides of Brisbane Road had been rebuilt. By 2012, he had wiped out any debt and reportedly invested around £8m.
In 2013/14, Orient reached the League One play-off final and had a rare chance to reach the second tier - but they lost 4-3 on penalties to Rotherham at Wembley. Within two months he had sold the club to Italian businessman Francesco Becchetti.
For nine years, Hearn was away from football. There was no shortage of work for him to be getting on with elsewhere.
Then, in July 2023, Matchroom sponsored the home shirt of Brentwood Town, the Isthmian League North Division side based three miles up the road from their headquarters.
The following year, Hearn took a minority stake in the club - and earlier this summer, a five-year partnership and "a significant investment" was announced.
"The reason Barry came over initially was we were doing something for Saint Francis Hospice, which he is a patron of, and he sat next to me for a game," says chairman Jez Dickinson.
"It was an entertaining game and Barry said afterwards, 'I'm never going to sit next to you again, Jez! Every time the ball went into the box, you were going up for a header and elbowing me in the side!' Barry is very much about passion and wearing his heart on his sleeve, so that's probably where we connected.
"We had some lunches and, after about the third one, he asked me what I wanted. I said obviously I wanted him to get involved, but I wanted him to get involved because he wanted to get involved, not because I was asking him - and he said he'd do it."
Hearn's name is, naturally, the one that catches the eye, but Dickinson has been the driving force since taking over as chairman in May 2019.
Before his appointment, he says there was "no pathway for the youth into the first team", "the bar was like a 1970s pub", and "the ambition was just to stay in the league".
They installed a brand new 3G pitch in the summer of 2024, won the Isthmian North Division in 2024/25 and last season lost the play-off final, where a place in the National League South was on the line.
Brentwood now have a Centre of Excellence, with 250 boys and girls between the ages of six to 12 in it. "It's hollow if that isn't there," he says.
Dickinson has spent seven years building the foundations so far - and Hearn's involvement provides the chance to take the club to another level.
So how does the partnership work?
"I speak to him probably once a week, maybe twice. It depends what's happening," says Dickinson.
"He's hands-on in as much as he's available for anything we talk about. We'll sit down every couple of months, look at the financials, how we're getting on. He loves his numbers!
"Though he's a minority shareholder and he owns some of the club, he doesn't want to run it. He says: 'I look at you, Jez and you're stressed enough, I don't want any of that!'
"What he does is actually raise the bar, subconsciously, for what I want to achieve. We'll have a catch-up at Matchroom and it is quite inspiring and you come away thinking, 'let's go for it'.
"I don't underestimate that. It's probably 10 times as important as the financial stuff he does - not that I don't want the financial support as that's really important!
"He's a fantastic ambassador for the club as well as a sponsor and partner. I was speaking to a potential partner recently and they said they were interested because if he's committing to five years, he doesn't do things by halves and won't give up easily. It creates confidence with us and people looking to be partners."
Dickinson says Brentwood - who sit 18th in the Isthmian Premier Division after eight games - are currently averaging attendances of just under 700, with aims of reaching 1,000 this season.
There are plans for a 1,000-seater stand in place, but their purchase of the Brentwood Centre Arena needs to be completed before any progression can be made on that front.
Where does Dickinson think the partnership with Hearn and Matchroom will take Brentwood over these next five years?
"Barry decided on a five-year partnership to drive the club to the highest level of the pyramid possible. Hopefully after those five years, there'll be another five years!
"Realistically, if we're playing National League football in five years, that will be pretty successful for us. That would be excellent.
"It shows how much faith he and Matchroom have in us - it's down to us to deliver."

Wanderlog, Stippl, Polarsteps, and TripWaffle can turn flight, hotel, train, and other confirmation emails into organized travel plans. They differ in AI planning, maps, collaboration, trip tracking, alerts, and pricing, so the best choice depends on how you travel.
While traveling is something we all look forward to, the preparation behind it is sometimes quite grueling. Especially when you are doing everything by yourself. You book a flight on one site, a hotel on another, and a rental car through a different source, maybe through a referral link sent to you on WhatsApp. Traveling isn’t just about downloading the right apps before you board the flight. It is also about having all your important info at your disposal.
Just to know whether your hotel booking said 2 PM or 12 PM, you have to dig through your inbox. This is such a universal travel headache that an entire category of apps has been developed just to fix this. This list contains 4 AI travel planner apps that can convert your forwarded emails into a clean, day-by-day plan — flights, hotels, activities all lined up in order.
Table of Contents
Best AI Travel Planners
I went over the internet and actually dug through four of the more talked-about names in this space — Wanderlog, Stippl, Polarsteps, and the newer, scrappier TripWaffle. These apps were put to the test to see what they are genuinely good at, where they fall short, and which one deserves a spot on your phone before your next trip. Let us go through them one by one.
Wanderlog: The one that does almost everything, and does most of it well
For me, Wanderlog has become the default travel planner app, and for good reason. The email trick works two ways here. You can either forward your flight and hotel confirmations email to a special address Wanderlog gives you, or you can just link your Gmail account and let it quietly scan your inbox for bookings automatically on its own. The details show up straight in your itinerary, and it eliminates typing in flight numbers and copying and pasting confirmation codes.
However, there is one thing that makes Wanderlog stand out from a plain inbox-scanner. After your bookings are in, Wanderlog does not just leave them sitting there as a list. It pins everything onto an actual map. You can drag your stops, reorder your day, and there is a route optimizer that can rearrange your stops to save you driving time. Wanderlog also works like a shared Google Doc. Add your travel companions by email, and everyone will have access to edit the same trip at the same time, see live changes, and more. For a group trip, this is a great thing to have.
Community members also contribute travel guides right inside the app, so you have all the interesting information about a new city you have landed. Speaking of the cons, some users have reported that once a trip is created, there is sometimes no way to edit locations cleanly, forcing them to delete and redo it. Then there is the paywall issue, where features such as offline access and automatic Gmail scanning are locked behind the Pro subscription.
Download Wanderlog: Android | iOS
Stippl: The AI-first planner that tries to be your whole travel toolkit
Stippl leans hard into AI to get there. You just need to tell it what kind of trip you want (relaxed, adventurous, culture-heavy, offbeat) and it generates out a full day-by-day itinerary for your destination in under two minutes. If you already have a rough plan and just need a day filled in, you can use Stippl for that too. Simply tap a single day, and it will generate activities, restaurants, and transport suggestions just for that slot.
For emails, it works the same familiar way. You just need to forward your booking emails, and Stippl will pick up flights, hotels, trains, and restaurant reservations and feed them to your trip automatically. Everything also gets synced to the calendar, so your itinerary shows up right alongside your regular meetings and reminders. Stippl sets itself apart from the other three by the fact that it leans into being a memory-keeper as well as a travel planner.
There is a scratch map feature that adds every country you have already visited. It gives the feel of a passport stamp collection you can show off. It can also stitch your trip photos into an automatic travel reel or photobook once you are back home, no editing required from your end. You can also purchase an eSIM from the app. Coming to the con, the AI-powered itinerary generation and offline mode sit behind a paywall. Some users have reported having run into crashes, slow email imports, and the odd date or flight not saving correctly, especially with overnight flights or long layovers. Do keep that in mind.
Download: iOS
Polarsteps: Built for tracking your journey, now sneaking in planning too
Polarsteps is a bit different than the other three apps on this list. It did not start as a booking organizer at all but as a way to automatically track where you have already been and turn it into a beautiful, shareable map, eliminating manual check-in anywhere. You just have to carry your phone, and the app quietly traces your route in the background using WiFi and mobile data with constant GPS pings. That said, Polarsteps is also slowly gaining proper trip-planning tools, and the confirmation-email feature is now part of it. You can forward your hotel or flight booking to the app, and it pulls out the address and other details automatically.
Polarsteps has also introduced an AI-powered itinerary builder. There is also the ability to manually add flights by looking them up by airline and flight number, though you cannot book through the app. Since tracking is Polarsteps’ specialty, once your trip ends, it can turn the whole route into a digital travel book that you can order and keep.
Speaking of the shortcomings, compared to Wanderlog or Stippl, Polarsteps’ booking-import feature is newer and less complete. Polarsteps traditionally allows just one person to add content per trip. This means that if you are planning a group trip, Polarsteps, as a travel planner, won’t be a good option. It is meant for solo travelers and backpackers, who care as much about documenting the journey as planning it.
TripWaffle: The newcomer that’s focused on one job
TripWaffle may be the least-known name here, but that is one of the reasons why it makes it to this list. It’s built by a small, independent team (led by a single developer, Guy King, based in Australia). Instead of trying to be a do-everything travel app, it does one thing and focuses on, which is turning forwarded confirmation emails into a clean itinerary.
The setup is about as simple as it gets. You sign up and send your booking confirmations to it from providers. Using AI, TripWaffle reads the email, pulls out the dates, times, confirmation numbers, and addresses, and puts everything into a day-by-day timeline with time zones and connecting flights already planned out.
TripWaffle earns its keep in the details that it can keep. You get live flight tracking with real position updates, alerts about delays, gate changes, and a “flight reliability score,” which tells you how a specific flight number has historically performed. You receive a pre-trip checklist email covering visa requirements, weather, and packing suggestions just a day before your departure. TripWaffle is completely free with no ads, no Pro tier, and no upsell, which is something none of the apps in this list provide. You do not get crowd-sourced attraction guides or any AI-generated itineraries from scratch.
So which one should you actually download?
Honestly, it depends on what kind of traveler you are. I travel a lot, and most of my stay is outside my home country. I would suggest you try multiple apps and then decide on the one that you want to keep. For me, the above apps do the job, and you should definitely check them out and see if they fit your bill or not. Before you purchase a subscription to any of the paid apps, do go through the free version thoroughly and see if that is what you are looking for or not.

Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers.
The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison. About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US. Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next.
Human rights advocates and experts have warned for months that conditions at the Hotel Bamy – a run-down establishment that has served as a detention center for US deportees – are dangerous.
The US has sent at least 66 people from different African countries, Cuba and Brazil to Equatorial Guinea, which has received $7.5m as part of a deal to cooperate with the US deportation program. The Trump administration has pursued dozens of similar deals with countries to take in immigrants that the US cannot deport directly to their home countries, where judges have deemed they would face torture or persecution. In the past, the US government allowed those people to live and work in the US indefinitely.
The Trump administration, however, has sought instead to expel them to third countries where they have no ties, do not speak the local language and have no legal status – trapping them in limbo.
Advocates have been especially concerned for deportees sent to Equatorial Guinea, where the authoritarian government is notorious for human rights abuses, including torture, according to the US state department. Detainees held at Hotel Bamy have told the Guardian that armed guards keep watch over them 24/7, and that they have not been provided any medical care or even fresh clothes since arriving there. One of the detainees, who has a severe stomach hernia that requires visits to the hospital to drain his stomach due excessive fluid build-up, said he has been unable to see a doctor since arriving at Hotel Bamy.
Other detainees have managed to obtain medication for HIV, diabetes and other conditions via human rights lawyers, but remain fearful that access to medications will be arbitrarily cut off.
The two men who were tortured – Ahmed Soliman, 31, of Egypt, and Samson Birhane, 47, of Eritrea – have since been transferred to a prison in Malabo. Multiple witnesses recounted that the police officers shouted, “Where is the phone? Where is the phone!” as they beat the men, who had initially been accused of breaking a mirror at the hotel before they were pulled aside and arrested.
The beating, which occurred on 11 September, followed the release of a video first reported by Reuters showing conditions at the hotel and the violent behavior of the guards. The detainees had been using cellphones to communicate with lawyers and the media about the conditions they were facing.
In the video taken by Soliman, which lawyers shared with the Guardian, authorities are seen pointing guns at the deportees. A Cuban man asked the officer for the return of his confiscated mobile phone so he could contact relatives and a lawyer, but was ignored. When officers noticed Soliman filming the exchange with his mobile phone, multiple officers rushed at him and others standing nearby, pointed their guns, and told Soliman to remain on his knees with his hands up for 10-15 minutes.
In another video, Soliman was able to film authorities forcibly sending US deportees to Ethiopia, where they are likely to face torture. When deportees resisted going with authorities, officials gave them the option to “go back to their home country” or “go to prison”. At least 12 people have been returned by Equatorial Guinea to their home country, where they face persecution.
In May, human rights experts at the United Nations issued a rare public appeal asking Equatorial Guinea to halt plans to return deportees to their home countries and to comply with international human rights standards and avoid refoulement, or the expulsion of people to countries where they face persecution.
“This is a human rights catastrophe,” said Bella Mosselmans, director of the Global Strategic Litigation Council, who represents several of the deportees at Hotel Bamy. The US and Equatorial Guinea “must be held accountable for the atrocities they are committing”, she added.
In the week since Soliman and Birhane were beaten, police have also been searching the other detainees’ hotel rooms for cellphones, and have confiscated them. They have also barred lawyers from seeing the deportees. Authorities have told the 29 US deportees who remain at Hotel Bamy that they may never see Soliman or Birhane again, according to lawyers. One detainee who witnessed the beating said authorities treat them as if they are “blanks” who “don’t even exist”. Another detainee said an officer told her: “You will disappear from the earth. I am the law.”
Witnesses said they feared for the lives of Soliman and Birhane, who came to the US as children.
Soliman is a gay man from Egypt who had lived in Phoenix for most of his life. He had a green card, but lost status after he was convicted of drug possession. He served time for his crimes, and in October, a judge had determined he would face persecution and torture if he were to return to Egypt due to his sexuality.
Birhane had come to the US as a refugee when he was 13, but lost status after a conviction for robbery when he was in high school, in 1988. He was allowed to remain in the US after a judge ruled he faced torture in Eritrea, and had been regularly checking in with Immigration and Customs Enforcement as required.
Lawyers for the deportees shared copies of multiple emails they had sent to the US embassy in Equatorial Guinea alerting them to threats and violence against those detained at Hotel Bamy, but those messages have gone unanswered, they said. In July, amid a lawsuit challenging conditions for deportees, the African Commission issued an urgent interim order instructing the government of Equatorial Guinea to refrain from deporting, transferring, or relocating deportees against their will.
The US Department of Homeland Security did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.
A spokesperson for the state department said: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”
The agency did not respond to questions about whether it was aware of how Equatorial Guinea was treating US deportees, nor would it acknowledge whether any measures have been taken to intervene.
“As a general matter, we do not comment on the details of our private diplomatic communications with other governments,” the spokesperson said.

New York, Sep 23: On a day of high-stakes diplomacy on the global stage, President Donald Trump began his United Nations visit by telling a prominent US journalist, “You should not be here.”
“It's an honour to be here,” Trump said as he entered UN doors Tuesday ahead of his speech to the General Assembly and faced Kaitlan Collins of CNN, a frequent target of his ire.
“I'm surprised that CNN is here covering me. You should not be here covering me. You said you weren't going to cover me.”
As Collins noted later on air, CNN said nothing of the kind. The administration had banned CNN from White House grounds days earlier — along with MS NOW and Politico — and removed the network from pool duty. But CNN had been admitted into the UN as regularly credentialed media.
In any case, the tense moment was a stark reminder of how dramatically the bitter conflict between Trump and news outlets whose coverage he objects to as “fake news" has escalated in just a few days.
The current ban was the subject of a joint lawsuit filed Monday by the three outlets, asking a judge to find the administration's move unconstitutional.
The White House had until Tuesday to respond, and a hearing is scheduled for Wednesday afternoon.
Later Tuesday, Trump doubled down on his remarks and said negative coverage was dangerous for the country.
Asked whether he would allow the outlets back in if the court rules against the White House, he said, “Well, it probably will, because this is a judge who's not a particularly fair judge.”
He was referring to US District Judge Timothy Kelly, whom he appointed in 2017 and who ordered a CNN journalist's access restored in a similar case in 2018.
“So you never know,” Trump added. "I think we have a right to clean out fake news."
Trump's comments echoed others he's made since announcing the ban Friday. He has referred to “purposely negative stories,” but cited no specific stories — only generally “fake news” — as justification for the ban.
The ban and lawsuit are part of a long-running conflict between the president — especially in his second term — and media outlets he finds unfavourable.
Trump has responded in the courtroom, or with regulatory action. He's also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media, sometimes in strikingly personal terms — as he has with CNN's Collins, most recently in a speech at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner.
On air, after her exchange with Trump on Tuesday, Collins said: “We never said we were not going to cover the president. We will do our best to cover him each and every day.”
Tuesday began with an item missing from the daily press schedule issued by the White House: It did not list the US network pool, a departure from the norm.
CNN had been the designated pool network for the president's trip to New York, according to a schedule that divides coverage of certain events between the five major networks. But Trump's ban removed it from pool duties.
The other pool members agreed, in solidarity, not to replace CNN with another network on the coverage, and further to suspend all pool coverage until further notice.
Other news outlets also took steps in solidarity. The Associated Press joined a number of news organisations, including The Washington Post and The New York Times, in a decision not to publish photographs of presidential events Monday.
It remains to be seen how long both the ban and the collective media action will continue.
In speeches and meetings Tuesday, Trump was seen plenty by global audiences, thanks to UNTV — the official United Nations broadcast arm — and pool journalists covering other international leaders.
Meanwhile, a sign was spotted in the White House workspace: “I stand with AP, CNN, MS NOW, Politico.”
One longtime TV analyst says the lack of constant coverage will prove damaging to a spotlight-loving president — which may be one reason the standoff ultimately ends.
“This ban is not going to go on forever because he doesn't want that to happen, anymore than anybody else,” said Robert Thompson, director of Syracuse University's Bleier Centre for Television and Popular Culture.
In the short term, Thompson said, audiences won't feel the impact in a lasting way — after all, he noted, there are many ways people get news outside of network coverage.
“We are not going to be deprived of important civic information,” Thompson said, as might have happened years ago when outlets and options were fewer.
On the other hand, if viewers were interested in what Trump said as he inaugurated a helipad at the White House on Monday, they were out of luck: The sound of Trump's whirring, waiting helicopter drowned out his remarks. TV network crews usually work to capture clearer audio.
On a deeper level, Thompson said, news consumers will be impacted in a more serious way. He called out Trump's remarks labelling negative media coverage "dangerous" as troubling.
“These casual remarks, not even disguised, about what we always considered basic freedoms of the press ... that, I think, is a lot more serious,” he said.

Researchers at the BRIC-Rajiv Gandhi Centre for Biotechnology (BRIC-RGCB) here have developed a nanopore-based sensing technology that could pave the way for early detection and monitoring of biomarkers linked to neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
A research team led by Mahendran K.R., with contributions from PhD student Varsha Shaji and postdoctoral researcher Neethu Puthumadathil, designed the ‘self-assembling dual-diameter’ nanopore sensors that are capable of detecting such biomarkers with high sensitivity, the RGCB said in a statement.
The research published in Nature Nanotechnology represents a significant advance in nanoscience and biomolecular sensing, the RGCB said.
Indicators of diseases
Biomarkers are indicators of diseases that can be used for early detection. Nanopores are extremely small hollow structures. Detecting biomarkers at an early stage using conventional techniques, however, remains challenging as many of these biomarkers occur at extremely low concentrations.
“In the new approach, the researchers designed short peptides that form pores of varying sizes, providing a versatile platform for sensing biomolecules with different shapes and dimensions. The sensors distinguish disease and non-disease-associated forms of the biomarkers, even when they were present in complex protein mixtures at very low concentrations,” according to the RGCB.
In future, these sensors can be used to develop point-of-care devices that detect biomarkers associated with various diseases, such as cancer, directly from biological fluids, including blood, the institute said.
Major challenge
Early and accurate detection remains a major challenge in managing neurodegenerative diseases, BRIC-RGCB director Beena Pillai said. “The nanopore sensor platform demonstrates how advances in nanotechnology and biotechnology can come together to address a critical unmet need in health care,” she said.
The work was carried out in collaboration with Ulrich Kleinekathöfer’s group at Constructor University, Germany, and Krishnananda Chattopadhyay’s group at CSIR-Indian Institute of Chemical Biology (CSIR-IICB), Kolkata. The study was supported by grants from the Department of Biotechnology, the Department of Science and Technology, the Indian Council of Medical Research and the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.
See more information on the partnership between Netherlands and WHO.

Anthropologists and community leaders from Nagaland, a remote state in north-eastern India bordering Myanmar, have expressed joy and relief that human remains belonging to their ancestors that had been on display in a British museum for nearly a century are finally being returned.
On Monday, the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford announced that 39 pieces of human remains – including parts of skulls, a finger and a piece of skin with hair – belonging to the Naga tribes, will be returned to Nagaland after six years of negotiation between the community and the museum.
For the Nagas, the repatriation is not just about “bones and ancestral remains … It is about memory returning to where it belongs,” the community said in a statement.
“We are at peace,” said A Peihwang Wangsa, an Indigenous Konyak man involved in the repatriation negotiations. “Our forefathers are coming back.”
Wangsa, whose ancestors’ remains are among those being returned, added that the homecoming would be a moment of “mourning and celebration”.
NT Thamlong Phom, a Naga community leader from the Phom sub-tribe, said: “I feel joy, I feel blessed.
“Ever since the announcement was made, my entire community has felt happy,” he said. “Our ancestors’ spirit will have a final resting place.”
Thejao Vihienuo, who is also part of the repatriation discussions and went to Oxford in 2025, said he had been “angry and unhappy” to see the remains of his ancestors, which he said had been “taken in a most dubious manner”.
“It was displayed as if it was a trophy, but they silently spoke of the atrocities the British committed on our people,” he said.
The return caused “mixed feelings”, he said, but added: “We owe it to our ancestors to bring their remains back and put them to peaceful rest. And also to our younger generation to decolonise their minds and show that our children are not inferior to any white man.”
The Nagas are a transnational Indigenous group of tribes living in India’s north-east and parts of Myanmar, once associated with headhunting but now predominantly Christian.
The Pitt Rivers Museum, home to one of the world’s largest ethnological collections, has more than 6,500 Naga objects, 898 of which were on display. Most of the collection was “coercively” acquired by the colonial administrators James Philip Mills and John Henry Hutton.
The human remains were displayed at the museum for 80 years. In 2020, they were put into storage during a revamp aimed at addressing the institution’s colonial past and how exhibiting human remains “reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking” of other cultures.
The museum said in a statement: “Thirty-nine Naga ancestors will soon begin their journey home from Oxford to Nagaland.”
In November, a Naga delegation will visit Oxford for a handover ceremony and the remains are expected to arrive in Nagaland before the end of the year. They will be laid to rest in a traditional community ceremony in the state capital, Kohima.
The repatriation negotiations were led by representatives from all of the Naga tribes.
“It has been a journey of redemption,” said Prof Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist. “This shows that we are no longer victims of colonial violence. We embrace our roles as people who find redemption and healing by giving dignity and honour to a very violent past.”
The negotiations started in 2020, when Kikon wrote to the museum after reading “an article in the Guardian that they were doing an ethical review” of the collection. “They replied within 24 hours,” said Kikon.
That was just the beginning of a lengthy process that soon expanded into a wider community-led campaign.
The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a community peace group, assembled a team known as Recover, Restore and Decolonise, bringing together Naga volunteers from across the region to work on the repatriation effort.
“They travelled to villages and organised meetings to inform people about the remains,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a Naga anthropologist who worked closely with Kikon to lead the initiative, which he described as “open and transparent”.
“It was an intergenerational journey that brought together students, civil society, tribal leaders and the church,” said Longkumer, who teaches at Edinburgh University.
A Naga delegation, including tribal leaders, visited Oxford in 2025 to officially register a claim to the remains.
“I had never known our ancestral human remains had been taken away like that,” said Wangsa. “I felt angry when I saw them.”
Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum and a professor of museum studies and ethics at Oxford University, said the museum was completing paperwork to enable the return of the remains.
“We will then start working towards the ceremonial aspects so we can have everything ready,” she said. “In our experience, handover ceremonies can be very emotional.”

A young boy who was allegedly shot at a home in Sydney’s north-west earlier this week has died.
Police said that the boy, who had been in a critical condition since being found with a gunshot wound at a unit in Norwest on Monday, died in hospital at about 8pm on Thursday.
Police had been called to the unit in Fairway Drive at about 5pm on Monday after reports of a shooting.
Officers found the 11-year-old boy had sustained a gunshot wound to his face and neck.
He was treated at the scene by NSW Ambulance paramedics before being taken to at Westmead Children’s hospital in a critical condition.
Five other people who were in the home at the time of the incident were not injured.
Three men, all aged 18, were arrested. Two were taken to The Hills police station and later released pending further inquiries.
One of the men, Isaac Bechara, was charged with concealing a serious indictable offence, while two of the other men were arrested and released pending further inquiries.
He appeared at Blacktown local court on Tuesday morning , where he made no application for bail, which was refused.
Det Supt Naomi Moore told reporters on Tuesday afternoon that police were “aware” of the unit where the shooting had occurred and had “engaged with the occupants previously”.
“This shooting at this stage does not appear to be linked directly to current conflicts however a number of individuals who were inside the unit at the time are well known to NSW police,” she said. “Their association with organised crime is being considered by investigators.”
Police said the investigation was continuing.

Essex cricketer Das charged with two counts of rape
- Published
Essex cricketer Robin Das has been charged with two counts of rape.
The 24-year-old will appear at Inner London Crown Court on Friday, 9 October after he was charged on 23 July.
Das was arrested on 27 August last year following reports of a woman being raped in Brixton in March 2024.
The Metropolitan Police said in a statement: "Robin Das of Queens Road, Waltham Forest, was charged on 23 July 2026 with two counts of rape.
"The charges follow his arrest on 27 August 2025 following reports of a woman being raped in Brixton on 30 March 2024. The woman continues to be supported by specialist officers."
Das, a top-order batter, has made 60 appearances for Essex and last appeared for the club in a One-Day Cup match against Middlesex on 21 July, his only senior appearance in the 2026 season.
Essex have confirmed that he has been suspended since his arrest, two days after his last appearance for the club.
Essex said in a statement: "Essex County Cricket Club can confirm that a male member of the playing staff, currently under contract with the club, recently appeared in court in relation to an incident that took place outside club activities.
"Throughout, the club has remained in contact with the ECB, PCA, the Cricket Regulator and the player with regard to the matter, which included an immediate and ongoing suspension. The club will continue to follow all appropriate legal processes and guidance.
"As a club we have strict safeguarding and HR procedures in place, and all employees of Essex County Cricket Club are required to meet the highest standards of professional conduct at all times.
"As legal proceedings are in progress, the club are unable to make any further comment at this time."
Das made his debut for Essex in 2020 and has made nine first-class appearances for the county, along with playing 29 games in 50-over cricket and 24 matches in T20s during his career. Two of the T20 appearances were for Dhaka Dominators in the Bangladesh Premier League.

“Treatable conditions can masquerade as Alzheimer’s disease, including autoimmune disorders and thyroid inflammation,” said Ennapadam S. Krishnamoorthy, founder and behavioural neurologist and neuropsychiatrist, Buddhi Clinic, stressing the importance of a specific diagnosis in people presenting with cognitive symptoms.
He was speaking at The Hindu Wellness Series webinar on Alzheimer’s dementia and the promise of brain stimulation, held on Sunday by The Hindu in association with Buddhi Clinic, marking World Alzheimer’s Day.
Dr. Krishnamoorthy said a detailed, case-based assessment was important to distinguish Alzheimer’s disease from other conditions that can cause cognitive symptoms and may be treatable. He also stressed the need to tailor care to the individual, noting that some medications may offer limited benefits or cause harm in certain patients. He said non-pharmacological interventions also had an important role in dementia care.
Vivek Misra, senior consultant – Neuromodulation and Clinical Neurosciences, Buddhi Clinic, discussed the potential of non-invasive brain stimulation as part of dementia care. The technique uses external stimulation to modulate activity in specific areas of the brain. “It does not require sedation or seizure induction and can be done in an outpatient setting,” Mr. Misra said.
He said brain stimulation should not be viewed as a standalone treatment, but as one component of a broader, precision-based approach to dementia care, with interventions tailored to the individual’s clinical profile and needs.
The session was moderated by Athira Elssa Johnson, Senior Reporter, The Hindu.

Sixty-three per cent of the 3,253 Water Supply Schemes (WSS) taken up under the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) in Jammu and Kashmir are non-operational despite expenditure of around Rs 7,000 crore, a House Committee of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly has found, raising serious questions over planning, execution, procurement, quality control and monitoring of the flagship rural drinking-water programme.
The findings are contained in the voluminous 1253-page report of the House Committee constituted to examine alleged irregularities in the implementation of JJM in the Union Territory. The report was laid before the Legislative Assembly on September 21 by committee chairman Justice (Retd) Hasnain Masoodi. The committee was constituted on April 9, 2025, to examine alleged irregularities in implementation of the Mission.
“The result is that 63 per cent of 3253 WSS involving an expenditure of Rs. 7000.00 crore are non-operational,” the report states. It adds that even the 37 percent of schemes claimed by the Jal Shakti Department to be functional were “not fully operational”.
The committee said the institutional mechanism established to oversee JJM had failed to discharge its responsibilities effectively, resulting in inadequate planning, supervision and monitoring.
“The House Committee is of the considered view that there has been complete abdication of authority,” the report said, referring to the Apex Level Committee, Executive Committee and District Level Committees.
The panel attributed the failure to achieve the Mission’s objectives within the stipulated timeframe to what it described as “gross negligence” on the part of these committees and the officers who manned them.
According to the report, 37 per cent of schemes claimed by the Jal Shakti Department to be functional were also “not fully operational” in several cases.
The committee also questioned official figures relating to Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTCs), saying discrepancies emerged between departmental records and ground conditions during field inspections.
The panel said records supplied to it contained what it described as “false claims” regarding the number of FHTCs provided in habitations and the number of habitations covered.
“On spot visits, the House Committee came to know that far less than the number of FHTC indicated in the record, have actually been provided benefit of the Safe and Adequate Drinking Water of the prescribed quality,” the report said.
The committee also questioned the department’s claim that 81 per cent of rural households in J&K had tap-water connections as of March 2025, saying the figures required physical verification.
The House Committee was headed by Justice (Retd) Hasnain Masoodi. Its 13 members were Mohammad Yousuf Tarigami, Ali Mohammad Dar, Altaf Ahmad Wani, Aijaz Ahmad Jan, Rajiv Jasrotia, Ranbir Singh Pathania, Tanvir Sadiq, Javaid Riyaz Bedar, Muzaffar Iqbal Khan, Rafiq Ahmad Naik, Arjun Singh Raju and Iftikar Ahmad.
The committee subsequently undertook field inspections to assess the implementation of JJM works. It inspected schemes in Rajouri and Poonch, among other areas, before finalising its findings.
One of the major concerns highlighted by the committee was the failure to establish the sustainability and adequacy of water sources before executing schemes.
The panel found instances where expenditure had been incurred on pumping systems, storage facilities, transmission networks and distribution infrastructure without adequately establishing the viability of the underlying water source.
In WSS Shirpora Bangil, the committee found high sulphur and iron content in the source and said this had rendered the scheme useless. It termed the expenditure “unfruitful” and directed fresh testing of the source.
“Providing of FHTC is immaterial in absence of safe and viable source,” the committee observed.
The report also cited schemes affected by land and source disputes. These included WSS Dachnipora in Pahalgam, WSS Lelhara, WSS Syed Mantaqi Khrew and WSS Greenland Wuyan. In WSS Bugam Dooniwari, the committee said Rs 10 crore had been spent without benefiting the targeted population because of a source dispute.
The committee has also scrutinised the decision to shift from GI pipes to HDPE pipes during JJM implementation.
It noted that the Jal Shakti Department, Jammu, authorised Executive Engineers in April 2023 to use HDPE pipes instead of GI pipes depending on site feasibility. However, an earlier technical committee had recommended modification of DPRs before the change.
The panel said the national-level communications cited in support of the shift did not mandate compulsory replacement of GI pipes with HDPE pipes and questioned why the decision was taken several years after the Mission’s launch.
It said the decision had significant financial and operational implications and “ought to have been taken by the Apex Level Committee”.
The report also records allegations made by retired IAS officer Ashok Parmar concerning procurement orders and changes in pipe specifications. Parmar alleged that procurement orders worth Rs 4,000 crore were placed without approval and that HDPE pipes were ordered in violation of approved DPRs. The committee recorded these as allegations and evidence presented before it, rather than independently establishing every allegation.
The committee separately examined tube-well projects and raised concerns over tendering, technical qualifications, quality assurance and functionality.
It said some tube wells had failed to meet desired standards and noted submissions that water from certain sources was unsuitable for human consumption. The committee observed that quality-assurance mechanisms appeared to have been inadequately enforced.
The panel also questioned the effectiveness of third-party monitoring agencies hired for audit and inspection of JJM works. It said field observations regarding faulty execution indicated that such agencies had failed to discharge their obligations adequately despite being paid for monitoring and audit work.
The committee has recommended constitution of a High-Level Committee to conduct a comprehensive audit of JJM and retrofitting schemes, including procurement of DI, GI and HDPE pipes and execution of civil works.
It has recommended identifying officers and engineers responsible for irregularities and initiating action against those found responsible under applicable rules.
The panel has also called for scrutiny of officers who served on the Apex Level, Executive and District Level Committees from their constitution until March 31, 2025, with their actions and omissions examined against the respective terms of reference.
A comprehensive technical, financial and administrative review of tube-well projects has also been recommended, covering functionality, water quality, payments released, pending liabilities and possible additional expenditure.
The committee said the problems identified were not confined to isolated technical failures but indicated “possible systemic deficiencies in planning, procurement, quality control, contract administration and project oversight”.
Its central finding is that the success of JJM cannot be measured merely through construction figures or tap connections recorded in official databases. The ultimate test, the committee said, is whether households are actually receiving safe and adequate drinking water.

A video showing a large crowd gathered on a road and a flyover is being widely shared on social media, claiming that it shows the crowd at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event in Indore on 19 September 2026 (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video shows people gathered for Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event held on 19 September 2026 in Indore, Madhya Pradesh.
Fact: The viral video is old and unrelated to Rahul Gandhi’s event. It shows a rally organised in Indore on 9 August 2026 to mark World Tribal Day. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to a Facebook post by Vinoddj Vlog posted on 10 August 2026. The account confirmed in the comments that the video was recorded during the Adivasi Diwas (World Tribal Day) celebrations in Indore. Further, we found a YouTube video uploaded on 9 August 2026 by @DineshSolanki_indori, which features the same truck and location seen in the viral video. This video also identified the visuals as being from the World Tribal Day celebrations in Indore. This confirms that the video predates Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event, which was held in Indore on 19 September 2026.
Further, we also found similar visuals shared by Lokesh Mujalda, president of Jai Adivasi Yuva Shakti (JAYS), on Instagram on 9 August 2026. The post stated that a large number of people had gathered in Indore for World Tribal Day celebrations.
We identified the location seen in the viral video as Bhanwarkuan Square in Indore, which was one of the locations along the route of the World Tribal Day procession. A comparison between both can be seen below.
Media also reported that thousands of people participated in the World tribal day procession that took place in Indore (here, here). Actual visuals showing the ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event can be seen here and here.
To sum up, an old video of the World Tribal Day rally is being shared as visuals of crowd at Rahul
Gandhi’s Indore event.

Former Maine Governor Paul LePage says that federal immigration authorities were seeking to deport his son’s father-in-law, and he has called on officials to stop the removal.
LePage, a staunch conservative running for a seat in the U.S. House of Representatives, has made border policy a central focus of his political campaign.
However, as reported by The Washington Post, the candidate expressed strong objection to the federal action taken against his relative, who he said resides legally in the United States.
“That’s not right,” LePage said. “He has a work permit. He should be allowed to stay.”
LePage said that his relative faces deportation “because he came from a country that’s not the liking to certain people in Washington.”
The situation follows an increase in federal enforcement operations across Maine. In January, the Trump administration sent additional Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to the state — those tensions peaked six months later, in July, when an ICE agent shot and killed a man in Biddeford.
The Department of Homeland Security stated that agents fired after the victim, a 25-year-old Colombian national named Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, attempted to flee in his car during a targeted enforcement operation, as reported by the Associated Press.
Federal officials alleged that the driver posed a threat to public safety when officers confronted him. However, lawmakers and immigrant advocacy groups quickly challenged that account, noting that Durán Guerrero held a valid work permit and was not the intended target of the arrest warrant.
Witness accounts and local security footage showed federal officers surrounding the vehicle before gunshots were fired at the intersection of Pool and Hill streets. The fatal encounter sparked protests across southern Maine and prompted calls for an independent federal investigation into the agency’s use of force.
According to tracking by The New York Times, Durán Guerrero’s death came less than a week after federal agents in Houston fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in his car, bringing the count of people shot at by officers involved in the federal deportation campaign to 23. Six people, including three U.S. citizens, have been killed in these incidents, almost all of which involved agents opening fire on occupants inside vehicles.
Law enforcement experts noted that firing into vehicles deviates from standard protocols and federal rules, which state officers should only use deadly force when facing an imminent threat of death or serious injury. Although the government has charged multiple drivers with assaulting federal officers, seven of the 13 people charged following such shootings have had their cases dismissed in court.
Throughout his political career, LePage has consistently advocated strict law enforcement protocols and endorsed local Maine agencies working in coordination with federal immigration authorities.

A 19-year-old college wrestler from California has fallen to his death while hiking near a waterfall in Yosemite National Park, according to reports.
Ryan George’s wrestling team at Santa Rosa Junior College, about an hour’s drive northwest of San Francisco, announced the tragic news in a Facebook post Monday.
“This past weekend we received the tragic news that Ryan passed away at Yosemite National Park, following an accident,” the team wrote.
The Press Democrat, a local newspaper, reported that George was hiking with friends near Illilouette Falls on Sunday when he slipped and fell to his death. The waterfall is roughly 370 feet tall and flows all year long.
“If you knew Ryan, you know he was one of the most genuine, positive people you could ever meet,” his wrestling team said. “He had this way of lighting up a room, making you feel welcome, and bringing out the best in everyone around him. Always smiling, always encouraging, always full of life.”
Details surrounding George’s death, such as what led to the fall and the aftermath, are unknown. The Independent has reached out to the National Park Service and the Mariposa County Sheriff’s Office for comment.
George got into wrestling during his freshman year of high school. He was a football player at Montgomery High School in Santa Rosa and was too heavy to join the wrestling team. But that didn’t stop him.
“He worked really, really hard and he got his weight down,” Ian Hesz, who was George’s high school wrestling coach, told The Press Democrat.
George won an individual North Bay League title at Montgomery High, and then earned All-American honors last wrestling season as a freshman at Santa Rosa Junior College, according to the outlet. On Friday, just days before his death, George earned second place at the Dave Pacheco Invitational meet at Sacramento City College.
“It was good watching him find what he loved,” George’s older sister, Jaida, told The Press Democrat. “He was always playing and wrestling when he was a kid.”
The siblings’ father died when George was a baby and their mother died just weeks ago, according to the outlet.
In a GoFundMe page created on behalf of Jaida, a loved one wrote, “In July, we lost our Beloved Taji and now, just 2 months later, her daughter Jaida is facing another heartbreaking loss with the passing of her Little Brother Ryan Jr. this past Sunday.”
“She is grieving the loss of two people she loves deeply, while also facing all that comes with losing family members so unexpectedly, on top of it all being a New Mommy to her precious Son who is only 2 months old,” read the fundraising page, which generated more than $9,000 in donations by Wednesday.

Trump offers warm welcome as China's Xi arrives for US visit
- Published
US President Donald Trump has greeted his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping with a military flyover and 100ft (30m) red carpet to kick off their three-day summit in Washington.
In a rare move, Trump welcomed Xi's entourage at the airport as the US Air Force band marched on the tarmac and US and Chinese flags flew.
Trump and First Lady Melania Trump welcomed Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday evening in Maryland.
The high-stakes visit - Xi's first trip to Washington since 2015 - is expected to include closed-door meetings, a state dinner, and plenty to discuss, from AI, to the Iran war and Taiwan, and an extended trade truce.
The leader of China's Communist Party touched down in an Air China plane at 17:39 local time (22:39 BST). The colour and honour guard marched up to the aircraft and stood on both sides of the red carpet as two limos pulled up.
Xi and Peng exited their plane and the two couples shook hands. They spoke briefly before walking side by side down the red carpet and posing for photos.
Two B-1s flew over as the Army Air Force Band played the US national anthem. The supersonic aircraft are a key part of the US's combat arsenal.
After exchanging pleasantries, the two couples departed in separate vehicles to Washington.
This is the first time since 1962 that a US president has personally welcomed a foreign leader at the base, signalling the importance that Trump is giving this visit.
In 1962, then-President John F Kennedy greeted British PM Harold Macmillan.
Also on Wednesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the US and China will extend their trade truce to January. The agreement, which saw Trump lower tariff rates on some goods in exchange for Xi loosening restrictions on rare earth minerals, was set to expire 10 November.
Bessent, who spoke after meeting Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, said the two discussed if there can eventually be a more substantive trade deal between the two countries.
In a written statement published by China's state news agency Xinhua, Xi said both China and the US are "great nations, and their people are great people".
"The two countries should be partners rather than rivals," he said.
Melania Trump has said she has been involved intimately with the planning of the itinerary. She told Fox News that Trump made the decision to personally greet Xi himself at the airport "because they have a great relationship".
Xi is accompanied on the visit by Cai Qi, a member of the party's Politburo Standing Committee who's widely seen as his right-hand man, vice premier He Lifeng, foreign minister Wang Yi, as well as other delegates and ambassadors from Beijing.
"Realising the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can fully coexist, reinforce each other and benefit the world," Xi said in the statement carried by Xinhua, where he also expressed confident that the visit would "yield fruitful results".
It is unclear if Xi has brought any business executives with him. Bringing Chinese firms to the US may also raise questions about Chinese business practices, subsidies and overcapacity, all of which may draw more fire and questions than Xi or his party would like.
During Trump's visit to Beijing in May, he was accompanied by a group of tech executives from some of the largest US firms, including Apple's Tim Cook, Tesla's Elon Musk and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
Leaders of US AI companies are slated to attend the lavish state dinner set for Thursday. Xi's visit will end on Friday.
Trump has dismissed recent warnings about the potential dangers of AI from within the industry as a "hoax" and both countries are racing to try to achieve dominance in the sector.
Trump will aim to achieve other deals around trade and tariffs – like lowering Chinese tariffs on American products, increasing imports of Chinese rare earth minerals, and increasing exports of US agricultural products, according to David Firestein of the Bush China Foundation.
But China appears have reneged on promises to buy more American agricultural products and to sell more rare earth minerals to the US.
Firestein expects Xi to encourage Trump to further stall - or kill - a congressionally approved $14bn (£10.5bn)-arms sale to Taiwan and deepen US-China trade integration.
These are the same US-China issues for the ages, he said, but, this time, "there seems to be a greater degree of, let's say, stability within the relationship, or less volatility relative to where we were last year in 2025".
Xi's visit comes at a time when American attitudes towards China appear to be warming.
A recent poll by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs indicated that 41% of Americans see China's territorial ambitions as a threat to the US. That number is down from 52% in 2022.
More than half of Americans - 57% - believe the US should cooperate and engage with Beijing. Notably, that statistic cuts across the US political spectrum.
Of Republicans who do not identify as Maga, 57% favour cooperation, as do most Democrats, both moderate and liberal.
However most of Trump's loyal base - 63% - favour limiting US relations with China, putting them at odds with his warm welcome of Xi.
Aside from the arrival ceremonies at the White House, Melania Trump has also planned a visit to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art to show her Chinese counterpart the cultural connections between the two countries.
The landmark visit will end on a historical note at the National Archives building where the couples will view important records including those of "significant to the American and Chinese relationship," the White House has said.

It is sometimes called "momnesia," "mommy brain," "pregnancy brain" or "baby brain" — the forgetfulness, mental fogginess and cognitive changes that many women may experience during pregnancy. For instance, a woman might walk into the kitchen and forget why she did, or perhaps misplace her car keys in the bathroom.
Scientists know it is a real biological phenomenon, and now have found a possible explanation, identifying a specific brain circuit that becomes disrupted under the sustained high levels of oestrogen that accompany pregnancy.
They conducted experiments using laboratory mice designed to mimic the sustained elevated oestrogen experienced during pregnancy, finding that this led to temporary memory impairment in the animals without mood changes.
Underlying this in the mice, they found, was how the high oestrogen affected a neuronal pathway between two brain structures — the hypothalamus, which acts as a control center and integrative hub, and the hippocampus, which is central to memory formation.
High oestrogen increased the activity of hypothalamus neurons, which in turn suppressed activity in the hippocampus and impaired memory, they found.
"Momnesia" becomes most evident in late pregnancy and may continue into the postpartum period but usually dissipates after childbirth. Short-term and long-term memory can be affected, including spatial, social and verbal memory such as having difficulty remembering names or words, or struggling to recall familiar information.
"It is not serious or medically disabling, although it does affect daily functioning and confidence," said Zheng Sun, a professor of medicine at Baylor College of Medicine specialising in endocrinology and molecular biology and one of the leaders of the study published in the journal Science Bulletin.
"Typical examples include forgetting why one entered a room, misplacing an item, losing the thread of a conversation or needing reminders for appointments. It is widespread. About 80% of pregnant women notice those changes, but that figure largely reflects self-report and subjective experience rather than objective testing," Dr. Sun said.
The findings suggest that the phenomenon does not represent a general decline in cognitive ability.
"The important point is that pregnancy does not simply make someone 'less intelligent.' The effects appear to be more subtle and specific to certain cognitive tasks," said Yanlin He, director of the Brain Glycemic and Metabolism Control Laboratory at Louisiana State University's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and another of the study leaders.
Mouse experiments
The mouse experiments shed light on what is happening in the brain. Oestrogen is a hormone that governs a woman's pregnancy, menstrual cycle and puberty, spurring physical changes that help the body support the fetus, foster fetal development and prepare for childbirth. Its levels increase during pregnancy, peaking in the third trimester.
The researchers found that a protein called "oestrogen receptor alpha" transmits estrogen's signals into cells in the hypothalamus.
This region has abundant brain cells called GABAergic neurons that typically transmit calming signals to other parts of the brain. The study showed that high oestrogen levels over-activate the inhibitory signals by these neurons in the mice, and this directly affected the hippocampus.
The researchers performed memory tests including object and location recognition, finding impairment in mice given high oestrogen levels compared to those that were not.
When the researchers experimentally turned off the hypothalamus-to-hippocampus neuronal pathway, the mice no longer experienced oestrogen-induced memory problems. But experimentally activating the same pathway impaired memory in the mice, even without higher amounts of oestrogen present.
"When we genetically removed estrogen receptors from these hypothalamic neurons, estrogen-induced and pregnancy-induced memory problems in mice were also reversed. We suspect that a similar circuit may play a similar role in humans, although you cannot do this type of invasive study directly in humans," Dr. Sun said.
The researchers complemented the mouse experiments with a study assessing memory performance in 70 women, including some across different stages of pregnancy and some who were not pregnant, using tests of long-term, short-term and working memory. These tests revealed memory impairments that manifested during late pregnancy, correlating with high circulating oestrogen levels.
"Importantly, higher circulating estrogen levels were associated with poorer performance on several memory-related measures even after accounting for other potential contributing factors. This provides human evidence consistent with the mechanism we identified in mice," Dr. He said.
"However, we should emphasise that we did not directly manipulate or measure this specific neural circuit in pregnant women. Therefore, the human findings support the hypothesis but do not establish the same level of causality as the mouse experiments," Dr. He said.

Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious
- Published
An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage.
That the match is even taking place had been in doubt - one side had to vote on a motion confirming whether or not they would participate amid significant opposition from fans, pundits and politicians.
But the vote confirmed the fixture would go ahead, and now the Republic of Ireland will travel to Debrecen, Hungary, for a Uefa Nations League 'away' match against Israel, played against a backdrop of ongoing and increasingly volatile disagreement between the two countries about Israel's military offensive in Gaza.
And on 4 October, the Republic will face the same opponents in a 'home' match in Backa Topola - a small town in Serbia.
No tickets have been sold to Irish fans for either fixture, and Irish public broadcaster RTE will air a stripped-back version of match coverage, with no commentators, pundits, or half-time analysis.
So how did a Uefa Nations League match become one of the most contentious fixtures in football?
Venue changes have not quietened protests
As soon as the Republic of Ireland were placed with Israel - plus Austria and Kosovo - at the Nations League draw in February, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) faced calls from some to boycott the matches because of Israel's military action in Gaza.
The FAI eventually took a vote of its delegates in July, in which 75 members voted to play the matches and 32 voted to boycott.
Not playing the matches could have harmed Irish football in the long-run, the FAI said, amid the possibility of Uefa sanctions for refusing to fulfil the fixtures and the potential loss of millions of euros in income.
As well as curtailing its coverage, RTE will not take advertising or sponsorship income from the matches, saying it will only "meet its contractual obligations" to broadcast the fixtures.
No tickets are being sold to Irish fans for either the 'home' or 'away' matches, with a small allocation available for Israeli fans for the first fixture, which has been the case at multiple previous Israel home games held in Hungary.
Hungary has been deemed a suitable host nation for Israel matches because the two nations enjoy stronger diplomatic ties than those between Israel and many other European nations, and it has been willing to provide the necessary policing and security arrangements for matches to operate smoothly.
The FAI decided in the summer to play its 'home' fixture against Israel at a neutral stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil".
Reports have claimed the FAI was concerned protests could prevent the match from taking place in Dublin.
The FAI gave no official reason for the selection of Backa Topola, but choosing a venue in Serbia - in a town so remote - in theory renders security management easier and reduces the possibility of protest.
In 2025, Serbian foreign minister Marko Duric described Israel as one of Serbia's "closest friends and strategic partners". Serbia has also purchased military equipment, including drones and missiles, from Israel in recent years.
The decision to play in neutral stadiums has not curtailed opposition.
Fans of various Irish clubs have demonstrated against the matches during domestic fixtures in recent weeks, and on Monday more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine group urging a boycott. The signatories include boxer Tyrone McKenna and former European champion athlete Ciara Mageean.
FAI CEO David Courrell said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the teams to be kept apart in future draws, director of football John Martin described the games as a "very uncomfortable situation for everyone". Manager Heimer Hallgrimsson, meanwhile, said playing the match did not constitute legitimisation of Israel's "genocide".
"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," Hallgrimmson said. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."
In response, the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity".
The Republic of Ireland faced Israel in Women's EuroBasket qualifiers last autumn and earlier this year after "extensive deliberations".
Irish support for Palestinians is long-standing
The Republic of Ireland has been among the European countries to most keenly show support for Palestinians since the start of Israel's military offensive in Gaza in October 2023.
More than 73,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations (UN).
In May 2024, alongside Spain and Norway, Ireland officially recognised a Palestinian state, and later that year joined South Africa's Gaza genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice.
The country has also boycotted Eurovision since 2025 because of Israel's ongoing participation in the song contest, was the first EU country to ban goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and has issued travel bans for Israeli government ministers.
On Monday, Irish foreign minister Helen McEntee said: "Ireland's view is clear - international law is being breached. We are seeing an attempt to erase a population."
Israel has criticised Ireland's standpoint and claims its actions in Gaza constitute self-defence, after the armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.
Last summer a UN commission of inquiry found that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, and this year a further investigation determined that the country has deliberately targeted children with military force, resulting in genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations it has committed genocide.
The Republic of Ireland is not the only nation to have expressed reluctance to face Israel in international football.
In 2024, Belgium refused to host Israel on home soil, and the match was held instead in Debrecen.
The president of the Norwegian Football Association, Lise Klaveness, made a public statement last year saying Israel should be suspended from European competitions, and Turkey also called for Israel to be banned.
BBC Sport reported last autumn that Uefa executives were considering a vote on whether to ban Israel, under pressure from representatives from a number of nations.
But any plan to hold a vote was pulled when the first phase of a ceasefire was announced last October.

A planned executive order that would have greatly enhanced White House influence over grants at the National Institutes of Health is “looking dead,” according to one person familiar with the decision and Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine).
On Tuesday, Collins, the Appropriations Committee chair, sent a letter to Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, decrying the White House plan to establish a commission of political appointees, including Vought, with veto power over grant awards. The tempering of the executive order was first reported by Semafor.
“I urge you not to move forward with this proposal, which would undermine … the Federal government’s objective of funding biomedical research projects based on scientific merit and value rather than political ideology,” Collins wrote in the letter.
Her concern was shared by several other lawmakers, who released their own statements earlier this week. By Wednesday, some of those same officials were celebrating the Trump administration’s seeming reversal.
“It shouldn’t take public outcry to prevent President Trump and Russ Vought from laying waste to the NIH and defunding lifesaving research because they think it’s ‘woke’ or want to extort a university,” Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.), vice chair of the Senate Appropriations committee, said in a statement.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
The idea for the executive order came out of a widely reported Oval Office meeting Friday, when Vought accused the NIH of funding projects that do not comport with the goals of the Trump administration, The Washington Post reported. President Trump seemed to support the idea of moving NIH grants more firmly under political control in part so that he could further target research funding for Harvard University, according to Politico.
It was just the latest attempt by OMB to bring science funding more tightly under agency control by taking a more hands-on approach. Many of those efforts have been challenged by Congress, however. Last year, Vought mandated that the NIH fund grants in their entirety up front, rather than dispersing funds on a yearly basis. This meant that the agency had less cash on hand for new grants. But that funding strategy, called “Multiyear funding,” was curbed in the 2026 appropriations bill, which also slightly increased the NIH budget after OMB proposed a massive cut. Congress is on track to do so again this year.
Earlier this year, OMB delayed signing off on NIH spending in its 2026 budget. The agency similarly last year instituted a brief pause on NIH being able to spend any money. And in May, OMB rocked the scientific community by proposing a rewrite to the bedrock guidance for all federal contracts that deemphasized peer review and empowered political appointees in driving decisions. The proposal received tens of thousands of comments in opposition, and its implementation was blocked by Congress’s stopgap spending bill.
Its most recent executive order also received immediate pushback from Congress members on both sides of the aisle, and in both chambers.
Daniel Payne contributed reporting.

After years of accusations that the Hyderabad Cricket Association (HCA) has been ignoring cricket in rural areas, it is now pushing ahead with an ambitious plan to revamp the cricketing structure in the State. Mahabubnagar and Karimnagar are set to be the first to see these winds of change, with both set to get functioning academies by summer.
“Karimnagar and Mahabubnagar will get floodlights soon. Apart from that, we are also focusing on Khammam and Warangal. Once land is acquired everywhere, by December hopefully, and handed over to HCA, we will take up the works,” HCA secretary M. Jeevan Reddy said at a press conference here on Wednesday.
The association, however, will continue to rely on private grounds in Hyderabad owing to the expensive land costs in the city.
HCA is also looking to expand its administrative footprint to cover all districts of Telangana. Plans are being drawn to bring them all under its umbrella and then decentralise the operations across the State.
Former secretary T. Shesh Narayan, who now heads the District Infrastructure Development Committee, stated that tenders will soon be called for investing in the infrastructure of Karimnagar and Mahabubnagar. He said that the focus will not be solely on developing cricketers.
