“We need to explore all talent in the districts, not just the players but also umpires, physios, trainers and more. Once they are identified, they can be trained in Hyderabad and then get full-time jobs,” Shesh Narayan, who also serves as the HCA spokesperson, explained.

Public health experts have called for tighter regulation of celebrity endorsements of harmful products following President Droupadi Murmu’s appeal to artistes to refrain from promoting substances detrimental to health, made against the backdrop of Maharashtra’s action over a Vimal Elaichi advertisement featuring Shah Rukh Khan, Ajay Devgn and Tiger Shroff.
The President, speaking at the 72nd National Film Awards in Gujarat on Tuesday (September 22, 2026), said popular artists, particularly those who influence children and young people, should promote disciplined lifestyles and refrain from endorsing substances harmful to health.
The remarks come as the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) examines whether the Vimal Elaichi campaign amounts to surrogate advertising for Vimal Pan Masala. The FDA has issued show-cause notices to the three actors, alleging that the advertisement creates an association with a pan-masala product whose manufacture, storage, transportation, distribution and sale have been prohibited in Maharashtra.
The issue has also reached the courts. The Delhi High Court on September 14 declined to entertain a challenge to the FDA notices on territorial-jurisdiction grounds and directed the petitioner to approach the appropriate court in Maharashtra. The court did not adjudicate on whether the advertisements amounted to surrogate advertising.
Public health advocates have long raised concerns that celebrity endorsements can give socially acceptable imagery to products associated with tobacco, areca nut and other harmful substances, particularly among younger audiences. Cancer specialists have also warned about the health consequences associated with tobacco and areca-nut consumption.
Also read| Due diligence: On surrogate advertising
The Vimal campaign is not the first instance in which Bollywood celebrities have faced scrutiny over such endorsements. Amitabh Bachchan, Salman Khan, Saif Ali Khan and Akshay Kumar have, at different times, been associated with advertisements for pan masala or related products. Kumar withdrew from a Vimal campaign in 2022 following criticism.
The renewed debate raises a broader public health question over whether regulations governing advertising are keeping pace with the influence of celebrity endorsements, particularly where advertisements for apparently permissible products may create associations with products that are restricted or harmful.
Speaking to The Hindu, Arun Gupta, convener of Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPi), said appeals to celebrities needed to be backed by a clear legal framework covering the endorsement and advertising of harmful products, including tobacco and ultra-processed foods.
“I wish appeals were taken seriously and work in India, especially when it comes to endorsement and advertising of harmful products which include ultra-processed food products and tobacco products,” he said.
Mr. Gupta said the government should act on the President’s appeal and enact a clearly worded law to prohibit the marketing of unhealthy products.
“This is the only way to curb the trend. Why I am saying this is because the current legal framework is more of self-regulation and is ineffective even though the government believes it to be working,” he said.
Sandeep Nayak, chairman — Oncology and executive director — Surgical Oncology and Robotic Surgery, KIMS Hospitals, Bengaluru, said the President’s remarks highlighted the public-health consequences of celebrity endorsements of tobacco-linked products.
“As oncologists, we witness daily the catastrophic impact of pan masala, alcohol and tobacco addiction in our clinics. When high-profile icons lend their names to these brands, they inadvertently glamorise carcinogenic products for millions of impressionable youth,” he said.
Dr. Nayak said products such as silver-coated cardamom and flavoured mouth fresheners marketed under tobacco-associated brand names could function as surrogate advertisements.
“Using identical brand titles, logos and colour palettes — whether for pan masala or alcohol extensions —” creates a strong association with the primary brand, he said, calling for tighter regulation of such brand extensions.
Giving an insight into the scale of tobacco use in India, the National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-21) found that 21.4% of Indians aged 15-49 used smokeless tobacco, with the prevalence higher among men (29.6%) than women (12.8%). The latest Global Adult Tobacco Survey (GATS), conducted in 2016-17, estimated that 28.6% of Indians aged 15 years and above — nearly 267 million people — used tobacco. The survey also found that smokeless tobacco was the most prevalent form of tobacco use in the country.
A World Health Organisation study estimated the economic cost of diseases and premature deaths attributable to tobacco at ₹1.77 lakh crore in 2017-18, more than 1% of GDP, while treatment of tobacco-related diseases accounted for 5.3% of total health expenditure. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has estimated that smokeless tobacco and areca-nut use caused more than 120,000 oral-cancer cases globally in 2022, with 88% occurring in South-Central Asia.

Indians are discovering the thrill of shopping without paying
- Published
You are hungry. Or you are not. It doesn't matter.
You open FoodNeverComes, pick from 22 cuisines and start scrolling. Butter chicken looks good. So does bibimbap. You add a few dishes, watch the total climb and hit checkout. A tracker says a rider is on the way.
Then you get a dummy AI-generated call from inside the site. He is outside your building, he says, but cannot find your street or door. Except there was never any food in the first place. The order exists only on the screen.
"Order the food. Skip the bill," says the site., external Its slogan is blunter: "The food never comes - but the dopamine does."
Built by two 26-year-old software developers - Purvansh Parmar and Anshul Sharma - from Udaipur in India's northern state of Rajasthan, FoodNeverComes says it has attracted more than 2.7m visitors since its launch in June.
It now offers 22 kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes, complete with fake prices, a simulated checkout and a fictional delivery experience.
FoodNeverComes belongs to a new internet genre: "dopamine sites", which recreate the rituals of consumption without the consumption. There are fake shopping sites, fake delivery services and even fake holidays.
The genre took off in South Korea, external and has since travelled well beyond, spawning a growing crop of sites - Dopamine Shop, external or Fakehaul, external, for example - that mimic everything from food delivery and shopping to travel.
What, exactly, are we enjoying when we enjoy buying something?
The idea began with the founders' own shopping habits. Parmar and Sharma met on a computer science diploma course and later started NeuroX AI, which builds software and AI products and makes Instagram content. They noticed it in their own lives: online baskets filling up with things they wanted, but never actually bought.
Sharma would browse electronics, fill an online basket and abandon it. Parmar's mother did much the same. "She would add things to the cart and say, 'I will order this later'," he recalls.
Parmar's own version ended at food delivery checkouts. During a two-month project in Mumbai, he says, he was spending 5,000-10,000 rupees a week on food, sometimes ordering treats he did not necessarily need: Belgian waffles, ice cream and, once, a large jar of sour cream he barely wanted and gave away to friends.
He believes "perhaps the real craving was not always for the food, but for the ritual of ordering it".
What begins as genuine hunger, the two argue, can become associated with the pleasure of ordering. Over time, boredom, anxiety or habit can trigger the urge even when the hunger has disappeared.
"Sometimes you're not hungry at all. You're bored or busy, and then you realise that ordering food makes you feel good. You start associating the act of ordering with that dopamine hit. Eventually, it's not just the food you want," says Parmar.
Ravi Dhar, director of the Yale Center for Customer Insights, calls this "anticipatory utility" - the pleasure of looking forward to consumption. It is especially strong with things that capture the imagination - a new pair of shoes, a holiday, a restaurant meal - because anticipation becomes part of the experience.
Sometimes, Dhar says, anticipation can be more pleasurable than ownership: "The thrill is in the chase." Once the object is acquired and the tension resolved, psychological arousal falls.
Neuroscience has a name for this gap between the chase and the catch, and it complicates a popular idea. Dopamine is not simply the brain's pleasure chemical, whatever the internet's talk of "dopamine hits" might suggest.
Kent Berridge, a University of Michigan neuroscientist who developed the theory of "wanting" and "liking", says they are separate processes. Wanting is the motivational pull towards something; liking is the pleasure of having it. They often travel together, but not always. Dopamine, in his account, drives the first, not the second.
Tempting food or products online are likely to activate this wanting system, which Berridge calls "incentive salience".
"Some situations can trigger 'wanting' by itself," he says. We can pursue something intensely even when the eventual pleasure is weak - or, in more everyday terms, want something more than we ultimately like it.
Dr Anna Lembke, a Stanford University addiction psychiatrist and author of Dopamine Nation, makes a similar distinction.
"To call dopamine a chemical of pleasure is an oversimplification," she told me. "Dopamine is the molecule that says 'get more of' or 'do more of', but it doesn't necessarily equate to pleasure."
What she adds is the role of ritual. Cues and habits attached to a reward can become reinforcing in their own right, she says: in addiction, the routines leading up to drug use can eventually matter as much as the drug itself. "Anticipation of reward can be as reinforcing as the reward itself," she says.
Can repeatedly ordering imaginary food satisfy a real craving? Berridge says the ritual could produce a "dopamine hit and strong 'wanting', and also evoke faint conditioned 'liking'".
But he would expect the "novelty to soon wear off", and would be "surprised" if many people returned to place more than about 10 imaginary orders.
Dhar is more open to the possibility that simulated consumption could serve as a kind of release valve.
"While we still need more empirical data to know if simulated shopping can satisfy a consumer urge, evidence from simulated consumption in gaming shows it can be highly effective," he says.
But there is an equally plausible danger: the ritual may simply rehearse the behaviour it is supposed to replace.
Lembke says the evidence is not in yet, and the effect may depend on the person. But her own bet is that, over time, the sites could "reinforce the same addictive neural networks they are trying to simulate".
"The one up side, though, is that people using these sites have on some level already admitted to themselves they have a problem, and that admission is often the first step in recovery," says Lembke.
Sharma ran an accidental experiment of his own. When his phone screen cracked, he spent a week on Amazon comparing six or seven replacements and adding them to his basket. Then he repaired the handset.
"I enjoyed the process of research and putting the phones in the cart," he says. "Eventually I didn't buy a phone."
He now catches himself doing the same on food delivery sites, particularly when anxious, filling baskets without checking out. "I realised that I suffer from this problem," he says.
The site's blog explores the "serious side" of the fake takeaway, from food-delivery addiction and why fake ordering feels good to cravings, guilt and the psychology of the shopping cart.
The founders have since taken the idea beyond food. A second site, TripNeverLeaves, lets users plan a holiday - destination, flight, seat, hotel and activities - then sends them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway. They say it has attracted more than 100,000 visitors.
Who those visitors are is harder to establish. But Lembke says younger people may be especially vulnerable to reinforcing digital rewards because the "developing brain is a vulnerable brain".
"In childhood and early adolescence, the front lobe, which acts like the brakes on appetite, is not yet fully connected to the emotion centres of the brain. Hence, teens are more likely to take risks without appreciating the negative consequences, and more likely to get addicted to reinforcing substances and behaviours, once exposed," she says.
For now, the founders say the sites are not about making money. They plan to keep them free and eventually share the data with neuroscientists and psychologists.
What looks like a joke about ordering too much food has stumbled into a bigger question about modern consumption: if so much of the thrill comes before we get the thing, do we need the thing at all?

Latest CDC report on youth behavior has some good news — and MAHA vibes
CDC survey finds mental health and suicide risk among U.S. teens has improved
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Mental health symptoms and suicide risk among American high schoolers improved in 2025 compared to two years prior. That's according to the latest report from the national Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance Survey, conducted by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) every two years.
The new report, which primarily highlights students' diets, physical activity and sleep, found improvements in the number of students who ate fruits and vegetables compared to the previous survey. While there was not much improvement in levels of physical activity, more students reported playing on a sports team compared to in 2023.
"We see in this report that our children are eating healthier, engaging in team sports, and experiencing fewer feelings of sadness and hopelessness," said Dr. Jennifer Shuford, CDC's Deputy Director and Chief Medical Officer at a press conference held last week to announce the report's findings. "This is good news for kids, for us, and for our country. The focus here is clear: healthier youth today, healthier adults tomorrow."
The survey, commonly known as the YRBS, has been running for more than 35 years. This year's report differs from previous years' which emphasized the dangers teens face from drugs, alcohol and sex. While the 2025 survey collected a range of information, the report highlights topics important to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his MAHA – Make America Healthy Again – movement. It talks about nutrition, exercise, sleep, screen time and mental health while leaving out things like teen smoking and vaping and exposure to violence.
It also leaves out discussion of health disparities among ethnic groups, which was a feature of past reports.
Improvements in youth mental health
In 2021, the American Academy of Pediatrics declared a national emergency in child and adolescent mental health.
"After the pandemic, we had our all time high of suicide attempts and ideation and visits to the ER with suicidality," says child and adolescent psychiatrist Dr. Vera Feuer, Chief Clinical Officer at the Child Mind Institute.
But the new report, which also presents trends over the past decade, shows a decline in suicidal thinking and behaviors, which initially showed up in the 2023 YRBS data. This year's report finds that levels of persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness among high schoolers have fallen in recent years – from 42% in 2021, to 40% in 2023 and 33% in 2025.
Similarly, the number of students who seriously considered suicide fell from 22% in 2021 to 14% in 2025. The number who made a suicide plan (which ups the risk of attempting suicide) also fell from 18% in 2021 to 12% in 2025.
While these percentages still represent large numbers of teens, the latest findings are "encouraging," adds Feuer.
"What we're seeing is that since 2021, there's actually been a really nice improvement in many mental health indicators for young people," says pediatrician Dr. Scott Hadland, chief of adolescent medicine at Mass General Brigham for Children in Boston. "I think that's a cause for optimism."
New emphasis on health and wellness
However, the new report stands apart from past years' reports in what's highlighted as well as what's not, says Hadland, who is part of the team that administers the survey in Massachusetts. The survey questions haven't changed but what the report emphasizes or omits has.
"There is a real emphasis on health and wellness," says Hadland. "And look, that's very important."
The highlights in the new report "align with the Make America Healthy Again initiative led by President Trump and Secretary Kennedy – who are committed to preventing chronic disease across our country, especially in our nation's youth," Shuford said at last week's press conference.
Missing pieces
But other factors that are also important in the health and wellbeing of the country's youth are missing in the report, says Hadland.
"As somebody who looks at this report every year, it really stood out to me that we were missing rich data on what's going on with substance use with young people," he says. In past years, the survey captured both positive trends – decline in smoking – as well as more troubling ones – rise in vaping in recent years, he explains.
Similarly, the new report is also missing information on sexual behaviors among teens, as well as their exposure to firearms and other forms of violence, which featured prominently in past reports. Guns, for example, remain the leading cause of death among children and teens in this country.
Another piece of data that's missing in the new report, says Feuer, is how connected students feel in their school.
"School connectedness and kids feeling like they belong in schools and that adults and children in schools care about them is a really important protective factor for mental health," she says.
The report also omits any mention of LGBTQ+ youth and has fewer details based on race and ethnicity of students, note both Feuer and Hadland.
"The extent to which we could observe health inequities by race and ethnicity and then by membership in the LGBTQIA+ community were really much more absent in this report," says Hadland.
"There are significant disparities when we look at behaviors among different groups of students," acknowledged Mike Underwood, acting director of the CDC's Division of Adolescent and School Health, in response to a reporter's question about data on LGBTQ youth.
He said that data was collected and is available on the YRBS website for anyone to look up.
"We encourage states and communities to go and look through their data," he said.

OpenAI and Anthropic both recently released new models aimed at lowering costs. Anthropic announced Opus 5.5, the latest version of its main mass-market workhorse model, used for tasks like coding and other complex knowledge work.
And OpenAI announced GPT-6 Sol and Luna, the latest versions of its middle-of-the-road or smaller models focused on efficiency and speed.
These new releases are not about groundbreaking new capabilities. Rather, they’re about efficiency. As both OpenAI and Anthropic target enterprise customers, they’re racing to compete with open-weight models as organizations have explored changing their practices and using model routers to use these pricey, frontier models less in favor of cheaper alternatives.
Anthropic and OpenAI argue that these new releases push the envelope at the frontier (albeit mostly in modest ways), while bringing costs substantially down.
Opus 5.5: A more affordable, more competitive flagship
Opus 5.5 is at the higher end of the models announced today, but the wider context here is that Anthropic is playing a bit of catch-up in its race with OpenAI. OpenAI earlier this month released GPT-6 Astra, which has sometimes been modestly beating Opus 5 in benchmarks and user sentiment. (By price and capability, Astra is competing with both Opus and Fable.)

Obama often criticized Fox News. He also did fewer interviews with Fox News and took fewer questions from its correspondents compared to other news networks. His administration also said it was willing to exclude Fox News from interviews. Some accused his administration of blocking the network's access in one instance, but a spokesperson claimed it was a communication error and the administration backtracked.
However, the Obama administration never outright blocked, banned or ejected Fox News reporters from press briefings.
In September 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump banned three major news outlets — CNN, MSNOW and Politico — from the White House. The outlets subsequently filed a lawsuit accusing the administration of violating the First Amendment.
Soon after, former President Barack Obama condemned Trump's ban and speculated about the consequences if he had banned Fox News during his administration. In response, some people online claimed Obama had retaliated against Fox News (archived) in a similar way during his first term. For example, television personality Piers Morgan wrote on X (archived), "Obama did ban Fox, and waged almost constant war against press freedom."
(X user @PiersMorgan)
As Snopes previously reported in 2018, while Obama criticized Fox News and snubbed the network's requests for interviews, he never banned the network outright from the White House. As such, we rate this claim as mostly false.
In October 2009, a New York Times report (archived) stated Obama's Treasury Department attempted to exclude Fox News from a roundtable interview with the executive-pay czar Kenneth R. Feinberg. Major news networks were sharing a "pool" camera crew for these interviews. According to the report, other networks protested Fox's exclusion.
However, a 2009 Talking Points Memo report referred to the situation as a "miscommunication." The report said:
TPMDC dug into it, and here's what happened. Feinberg did a pen and pad with reporters to brief them on cutting executive compensation. TV correspondents, as they do with everything, asked to get the comments on camera. Treasury officials agreed and made a list of the networks who asked (Fox was not among them).
But logistically, all of the cameras could not get set up in time or with ease for the Feinberg interview, so they opted for a round robin where the networks use one pool camera. Treasury called the White House pool crew and gave them the list of the networks who'd asked for the interview.
The network pool crew noticed Fox wasn't on the list, was told that they hadn't asked and the crew said they needed to be included. Treasury called the White House and asked top Obama adviser Anita Dunn. Dunn said yes and Fox's Major Garrett was among the correspondents to interview Feinberg last night.
A Treasury spokesperson told Talking Points Memo, "There was no plot to exclude Fox News, and they had the same interview that their competitors did. Much ado about absolutely nothing." Fox News did conduct the interview with Feinberg.
The Obama administration didn't hold back in its criticism of Fox News in the aftermath of the controversy. When questioned by NBC News about the administration's tone regarding Fox News, Obama said:
We're going to take the media as it comes. And if media is operating basically as a talk radio format, then that's one thing, and if it's operating as a news outlet, then that's another. But it's not something I'm losing a lot of sleep over.
Obama spokesperson Josh Earnest reportedly admitted that the White House had demonstrated its "willingness to exclude Fox News" from interviews, but that it had not done so, according to Talking Points Memo. Earnest added, "The president and other high ranking officials and people like Ken Feinberg have done interviews with Fox in the past and will do them in the future."
In a 2010 interview with Rolling Stone, Obama accused Fox News of focusing more on its point of view than objectivity. "It's a point of view," Obama said, "that I think is ultimately destructive for the long-term growth of a country that has a vibrant middle class and is competitive in the world."
As Snopes previously reported, former Fox News White House correspondent Major Garrett asserted that though there was "never an effort to shut me out of the briefing room," ongoing tensions between the Obama administration and Fox News hindered his ability to do his job. In a November 2018 interview with The Hill, he said:
The White House would always pull me aside and say "well, really, Major, we're not at war with you," and I said "stop talking to me like that because when you're at war with my network you by definition are questioning and assailing my journalistic credibility and the work I do here every day," he said. "So don't tell me it's not about me, it is about me."
"Now, they never tried to pull my pass, but they had this sort of arms-length relationship to Fox and tried to demonize it on a daily basis. So that's another part of American history and journalism in the White House press corps I think at least should be noted at this moment," he said.
As we previously reported, Fox News' White House correspondents were called on less during press briefings compared to other major television networks. In September 2009, when Obama made the talk show rounds to talk about healthcare reform, he snubbed "Fox News Sunday" and did not appear on the show until his last year in office in 2016.
In 2013, The Washington Post reported that Obama's Department of Justice surveilled a Fox News reporter and obtained a search warrant for his emails while conducting an investigation into national security leaks in 2009. The investigation also looked into other reporters but appeared to specifically target Fox News.
The Obama administration never banned Fox News outright, but no love was lost between the two groups. While Fox News accused the administration of cutting it out of one interview, the administration blamed it on miscommunication and gave the network access while not hiding its disdain for the network.
For further reading, Snopes previously covered the misrepresented claim that former U.S. President Joe Biden cut reporters from the press pool.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

Trump gets a Greenland deal
But the island is still a part of Denmark.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s campaign to take over Greenland has reached a peaceful end — for now.
What happened? Trump signed a new security agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland while at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, outlining an expanded US military presence on the island.
The deal is the result of months-long negotiations between the two countries and Greenland, which is a semi-autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark. Crucially, it reaffirms the “sovereignty and territorial integrity” of Denmark and Greenland, something Trump has spent the last year-and-a-half-plus threatening to sweep away.
What’s the context? Trump returned to office last year proclaiming that US “ownership and control of Greenland is an absolute necessity” for US national security, even though Denmark — and by extension Greenland — is a NATO ally.
That rhetoric quickly escalated, and by this January, Trump was suggesting that the US could even use force to take the island. “If we don’t do it the easy way,” he said — buying Greenland from Denmark, or perhaps bribing its residents to secede — “we’re going to do it the hard way.”
This, understandably, freaked Europe out, prompting multiple countries to deploy small numbers of troops to Greenland.
Does this mean Trump is done trying to take over? We can always hope. It’s possible Trump will claim this as a win and move on, even though Tuesday’s deal doesn’t fundamentally change the nature of the US-Greenland relationship. (Last week, he referred to it as “a dream come true” for the US.)
That being said, Trump’s desire to own Greenland always made more sense as an attempted legacy move than anything else, whatever his professed justifications. So while he might be happy to take the win for now, with the war in Iran still on and the midterms fast approaching, it shouldn’t be surprising if he’s clamoring for ownership again before his term is up.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

With cases of mumps being reported from various parts of Thrissur district in Keralam, the District Medical Officer (DMO) has urged the public to remain vigilant.
Mumps is a viral infection that spreads through air, particularly through droplets from coughing and sneezing, nasal secretions and close contact with infected persons. The disease is most contagious from about two days before the onset of swelling to four to six days after the swelling appears.
Children between five and 15 years are commonly affected, although adults can also contract the infection. The disease can be more severe in adults.
Symptoms
The most prominent symptom is swelling on the sides of the cheeks, below the ears. The swelling may affect one or both sides of the face. Mild fever and headache are among the early symptoms, followed by difficulty in opening the mouth, chewing and swallowing. Loss of appetite and fatigue may also occur.
The DMO has advised patients to seek treatment for fever and pain, drink plenty of fluids and take adequate rest. If proper precautions are not taken, the infection can, in some cases, affect the brain, testicles, ovaries, pancreas and prostate. Complications such as encephalitis may occur if the infection spreads to the brain. In adults, complications involving the reproductive organs can, in some cases, affect fertility.
Avoid contact
Teachers should immediately inform parents and health workers if children develop symptoms. Infected persons should remain at home until they have recovered. They should avoid close contact with others. Children with mumps should not be sent to school.
Disinfecting items used by infected persons, wearing masks, maintaining physical distance and washing hands with soap are among the measures recommended to prevent the spread of the infection. The illness usually subsides within one to two weeks.
MMR vaccine
The DMO has advised parents to ensure that children receive the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine at 16-24 months of age, as it provides protection against the three infections.
Anyone developing symptoms has been advised to consult a doctor promptly and seek appropriate treatment.

A video circulating on social media claims to show massive flames and thick black smoke following an airstrike on an airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia (here, here, here). Even a few mainstream media outlets reported these visuals with the same claim (here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video shows an airstrike on Riyadh Airport in Saudi Arabia.
Fact: This video is not from Riyadh. It shows a fire caused by a drone strike at the Sadovod market in Moscow, Russia, in June 2026. While there were reports of a Houthi attack on Riyadh airport in September 2026, the viral video is unrelated to that incident. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
We conducted a reverse image search of the viral video and found the same visuals in multiple videos published on 18 June 2026 (here, here & here). These reports confirm that the footage is from Moscow, Russia, and shows a fire at the Sadovod market following a drone attack.
According to news reports (here & here), the Sadovod market in Moscow was engulfed in flames and smoke following a drone strike on 18 June 2026. We also checked the location using Google Street View, and the surroundings seen in the viral video match the Sadovod market in Moscow, confirming that the footage is from Moscow.
However, several international news outlets (here & here) reported that the Houthis claimed to have targeted “sensitive sites” in Riyadh on 19 September 2026. On the same day, a fire broke out at a fuel storage depot near King Khalid International Airport, with large flames and thick black smoke visible from the area.
To sum up, an old Russian video is being shared as visuals showing an airstrike on Riyadh Airport.

Discord today is rolling out an age-verification system that estimates each user’s age and requires some users to prove they are old enough to access age-restricted content. Discord said it will take a few days for the global system to reach all user accounts.
Discord had announced a somewhat different plan for age checks in February, but scrapped it amid backlash from users concerned about privacy. The privacy concerns were heightened by a 2025 incident in which hackers stole government IDs of 70,000 Discord users from a third-party service that Discord used to verify ages in the UK and Australia.
The original plan was to require ID uploads or face scans from users seeking to access age-restricted servers and channels. The revised system, detailed yesterday by Discord CTO and co-founder Stanislav Vishnevskiy, will provide several additional options.
“In February, the only methods we’d planned for to confirm your age were facial age estimation or an ID scan. Based on your feedback, we committed to giving you more options that meet our high privacy standards,” Vishnevskiy wrote.
A Discord system will automatically estimate user ages and place each user into an adult age group (18+), a teen group (13-17), or an “unconfirmed” group for which there isn’t enough data to determine whether a person is an adult or teen.
For the teen group, message requests from non-friends will go to a separate inbox for review, and users will receive alerts about friend requests from people they don’t share mutual friends or a small server with. “Sensitive” images will be blurred or blocked, “and age-restricted servers, channels, and bot commands aren’t accessible,” Discord said. Teen users’ full profile details will be visible only to friends and people in smaller servers that they’re part of.
Age verification options
Discord estimates that more than 90 percent of users will not be asked to confirm their age. Adults who want to access age-restricted content, but are incorrectly placed in the 13-17 age group or put into “unconfirmed,” will have several options to prove they are old enough.

External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on Wednesday raised India’s concerns over the United States’ new Russia sanctions law during a meeting with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly High-Level Week in New York.
The talks focused on the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 (SRIA), which was signed into law by US President Donald Trump last week. The legislation gives the US president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue purchasing Russian oil and gas, including India and China.
Jaishankar said after the meeting that he had reiterated India’s “interests and concerns” regarding SRIA. The two ministers also discussed the situations in the Gulf and Ukraine.
The meeting comes as India assesses the potential implications of the new US law for its energy purchases and exports to the American market.
The legislation provides the US president with powers to impose additional tariffs on countries buying Russian crude oil and natural gas. However, the law itself does not automatically impose a 100% tariff on Indian goods. Instead, it creates statutory authority for the administration to impose such measures under specified conditions.
India remains among the major buyers of Russian crude, alongside China, making the issue particularly significant for New Delhi's energy and trade interests.
Following the passage of the legislation, the Ministry of External Affairs said India would take necessary steps to safeguard its economic interests and energy security.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 expands the US sanctions framework targeting Russia and provides additional trade-related measures against countries continuing specified purchases of Russian energy.
For India, the legislation creates the possibility of higher US tariffs on Indian exports if the administration invokes the relevant provisions.
The potential measures come at a time when India and the US are also engaged in discussions on a bilateral trade agreement, adding another dimension to the economic relationship between the two countries.

- The claim that Danish officials played "Send in the Clowns" when U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived at the signing of a U.S.-Denmark-Greenland agreement is unproven.
- The rumor stems from footage circulating online that social media users claimed showed Rubio entering the signing ceremony on Sept. 22, 2026, as Judy Collins' song "Send in the Clowns" played in the background.
- Two separate live streams of the event both showed that Collins' song did play while Rubio entered the signing ceremony with Greenland and Denmark's Ministers of Foreign Affairs. All three men were in frame while parts of the song that specifically mentioned clowns played.
- Therefore, the choice of "Send in the Clowns" was likely coincidental or accidental. If one delegation had chosen the song to mock another, it did not have the intended effect.
- A spokesperson for the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs said via email that "Denmark was not involved in selecting the music for the signing ceremony."
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We asked the White House whether its officials chose the pre-ceremony music and await a reply. In the meantime, we leave this claim unrated.
A claim (archived) circulated online in September 2026 that Danish officials played the song "Send in the Clowns" when U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived at the signing of a U.S.-Denmark-Greenland agreement.
The claim circulated after U.S. President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed the deal, which sought to end months of diplomatic squabble over Greenland, in New York City on Sept. 22, 2026.
For example, one Threads user wrote, "Listen, I'm not gonna say it's perfection, but the Danish delegation having 'Send in the Clowns' playing on the playlist as Marco Rubio entered to sign Denmark/Greenland stuff is very, very well played."
Other social media users shared the claim on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), X (archived), and Bluesky (archived). Some of those users posted a video that they claimed showed Rubio entering the room as "Send in the Clowns" played, suggesting Danish officials sought to embarrass or insult him. Snopes readers also contacted us about the claim.
Two separate live streams of the Sept. 22 signing event, which used two separate camera angles, showed that "Send in the Clowns" did play around the time Rubio and Greenland and Denmark's Ministers of Foreign Affairs Múte B. Egede and Lars Løkke Rasmussen entered the conference room where the ceremony was held.
A spokesperson for the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs said via email on Sept. 22, 2026, "Denmark was not involved in selecting the music for the signing ceremony." Snopes asked the White House whether its officials chose the pre-conference music and await a reply.
In the meantime, we leave this claim unrated.
What the streams showed
According to a livestream (archived) of the Sept. 22 signing event shared by MAGNO News, which said it provided "professionally licensed video content from accredited media providers," "Send in the Clowns" played as attendees at the signing ceremony were finding their seats.
The song started at time code 9:59 in the stream. Rubio, Egede and Rasmussen entered the room around time code 10:59 as Collins sang, "Isn't it bliss? Don't you approve? One who keeps tearing around, One who can't move. Where are the clowns? There ought to be clowns."
At time code 11:18, the camera panned to Rasmussen as Collins sang, "There ought to be clowns."
Later, at time code 12:22, Collins sang, "But where are the clowns? Send in the clowns. Don't bother, they're here," as the camera panned to Rubio and Rasmussen.
Finally, at time code 13:24, Collins sang, "But where are the clowns? There ought to be clowns. Well, maybe next year," as the camera focused on Rubio and Rasmussen.
Another livestream (archived) uploaded to YouTube by British newspaper The Guardian also included Collins' music.
"Send in the Clowns" started at time code 5:14 on the Guardian's stream. Egede and Rubio entered the frame at time code 6:24 as Collins sang "Where are the clowns? There ought to be clowns."
The song ended at time code 9:10, followed by the announcement and arrival of Trump, Frederiksen and Nielsen at time code 9:46.
Given the above, the choice of "Send in the Clowns" was likely coincidental or accidental. Officials for all three countries signing the deal were in frame while parts of the song that directly mentioned clowns played, meaning that if one delegation had chosen the song to mock another, it did not have the intended effect.
Additionally, Trump, Frederiksen and Nielsen entered the stage right after the song. Again, if one delegation had sought to call the head of another other a clown through Collins' song, that did not have the intended effect because the heads of all three delegations appeared together.
Greenland deal averts diplomatic crisis
Trump, Frederiksen and Nielsen's deal for Greenland followed months of threats by Trump to seize the Arctic island. Trump's wish to gain control of Greenland, which is an autonomous territory of Denmark, threatened the integrity of NATO in January 2026 when his administration refused to rule out using military force.
Both Denmark and the U.S. are NATO members. The alliance has an article that treats an attack on one member as an attack on all.
Negotiations for a new deal related to U.S. involvement in the island's affairs began in January and concluded with the signing in September.
According to the Associated Press, the deal allows the U.S. to expand its military presence on Greenland, but affirms the island's status as an autonomous territory of Denmark as well as Greenland's right to self-determination.
It also notes that non-NATO countries cannot open military installations on the island.
The Danish parliament will consider the deal, which can only come into force if that parliament approves it.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows the 136-year-old Gauripur Jama Masjid near Kolkata Airport being demolished by religious extremists to make way for a Ram temple. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows the 136-year-old Gauripur Jama Masjid near Kolkata airport being demolished by religious extremists to make way for a Ram temple.
Fact: The video shows an angry mob vandalising the house of Mustafa Pramanik, an accused in the rape and murder of a 10-year-old schoolgirl in Pabna, Bangladesh, in September 2026. It has no connection to the 136-year-old Gauripur Jama Masjid near Kolkata airport. While the mosque is set to be relocated due to airport security and runway expansion plans, there are no credible reports of it being vandalised. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we searched Google using relevant keywords and found (here, here) that the 136-year-old Bankra Masjid, also known as Gauripur Jama Masjid, is located within the premises of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport in Kolkata, about 165 metres from its secondary runway. It was built in the 1890s. In July 2026, prayers were suspended, and authorities supported relocating the mosque, citing airport security and runway expansion plans. The mosque will be moved, as stated by West Bengal Chief Minister Subhendu Adhikari. However, at the time of writing this article, we could not find any credible reports of the mosque being vandalised.
We then conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to several Bangladeshi news reports (here, here, and here) from September 2026 featuring the same visuals as the viral video. According to these reports, an angry mob attacked and vandalised the house of Mustafa Pramanik, who was accused in the rape and murder of a 10-year-old schoolgirl in Pabna Sadar Upazila. The incident took place in the Kulunia area. Pabna Sadar Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Md. Tariqul Islam said that the schoolgirl’s body, wrapped in a sack, was recovered from a pond seven days after she went missing. Local grocer Md. Mostafa Pramanik, 55, and his tenant, Md. Yasin Ali, were arrested in connection with the incident and sent to jail by a court.
To sum up, an unrelated video from Bangladesh is being shared as visuals of the demolition of a 136-year-old mosque near Kolkata Airport.

Fiji has declared an HIV national emergency after data showed one in 60 people in the South Pacific island nation is now estimated to have the bloodborne virus.
The country says it is boosting testing and treatment efforts to fight a surge in new infections, which have increased 12-fold over the last 15 years, according to the Joint United Nations Program on HIV and Aids (UNAIDS).
Latest figures showed there was about 9,000 people living with HIV in 2025 in a country which has less than a million people, according to the UN agency. It said only 39 per cent of patients knew their HIV status and just 22 per cent were receiving antiretroviral treatment.
Fiji said that one in every 60 adults in the country has HIV, compared with one in 167 five years ago.
"This means HIV is now a national crisis and the government is treating it like one. No more business as usual," Fiji's Health Minister Antonio Lalabalavu said in a video statement on Facebook. “More people in Fiji are living with HIV than ever before.” The government said it was finding more cases because its testing efforts are reaching more people. It will provide more free testing, clean needles for drug users and free treatment for people who test positive.

United Nations, Sep 23: In his inaugural speech at the UN General Assembly, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said world leaders must set up global standards to oversee artificial intelligence because “fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance”.
Burnham said the UK will try to persuade other countries to adopt rules on transparency and access to AI models - and, even tougher, to get tech companies to sign on, too.
He said AI has immense potential but will also be “a source of disruption to the way we live and work - and a multiplier of risk”.
Burnham also said Russia and other states are using AI-augmented misinformation and disinformation to corrode democracy, something he said Britain has faced in the decade since it voted to leave the European Union.
He said he has asked British security chiefs to set up a National Centre for Information Defence to counter the threat.
Burnham also chaired a meeting at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday on the Israel-Palestine issue, alongside French President Emmanuel Macron, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan.
He said the two-state solution to Israel-Palestinian conflict must be kept alive.
Burnham said failure to deliver a two-state solution will “corrode trust” in politicians who have talked about the issue but not taken action.
He told delegates from dozens of countries that the UK has banned trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank because the “E1” settlement expansion plan is “a deliberate attempt to block a two-state solution.”
“We all live in an era of low trust in politics. Many people in this room, many politicians around the world, have spoken for decades about a two-state solution. But if we fail to back those words with deeds, we will further corrode trust in the political, diplomatic and international process,” the UK prime minister said. (AP)

The Embassy of the State of Palestine to India has questioned the description of the 1918 Battle of Haifa as the “liberation of Haifa”, saying that Indian soldiers who participated in the battle were serving under British command as part of an imperial military campaign that resulted in the occupation of Palestine.
In a five-page position paper titled “Rewriting of India–Palestine history: The battle of Haifa: liberation or occupation?”, the Palestinian Embassy said the terminology surrounding the battle required “careful and scholarly reflection” and argued that the event should be understood within the historical context of British military occupation of Palestine.
The Embassy said Palestine, including Haifa, was under Ottoman rule before 1918 and that British forces defeated the Ottoman Empire during the First World War, bringing Palestine under British occupation. Indian soldiers participated in the campaign as part of the British Indian Army, under British command.
It argued that describing them retrospectively as having “liberated Haifa” risked attributing to India a sovereign military decision that the country did not possess in 1918, when it was still under British rule.
The paper pointed to contemporary British terminology, saying military and parliamentary records referred to the operations in Palestine using terms such as “capture”, “take”, “fall” and “conquer”. It also noted that following the British military campaign, Palestine was administered under the Occupied Enemy Territory Administration (OETA) until its replacement by a civil administration in July 1920.
The Embassy also cited India’s own historical records, including the 2014 publication Indian War Memorials Around the World, saying it does not describe the event as the “liberation of Haifa”.
According to the paper, the publication records that the “fortified town of Haifa fell to a cavalry charge by the Jodhpur Lancers” and that the 15th Imperial Service Cavalry Brigade “broke through and took the town”.
It also referred to the Teen Murti Memorial in New Delhi, stating that the memorial was established during British colonial rule to commemorate Indian soldiers who served and died during the First World War, and was not originally intended to commemorate relations between India and Israel.
The Embassy said the memorial refers to “Palestine and some of its cities” among the places associated with the military campaigns in which Indian soldiers served.
The paper further cited official Indian records to state that 491 Indian soldiers are recorded at Ramleh War Cemetery, 109 at the Gaza and Deir el Balah War Cemeteries and 47 at the Haifa Indian Cemetery, besides soldiers commemorated at other cemeteries and memorials across historical Palestine.
The Embassy questioned why Haifa had become the centre of a commemorative narrative when Indian soldiers had fought across a much wider region, including the Suez Canal, Gaza, Jerusalem, the Jordan Valley, Damascus and Aleppo.
It also said the first formal Israeli public ceremony commemorating the Indian soldiers was held in 2010, nearly a century after the battle.
The paper argued that Britain, rather than India, was the principal military power behind the campaign, as it financed, armed and commanded the operation. It questioned why the “liberation of Haifa” narrative centred on Indian soldiers while Britain’s role was not similarly emphasised.
The Embassy also stressed that the soldiers described as “Indian soldiers” served in the British Indian Army and came from different regions, communities and religions across British India, whose geographical and political boundaries differed from those of the present-day Republic of India.
The position paper placed the soldiers’ participation within the wider history of British colonial rule, noting that Indian troops were deployed in military campaigns far from their homeland.
It also referred to the Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, arguing that the broader record of British rule should be considered when interpreting the role of Indian soldiers in the First World War.
The Embassy cited Mahatma Gandhi’s opposition to the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine at the expense of its indigenous population, including his statement that “Palestine belongs to the Arabs in the same sense that England belongs to the English.”
It further pointed out that India voted against UN Resolution 181 in 1947, which proposed partition and allocated Haifa to the proposed Jewish state, and questioned how the 1918 battle could subsequently be presented as a foundation for India-Israel historical ties.
The Embassy said describing the 1918 occupation of Haifa as a liberation “raises serious questions and concerns in Palestine”. It maintained that Haifa should be recognised as a Palestinian city at the time and that the battle took place in the context of the British military occupation of Palestine.
At the same time, the Embassy said its position was expressed with “full respect” for the sacrifice and memory of Indian soldiers and for India’s sovereign right to commemorate its history and fallen soldiers.
It called for historical remembrance of the Battle of Haifa to remain grounded in accuracy, balance and respect for the historical experiences of all concerned, while emphasising that the document represented the Palestinian Embassy’s perspective and was intended to contribute to discussion on the historical and legal questions surrounding the battle.

Every bird enthusiast has probably heard of Birdfy and Birdbuddy smart bird feeders, but a handful of competitors have quietly been refining their models over multiple generations—to the point where they’re starting to outpace the OGs in engineering, features, and design. Kiwibit is one of them.
I tested Kiwibit’s first feeder, the Beako, in mid-2025 and was impressed by its robust plastic body, removable dual-sided seed reservoir, and three-minute video captures—there was nothing quite like it at the time, and almost all of its features were available sans subscription. However, the optional rooftop solar panel stopped working after six weeks, which kept it from being a pick in my guide to the Best Smart Bird Feeders.
The Beako’s subsequent update, the Feeder 2, made the solar panel standard on all units, upped the panel’s output from 4.4 to 5 watts, and fixed the longevity issue—it’s currently my top pick for Best Design. The Feeder 2 Pro, meanwhile, has totally redone the camera to offer phase detection autofocus (PDAF) in 4K HDR—one of the most impressive smart feeder hardware offerings on the market. The companion app upgrade, however, still has some kinks to work out.
OK Computer
I tested the Feeder 2 Pro for a total of four weeks: one week at the non-subscription tier, and three weeks with Kiwibit Plus (also alternately referred to as “Family Premium” or “Premium Family), which at $90 a year offers AI ID, 60-day cloud recording (the feeder also supports microSD storage up to 512 GB), and new gallery views and roundup reports.
Without a subscription, camera quality is the same (some other feeder brands, like Birdbuddy, will paywall higher resolution), but here you’re limited to a bare-bones feed of video captures, and there’s no AI ID to sort or identify them—you’ll have to look at every image to make sure you didn’t miss anything interesting. This can be especially laborious if the same bird visits 15 times or more per day, especially since the camera placement means the thumbnails often show only the top of the bird’s head, if they show anything. This is atypical for a feeder with an MSRP of $290—most models at this price point include a lifetime subscription.
Thankfully, it is still easy to download and share 8-MP images and videos, and the camera records as long as the bird is there—up to three minutes—to ensure no movements are missed. The PDAF works to minimize blur and ensure all features are sharp. At various points during my test, I did notice the motion of the lens zooming in and out being clocked by multiple birds, who either immediately stopped eating to watch the camera warily or flew away. It didn’t happen often enough for me to wish the feature didn’t exist, but it is something to consider if your local birds are easily spooked.
The subscription gives you the same feed of video captures, but with labels of the bird species so you can skip past the ones that aren’t worth opening. There’s also a tile view under “Visits” that shows which birds have visited over the feeder’s lifetime and when they were last seen.
However, this is only so useful given that the AI ID is wrong a hefty percentage of the time—fish crows, Cape May warblers, mangrove warblers, red fox sparrows, and grackles are not found in western Washington state, where I live, but according to the Kiwibit app they are frequent visitors to my backyard. (I even had a “pileated woodpecker” visit the feeder, which would have been exceptionally rare, except the misidentified bird was a crow.) Also note that, unlike Birdfy feeders, the camera is not able to ID multiple birds on the feeder at a time.
Premium Pictures, Premium Fees
One area where Birdfy and Birdbuddy still beat their competitors is their intuitive, user-friendly apps. While Kiwibit’s non-subscription view has a simple interface, the subscription experience is a bit chaotic, as Kiwibit tries to cram a lot of information into too many places. There’s the tile view under “Birds,” the list of captures under “Feeds,” and a live view under “Live,” which you can click into to see a calendar of captures by day. Then, under “Me,” there’s a different calendar view with the number of bird visits per day, and a weekly Report tab that gives stats on that week’s visits. Even after four weeks of testing, I’m still not sure where I should first look when I simply want to see the birds that visited that day.

The Guardian and mk2 films have announced global release plans for Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s bombshell documentary NAZA.
The partners said that The Guardian-produced documentary will be released theatrically from September 28 onwards in more than 50 territories, having secured theatrical distributors in 56 territories since its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival on 10 September.
In an unprecedented move, The Guardian will make NAZA available for global audiences for free on its website, after the theatrical run later this fall. The partners said this move was due to the “worldwide interest” in the documentary as well as The Guardian’s “commitment to fearless, independent journalism”.
The investigative documentary, exposing the calculated targeting of civilians in Gaza in missile strikes by Israeli military through the testimony of intelligence personnel and soldiers involved in the killing, has caused a sensation since its Venice debut.
Watch on Deadline
It landed a record 25-minute ovation its Venice premiere Film, but has since been attacked by Israeli politicians including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has threatened to strip the directors of their Israeli citizenship even though he has no power to do this under the country’s laws.
The Guardian and mk2 said the film has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel, and they will be exploring other ways to enable the film to be seen in the occupied Palestinian territories.
They added that, as previously announced, the film will receive its North American premiere on 26 September at New York Film Festival, and will open in U.S. theaters on September 30, launching exclusively at the IFC Center in New York City.
It will expand to Los Angeles and other key markets on October 9, ahead of a national roll out in the weeks to follow.
NAZA is produced by The Guardian and James Wilson (JW Films); and executive produced by Oscar-winning filmmaker Jonathan Glazer.
The documentary builds on a series of revelations first published by the Guardian, +972 Magazine, a Israeli-Palestinian publication, and Hebrew-language outlet, Local Call between 2023-2025, including groundbreaking investigations into how Israel uses AI to identify targets in Gaza.
It follows Abraham and Szor’s No Other Land, winner of the Best Documentary Academy Award in 2025. Co-directed with Palestinian filmmakers Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, it documented Israeli army-backed efforts to erase the West Bank Palestinian villages of Masafer Yatta, while painting a wider picture of Israeli occupation.
“We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israelis to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible,” said Abraham and Szor in a joint statement as the NAZA release plans were unveiled.
“The threats from the Israeli government to revoke our citizenship and the death threats do not change that and will not stop the film. We thank our colleagues for the solidarity and look forward to sharing NAZA all over the world very soon.”
	Harry Davies, a Guardian investigations correspondent and one of NAZA’s producers, added: “NAZA is grounded in rigorous journalism published over the past three years, but it is also a powerful piece of cinema that will soon be available on screens, large and small, around the world.”
“The initial response from those who’ve seen it shows audiences are engaging deeply with the urgent questions the film raises. We’re working with MK2 and international partners to bring the film to global audiences as soon as possible.”
The 56 territories sold by Paris-based mk2 film, which boarded international sales on the documentary ahead of its Venice premiere, include France, UK, Italy, Spain, Germany, Belgium, Netherlands, Austria, Switzerland, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Greece, Portugal, Poland, Lithuania, Romania, Bulgaria, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Thailand, Canada, Brazil, Turkey, Central America, and the Middle East.

UK to review Chagos Islands deal after Trump's latest criticism
- Published
The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said.
Wes Streeting confirmed the deal was being looked at again after US President Donald Trump called it "terrible" at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.
The original agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of £101m ($136m) per year to lease back a joint UK-US military base there, prized for its strategic location in the Indian Ocean.
In April the deal, agreed under Sir Keir Starmer, was paused indefinitely because Trump pulled his support.
Streeting said "we have to" review the deal "because the United States doesn't support it".
"What President Trump said yesterday wasn't new but I think it does provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing," he told BBC Breakfast.
"So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where he can support it."
Streeting said the focus now would be to secure a long-term certainty for the base on Diego Garcia, the Chagos archipelago's largest island.
He said it had been the view of every UK prime minister since Boris Johnson that an ongoing legal process - as Mauritius argues it was illegally forced to give away the islands in 1965 to gain independence - risks the security of the base.
During Trump's first face-to-face meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the UN General Assembly in New York, the US president criticised the "terrible deal" and said the UK was "going to be looking" at it.
Burnham replied: "Yep."
He later told broadcasters he has "inherited the situation and we need a resolution".
Burnham added: "It's critical to safeguard the future of the base, and that matters to us for security reasons, but also clearly to the United States as well.
"What I said in the meeting is that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides, and we'll work hard to find it."
The prime minister had spoken to his Mauritian counterpart, Navin Ramgoolam, ahead of his trip to New York.
An official readout from that meeting said Burnham "reiterated his commitment to continue doing everything possible" along with the US to ratify the deal.
Prior to the pause in April, the UK and Mauritius had signed an agreement in May 2025 but a final draft of the bill to hand over sovereignty of the islands had not passed Parliament.
Under the terms of the deal agreed in 2025, Britain would hand sovereignty over the Indian Ocean archipelago to Mauritius but lease back the Diego Garcia base for 99 years, with official figures giving the total as £3.4bn.
However, Sir Keir, who was then prime minister, came under heavy criticism from opponents who said the real cost of the deal could amount to about £35bn, adjusting for inflation, and risked allowing China to establish a presence on the archipelago.
Trump has been a frequent critic of the deal, previously branding it a "a blight on our great ally" and an "act of total weakness".
Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday that no money would be handed over to Mauritius "at this stage" while officials review the deal.
Describing the Diego Garcia base as "one of the most sensitive and valuable national security assets", he said work was underway to find a deal "that maybe not everyone loves, but everyone can live with".

Salt, as an essential electrolyte, sits at the centre of human well-being, but being most prone to overuse and misuse, the condiment remains at the heart of illness as well. When Tamil Nadu Health Minister K.G. Arunraj took salt to the floor of the Assembly, he dragged it willy-nilly into public discourse. He announced plans to launch a multi-pronged mission to reduce salt intake, turning attention to the right quantities and forms that must be consumed. The Minister’s speech made it clear that the government’s plans were not merely about a dietary tweak, but instead, a recalibration of how wellbeing is perceived.
Salt, in the right proportions, facilitates hydration, nerve signalling, muscle function, and digestion and also has a role to play in stress physiology. However, in excess, or in ultra-processed foods, it can have a deleterious impact on health, increasing the risk of stroke, heart disease and kidney strain over time. On the other hand, very low salt intake can contribute to hypotension, fatigue, dizziness and brain fog, as well.
The health difference comes from the quantity of salt consumed and the overall diet patterns, undergoing rapid changes in favour of ultra-processed, packaged foods, and fast foods, that tend to be high in salt. The Indian diet itself, with its pickles and spicy curries, lends itself to tilting the salt cellar over a little too often. Surveys by the Indian Council of Medical Research show that in India, men consume an average of 8.9 gms daily, while women consume about 7.1 gms. Urban areas tend to consume higher amounts of salt, averaging around 9.2 gms a day. The WHO, which recommends keeping the intake under 5 gms of salt per day, released a set of guidelines in January 2025, recommending the use of lower-sodium salt substitutes, essentially including potassium chloride, and reducing the percentage of sodium chloride in table salt.
In Tamil Nadu, hypertension is a major public health concern. A 2024 study by Selvavinayagam T.S. et al., published in PLOS 1, showed adult prevalence of hypertension hovering around 33.9%, much above the national average of 28.5%. There is a direct link between consuming excess salt and hypertension — eating too much salt causes the body to retain extra water, which increases blood volume and puts higher pressure on the artery walls, leading to clinical hypertension.
Action plan
The Tamil Nadu government’s plan is appropriately comprehensive. For the first time, a statewide survey using urine samples will scientifically measure salt consumption. Salt will be gradually reduced in government-run kitchens, including the Nutritious Meal Programme, ICDS centres, government hospitals and hostels. The feasibility of introducing a low-sodium salt substitute will be examined.
This will be backed by a state-wide awareness campaign on how to read labels on packages, tasting before adding salt and using natural flavour enhancers. Researchers of a randomised, double-blind, controlled trial reported in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, in 2021, wrote that the replacement of salt with a reduced-sodium, added-potassium salt substitute is an acceptable and effective dietary intervention for lowering systolic blood pressure in persons with hypertension in rural India.
The State also intends to step up its hypertension control activities through its community health outreach programme ‘Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam’ and other public health care institutions. People diagnosed with hypertension will receive systematic counselling and anti-hypertension drugs. There is evidence that such closely-monitored health interventions succeed. A study published recently in Nature, Archana Ramalingam et al., studying the cascade of care between 2019-20 and 2023-24 in Tamil Nadu, showed that overall, hypertension care in Tamil Nadu improved, with increased use of public health facilities for treatment.
The Sapiens Health Foundation has welcomed the new salt reduction campaign of the Tamil Nadu government. Founder Rajan Ravichandran says: “This is a wonderful surprise; we have been knocking at many doors to bring in awareness of salt reduction in the public health sector. It can be very powerful in changing the way people consume salt. We just have to go back to 2005, when the campaign initiated by Graham MacGregor of the World Action on Salt, Sugar and Health resulted in a reported 30% reduction of salt in bread in the United Kingdom,” Dr. Rajan adds.
G. Sengottuvelu, senior interventional cardiologist, Apollo Hospitals, explains further: “Excess salt is one of the most important and preventable contributors to high blood pressure, heart attack and stroke.” His argument is that Indians’ preference for salty food is largely an acquired habit, often beginning in childhood, and the palate can adapt when salt is gradually reduced. Cutting down salt is a simple change that can make a major difference to cardiovascular health — less salt today can mean lower blood pressure, fewer heart attacks and fewer strokes tomorrow.
Incidentally, the regulator Food Safety and Standards Association of India’s submission of guidelines for ingredient labelling on packaged food has grabbed eyeballs. While experts point to lacunae within the labelling guidelines, it does seem that momentum is growing towards building a society that is aware of the importance of salt and regulating it, and reclaiming the kitchen staple as a transformative touchstone for improved public health. As Tamil Nadu rolls out its programme, hopefully with scientific vigour and cultural sensitivity, other States will do well to watch and emulate. If it is possible to cut down hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and kidney disease with adjusting the size of a single pinch, then, the question is why not?

Indian Startup IPOs In Full Swing Indian startup IPO spring is in full bloom. Snapdeal parent AceVector is all set to list on the bourses next month, Spinny has filed its draft IPO papers, and Furlenco is pushing the needle on its D-Street debut. Snapdeal’s IPO Deck: In its second attempt at a listing, the Snapdeal parent’s ₹420 Cr issue blends a ₹287 Cr fresh raise and a trimmed OFS of 4.16 Cr shares. It has also set the IPO price band at ₹30-₹32, valuing the company at ₹1,741 Cr at the upper end of the spectrum. The IPO will open next week. What works in AceVector’s favour is its healthy top line, improving unit economics, non-metro focus, value ecommerce play and a stake in Unicommerce. Spinny Files DRHP: The used car marketplace has confidentially filed its DRHP for a ₹2,500-₹3,000 Cr IPO, targeting a 2027 listing. With revenue nearing ₹6,000 Cr in FY26 and losses narrowing, Spinny is betting on its full-stack retail, financing and ancillary services to sustain growth and woo investors. Furlenco Gears Up For IPO, Too: Following rival RentoMojo’s suit, Furlenco has also kicked off its IPO proceedings. The startup plans to soon appoint ICICI Securities as an advisor for its up to ₹1,200 Cr public issue, which will target a valuation of around ₹7,000 Cr. Furlenco is looking to launch the IPO in FY28. The Broader IPO Wave: New-age tech companies continue to make a beeline for the public markets. As per Inc42 data, 24 startups have already filed their DRHPs, while over 25 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO, Razorpay and Zetwerk alone could raise over ₹34,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs. Startups now see IPOs as a credible exit and growth capital source. Recent strong debuts, policy support and investor appetite for niche businesses are further encouraging founders. With much on the anvil, here is all about who is debuting on the bourses next… From The Editor’s Desk 🏭 Zetwerk-Ayr Settle Dispute The two companies have reached a settlement by agreeing to dismiss all claims asserted in lawsuits, pending before a US business court and a Bengaluru court. The financial and other terms of the settlement have not been disclosed. Zetwerk had alleged that Ayr founder Anirudh Reddy downloaded hundreds of files and used the data to pursue Zetwerk’s clients. Ayr denied the allegations and filed counter claims accusing Zetwerk of trade-secret theft and trademark infringement. The resolution removes a major legal overhang as Zetwerk prepares for its IPO. The B2B manufacturing startup last month filed its DRHP with SEBI for a public issue, which comprises a fresh issue of shares worth ₹2,600 Cr and an OFS of up to 9.6 Cr shares. 🤖 Sol Foundry Bags $4 Mn Emerging out of stealth mode, the AI startup has raised ₹38 Cr in a funding round from General Catalyst, Nexus Venture Partners and others to fuel R&D, AI model development and hiring. Founded in 2025, Sol Foundry’s AI assistant can research a topic, assemble a document, find calendar slots and draft replies using context drawn from scattered email conversations. The model-agnostic platform initially plans to target professionals. The startup is pre-revenue and has not yet finalised pricing. It plans to explore usage- or outcome-based billing plus a fixed component. It is also pursuing a prosumer-first model, allowing individuals to sign up before expanding into enterprise sales. 📉 Captain Fresh’s FY26 Show The B2B seafood brand claims to have retained profitability in FY26. This came on the back of consolidated net revenue zooming 52% YoY to ₹5,169 Cr in the fiscal under review and adjusted EBITDA nearly tripling YoY to ₹371 Cr. Meanwhile, Captain Fresh was saddled with a debt of ₹2,300 Cr at the end of FY26, which the startup attributed to higher working capital requirements during the fiscal. The company now claims to be on track to achieve ₹10,000 Cr in revenue in FY27. Founded in 2020, Captain Fresh operates a global packaged seafood business. It sources seafood from more than 30 countries and serves nearly 2,500 customers. The IPO-bound startup has raised nearly $250 Mn to date. 📱 PhonePe Sets Eyes On The UAE The Walmart-backed fintech giant has received in-principle nod from the Central Bank of the UAE for two payment licences. The approvals will enable the startup to offer retail payment services and issue stored-value products such as digital wallets. This takes PhonePe another step closer to launching its payments operation outside India. However, the fintech major will still have to fulfil the remaining regulatory requirements to begin commercial operations in the Middle Eastern nation. The development comes days after PhonePe’s monetisation prospects in India received a boost from the reintroduction of MDR on certain UPI transactions. On the back of this, the startup has revived its IPO plans and is now targeting a public listing by March 2027. 🔍 ED Chargesheets EMT Cofounder The Enforcement Directorate has filed a chargesheet against EaseMyTrip cofounder and chairman Nishant Pitti in the Mahadev online betting app money laundering case. Pitti said he was not aware of any chargesheet and would contest any such charges. The agency also provisionally attached demat shares belonging to Pitti worth ₹59.6 Cr under the PMLA. The ED has also sought a special PMLA court’s permission to confiscate the shares, alleging that they constitute proceeds of crime. The agency has accused him of facilitating the entry of alleged illegal betting proceeds into the Indian stock market through FPIs. Even last year, ED had alleged that Pitti was connected to a network that used betting proceeds to manipulate several stocks. Inc42 Markets Inc42 Startup Spotlight Can Agriculture Fund Vaimanika’s Defence Ambitions? India’s drone industry is growing. But farmers still lack access to affordable drone spraying, while defence forces need mission-ready UAVs for high-risk operations. Vaimanika Aerospace is addressing both needs through drone services and a vertically-integrated stack. A Full-Stack Operator: Founded in 2022, Vaimanika operates an agriculture-focused drone-as-a-service network. Farmers and institutional customers can access precision spraying on a pay-per-acre basis. The startup also earns through drone sales, pilot training, maintenance and franchise-led services. Its agriculture network includes around 210 drones and has generated nearly ₹35 Cr in spraying revenue. The Defence Portfolio: Vaimanika’s second growth engine is defence. Its portfolio spans heavy-payload UAVs, ISR platforms, FPVs and counter-UAS systems. Its systems have undergone field validation with Indian Army formations, including high-altitude trials and a 105 kg payload test. Integrating Vertically: The startup is developing its own airframes, avionics, ground-control stations, communications hardware, battery systems and autonomous-flight software. Greater control over these mission-critical components could help Vaimanika customise systems for difficult terrain and reduce reliance on external suppliers. Eye On The Prize: Vaimanika claims to have clocked ₹52.6 Cr in revenue in FY26 against a profit after tax of ₹9.47 Cr. The startup is now converting the cash and engineering base from its agri-focused drone business to fund its defence UAV pitch. So, can Vaimanika disrupt the status quo and build a scalable drone tech business?
