International watchdog calls for protection of journalists ahead of Serbia election
An international media watchdog says that journalists in Serbia are increasingly under threat of violence and hostility ahead of a high-stakes early parliamentary election that will test populist President Aleksandar Vucic’s rule
BELGRADE, Serbia -- An international media watchdog has warned that journalists in Serbia are increasingly under threat of violence and hostility ahead of a high-stakes early parliamentary election next month that will test populist President Aleksandar Vucic 's rule.
The Committee to Protect Journalists urged Vucic's government this week to ensure that journalists can follow the Oct. 25 ballot “safely and without fear.”
“Journalists covering the polls are at serious risk of threats, violence and hostility of the sort that has become increasingly common” during Vucic's term, CPJ said in a statement released on Tuesday.
The group called on “Serbia's European partners to monitor the situation closely, encourage Belgrade to guarantee the rule of law is respected and speak out to challenge violations of press freedom.”
The Serbian government did not immediately respond to an Associated Press request for a comment. In the past, Serbia's Ministry of Information has told the AP it condemned any attacks on journalists and urged a quick state reaction.
An international mission in March documented escalating police violence, smear campaigns fueled by public officials, persistent impunity, legal and digital threats and the ruling party’s efforts to tighten its grip over the media, CPJ said.
Serbia is formally seeking membership in the European Union but the effort has stalled under Vucic, who has faced accusations of clamping down on democratic freedoms, including the media. Since coming to power in 2012, the ruling populist party has gradually established control over mainstream media while often describing embattled critical outlets as enemies of the state.
Danica Vucenic, who works on N1 regional television, in June received a letter threatening both her and her family. She told the AP over the phone that she routinely reports all threats to the authorities but there has been no result.
“It's a waste of time because I will receive more threats and report again,” Vucenic said. “It will not end until Serbia becomes a democratic country.”
Vucic and his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party face a challenge in the October vote from a youth-led movement that was behind nearly two years of street protests triggered by a train station tragedy in November 2024. Tensions are expected to be high as the populists seek to stay in power despite widespread popular discontent.
Attila Mong, CPJ’s Europe representative, described the reality for journalists in Serbia as “alarming.” He cited violence in the streets, threats and “relentless” efforts to discredit their work, often coming from senior government officials.
“Ahead of the October elections, conditions for journalists are getting worse,” he said. “We have multiple reports of journalists being assaulted while out doing their jobs at rallies and other political gatherings, and online the atmosphere is increasingly febrile.”
CPJ listed recommendations for the authorities that included public instructions to the police, rapid response to threats and condemnation of violence, while ensuring protection for journalists and availability of election candidates.
Vucenic, who is an experienced journalist with a long career in Serbia's independent media, also told the AP that she is trying to ignore the threats and live and work normally. She blamed Serbia's political authorities for the atmosphere.
“Journalists are being treated as enemies of the state,” she said. “That has made our existence unsafe.”

Mohamed Salah given six-month driving ban
- Published
Former Liverpool footballer Mohamed Salah has been banned from driving for six months after his Rolls-Royce was clocked speeding.
Salah failed to tell police who was at the wheel when the car was caught by a speed camera driving at 36mph (58 km/h) on a 30mph (48km/h) stretch of road in Wilmslow, Cheshire, on 27 March, according to court documents.
The 34-year-old did not respond to the notice of the prosecution, brought by Cheshire Police, and did not enter a plea to the charge.
He was handed a six-month driving ban and ordered to pay £1,044 in a hearing at Warrington Combined Court.
A court spokeswoman said Salah was prosecuted under the Single Justice Procedure, which sees magistrates sit in private hearings, and was convicted of failing to give information relating to the identification of the driver of the Rolls-Royce.
The speeding offence came days after the Egypt captain announced he would be leaving Liverpool following nine years with the team.
Announcing his departure on 24 March, the club said he had "firmly established himself as one of the greatest players in Liverpool's history".
He scored 257 goals in 442 appearances for Liverpool, before transferring to Turkish side Trabzonspor following the 2025-26 season.

Japan’s 17-year-old wunderkind Shin Ohashi set the men’s 200-meter breaststroke world record on the way to Asian Games gold on Thursday, soaking up the moment in front of a thrilled home crowd.
Ohashi’s blistering time of 2:04.83 at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre eclipsed the previous mark (2:05.48) set by China’s Qin Haiyang at the 2023 world championships in Fukuoka.
“The world record was my goal so I’m very happy to get it,” he told reporters.
“Thanks to my fans, my family, all who supported me.
“My next goal is for the gold medal at the world championships.”
Ohashi’s triumph comes days after French great Leon Marchand, the Olympic 200m breaststroke champion, praised the Japanese swimmer as a major threat, saying he was “scared” of his potential.

Meta is building a dedicated hardware device for its new Muse AI agent. The product, called Muse Charm, was briefly shown off by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg at the end of his Meta Connect presentation. It looks almost like a chunky smart watch without the strap — just a big screen, plus a little lanyard for carrying the device around.
Meta is making a standalone Muse AI gadget
The Muse Charm doesn’t require a phone, and it’s supposed to ship this year.
The Muse Charm has a fingerprint sensor on the top right corner, which you can press to activate and begin speaking to the agent. There appears to be a small camera on the device as well, plus what looks like at least three holes for microphones on the front. Zuckerberg said you don’t have to unlock a phone or open an app to use the Charm, but he didn’t share how it’s actually connecting to Meta’s servers.
Meta plans to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but as of now Zuckerberg says the company has “only built a few of these so far.” The company still needs to finalize “the finishing material,” he said. Throughout the keynote, he teased the device and made references to a translucent exterior that would let you see the gadget’s internals. He referred to it as an “elevated hacker aesthetic.”
Zuckerberg promised to share more details “soon.”

Ex-Tottenham midfielder Bissouma set to join Ajax
- Published
Former Tottenham midfielder Yves Bissouma is on the verge of joining Ajax on an initial deal that runs until the end of the season.
The defensive midfielder, 30, was out of contract following his release from Spurs in June but is now set for a return to football in the Netherlands.
It is understood Bissouma has agreed a deal until the end of the season with the option of a further 12 months.
The Mali international is currently in Amsterdam finalising the move to the Eredivisie club.
Bissouma joined Spurs in 2022 and made 111 appearances for the north London outfit following a high-profile move from Brighton.
In August 2025, the then Spurs manager Thomas Frank left Bissouma out of his squad to face Paris St-Germain in the Uefa Super Cup because of persistent lateness.
Bissouma made 11 appearances for Tottenham in his final season with the club, with all of them coming in the Premier League as they finished 17th for the second consecutive season.

Ex-NFL star Antonio Brown to avoid prison for 2025 shooting with plea deal, lawyer says
The Super Bowl-winning wide receiver was extradited from Dubai in November 2025 after an arrest warrant was issued

Former NFL star wide receiver Antonio Brown plans to accept a plea deal on an attempted murder charge in Miami that avoids prison as part of an agreement that his lawyer was too good to turn down.
Brown is scheduled to appear in court on Sept. 30 to make the deal final. He could have faced up to 30 years in prison if convicted of the charge.
Brown is accused of grabbing a handgun from a security staffer after a celebrity boxing match in Miami on May 16, 2025, and firing two shots at a man he had gotten into a fistfight with earlier, according to an arrest warrant. Zul-Qarnain Kwame Nantambu told investigators that one of the bullets grazed his neck.
“This was not an easy decision,” defense attorney Mark Eiglarsh said in a statement Wednesday. “Antonio believes in his innocence. He believes strongly in his Stand Your Ground defense, and he believes he would ultimately prevail at trial. But when prosecutors put an offer on the table that transforms a potential decades-long prison sentence into a significantly reduced charge and probation, there was simply no way he could reasonably turn it down.”
Florida’s so-called Stand Your Ground law allows people who believe they face death or serious injury to use deadly force to defend themselves without a duty to retreat.
The Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office declined to comment on Wednesday, with spokesperson Ed Griffith saying the details would be “fully clarified” at next week's hearing.
Brown has said on social media that he was defending himself from an attack and that others were trying to steal jewelry from him.

He spent much of his career with Pittsburgh. For his career, Brown had 928 receptions for more than 12,000 yards and accounted for 88 total touchdowns, counting punt returns and one pass.
Brown was extradited in November 2025 from Dubai, where he has business interests, after an arrest warrant on the attempted murder charge was issued in June 2025.
Brown has dealt with several legal problems over the years. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on Friday said it has initiated legal action against Nestle India Ltd for alleged non-compliance with food safety norms in three infant nutrition products.
According to FSSAI, it examined NAN Excella Pro Stage 1, Lactogen Pro 1, and a follow-up formula along with their promotional material available on e-commerce platforms.
In NAN Excella Pro Stage 1, the regulator flagged claims relating to "5HMOs" and "Whey Protein," while in Lactogen Pro 1, it observed a claim describing "Whey Protein" as easy to digest, the regulator said in a social media post.
FSSAI said it had sought clarifications from Nestle India on these claims.
Both the products were found to be in contravention of Regulation 4(2) of the Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, which restrict promotional claims or material aimed at increasing the saleability of infant foods, as well as Section 3 of the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992, which bars the advertisement or promotion of such products.
Separately, a sample of a follow-up formula manufactured by Nestle India was found sub-standard for Biotin content during laboratory analysis. The sample was sent for re-analysis, and the referral laboratory also found it non-conforming with the Biotin requirement prescribed under the 2020 regulations.
In light of these findings, FSSAI has filed three separate adjudication cases against Nestle India in respect of the three products, it added.
At 1.10 p.m., shares of Nestle India were down nearly 2% at ₹1,345.45 on the BSE.

Aaditya Thackeray responds to Satish Salian's notice, refutes allegation of defamation
Satish Salian sent the Sena (UBT) MLA a notice on September 17 alleging that Thackeray had defamed him in two posts.
Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Aaditya Thackeray on Wednesday refused to apologise to Satish Salian, late celebrity manager Disha Salian's father who sent him a ₹500 crore defamation notice last week, and dismissed his allegations as "frivolous".
His social media posts did not even mention Satish Salian, Thackeray said in his reply sent through advocate Anshuman Sinha.
Satish Salian sent the Sena (UBT) MLA a notice on September 17 alleging that Thackeray had defamed him in two posts published in English and Marathi on X the previous day.
"My client's posts addressed the sustained campaign by political actors, vested interests and sections of the media that have repeatedly linked his name with this tragic case without placing verified evidence in the two SIT investigations," Aaditya's reply said, adding that he had made no defamatory statement about Satish Salian.
"The real concern is the political use being made of this tragedy by persons seeking to advance their own agenda," it said.
Thackeray firmly stood by his earlier public statement that he had never met or known Disha Salian, the reply said.

'Be comfortable in your own identity' - Agassi's advice to Raducanu
- Published
As Emma Raducanu plots a route back to the pinnacle of tennis, the Briton has been taking inspiration from Andre Agassi's 2009 autobiography.
Five years have passed since Raducanu's remarkable US Open triumph, when at the age of 18 she became the first qualifier in the Open era to win a Grand Slam.
American Agassi was a teenage prodigy himself and later claimed the first of his eight major singles titles at Wimbledon in 1992 aged 22.
But between the peak years of his career, he had to overcome a challenging period when he went four years without a major and dropped to 141st in the world rankings.
"I was especially intrigued by the passage where he got out of his slump in the late 1990s by creating his own training regimen and finding his way back to the top," Raducanu told Uniqlo.
"It speaks in depth about his early successes and the lows he reached, perhaps as a result of them.
"A lot of it was so relatable."
Agassi said his hope was for his experiences to help other players going through similar periods in their own careers.
"It's wonderful to hear that anybody can relate," Agassi told BBC Breakfast.
"It was literally the hope that if one person read it and it gave them hope, some tools to understand that they're not alone, they can figure it out and get to a healthier place without having to direct their frustrations at the game of tennis, then it was a success for me.
"So, hearing that 17 years later it can still impact somebody, especially in this game, it does make me feel good."
Raducanu reached a career-high ranking of 10 in July 2022, but the 23-year-old has slipped to 98th in the world.
Her progress continues to be hampered by physical issues, and she most recently missed the US Open as she continues her recovery from a stress fracture in her lower right leg.
A foot injury disrupted her pre-season training before she spent two-and-a-half months off court with a post-viral illness earlier this year.
But Raducanu enjoyed one of the best weeks of her career at Queen's Club in June, reaching her biggest final since her triumph in New York five years ago.
Agassi won all four of the sport's Grand Slams and claimed Olympic singles gold at the 1996 Games.
Asked what advice he would give Raducanu, Agassi said: "I would encourage her to focus on being the best of herself on a daily basis, but don't judge that by results or thinking that somehow you have to be 100%.
"You have to learn to be 100% of whatever percent you're at [and] be comfortable in your own identity inside of that - not what people say.
"Back in my day, I could just put down the paper and not read it. Now it seems like it's harder for these youngsters to avoid."

For Agassi, tennis was by no means a childhood passion. His father, keen for his son to become the very best, would introduce him to others as a future number one tennis player.

'It was scary' – Jacks goes from hospital bed to England match-winner
- Published
Will Jacks was supposed to be going to Edinburgh last month to celebrate his mum's 60th birthday.
Instead, what the England all-rounder thought was a "tummy bug" turned out to be appendicitis.
From there, a rushed visit to the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh and emergency surgery followed.
"It was just really bad really quickly so we had to go," Jacks, 27, said.
"It was, obviously, completely random and quite scary. I was lucky to be looked after really well by the NHS."
Jacks was given an initial four-week recovery period but ended up returning a few days early to captain the Lions in a warm-up against Sri Lanka on 11 September.
Afterwards he played in all three T20s in England's series sweep against the same opponents, and on Tuesday took career-best 50-over figures of 5-22 in the first one-day international in Chester-le-Street.
"Luckily they were able to do a slight incision and not have to rip me open completely," he said.
Appendix operations are not rare but they do not fit naturally with the twisting and turning of a spin bowler's action, meaning Jacks has been doing extra work behind the scenes to rebuild his core strength.
It makes the 4.3 degrees of turn Jacks found at Chester-le-Street – the most he has produced at home in his ODI career – even more impressive, albeit helped by a slow pitch.
His figures were also the second best by an England spinner in one-day internationals.
"It was more of a confidence thing," he said.
"It helped that we were playing the T20s first and I was bowling a maximum of four overs.
"If I am honest, I only bowled five days before the first game because I was building up my strength and trying to get some fitness back.
"I didn't bowl too much in the T20 series, which probably benefited me. It has been OK."
Jacks' match in the north east also included an important 46 not out with the bat.
Though he was eventually left stranded, he batted responsibly, hitting only one four in his first 43 deliveries, to make sure England's innings was extended from 211-7 in the 39th over to 265 in the penultimate.
"I came in and found it really difficult to start off," he said.
"I just re-evaluated what I thought was a good score and obviously what then happened with wickets falling around me a change of the role, just try and bat out the overs."
For so long "batting out the overs" has not been the England way, but Jacks is a player growing in maturity.
He is also vice-captain to Harry Brook for these Sri Lanka series in the absence of Jacob Bethell and has become an increasingly vocal member of the group.
It was telling that when England's T20 World Cup campaign began earlier this year amid the cloud of Brook's Wellington episode, Jacks was first put up to speak to the media.
"He's just a good leader," Brook said, plainly.
Reliable off the field, Jacks is becoming increasingly so on it.
It is 18 months since he moved from the top of the order to the middle as England's finisher in T20 and 50-over cricket.
After obvious success as England's player of the tournament at the T20 World Cup in India and Sri Lanka, this was another sign of his growing confidence and ability to do what is needed. Finishers rarely arrive in ideal situations, but their impact can often be match-defining.
"I feel very comfortable going out there on the day and any situation can arise which I really enjoy," Jacks said.
"It is not the same every day which you get opening so it keeps that fresh element to the game.
"At the beginning of my career it felt like you are just fighting to play in the next game, which is not the best place to be.
"It is a luxury to know, say when we go to Headingley [for the second ODI], that I will be in the team. You can't take that for granted and appreciate the hard work you have done to get there."
It is also easy to forget Jacks began the year in England's Test side, as their spinning all-rounder during the Ashes - a role now filled by Dan Lawrence.
Jacks, who met new Test coach Stephen Fleming when the New Zealander joined the white-ball squad at Old Trafford last weekend, has is signed up for a stint with MI Cape Town in the SA20 this winter.
There would no clash there with Fleming's first tour in charge in South Africa over Christmas, but the later part of the T20 competition overlaps with England's two Tests in Bangladesh, where English spinners will be needed.
"I don't know about what would happen or even if they would want me," he said.
"We will finish the summer before getting into the winter."
For now, Jacks will focus on white-ball trips to Pakistan, Australia and South Africa as England build towards the 50-over World Cup next autumn.
One downside of a Test recall would be losing more time to rearrange that Edinburgh trip.
"It didn't go how we planned but we will have to find time to redo it," Jacks smiled.

Out of nowhere, a woman’s right arm and leg started shaking uncontrollably. In the moments leading up to the experience, she seemed well; she had no headache, confusion, or weakness. But for about a minute, half of her body juddered.
The woman, a rice farmer in the Philippines, headed to the emergency department. There, doctors gave her a physical exam and found nothing out of the ordinary. Then they took a look at her brain. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a bright cluster of nodules surrounded by fluid in her left frontal lobe. The doctors had an immediate guess as to what they were: worm eggs.
In a case report published in the latest issue of the New England Journal of Medicine, doctors write that they suspected the woman had neuroschistosomiasis, an uncommon complication of an infection with a Schistosoma parasitic worm, aka a blood fluke. In the Philippines, the most common fluke is S. japonicum. It’s also found in China and part of Indonesia; despite its name, it has been eliminated from Japan.
An unfortunate fluke
S. japonicum, like its relatives, has a diabolical life cycle, which starts with its eggs being shed in the urine or feces of various animals, including humans. When conditions are right, the eggs hatch into a free-swimming larval form. These seek out specific types of aquatic snails, which they bore into and inhabit to go through two life stages. Late-stage larvae then burst out, grow a forked tail, and swim to find an animal host. These tailed larvae, called cercariae, have the ability to tunnel through intact skin and take a trip through the vascular system—visiting the lungs, heart, and then liver, where they develop into adults.
The adult male and female worms live paired together with the slender female worm tucked into a groove within the thicker male. Adult worms typically move to large blood vessels in the abdomen connecting the liver to the intestines. From there, the cuddly couples spew out eggs that make their way into feces and urine.

The resignation of Congress MLA Yashwanthrayagouda V. Patil of Indi taluk in Vijayapura district over the failure to declare his constituency drought-hit embarrassed the D.K. Shivakumar-led government in the Legislative Assembly on Wednesday (September 23, 2026).
Mr. Patil submitted his resignation to Speaker G.S. Patil on September 22, saying he was unable to meet the expectations of people in his constituency amid the drought situation. He said farmers had suffered crop losses, and people and livestock were facing water shortages.
Mr. Patil’s resignation was his second such move this year. In August, he had resigned from the Assembly after being denied a Cabinet berth but withdrew it following persuasion by Congress leaders.
BJP takes up issue
Raising the issue during the debate on drought, Leader of the Opposition R. Ashok demanded that the Speaker announce whether he had accepted or rejected the resignation or kept it pending. BJP members raised slogans of “shame, shame” against the government.
Mr. Ashok recalled Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar’s earlier statement that he would accept a resignation within minutes if any legislator resigned and questioned the delay in deciding on Mr. Patil’s resignation. He said the resignation reflected the government’s failure to handle the drought situation, leading to heated exchanges between the Opposition and Treasury benches.
In his resignation letter, Mr. Patil said farmers in Indi had borrowed money to sow crops and purchase fertilisers after receiving some spells of rain. However, the subsequent failure of timely rainfall had resulted in crop losses and shortages of water for people and livestock.
He said he had submitted representations to the Chief Minister, Deputy Chief Minister G. Parameshwara, who also holds the Revenue portfolio, on August 28, seeking that Indi be declared drought-hit.
Of the 13 taluks in Vijayapura district, 11 have been declared drought-hit, while Indi and Chadchan have been left out, he said. The State has so far declared 188 taluks drought-hit.
‘Pressure tactics work’
“As an MLA from the ruling party, I did not want to cause embarrassment to the government and adopted a nuanced approach. There is no value to my words or feelings,” Mr Patil said in his letter. He added that, in the prevailing political atmosphere, those who were powerful or used pressure tactics were able to get things done, while there was little space for those who adopted a gentle approach.
During the heated debate, Mr. Parameshwara blamed the BJP-led Union government for restricting the State’s ability to declare more taluks drought-hit. “We have written 10 letters to the Centre seeking relaxation in the drought manual,” he said.
Mr. Shivakumar said the government was not discriminating against constituencies on the basis of political affiliation. “I cannot decide on declaring drought taluks. There are parameters. Many MLAs are asking us to declare their constituencies drought-hit,” he said.
Describing Mr. Patil’s resignation as an emotional response, Mr. Shivakumar said, "The Indi MLA was emotional. I have pacified him.”
After the Opposition and the government presented their arguments, the Speaker told the House that he had rejected Mr. Patil’s resignation, as it did not comply with the rules.
Mr. Patil’s latest resignation came a day after senior Congress legislator and former Minister H.K. Patil said he would resign if Gadag taluk was not declared drought-hit by October 10. Now, the Gadag taluk has been given the drought tag.

Poland accuses Russian military helicopter of violating its airspace
- Published
Poland has said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing the Nato member to scramble fighter jets while ground forces remained on alert.
Its military said the Mi-8 aircraft had crossed from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on Wednesday morning, penetrating Polish airspace to a depth of about 300 metres (328 yards) and staying for 42 seconds north of Braniewo.
It said "the nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence". Moscow did not comment immediately.
Poland and other European Nato members have recently said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine - Moscow denies this.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states.
By contrast, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said this month that it was Europe that was constantly talking about preparing for war, and he warned: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short."
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014.
In a statement, the Polish Army Operational Command said the brief incursion had happened at 11:08 (09:08 GMT), and the helicopter had been tracked by radar.
Poland's air defence units were operating around the clock ready to "ensure the safety of Polish airspace", it added.
A number of Russian drones and one unarmed Russian missile have landed in Poland since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which is not a member of Nato.
Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank.
"In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans... has intensified," he said.
"The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine."
French President Emmanuel Macron said shortly afterwards that his country had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks, vowing that this would not be left "without a response".
Macron said he had already ordered a plan to protect the country's critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.
Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.
These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.
There have recently been a number of suspicious fires and blasts at defence facilities in a number of European Nato members from Italy to Bulgaria to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia.
Earlier this month, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig airport - an accusation denied by Moscow as "absurd".
And earlier this week, Lithuania's prime minister told the BBC that his country had already made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they would "not surrender" if attacked.
Ukraine said the drone's target "could have been the diplomatic train", while the Russian military said only that it had struck "railway infrastructure".

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has cautioned against the indiscriminate, repeated, or prolonged use of painkillers and antibiotics, citing the associated risk of chronic kidney disease and renal impairment.
In a circular dated September 21, 2026, the regulator said non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and antibiotics are regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the Drugs Rules, 1945, and are required to be sold and distributed on the prescription of a registered medical practitioner.
The CDSCO said most NSAIDs are included in Schedule H of the Drugs Rules and cannot be sold at retail without a prescription. Most antibiotics are included in Schedule H1 and carry warnings that they should not be taken except in accordance with medical advice and should not be sold without a prescription.
The circular directed stakeholders, including healthcare professionals, pharmacists, retailers, hospitals, and State drug control authorities, to ensure that such medicines are used only when clinically indicated, at the appropriate dose and for the appropriate duration.
‘Don’t self-medicate’
The regulator advised the public not to self-medicate with antibiotics or use them for conditions where they are not clinically indicated, including most uncomplicated viral infections. It also said antibiotics prescribed by a healthcare professional should be taken strictly as advised and should neither be shared nor used from leftover medicines.
People with pre-existing kidney disease or other risk factors for renal impairment have been advised to inform their healthcare professionals before taking NSAIDs. The CDSCO also urged people to seek medical advice if pain, fever, or other symptoms persist or recur instead of repeatedly taking painkillers or antibiotics on their own.
Advise for medical professionals
For healthcare professionals, the regulator recommended considering a patient’s age, comorbidities, other medicines and risk factors before prescribing these drugs. It said the lowest effective dose for the shortest appropriate duration should be considered when prescribing NSAIDs, particularly for those at increased risk of renal impairment.
Doctors have also been advised to follow antimicrobial stewardship principles while prescribing antibiotics and to avoid unnecessary combination therapy, inappropriate drug selection, incorrect dosing, and unnecessarily prolonged treatment.
Pharmacists and retailers have been directed to strictly comply with statutory requirements governing Schedule H and H1 drugs and not facilitate self-medication.
The CDSCO has also asked hospitals and healthcare institutions to strengthen systems for rational prescribing, prescription review, antimicrobial stewardship, and patient counselling. State and Union Territory drug control authorities have been asked to create awareness about the risks and regulatory requirements.

What is the cost of a life? For the wife and 20-year-old son Chongtham Vikram Singh, it is the lifelong grief and trauma of losing a family member. For Manipur, it is the loss of a homegrown musical talent, who began practicing his craft when he was a child, and made his way from Imphal to the big stages of Delhi. And for the rest of India, it is a reckoning with the systemic racism that has historically exposed Northeasterners living in other parts of the country to racial discrimination, harassment, bullying and violence.
The concerns are not new, nor were solutions entirely out of reach. The Bezbaruah Committee, set up by the Manmohan Singh-led UPA government to address the discrimination faced by people from the Northeast, had made a series of recommendations to the Modi cabinet in 2014. A key component of the proposals was making changes to the Indian Penal Code (IPC). Twelve years on, this is yet to be implemented.
Accused ‘Wanted to Teach a Lesson’ to the Manipuri Guitarist
Singh, a 55-year-old Manipuri guitarist, was allegedly beaten to death by a group of young men outside his home in Kilokari village of Southwest Delhi. On September 6, around 11:30 pm, Singh had objected to the loud noise and commotion being created by the accused outside his apartment.
According to the police complaint, when his son heard him shouting, he opened the door to see the group of men violently attacking Singh. After the altercation, Singh returned home but complained of breathlessness, he was then taken to Holy Family Hospital where he succumbed to his injuries at 6 am on September 7. CCTV footage showed the accused leaving the building. Seven men and a minor have been arrested in the case so far.
A Manipuri music teacher, Chongtham Vikram Singh, living in Delhi’s Ashram area was mob lynched by 8 people following a dispute over alleged noise and nuisance outside his residence.
Police said seven accused have been arrested and a minor detained in connection with the case.… pic.twitter.com/4V0LVeVLiJ
— Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear) September 7, 2026
The autopsy report revealed that Singh died of massive internal bleeding caused by severe physical trauma to his chest and abdomen. The accused allegedly kicked him on the chest and abdomen after he fell to the ground. During questioning, they told the police that they wanted to teach Singh a lesson.
While the police investigation so far has not revealed any racial motive behind the violent attack, his death has brought to the fore larger concerns around hate faced by people from the Northeast in the nation’s capital and beyond. It also brings the Bezbaruah Committee’s recommendations, and the fate of those recommendations, back into focus.
The Bezbaruah Committee and Administrative Inaction
The Bezbaruah Committee was formed in February, 2014, after the killing of Nido Tania, a 20-year-old hailing from Arunachal Pradesh, who was beaten to death with iron rods and sticks by three men after a verbal altercation in Delhi. The accused hurled racial slurs at Tania during the attack. The committee was constituted “to look into the various concerns of persons hailing from the Northeastern states who are living in different parts of the country, especially the Metropolitan areas, and to suggest suitable remedial measures which could be taken by the Government.” It submitted its report to the MHA of the BJP government in July, 2014. It can be read here.
The most crucial among the recommendations, perhaps, was a proposal to amend the provisions of the then IPC by adding Sections 153C and 509A. Section 153C would criminalise words, signs or acts that promote discrimination or violence on grounds of race or place of origin, with up to five years’ imprisonment and a fine. Section 509A would criminalise any word, gesture or act intended to insult a member of a racial group, with up to three years and a fine.
On January 2, 2015, then Union home minister Rajnath Singh said that the amendments were accepted and Sections 153C and 509A would be added as recommended by the Committee. However, In 2017, minister of state, home, Kiren Rijiju said in the Rajya Sabha the proposal was still under examination, with states’ views being sought. Later, when the IPC was being officially changed to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) in 2024 and discussions were being held from 2023, the recommended amendments were entirely overlooked. The provisions were never enacted.
On September 8, 2026, two days after Singh’s killing, the MHA’s monitoring committee on Northeast issues convened a meeting to discuss the recommendations made more than a decade ago. Joram Maivio, a special invitee to the monitoring committee, MHA, and member of the Bezbaruah Committee, spoke to Alt News.
“We were expecting most of the recommendations of the Bezbaruah Committee to be slowly implemented after we received a confirmation from the MHA in 2015. We deliberated extensively on this with the judicial division of the MHA, after which the recommendation was sent to the law commission and the law ministry. It kept going from one department to another. We were verbally, or in principle, informed that it had been accepted and that it would be included when the comprehensive amendment of the IPC took place,” Maivio said.
“The discussions continued through 2017, 2018 and 2019 as the Supreme Court had ordered the committee to meet at least every three years and in serious instances, meetings can be called at any point. In every meeting we kept discussing the issue of racial discrimination and questioning when the law would be amended so as to criminalise racism against Northeasterners. So when the comprehensive criminal law amendments came in 2023 — the BNS, BSA and BNSS — we were expecting this recommendation to be included. But surprisingly, it did not come up,” he added.
Maivio said that he had flagged this on the two or three MHA monitoring committee meetings and questioned the ministry why the amendments had not taken place, but did not receive any concrete answer.
Meanwhile, Delhi police data accessed by The Indian Express in June 2026 showed that more than half of the accused in cases registered over the past 12 years for crimes against people from the Northeast in Delhi remained “untraced” despite “the creation of a specialised police unit intended to address such cases”. Out of the 2,656 FIRs filed between 2014 and April 30, 2026, in 1,465 (or 55%) cases, the accused were classified as untraced. Only 33 cases resulted in conviction, producing a conviction rate of 1.82 per cent.
Asked about what transpired at the September 8 review meeting, Maivio said, “The committee director and joint secretary said that the amendments would be taken up but we were not given any clear timeline as to when.”
“We will keep following up to ensure justice to people from Northeast as incidents of racial violence are chronic and recurring. There is no quick-fix solution, but by denying the reality, we cannot solve the problem. The Government must continue to act decisively to address it and prevent such incidents,” he asserted.
Maivio noted that some measures were implemented in Delhi, including the creation a Special Police Unit for North East Region (SPUNER) with the helpline number, 1093, two special Delhi Police recruitment drives in the Northeast, and plans for a Northeast Social and Cultural Institute in Dwarka. However, he acknowledged that implementation has largely remained confined to Delhi, with little progress in other states.
Northeasterners Condemn Killing, Speak out Against Discrimination
The North Eastern Students’ Organisation (NESO) condemned Vikram’s killing and demanded an impartial probe. Chairman Samuel B Jyrwa, who in 2024 also demanded that Prime Minister Narendra Modi “breaks his silence” and visits the crisis-struck Manipur, told the media: “It is deeply disturbing that a person can lose his life merely for raising an objection to disturbance outside his own home…For years, Northeastern citizens living, studying and working outside the region have repeatedly reported being subjected to racial slurs, verbal abuse, physical attacks, social discrimination and other forms of humiliation because of their appearance, identity and place of origin.”
“It is a very big loss not just for us but also for the music fraternity…We want justice and we want the government to ensure that people from the Northeast are treated as Indians in Delhi,” said Singh’s brother, Chongtham Vivek, as the former’s mortal remains were brought back to Imphal.

It is a very big loss not just for us but also for the music fraternity. We want justice. An atmosphere should be created in the capitals of India… pic.twitter.com/QmHjnTkk3W
— ANI (@ANI) September 9, 2026
Speaking to Alt News, the convenor of Delhi-based The Mizo Welfare Association, Thangzamang Henry Simte, condemned the killing and said, “Our organisation was built to create a community and safe space for people from Mizoram and the Northeast living in Delhi, who regularly face racial discrimination and stereotyping in educational institutes, office spaces, or even while taking public transport. The root cause is lack of education in the rest of the country about the Northeast. Some people in Delhi don’t even know which part of India is Mizoram or Nagaland…they do not know the difference between foreigners from other Asian countries and Northeasterns of their country.”
Simte left Nagaland around 26 years ago and moved to Delhi due to ethnic conflicts in his region. He said in 2003, when he was still new to the city, he was routinely referred to as ‘Nepali’ by passerby on the road. “In one particular incident that stayed with me, a man in a suit and tie who was sitting next to me at a bike servicing centre, suddenly yelled ‘Nepali’ at me unprompted. When I retorted sharply, he asked me where I was from. As I replied ‘Mizoram’, he bluntly asked, ‘where is that? Is that in India?”
Alt News spoke to people from the Northeast living in various parts of India, who, like Simte, revealed the daily, oft-normalised patterns of racial stereotyping and harassment they continue to face.
Gopi Kishan Baro (28), who hails from Assam and is currently working as a graphic designer in Gurgaon, alleged that he was systematically discriminated against and bullied by a senior colleague at work. “A few weeks ago, when we were in the lift, he kept mocking me and said something which sounded rather like a warning, ‘Tumahari aankhein choti hai aur hum dikhte nahi, iska ye matlab nahi hum gayab ho gaye hai’ (Your eyes are small, so we are not visible to you but that doesn’t mean we have disappeared). It made me quote uncomfortable but I tried to laugh it off because I did not want to create a scene,” he alleged.
He continued: “Last Wednesday, when I was having tea by myself, he appeared and claimed I stayed aloof most of the time because I came from such a faraway corner. By the end of the conversation when I was leaving, he shouted at me, ‘Waapis chale jaa apne desh’ (Go back to your country). I wrote a formal email to the HR about his racist behaviour. They simply let him off with a warning, while I continue to live in anxiety and disgust, knowing that these insults are directed not just to me, but at my kin, my community, and the entirety of Northeast India as well.”
Heightened Racism During Covid-19
COVID-19 brought this prejudice into sharper focus, as Northeasterners in several places were subjected to racial slurs, harassment and stigma.
Twenty-eight-year-old musician Abhibyanjana, who hails from Sikkim, lived in Pune for her studies and later in Mumbai for work. “When I was studying, as part of my course we were required to visit several slum pockets for a survey in early 2020, during the beginning of the pandemic. I was constantly referred to as ‘Covid’ or ‘Corona’ by locals there. I was jeered at and humiliated but I continued my work regardless, I realised that if I cannot fight back deeply indoctrinated prejudice against people who look like me,” she said.
“I have to move to cities like Mumbai for opportunities because it is scarce in Gangtok. But as a musician working in Mumbai, I am often treated as an ‘outsider’. The discrimination and otherisation against the people of Northeast is pervasive and crimes against our people hardly receive national focus. On the flipside, this has created solidarity within our community, we look out for each other wherever we go,” she added.
A 2022 study, published in the International Social Science Journal, titled ‘‘You people have brought the virus here’: Othering experience of northeastern people amid COVID‐19 in Delhi, India’, focused on how the Covid‐19 pandemic exacerbated discrimination, violence, and othering against Northeasterners living in Delhi, by analysing nineteen qualitative interviews.
The study, conducted to understand their lived experiences in Delhi before and after the pandemic, found that the pandemic disproportionately impacted the Northeastern people living away from their home states. “The Mongoloid features make them ‘non‐belonging’ and outsiders. The experience of othering is an everyday phenomenon for northeasterners… Northeasterners’ experience amid COVID‐19 is dominated by stigmatisation and bullying, as they are being targeted and arbitrarily accused of spreading the virus,” the study highlighted.
An earlier study, commissioned by the Indian Council of Social Science Research (ICSSR) in 2021, further confirms the heightened harassment, abuse, stigmatisation and blatant labelling as ‘coronavirus’ that Northeasterners faced living in other parts of India during the pandemic. Over 60% of the respondents said that their studies, work, and psychological health was impacted by these experience.
“The highest number of incidents were reported from Mumbai (44.7%)…78% of the Northeast people believed that physical appearance was the most important reason for prejudice against them,” the study noted. Mumbai was followed by by Chennai (72%), Pune (67.3%), Delhi (64%), Hyderabad (48.7%) and Bengaluru (43.3%) in racial discrimination comprising offensive and abusive language against Northeasterners.
‘You Look Like a Chinese’
Caroline Devi-Singh (52), who hails from Manipur, moved to Delhi in 1994 to pursue her graduation at Delhi University. She later moved to Chandigarh and subsequently Chhattisgarh. She told Alt News that her experiences living in North India for so many years had been varied, but racial stereotyping was a constant. “In college, we were often called racial slurs, either ‘Chinese’ or ‘Chinki’ or ‘Momo’. As a young girl, I was always taught to be extra cautious, to a point where dressing how we do at home was a threat to my safety,” she said.
“So many years later, my son [now 25-years-old] faces the same racial attacks. He has grown up with the awareness of his rights, but the rest of India still lacks awareness… Nobody thinks twice before resorting to violence against Northeastern. We have been ignored by all the governments and the media has never paid attention to our issues. I stay in a small town now and I see that even educated people cannot differentiate between a person from China and a person from the Northeast… This comes from ignorance and a lack of information. I blame the overall education system and the government for this,” she asserted.
China call us Chinese, mainland Indian call us Chinese, but we call ourselves Indians. 🙂
— Neha Gurung (@nehaGurung1692) November 27, 2025
A former student of Ashoka University, who now lives near the campus in Sonipat, said, requesting anonymity, “I moved here in 2021 from Manipur. In university, I have faced racial slurs regularly. Whenever I have brought it up with the administration, they have simply let the accused go with a warning. Racism is not taken seriously on this campus, or in the NCR region at large.”
“When Northeasterners face racism, people think it is only our responsibility to speak against it… We are always on high alert because what happened to the Manipuri musician could’ve been me. It could’ve been any of us,” he added.
A Violent Pattern Entrenched in History
The cases point to a continuum of discriminatory mindset against the people of Northeast that stretches from racial slurs and stereotyping to intimidation, physical assault and, in the most extreme cases, death. In December 2025, 24-year-old Anjel Chakma, an MBA student from Tripura, died after being allegedly attacked by a group of men in Dehradun. Anjel and his younger brother Michael were reportedly subjected to racial slurs, including being called ‘Chinki’, ‘Chinese’ and ‘Momo’, before the confrontation turned violent.
In July, 2014, 29-year-old Akha Salouni from Manipur was allegedly beaten to death by five youths in Delhi following a road rage incident. Following his death, the deceased’s family and members of the Northeastern community held a candlelight vigil at Jantar Mantar, which also saw the participation of the mother of Nido Tania.
In May 2013, 22-year-old Manipuri girl Reingamphi Awungshi was found dead in her home in Delhi under suspicious circumstances. Delhi police initially said she died by suicide, stating that severe injuries on her face and body were caused by rodents. However, her family and rights groups demanded a deeper investigation, claiming that she was sexually assaulted and murdered, pointing to local stalking complaints and police bias against Northeasterners. After 11 years, in March 2024, the Supreme Court ordered a CBI probe into Awungshi’s case. Two years on, no headway into the investigation has been publicly reported.
More recently, in February 2026, three women from Arunachal Pradesh alleged that their neighbours in Delhi’s Malviya Nagar subjected them to racial and sexist abuse during a dispute over repair work at their rented home. The women said they were called ‘dhandhewali’ and ‘momo’ and that ‘Northeastern people are shit’. In a viral video, the accused woman can be heard asking the Northeastern women, “Rs 500 mei massage parlour mei kaam karne waali dhandhewali (You work at massage parlours as sex workers for Rs 500). Are you sitting here to do business? Have you opened a massage parlour at home?” Delhi police registered an FIR and later arrested the neighbours, a couple, invoking provisions of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.
While speaking to Alt News, Maivio admitted that lack of awareness about the Northeast was the primary cause behind cases of racial discrimination. “We had recommended inclusion of the history and culture of the Northeast in school curricula and textbooks throughout the country. In our last meeting, we called the NCERT to find out what had been done so far. They said that they have included some content in Classes 9 and 10 in certain cities and that they would share it with us, which they are trying to implement countrywide. They are also preparing a documentary to be released countrywide, building awareness on the Northeast. But these have largely been verbal assurances, and we will have to see what has actually been included and whether it is sufficient,” he added.

Typhoon Dujuan has killed at least two people in Japan, while tens of thousands of houses near Tokyo remained without power after the storm swept through the region, authorities said on Tuesday.
Dujuan – which brought violent winds of 144km/h (89mph) – was moving away from Japan on Tuesday morning, allowing authorities to downgrade most heavy rain and landslide warnings.
But the typhoon had already caused deaths, destruction and widespread chaos, including disruption of some events at the Asian Games and forcing the early closure in Tokyo of the one of the world’s biggest video game trade fairs.
The city of Yokosuka in Kanagawa prefecture, near Tokyo, reported multiple landslides because of the torrential rain. Mud flowing into a home killed a woman in her 60s in Yokosuka, the public broadcaster NHK said. Another person died in Chiba.
Search operations were continuing for four people missing after the landslides, NHK said, while almost 50,000 households were still without electricity in Chibam near Tokyo on Tuesday morning.
The storm forced Japan Airlines to cancel 135 flights and All Nippon Airways to scrap 140, and more than 1.6 million residents in and around Tokyo were urged to evacuate on Monday, according to the Fire and Disaster Management Agency. The evacuations were not mandatory.
Although Dujuan weakened as it moved north-east, it dumped record rainfall in parts of the Tokyo area.
Oshima, an island about 120km south of central Tokyo, was drenched with 832mm of rain over 48 hours, more than double its average rainfall for the whole of September, NHK reported.
Rainfall in Tokyo’s Edogawa ward reached a record 282.5mm over 24 hours.
Japan often sees strong typhoons in the late summer and early autumn. But scientists say human-driven climate change is intensifying the risk posed by heavy rains because a warmer atmosphere holds more water.
Typhoon Dujuan is the latest extreme weather event in a year of unusually intense rain, floods and tropical cyclones that have hit regions across the globe, from east Asia to North America and Europe.

The L.69 group comprises pro-reform member states, including primarily developing countries from Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, Asia and the Pacific, with a united common desire to achieve comprehensive reform of the Security Council.
"As directly impacted stakeholders, L.69 and C.10 members join forces to keep pushing for UNSC reform," he said, also referring to the Committee of Ten African Ministers of Finance and Central Bank Governors (The C-10) established by the African Union in 2016.
Jaishankar, who arrived in New York City on Sunday, is leading the Indian delegation for the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.

Streaming and local film are set to send spend on content in seven major Asian markets over the $15B mark this year, according to a study.
Media Partners Asia (MPA) reports that content investment will rise from $14.8B in 2025 to $15.1B this year and on to $15.4B in 2031.
While TV currently accounting for 60% of the spend, followed by online video at 30% and film at 10%, MPA’s ‘Asia Video Content Dynamics 2026’ report noted “virtually all incremental growth comes from streaming and film as television budgets decline.”
The report assessed spend in India, Indonesia, Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam, with key findings being that while Asian video industries command large audiences and have valuable brands, this is not always “converting into attractive financial returns” and many “established media companies” are trading “well below equity book value.”
MPA is predicting those that spend wisely, rationalize costs and protect “genuine content advantages” will “increasingly separate” those that don’t.
Watch on Deadline
Within the $14.8B figure from 2025, Korea accounts for $6.9B, with India second at $5B, which is approximately 80% of the total.
MPA noted streaming has overtaken TV in India with online video accounting for 46% of content investment in 2025, compared to 42% in television. Indian audiences streamed 420 billion hours last year, with JioHotstar leading the way with a 58% of the premium VOD viewing. Sports is driving demand, with JioHotstar experiencing a boost in reach during the IPL cricket season.
In Korea, Netflix leads the way with domestic streamer TVING a clear second, while Indonesia’s Vidio, which has been profitable since the fourth quarter of last year, leading that market with six million paying subs. TVING’s extensive baseball rights helped expand its subs base from 5.3 million to 6.5 million, according to MPA.
Local film represents “the region’s clearest growth opportunity,” MPA added. This was evidenced by Vietnam’s box office rising 20% to $213M in 2025 with local titles accounting for 69%. There were similar figures in Indonesia, while India posted a record box office total of $1.41B, and local titles were attributed for a “substantial theatrical recovery” in Korea this year.
TV advertising, on the other hand, fell, with MPA suggesting “several television industries still carry more legacy capacity than their advertising economics can support.”
Stephen Laslocky, Vice President, MPA, said: “Asia’s video industries are not short of audiences or creative capability. They are short of structures that convert both into sustainable returns. As the margin for error narrows, management quality will become decisive.
Companies that rationalise legacy costs through restructuring and the adoption of new technologies such as AI, collaborate where independent investment no longer makes sense and protect the content that gives viewers a reason to stay will increasingly outperform, and the valuation gap between winners and losers will widen.”
Another MPA analyst Myat Pan Phyu (May), added: “The viewership data shows demand is intact. Premium VOD engagement continues to grow across India, Korea and Southeast Asia, streaming now leads content investment in India, and local stories are winning at the box office from Hanoi to Jakarta and Mumbai. This is a story of reallocation rather than retreat as capital moves toward streaming and local film, where both audiences and returns are growing.”

Ahead of opening its initial public offering (IPO) for bidding, fintech unicorn Moneyview has raised ₹327.5 Cr from anchor investors by allocating 9.63 Cr shares at an issue price of ₹34 per equity share, the upper end of the IPO's price band. Seven domestic mutual funds via fourteen schemes netted 6.96 Cr or 72% of the anchor round. SBI Mutual Fund's SBI Banking and Financial Services Fund lapped up the highest 1.47 Cr shares or 15.27% of the anchor round, investing over ₹50 Cr. Via three of its holding entities, HDFC Mutual Fund also bagged 1.47 Cr shares of the company. Motilal Oswal, 360 One, Goldman Sachs, ICICI Prudential's iSIF Ex Top 100 Long- Short Fund were some of the other investors that picked up a stake in the IPO-bound digital lending company. Moneyview's ₹1,092 Cr IPO is set to open for public subscription tomorrow (September 24). At the upper end of the price band of ₹32-34, the company is seeking a valuation of around ₹5,985 Cr ($624 Mn). This is about half of the $1.2 Bn valuation the company commanded post its last equity funding round of $4.6 Mn in September 2024. The IPO comprises a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹750 Cr and an OFS of up to 10.05 Cr equity shares. The fresh issue portion was halved from the ₹1,500 Cr proposed in Moneyview’s draft IPO papers, while the OFS was reduced from 13.6 Cr shares. The company had filed its DRHP with the SEBI in March 2026 and received SEBI’s nod for the public issue in July. The lending tech company, which offers users personal loans, payments, investments and insurance via its digital platform, intends to utilise ₹325 Cr of the fresh issue proceeds to support loan disbursals under default loss guarantee arrangements. Besides, ₹250 Cr will be infused into its NBFC subsidiary Whizdm Finance to augment its capital base, while the remainder will be used for general corporate purposes. The platform had 140.28 Mn registered users and 48 financial partners as of June 30, 2026. Its managed AUM stood at ₹22,520 Cr. Meanwhile, the OFS component of the IPO will see cofounders Puneet Agarwal and Sanjay Aggarwal plan offload up to 1.35 Cr shares each. Other investors like Tiger Global, Accel India, Crimson Winter, Ribbit Capital, among others, will also offload shares via the IPO. On the financial front, Moneyview Q1 FY27 net profit more than doubled year-on-year to ₹173.8 Cr in Q1 FY27 while its operating revenue rose 50.2% to ₹1,041.1 Cr from ₹693 Cr during the quarter as per its RHP. For FY26, Moneyview’s operating revenue grew 43.3% to ₹3,351.2 Cr from ₹2,339.1 Cr in FY25. However, its consolidated profit remained largely flat YoY at ₹242.7 Cr due to an exceptional loss of ₹206.7 Cr.

Luke Littler: Does world champion need to change approach to hostile crowds after whistling at World Series of Darts Finals?
Luke Littler's treatment by the crowd at the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam overshadowed the world champion's failure to deliver on stage; watch Littler's World Grand Prix defence live on Sky Sports from September 28
Wednesday 23 September 2026 18:05, UK
Following Luke Littler's latest run-in with a hostile crowd over the weekend, the Sky Sports Love The Darts Podcast has debated whether it is time for the world champion to change his approach.
Littler's bid for a clean sweep of all major PDC titles in 2026 was ended on Sunday after a crushing 10-4 defeat to Jonny Clayton in the last eight at the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam, but the action was overshadowed by the Brit's unhappiness at being repeatedly whistled at by the Dutch crowd.
After facing significant hostility during his win over home favourite Danny Noppert on Friday, Littler threatened to boycott future tournaments in the Netherlands after being booed and whistled at during his victory over Nathan Aspinall on Saturday, prompting referee Charlie Corstorphine to intervene.
- Darts in 2026: Tournament calendar and winners
- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream no contract
- Listen to Sky Sports' Love the Darts podcast
Littler has taken a stance against volatile crowds before, refusing to travel to European Tour events in Germany as a result of his treatment from fans there.
On the latest episode of the Love The Darts Podcast, World Series of Darts Finals champion Ross Smith explained his own approach to hostile crowds, which he admits is inspired by three-time world champion Michael van Gerwen.
"It's a real difficult situation," Smith said. "I can't speak for Luke because I'm not him and I wasn't in his position, I wasn't on stage at the time. I didn't really experience the whistling too much. I try not to rise to it because I know you're just going to get more stick.
"My manager once said to me, if you look at Michael van Gerwen, he never reacts, not once will he ever react to the crowd. He'll always thank them and he never really gets too much stick and he's very professional about how he does things. So, I admire him for that and I try and learn off of other people.
"I had a bit with Kevin Doets, obviously the crowd, rightly so, they're cheering their local guy on. Same with Gian [van Veen], they're doing exactly the same, but I think if you're aggressive towards the crowd and you're letting them know that it's affecting you and you're making them unhappy, it's not a good thing.
"I tried to, with Gian, I had more banter with them, you know what I mean? Just like thumbs up to them, but smiling, not in an aggressive way and they sort of laugh with you, it's not a problem.
"I think it's how you can react on stage, if you're aggressive towards them, it's going to create problems for you. But like I said, I can't really comment on Luke because I wasn't playing in the games with Luke and I don't know what he actually went through, but they can be brutal at times."
Nicholson: Maybe Littler can learn from others
Former world championship quarter-finalist Paul Nicholson praised Smith's approach, and suggested that Littler could benefit from learning from some of his rivals.
Nicholson, who himself was known for often having fractious interactions with crowds, also pointed to the way 2021 world champion Gerwyn Price has adapted his behaviour on stage.
Following on from Smith's comments, Nicholson said: "That's a really, really good way of looking at it, what Ross has just said, because from my standpoint, I tried to be aggressive because I wanted to be different and it was something that I had my entire career for, more than 10 years.
"Gerwyn Price has taken years to figure it out. Now he gives the smile with the aggression, and the crowd are with him more than they ever have been.
"So, it just goes to show that Ross is looking at this right, in order to make sure that his career is in the right place moving forward.
"So, we learn from mistakes, but we actually learn from what other people are going through as well. We don't want to see Littler not going to events, but maybe he can learn from what other people are doing as well."
Why whistling is worse than booing for players
Nicholson also explained why Littler and other players may become particularly frustrated at being whistled.
He added: "We have seen Littler have some banter with the crowd, which we're all for by the way, because we want people to have that connection. One of the greatest things about this sport is that there is a connection between the fans and the stars.
"But what we have at the minute is a trend of people using whistling as a way to make themselves feel heard. Dart players don't like it because it's piercing. It gets in your ear and it happens in a very short, sharp way, and it comes from nowhere.
"You don't know if it's going to come when you're throwing a match dart, a leg dart, or even going for a treble. If it comes out of nowhere, it can put you off and your shoulder jolts, and you don't want that.
"A boo is a lesser frequency and it's more mundane, you can handle them a lot better. But these short, sharp whistles, which is what they are, they're horrible.
"And the worst thing is, if it happens once, you are thinking about whether it's going to happen again, and you can't fully focus."

Microsoft said Tuesday that it led an industry-wide disruption of a subscription-based scam platform that used an AI chatbot to compromise 12,000 Microsoft accounts over a few-month span.
Named EvilTokens, the platform was introduced over a Telegram channel in February and charged an initial $1,500 fee and a recurring $500 charge each month after that. EvilTokens provided a single service for streamlining most steps required to compromise email accounts in large numbers. From there, the platform helped customers analyze inboxes, select targets that would provide the biggest potential payouts, and draft follow-up emails that provided realistic ruses for tricking company employees into transferring funds to attacker-controlled accounts.
Minutes, not days
“While EvilTokens helped cybercriminals access email accounts, at the center of the service was an AI-style chatbot that could analyze a victim’s inbox and help criminals identify trusted relationships, payment authorizations, and sensitive responsibilities, as well as other circumstances where fraud was most likely to succeed,” Microsoft said. “The platform could even recommend fraud strategies, including drafting messages that impersonated trusted contacts to help criminals trick victims into taking action.”
Microsoft said users of EvilToken compromised 12,000 customer accounts belonging to 10,000 organizations around the world, with the highest concentration of them located in the US. Countries with the next-largest numbers were Canada, the UK, Australia, India, and France. Victim organizations included wholesale distribution, construction, financial services, real estate, higher education, and healthcare. SpyCloud, a security firm that assisted in the disruption operation, has more details about victims here.
Using a legal process and a network of partners, Microsoft seized 50 websites and 150 more domains used to operate EvilTokens. The UK’s Metropolitan Police Service arrested two men on suspicion of offenses allegedly connected to the crime platform.
Account compromises were achieved through a legitimate OAuth process known as device code authentication. This form of authentication is designed for TVs and input-constrained devices, meaning those that lack the interface for performing normal log-in processes. In this model, the device being signed into presents a code and instructs the user to enter it into a browser on a separate device. The new device is then authenticated.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.

UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh

The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

The Trump administration must restore press credentials for staffers at CNN, Politico and MS NOW, a federal judge ruled early Thursday morning, delivering a rebuke to the president’s efforts to ban the outlets from the White House grounds.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, granted a temporary restraining order to the media outlets, after they sued Trump and other top administration officials, claiming violations of the First and Fifth amendments. The temporary order is set for a duration of 14 days. Generally, such orders are given to allow the court to consider a case more thoroughly.
Trump has previously sought to revoke the credentials of individual reporters, but his latest ban was a sweeping effort to punish the media for negative reporting on him. Although the government later claimed national security concerns, attorneys for the outlets said that was a post-ban rationalization, violating their due process rights.
Watch on Deadline
Earlier today, a collection of more than four dozen media groups and news outlets urged the judge to rule to end Trump’s ban. They included Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, the White House Correspondents’ Association and 49 other media organizations. Among those signing on to the brief were the Associated Press, Reuters, NPR, the National Press Club, CBS, NBC, ABC, Fox News and the Dow Jones Co.
After CNN was restricted from the network TV pool rotation at the White House earlier this week, four other networks — ABC News, CBS News, NBC News and Fox News — said that they would suspend their participation in an act of solidarity.

Terming it a "broad daylight dacoity" against patients, the Supreme Court on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) expressed shock over the overpricing of essential cancermedicines, noting that one drug carried an MRP of ₹27,000 despite being supplied to retailers for ₹2,700.
"It is very surprising that the authorities who are supposed to take action on this are silent," a Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta said.
The observations came when the Supreme Court was hearing two petitions that raised drug-related issues, including that of ensuring strict price control over medicines.
The court termed it "absolutely shocking" that the printed MRP of an essential cancer drug was ₹27,000 when the price to retailer (PTR) was ₹2,700.
"The MRP is 10 times the rate at which it is provided to the retailers. If this is not extortion, then what it is? People sell their houses, ornaments to get treatment," the Bench said.
"This is absolute rampage and carnage. This is broad daylight dacoity with patients," it said.
The Bench questioned how the patients could be cheated like this.
One of the petitioners told the Bench that his plea also raised the issue concerning the prescription of generic medicines by registered medical practitioners. He said fixing MRP of medicines was of critical importance.
Additional Solicitor General K.M. Nataraj, appearing for the Centre in one of the pleas, said the government was not treating it as an adversarial litigation.
The Bench observed that price fixation was a major issue.
It posted the matter for further hearing on September 29, 2026.
Price control
One of the petitions sought a direction to authorities to make drug formulations more cost-effective by preventing alleged unethical overpricing of essential medicines by pharma companies and retailers.
It also sought directions to ensure strict price control under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, to prevent violations of the price-fixing mechanism in the drug supply chain and disproportionate profit-making by retailers through unfair trade practices.
The other plea has sought disciplinary action against medical practitioners for not prescribing generic medicines to patients.

Trump wants to redefine AI. The name he chose is extremely telling
In 2014, a philosopher saw almost all of this coming and wrote a famous book about ‘superintelligence’. At the UN this week, Trump championed the term. It seems that he and his Silicon Valley friends are having some deeply concerning conversations, writes Holly Baxter
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
