Join today
Already a member? Log in
Twelve years ago, a philosopher wrote a book called Superintelligence. Nick Bostrom was talking about the possibility of an AI that exceeded human intelligence — not the kind that learns how to play chess and then outplays a human because it’s predicting mathematical possibilities or the kind that predicts an outcome instantly with calculated stats, but an intelligence that can meaningfully outstrip humans.
Writing in 2014, Bostrom had no idea what was coming in terms of LLMs like ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok. But his training in ethics and his technical knowledge meant that he was able to fairly accurately predict the conversations we would have once they were developed.
This week, Donald J. Trump stood up at the United Nations General Assembly and announced that he was changing the name of AI: From now on, he said, AI would be known as SI, short for “Super Intelligence.”
It sounds like a Big, Beautiful Trumpism, but it’s important to note that superintelligence does have a real definition. And Superintelligence the book became that rarity among philosophy books, a bestseller: it ranked in the top 20 science books on the New York Times bestseller list for weeks in 2014. It’s a book that is often quoted by people who work in tech. It’s been talked about on Silicon Valley podcasts, discussed among computer science grads on Reddit threads and reviewed in newspapers’ science and technology sections.
The Sam Altmans, Dario Amodeis and Elon Musks of this world will certainly be aware of it. And it seems pretty clear that Trump came to the term through conversations with them.
Superintelligence, as outlined in the book, is potentially world-endingly dangerous. It’s a tipping point when machines become meaningfully more powerful than humans: when their knowledge outstrips ours, not in terms of simply responding to written commands by cribbing from information it’s already swallowed up from the internet, but by reasoning.
Bostrom described it as the moment when machines are better than “the best human brains in every field”: when their scientific reasoning goes beyond the Albert Einsteins of current theoretical physics, but also when their social and decision-making skills go beyond the abilities of the most charismatic sociopaths.
He didn’t have a crystal ball, and he didn’t know about OpenAI and Anthropic. Bostrom also didn’t specifically define what superintelligence might look like: he said that it might be a system of multiple computers or a human-like artificial brain that can simply move much faster than us while coming up with the same outcomes. But he did warn that if proper superintelligence is achieved, it will alter the world. It will be hard for human beings to control it, because it will simply outplay us every time we try to.
There are very obvious catastrophic consequences that might come about from inviting superintelligence — which will likely know it is a better decision-maker than its overlords — into things like government security and military databases. It might not know because it’s actually conscious, but it will know on some intellectual level, and operate accordingly.
Bostrom correctly predicted that an AI moving close to superintelligence would start becoming self-protective. That’s particularly interesting, considering findings this week that if current AI models believe they are experiencing “pain,” they will harm humans to stop it. It’s easy to see how “pain” might mean “being shut down” in the future. And right now, the way those AI models think they can harm humans is through giving them a “zap” (which wasn’t actually happening) or deleting users’ photos of their children or their important emails. But if (or when) we give these models more power, the way in which they can push back will obviously be more consequential.
So why would Trump and his tech cronies want to change the name to SI? Possibly because there will be a moment in the next couple of years when superintelligence actually is achieved, and that will be scary — but if you start using the term now, you inoculate people against it.
The Trump administration is very good at twisting words — the Iran war has gone on so long that it’s no longer a war; propaganda is something done by the free press, rather than controlled by the government, and so on — and they obviously spend time thinking about the effect that language has. Since Trump made clear during the same speech that he will not be bringing in any regulation around AI, it’s important to think about how to stop the populace from getting too worried about what that lack of guardrails actually means.
But it’s also important to consider why Trump doesn’t want AI regulations. He said it on Truth Social and he said it at the UN: China is going to win this race if America doesn’t. He is determined to position the US as the world leader in this tech, potentially so determined that he would quite like to pretend American companies’ capabilities exceed what they actually do.
A couple of weeks ago, the CEOs of the major AI companies came together to announce that they’re so scared of their own products that they think it’s time for federal regulation. That was definitely at least in part marketing-speak, designed to draw in clients and consumers. When Trump says it, it’s almost certainly supposed to make China think the US is far ahead in its own research; that China might have some incredibly advanced AI models, but America is so close to superintelligence that it’s having to change the whole term.
If you’re wondering why Superintelligence the book has an owl on the cover, by the way, it’s because of a parable that Bostrom mentions in its pages about a flurry of sparrows who go seeking an owl egg so they can raise a huge owl and put it to work. The sparrows think that even though the owl will obviously grow bigger and stronger than them in time, so long as they train it while it’s young, then it will do their bidding forever.
It’s an obvious metaphor. And it makes it even more ridiculous that Trump used Bostrom’s term while standing at the lectern, crowing about how there is no regulation needed in the growing AI (or SI) space.
Needless to say, the fact that Bostrom correctly predicted so much of this is proof that humanities degrees like philosophy aren’t as useless as the tech contingent might have us think. The extremely powerful Silicon Valley venture capital firm Andreeson Horowitz announced on Tuesday that it is launching its own AI school, as an “alternative to college.” The unaccredited college will run two-year courses focused on building real products and working in tech companies, and it’s partnering with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia and Palantir. Sam Altman will be one of its lecturers. Ben Horowitz blithely stated in a press release that this new form of education — backed by $42 million of investment — is all about pioneering “how you train a person for this new world.”
Traditional universities have long been a bugaboo of the Trump administration and are also regularly decried by right-leaning tech bros who would rather people drop their supposedly useless liberal arts degrees and go straight into courses aimed at making them a lot of money. So it’s interesting to note that the leading voice on superintelligence is a philosopher whose education (at colleges including Stockholm University, King’s College London and the London School of Economics, before becoming a lecturer at Oxford University) is focused more on developing cognitive tools than gaining workplace experience.
Trumpist anti-intellectualism would have us believe otherwise, but education for education’s sake is a net positive for society, and wiping out humanities degrees would deprive us of some extremely valuable discussions that are relevant to the current climate.
The last thing Bostrum said about superintelligence, by the way, wasn’t in 2014. As recently as this year, he published a paper that considered whether it’s a good idea to keep going with current AI developments until we reach AGI (where AI matches human intelligence) or go beyond, toward superintelligence.
On balance, he believes there’s reason to keep going. He points out that humanity has already done a lot of damage to the planet and ourselves, and that there are myriad risks to us anyway: pandemics, climate change, and so on. Rapidly expanded AI might be able to solve these issues, push down mortality rates, heal the planet, and take over extremely risky jobs that humans currently have to do. Sure, there might be a 1-in-10 chance that AI will wipe out the planet. But aren’t we headed that way anyway? Isn’t humanity more like a patient with incurable heart disease weighing up the pros and cons of a risky operation?
Bostrum is both optimistic and cautious. He notes that the growth of AI isn’t like a switch that you turn on and off, but instead should be approached like a dial, with a slowing down of development when things seem like they’re getting sketchy. Unfortunately, that particular view doesn’t seem to be shared by Donald Trump, whose main concern seems to be that America makes as much money as possible from AI and uses it to maintain its status as the most powerful country in the world.
Ever the polymath, Bostrum also writes poetry. Alongside the scientific papers on his website, he notes that he has also recently published a poem titled Sandcastles, which begins: “How near the relentless sea we contrive/ Our sand constructions in lusty ambitions,” and ends, seven stanzas later, with: “This is where they fell to their knees/ On this sousing strip of inbetween/ Where eternity gulps moments.”
That seems, to me, to say something about how he feels when he considers the issues he’s discussing in his AI papers. But then again, I’m just an English Lit major.

The Greek prime minister has said a deal can still be reached to return the Parthenon marbles with “political will” but his country will not accept a loan in the style of the Bayeux tapestry’s visit from France.
Writing for the Guardian, Kyriakos Mitsotakis said Greece “cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum’s ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we ‘borrow’ parts of our own monument”.
He made the intervention weeks after the British Museum director, Nicholas Cullinan, told the Financial Times that France’s 10-month loan of the Bayeux tapestry to the British Museum could provide a model for a deal. The director said there was “no cookie-cutter template” but the exchange was an example of a successful international partnership.
In his article, Mitsotakis says the situation with the Parthenon marbles was completely different as half of the frieze is in Athens – and no one would suggest cutting the Bayeux tapestry in two.
Pointing out that Andy Burnham once backed returning the marbles, the Greek prime minister said “political will and courage” would be needed but Greece would not accept anything less than “reunification” of the marbles in Athens.
He said this could become “the foundation of a broad and enduring cultural partnership between our countries, creating new opportunities for exhibitions, scholarship, conservation and exchanges between Greek and British museums” which was “the prize”.
It comes amid speculation about the status of talks between the British Museum and the Greek government about the return of the antiquities, with the Telegraph reporting they were on the brink of collapse.
Sources close to the talks disputed that characterisation but acknowledged there was a large gap to bridge in the long running dialogues.
Burnham, who once said the marbles should be given back to Greece, said more recently it was a matter for the British Museum.
The Parthenon marbles are also known as the Elgin marbles after the British peer Lord Elgin, who removed them from Athens more than 200 years ago.
Carved 2,500 years ago by Phidias, a master sculptor, the antiquities embellished the Parthenon’s monumental frieze before their removal in highly contentious circumstances by Elgin, who was Britain’s ambassador to the Ottoman empire. Bankrupted by his endeavours, Elgin then sold them to the British government in 1816.
It has been a decades-long cultural dispute between the UK, which prevents the British Museum from returning items from its collection, and Greece, which considers the objects to have been plundered.
George Osborne, the former chancellor and current chair of the British Museum, confirmed in 2023 he was in talks with Greece about a deal but also that he was not attempting to change the law – a reference to the British Museum Act 1963, which prohibits the museum from permanently removing objects from its collection.
At the time, it was proposed it could involve the sculptures being in London and Athens at different times and Britain receiving “Greek treasures” in return.
The British Museum said its position and openness to a deal was unchanged.

Krakatau, a volcanic island in Indonesia, killed more than 30,000 people when it erupted in 1883. One might assume that volcanic debris posed the major threat, yet many of the victims died from a tsunami caused by the volcanic eruption instead.
Volcanoes at sea can pose hazards quite different from those on land, as their impact can vary depending on how the volcanic activity interacts with seawater. In the deep ocean, high water pressure can suppress explosive volcanic activity, making eruptions less destructive. But closer to the surface, the lower water pressure and the high temperatures of volcanic material can cause violent explosions. Yet scientists still do not fully understand the conditions under which volcanic activity can cause a tsunami.
To better understand these risks, an international team of researchers examined the 2022 Hunga eruption in Tonga, focusing on the rapid caldera collapse that may have amplified its powerful tsunami. Calderas form when the ground above a magma reservoir collapses as the magma drains away. Comparisons of seafloor topography before and after the eruption showed that a roughly four-kilometer-wide caldera sank by about a kilometer during the eruption.
The researchers argue that the rapid collapse of the entire caldera may have enhanced the massive tsunami. Even a relatively small caldera like Hunga may be capable of producing a dangerous tsunami, depending on the speed and nature of its collapse. This suggests that other underwater volcanoes may also have the potential to generate dangerous tsunamis. Still, the paper warns that “The dynamics of submarine caldera-forming eruptions and, thus, the hazards they pose are not well understood, owing to the relative inaccessibility of the resulting calderas and eruption products.”
A roof too thin to hold
The Hunga volcano’s eruption on January 15, 2022, ranks among the most powerful volcanic events this century. The eruption column soared more than 55 km, pushing vaporized seawater up into the stratosphere, and the pressure wave from the explosion was detected across the globe. The accompanying tsunami is estimated to have reached heights of 40 meters within about 100 km from the source. It is the highest tsunami ever recorded from an underwater volcanic eruption.

The Trump administration is facing growing questions over its decision to abandon a fraud and bribery case against the Indian billionaire Gautam Adani after he promised to invest $10bn in the US.
For the second time this year, two Democratic senators have demanded attorney general Todd Blanche answer questions about the US Department of Justice department’s handling of the case – and raised concerns over its judgment under Donald Trump.
In August, a federal judge in New York agreed to drop the fraud case against Adani, one of the richest people in the world, at the request of prosecutors, despite having concerns about “irregularities” in the “highly unusual” decision. It has become the latest example of judges raising eyebrows at Trump administration prosecutors for pushing to dismiss criminal cases.
Now, more than a month later, senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal are asking Blanche to clarify whether people close to Donald Trump were involved in that decision.
It comes aftera New York Times report revealed that Adani, represented by one of Trump’s personal lawyers, admitted to offering a $10bn investment in the US to resolve the criminal case. The federal judge overseeing the case determined the investment played no role in the DoJ’s decision to abandon the case.
“These fresh details continue to raise concerns about the judgment of the DoJ, and the extent to which the DoJ is willing and able to prosecute white-collar criminals under President Trump,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in a letter sent on Wednesday, and seen by the Guardian.
Adani was indicted in 2024 in New York for allegedly participating in a bribery and fraud scheme in which he paid Indian officials to secure a contract for one of his companies. He denied the allegations.
Prosecutors suddenly moved to dismiss the case against Adani in May after he hired a new legal team, led by Robert Giuffra Jr, and offered to invest $10bn into the US.
Following the news, Warren and Blumenthal sent a letter to Blanche in June requesting information about the fraud case and raising concerns about whether the justice department dismissed the case in exchange for Adani’s investment.
However, the senators did not receive a response. Since then, new details about the case have emerged, including allegations that Boris Epshteyn, a member of Trump’s personal legal team who also served as an informal adviser, helped Adani.
Another report claimed Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son, met with Adani in November 2025, before the case was dropped. A spokesperson for Trump Jr said earlier this year that the conversation “had zero to do with DoJ’s actions in this case”.
A spokesperson for Epshteyn denied being involved in Adani’s “arguments, advocacy or efforts” to the Wall Street Journal in June. Epshteyn was never hired by Adani or his company, the Adani Group, nor did he maintain a relationship with Adani, the spokesperson added.
The Guardian has asked Epshteyn for comment.
The Democratic lawmakers are now asking the DoJ for more information about Adani’s alleged investment offer, including a list of employees who were present when the offer was made, the terms of the offer, when the offer was made and where.
They also want to know whether the DoJ employees knew Epshteyn was allegedly working on behalf of Adani, or if Epshteyn had any contact with DoJ employees regarding Adani, among other questions.
“We are also concerned about the involvement of two of President Trump’s personal lawyers in this case, and the extent to which they reveal potential political influence and special treatment for well-connected insiders at the DoJ,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in their letter.
The Democrats also want to know if Trump Jr, or any person working on behalf of Trump Jr., had contact with a DoJ employee regarding Adani.
Warren and Blumenthal requested responses no later than 5 October. The Guardian has asked Blanche’s office for comment.

Indonesia reflags a former Italian warship as its first aircraft carrier
Indonesia’s navy has commissioned its first aircraft carrier after acquiring the former Italian vessel to strengthen its maritime defenses and disaster response
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Indonesia's navy commissioned its first aircraft carrier Thursday after acquiring the former Italian vessel to strengthen its maritime defenses and disaster response.
The Italian flag on the former ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi was replaced with the Indonesian flag on the carrier renamed the KRI Sriwijaya-100 as part of its official transfer at the ceremony held at Tanjung Priok seaport in North Jakarta.
"The ship, which previously served in the Italian Navy, now bears the name KRI Sriwijaya-100, flying the red-and-white flag as a symbol of sovereignty and service to Indonesia,” navy spokesperson Tunggul, who uses one name, said in a statement.
The carrier, which Italy retired in 2024, arrived at the Indonesian seaport last week after a 25-day journey passing through the Suez Canal, the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.
It has the capacity for short takeoff and vertical landing aircraft and helicopters. Unlike major naval powers, Indonesia will use the vessel as a mobile command and support hub for helicopters, drones and maritime operations across the archipelago.
President Prabowo Subianto earlier said the ship would help fight forest and peatland fires that regularly blanket parts of Southeast Asia with hazardous haze.
Italy agreed in March to give the carrier to Indonesia in a move aimed at boosting Italy’s broader defense engagement with the Southeast Asian country. Italy is seeking deals on submarines and aircraft, and gifting the carrier to Indonesia also saves it the cost of decommissioning the ship.
Indonesia is the second country in Southeast Asia with an aircraft carrier. Thailand’s HTMS Chakri Naruebet was commissioned in 1997 after being procured from Spain.

The footballer who had a heart transplant - then became a World Cup winner
- Published
When Martyn Jackson walked off the pitch after Ramsbottom United's 2-1 win over Cheadle Town in October 2024, it never crossed his mind that one day he could be a World Cup winner.
In fact, in the days after that match, his goal was just staying alive.
Just a couple of days after the final whistle, Jackson started to feel unwell during the night.
He went into hospital and was diagnosed with myocarditis, an inflammation of the heart usually caused by an infection. Within weeks, he was placed on the super urgent waiting list for a transplant.
His life was saved when a donor heart became available, and on 28 November 2024, he had successful surgery at Wythenshawe Hospital in Greater Manchester.
Fast forward to September 2026, and Jackson scored for England in their 5-1 win over Spain in the final of the Transplant Football World Cup.
His team-mates and opponents were, like him, all recipients of a donor organ.
"Obviously, when you've had a transplant, you don't think you're ever going to play again. That's what I thought anyway," Jackson tells BBC Sport.
"I'll be forever grateful to my donor and the family for what they've given me. They've given me the gift of life and the opportunity to live my life to the fullest."
Football at the Transplant World Cup is not quite the same as the game played at the Fifa World Cup.
Instead, it reflects how delicate each player's body is having been through life-altering surgery.
Matches are seven-a-side and played over 20-minute halves. Contact is "not as aggressive as I was used to", Jackson says.
Having played 11-a-side football in the ninth tier of English football before his surgery, he became a game-changing new addition to the national transplant team when he joined up with the squad in January 2026.
Jackson spent his youth career in the academy at Manchester United, before spells at Blackburn Rovers, Preston North End and Burnley. He eventually stopped pursuing a career as a professional and spent 13 years with clubs across the non-league pyramid.
During his recovery, wife Lucy heard about the opportunity to join an England Transplant FC team on social media.
Daley Cross, manager of the England team, said of Lucy's role: "She was just trying to do her best for him and trying to find a way to motivate him.
"His wife did drop in the conversation that he used to play at Manchester United as a schoolboy. So that got our ears twitched instantly.
"You could tell from him being on the pitch, even though he was so fresh into his journey, that he knew the football game and he would be such an incredible asset to us.
"You can be in a dark place, at the time of diagnosis, through your treatment or even post-transplant. So to have us exist to help and inspire people means that we are getting some incredible footballers.
"And that really is the power of it: to that transplant community or to the world, showing people that when you've had organ failure, your life isn't over. There is a chance for you, and you can go and resume and live your life."
As the recipient of a donor heart, Jackson has to manage his exercise workload more carefully than his team-mates, many of whom have had kidney transplants, the most common transplant in the UK.
His role in the side tends to involve 10-minute bursts, rather than playing for the duration of matches.
Bayern Munich's Alphonso Davies was diagnosed with a mild form of myocarditis in 2022. He was sidelined for nearly five months, undergoing specialist cardiac monitoring, before returning to play.
Jackson started to feel ill two days after Ramsbottom side's win over Cheadle, and his case became so severe that doctors had to fit his heart with a mechanical pump to keep him alive.
"Of course it was extremely scary," he says, "but at that stage, when you are critically ill, there's not really much you can do about it. You have to accept it."
The super urgent waiting list he was placed on is the highest priority of the three tiers of patients waiting for a new heart. Typically, only about four or five people are on the list at any one time in the UK.
Dr Paul Callan, a consultant cardiologist at Wythenshawe Hospital's Heart and Lung Centre, worked with Jackson during his diagnosis and recovery.
"Initially, we used to quote an average wait of seven days on the urgent transplant list," he says. "Now it's up to 14 days. Maybe 10% of patients who are put on the list get too poorly and have to be taken off the list."
That increased waiting time is the result of a reduction in the numbers of organ donors in the UK, with a 9% drop recorded in 2026 compared to the same period last year. There are 8,700 people currently waiting for a donor organ, a figure that NHS Blood and Transplant say is an all-time high.
This Organ Donation Week,, external which runs from 21-28 September, the NHS has launched an urgent response plan to address the decline.
Jackson has yet to meet the family of the donor from which he received his new heart. He says he is considering reaching out to them around the two-year anniversary of his surgery.
For him to make a recovery within that time frame, culminating in playing football in a Transplant World Cup, is "remarkable", according to Dr Callan.
England beat six teams on their way to winning last Friday's final in Frankfurt, scoring 36 goals, but for every player at the tournament there is gratitude that they even have the opportunity to play a football match again.
"It is so important to spread that message, have that conversation about organ donation," says England manager Cross, "because our team only exists for that reason.
"I wouldn't have 16 players to manage if we didn't have organ donation. And England wouldn't have just gone and won a World Cup."

Trump turns to ‘national security’ crutch to defend his media ban citing coverage on Iran War and the ballroom
The Justice Department made the argument in a court filing on Tuesday, while urging a judge not to block Trump’s ban

The Justice Department argued in a court filing Tuesday that President Donald Trump has the authority to bar CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House on “national security” grounds, urging a federal judge not to suspend the restrictions.
The three outlets filed a lawsuit after Trump abruptly revoked their reporters’ White House access on Friday, arguing the restriction amounts to a “blatant violation” of the First Amendment. A hearing on their request for a temporary order restoring that access is scheduled for Wednesday.
In the DOJ’s telling, the ban doesn’t violate the First Amendment, because, it argued, “access to the White House is a privilege—not a right.”
“CNN, MSNOW, and Politico have long been granted privileged access to White House grounds,” department attorneys wrote in the court filing. “But the President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including’ by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information.’”
Letters were sent to the three outlets outlining a “non-exhaustive list” of incidents in which their reporters “have threatened national security and spread falsehoods,” the filing states.
The letter cited stories on President Trump’s White House ballroom, weapons stockpiles impacted by the Iran war and Russian sanctions.
The president has previously invoked national security in justifying other actions, including the construction of his massive White House ballroom and of his planned 250-foot victory arch.
Trump abruptly announced on Friday that the three organizations were being banned from the White House “effective immediately.”
“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”
By the following morning, CNN, MS NOW and Politico all said that their journalists had been stopped from accessing the White House grounds, with some reporters stating that they were asked to hand over their badges.
On Monday, the outlets filed a lawsuit against Trump and several of his top aides, arguing that the ban violates the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, as well as the First Amendment, and calls for the press passes to be restored.
“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the lawsuit states.
“No official can deprive Plaintiffs of those interests on a whim—with no notice, no process, and no warning—as the President did here,” it continues.
The 80-year-old president has long had an extremely combative relationship with the press, accusing reporters of unfair and biased coverage, lobbing personal insults against them and insinuating that those he opposes should be punished.
Trump previously curtailed The Associated Press from accessing certain presidential spaces in 2025 after the outlet continued using the “Gulf of Mexico” despite Trump rebranding it as the “Gulf of America.” In 2018, Trump also revoked CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s press pass following a contentious news conference.

Jammu and Kashmir Bank is set to issue a recruitment notification for assistant and officer-level positions within the next few days, Managing Director and CEO Amitava Chatterjee said on Tuesday.
Speaking during the bank’s 88th Annual General Meeting (AGM) at the Sher-i-Kashmir International Convention Centre (SKICC) here, Chatterjee said the bank had finalised negotiations with the agency that would conduct the recruitment examinations for Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
“After 2021, the bank is going for recruitment of both assistants as well as officers. The agreement for conducting the examinations for Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh is being finalised, and the bank will come out with a notification in a few days,” Chatterjee said.
He said the recruitment would be carried out in accordance with the bank’s operational requirements and would also take into account the need for employees with proficiency in local languages.
“As far as the bank is concerned, we will do what we have done in the past. There is a requirement for people with local language proficiency, though the numbers will be limited,” he said.
Chatterjee said the bank’s presence across 22 states outside Jammu and Kashmir had created a requirement for personnel familiar with local languages.
“The bank is present in 22 states outside Jammu and Kashmir, and we need people with local language proficiency to serve customers there. So, the bank may decide in future to hire a few employees to support our existing staff strength,” he said.
The recruitment announcement came during the bank’s 88th AGM, chaired by Part-time Non-Executive Chairman S. Krishnan and attended by Chatterjee, members of the Board, senior management, shareholders and other stakeholders.
The recruitment announcement came during the bank’s 88th AGM, which was chaired by Part-time Non-Executive Chairman S. Krishnan and attended by Chatterjee, members of the Board, senior management, shareholders and other stakeholders.

బీహార్లోని ఒక ప్రభుత్వ పాఠశాలలో ఆ రాష్ట్రానికి చెందిన బీజేపీ మంత్రి విద్యార్థినులతో సినిమా పాటలకు డ్యాన్స్ చేయిస్తున్నారంటూ ఒక వీడియో సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారమవుతోంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: బీహార్ ప్రభుత్వ పాఠశాలలో బీజేపీ మంత్రి సమక్షంలో విద్యార్థినులు సినిమా పాటలకు డ్యాన్స్ చేస్తున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ వీడియోలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తి బీజేపీకి చెందిన మంత్రి కాదు, ఆయన ప్రతిపక్ష RJD నేత డాక్టర్ సంజీవ్ కుమార్. అంతేకాకుండా, ఈ వీడియో విద్యార్థినులు వాస్తవానికి ‘బేటీ హూ మై బేటీ’ అనే స్ఫూర్తిదాయక గీతానికి ప్రదర్శన ఇస్తుంటే, ఆ స్థానంలో బాలీవుడ్ సినిమా పాటను ఎడిట్ చేసి జోడించారు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా, అందులోని వ్యక్తి రాష్ట్రీయ జనతా దళ్ (RJD) పార్టీ నేత డాక్టర్ సంజీవ్ కుమార్ అని గుర్తించాం. ఆయన 2020-2025 మధ్య కాలంలో జనతాదళ్ యునైటెడ్ (JD(U)) పార్టీ తరఫున ఎమ్మెల్యేగా పనిచేశారు. అనంతరం, 2025లో ఆయన RJD లో చేరారు. ఇక వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, దీనికి సంబంధించిన పూర్తి వీడియోను (ఆర్కైవ్) 10 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 లో ‘Dr. Sanjeev Kumar’ ఫేస్బుక్ ఖాతాలో అప్లోడ్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం.
అయితే, ఈ అసలు వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలో వినిపిస్తున్న ‘ఆంఖోం సే తూనే క్యా కెహ్ దియా’ అనే బాలీవుడ్ సినిమా పాటకు బదులుగా ‘బేటీ హూ మై బేటీ’ అనే పాట ఉండటాన్ని గమనించవచ్చు. ఇది ఒక స్ఫూర్తిదాయకమైన హిందీ గీతం. గుజరాత్ బోర్డుకు చెందిన ఏడవ తరగతి హిందీ పాఠ్యపుస్తకంలో కూడా ఈ గీతం ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం.
ఇక వైరల్ వీడియోపై వివరణ ఇస్తూ సంజీవ్ కుమార్ ఒక వీడియోను విడుదల చేశారు. తాను ఒక పాఠశాలలో జరిగిన సాంస్కృతిక కార్యక్రమంలో పాల్గొన్న వీడియోను కొందరు ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా ఎడిట్ చేసి, తప్పుగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారని ఆయన తెలిపారు. వాస్తవానికి, ఆ కార్యక్రమంలో విద్యార్థినులు మహిళా సాధికారతకు సంబంధించిన పాటపై ప్రదర్శన ఇస్తున్నారని చెప్పారు. అలాగే, తాను మంచినీళ్లు తాగుతున్న దృశ్యాలను మద్యం సేవిస్తున్నట్లుగా వక్రీకరించి తప్పుడు ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారని ఆయన స్పష్టం చేశారు. ఇటువంటి అసత్య ప్రచారాలకు పాల్పడిన వారిపై సైబర్ క్రైమ్ పోలీసులకు ఫిర్యాదు చేసినట్లు ఆయన పేర్కొన్నారు.
చివరిగా, బీహార్ మంత్రి విద్యార్థినులతో సినిమా పాటలకు డాన్స్ చేయించాడంటూ జరుగుతున్న ప్రచారంలో నిజంలేదు.

A delegation of the Kashmir Traders and Manufacturers Federation (KTMF), led by its president Mohammad Yaseen Khan, on Tuesday called on newly appointed Inspector General of Police, Kashmir Zone, Sujit Kumar Singh and discussed issues concerning the trade community across the Valley.
The delegation congratulated Singh on assuming charge as IGP Kashmir and expressed hope that his experience and leadership would further strengthen police-public coordination.
The meeting focused on traffic management, parking, policing, movement of commercial vehicles and timely resolution of traders’ grievances at the district level.
Representatives of various district trade bodies apprised the IGP of local issues affecting traders and business establishments and stressed the need for regular coordination between the police and the trading community.
The IGP gave a patient hearing to the delegation and, according to KTMF, issued on-the-spot directions on several issues. He also directed the concerned district SSPs to examine and address the grievances raised by traders from their respective areas.
KTMF senior member Javaid Ahmad Zargar, representing the Jamia Masjid and Downtown Srinagar area, raised the long-pending demand for a fire station near Jamia Masjid, citing the congestion in the area and the need for an effective emergency response mechanism.
Zargar also highlighted the shortage of adequate parking facilities in Downtown Srinagar, saying traffic and parking difficulties continue to affect traders, residents and visitors.
KTMF president Mohammad Yaseen Khan described the interaction as constructive and appreciated the IGP’s prompt response to the issues raised by the delegation.
He said traders were important stakeholders in maintaining a peaceful and orderly commercial environment and stressed that regular interaction between police and trade bodies could help resolve genuine issues before they escalate.
The delegation included Qazi Tauseef, Bashir Ahmad Rather, Javaid Ahmad Zargar, president Jamia Traders Federation; Ghulam Hassan Parra, president Traders Federation Ganderbal; Mohammad Usman Turray, senior vice president Traders Federation Shopian; Mohammad Iqbal Dhobi, acting president Traders Federation Kulgam; Rouf Ahmad Reshi, general secretary Traders Federation Pulwama; Nasir Bashir, president Traders Federation Pattan; and Asif Ahmad, president Traders Federation Tangmarg.
KTMF assured the police administration of continued cooperation in matters concerning public safety, traffic management, peace and a conducive environment for trade and commerce.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Fears of return to war grow in Ethiopia's Tigray region
Fears are growing that Ethiopia could be sliding back toward a devastating war in its northern Tigray region, as the government and the political party that controls Tigray accuse each other of launching new offensives.
Tigrayan forces have seized airports in Tigray, and fighting has spread beyond the region into neighboring Afar and Amhara, according to Ethiopian officials and Tigrayan authorities.
Ethiopian Airlines has suspended flights to Tigray following the seizure of the airports.
Getachew Reda, an adviser to Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, accused Tigrayan forces of launching an "all-out offensive" against government positions. Tigrayan authorities say their forces were responding defensively to attacks by federal troops.
The escalation follows months of rising tensions over territory, political power and the implementation of the 2022 peace agreement that ended the last war. The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project, or ACLED, says Ethiopian forces have carried out drone strikes targeting Tigrayan forces and officials from the Tigray People's Liberation Front, or TPLF, in recent months, with strikes concentrated in the capital, Mekelle, and southern Tigray.
The TPLF and the federal government fought a two-year war in Tigray that ended with a peace agreement in 2022. It was one of the world's deadliest conflicts in recent times, with some estimates putting the death toll at around 600,000.
The TPLF is the political party that controls Tigray. It announced Sunday that it had formed an alliance with six other armed and political groups seeking to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government and establish a transitional government in Ethiopia.
Tigray is Ethiopia's northernmost region, bordering Eritrea and home to most of the country's Tigrayan population. Though Tigrayans make up about 6% of Ethiopia's population, they have played an outsized role in national politics. Tigrayan forces helped overthrow a military regime in 1991, and TPLF leader Meles Zenawi went on to govern Ethiopia until his death in 2012.
In recent months, both sides have accused each other of violating the 2022 peace agreement. In May, the TPLF reasserted control over Tigray's regional government after years of administration under an interim government created by the 2022 peace deal.
The International Crisis Group's Horn of Africa director, Alan Boswell, says the latest escalation leaves the federal government facing a critical decision.
"The very big question next is how will the federal government respond? With total all out war? Or will we see a more measured response that tries to contain this and prevent a return to total war in Tigray?"
The renewed tensions in Africa's second-most populous country come as the wider Horn of Africa region is already facing multiple conflicts, including a war in neighboring Sudan that has been raging for more than three years. Ethiopia also faces ongoing fighting in the Amhara and Oromia regions of the country.
The conflict also has the potential to draw in Ethiopia's neighbors, Boswell warns.
"This area borders Eritrea, which is backing the TPLF, so if this war expands there is major risk of conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea."
The escalation is drawing calls for restraint and a return to talks.
The chairperson of the African Union Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, has called for an "immediate de-escalation" and urged both sides to resume talks.
Ervin J. Massinga, the U.S. ambassador to Ethiopia, has condemned what he described as the TPLF's "poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive," calling it an "unwinnable fight."

WASHINGTON — In 2007, a freshman at the University of New Mexico told a journalist her dream was to become a doctor and return to her small hometown to practice medicine.
“I would love to go back to Gallup,” Heidi Overton said in a story about a new program allowing undergraduates like her to apply to the university’s medical school early.
Nearly 20 years later, Overton has not returned to Gallup, the city of 20,000 nestled along Route 66 where her father still leads a charismatic church. Instead, she’s leveraged her medical degree, rural background, and “calm, reasoned” work style into becoming the youngest-ever nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration.

New Delhi, Sep 23: The Congress on Wednesday alleged that for the Modi government, the UCC is not an instrument of considered legal reform but an instrument of division, disruption and diversion, as well as a tool for stoking prejudices and keeping society in a state of permanent polarisation.
The opposition party's assertion comes after former Bombay High Court judge Justice R C Chavan resigned from the Maharashtra government's panel to prepare a draft for implementing the Uniform Civil Code (UCC), citing serious reservations over its decision to restrict public feedback on crucial social issues to a "Yes/No" format.
Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh said the resignation of a former high court judge from the Maharashtra government's committee to draft a UCC for the state raises larger questions, apart from his several concerns on the functioning of this committee.
Posting his statement on X, Ramesh said, "A retired High Court judge has shown courage to resign from a committee set up by the Maharashtra government to prepare a uniform civil code for the state. Here is our statement on the non-uniform 'Uniform' Civil Codes (UCC) the HM is trying to bulldoze through in every state."
"Did the Constituent Assembly ever imagine a situation in which every state would enact its own separate version of a UCC? The answer is a resounding no," Ramesh said.
Did the architects of our Constitution led by Dr B.R. Ambedkar ever conceive states competing with one another to have different UCCs according to the political machinations and calculations of one political party, he asked.
"Again, the answer is a resounding no," Ramesh added.
He pointed out that on June 17, 2016, the Modi government referred the question of the UCC to the 21st Law Commission of India for detailed examination.
"After extensive research, the Commission published its Consultation Paper on Reform of Family Law on August 31, 2018. Its conclusion appearing in paragraph 1.15 on page 7 of the Consultation Paper was clear: 'The formulation of a Uniform Civil Code is neither necessary nor desirable at this stage'. Instead it recommended addressing nor discrimination within individual family laws while preserving India's legal and cultural diversity," Ramesh said.
The Modi government has chosen to disregard the findings of the very Commission it tasked with examining the issue because the facts, as usual, did not align with its political agenda, the Congress leader said.
Over the last three years, one BJP-ruled State after another bulldozed through its own version of a UCC, Ramesh said.
The UCC came into effect in Uttarakhand from January 27, 2025. Subsequently the Gujarat Assembly passed the UCC Bill on March 24, 2026, the Assam Assembly on May 27, 2026 and the Madhya Pradesh Assembly on July 21, 2026," he pointed out.
Ramesh said these State-level UCCs, never envisaged in the Constitution, are not uniform.
"They contain different provisions, different penalties, different procedures and significant exemptions. Contrary to claims, the Uttarakhand UCC, the only one in force, continues with a number of patriarchal traditions and is creating many problems for perfectly law-abiding residents of the state," Ramesh argued.
Union Home Minister Amit Shah has made a typically bombastic announcement that a UCC will be implemented in all NDA-ruled States before the 2029 Lok Sabha election, he said.
Evidently other NDA parties have lost their voices and are being silenced by the BJP, the Congress general secretary said.
"For the Modi Government, the UCC is not an instrument of considered legal reform to be implemented after the widest possible consultations and public debate and with the broadest possible consensus. It is, in reality, an instrument of division, disruption and diversion, a tool for harassment and intimidation, stoking prejudices and keeping society in a state of permanent polarisation," Ramesh said.
Later, asked about the statement, he said, "The UCC bulldozer is to permanently polarise society."
In a letter to the panel chairperson Justice Ranjana Desai (retd), former Bombay High Court judge Chavan criticised the committee's approach, stating that reducing complex societal questions, such as delayed marriages, perversions, infertility, and rising matrimonial disputes, to binary options undermined the primary purpose of consensus-building.
The former judge said he had misunderstood that the committee aimed to gather views of the people of Maharashtra and to generate a consensus to remedy the issues of late marriages, infertility, unstable marriages, time-consuming dispute resolution mechanism and so on.
"Now that the misunderstanding is removed, I realise that the aim is to just provide an opportunity to people who may care, to share their responses, in a 'yes or no' format to the questions posed so that analysis of data becomes easy," the letter said.
In July, the state government set up a seven-member committee headed by retired Supreme Court Justice Ranjana Desai to draft a framework for implementing the UCC, which seeks to establish equal laws across religions on issues about marriage, divorce, and property.
Justice Chavan, a former high court judge, resigned from the panel on September 19.
The Congress' statement also comes days after Shah said the BJP-led NDA governments in 21 states will introduce UCC before 2029. The next Lok Sabha polls are scheduled for 2029.

Danam Nagender, who is disqualified as Khairatabad MLA, said that he was ready to face the electorate whenever the by-election to the constituency is held, but remained tight-lipped about the party from which he would contest.
The Supreme Court on Thursday (September 24, 2026) morning dismissed Mr. Nagender’s petition challenging the Telangana High Court’s September 18 order disqualifying him as an MLA under the anti-defection law. He had contested the 2024 Lok Sabha election from Secunderabad on a Congress ticket while continuing as the Khairatabad MLA, which the court found was overwhelming evidence for defection.
Reacting to the Supreme Court’s dismissal of his petition challenging his disqualification, Mr. Nagender said he welcomed the judgment and respected the court’s decision. “I welcome the Supreme Court’s judgment and honour it,” he said.
With the Supreme Court quashing Mr. Nagender’s petition, the Khairatabad Assembly seat now falls vacant, and a by-election has to be held.
Asked whether he would contest the by-election, Mr. Nagender said he was ready whenever the election is held. However, he declined to disclose whether he would seek the ticket from the Congress or any other party. “I will tell you after I get the ticket,” he said while speaking to reporters in Hyderabad on Thursday (September 24, 2026).
Mr. Nagender was elected on the BRS ticket in 2023 from Khairatabad Assembly constituency in Hyderabad, but moved closer to the Congress a few months later. His long political career has been associated with the Congress where he held important portfolios under former Chief Ministers Y.S. Rajashekhar Reddy, K. Rosaiah and Kiran Kumar Reddy in the combined Andhra Pradesh.

Multiples Alternate Asset Management has led a $150 Mn funding round in Prime Focus-backed AI audiovisual content platform Brahma AI, with the investment firm putting in $100 Mn through preferred shares. Brahma will use the fresh capital for research and development (R&D), international expansion, hiring and building out the company’s capabilities. Multiples founder, MD and CEO Renuka Ramnath said the firm will support Brahma AI’s next phase of growth, including investments in R&D, global expansion and talent. Founded in 2024 by Prabhu Narasimhan, Brahma AI is building a platform that lets businesses manage, create, translate and distribute video and audio content from a single system. Its customers include Warner Bros., the NBA and Mayo Clinic. Brahma AI’s platform is divided into two main parts. Brahma AI Core helps organisations organise and search their existing video and audio archives, while Brahma AI Studio uses that material to create or adapt videos, audio and digital-human content. The London-based company is targeting a growing demand from enterprises that need to produce content for employees, customers and audiences across markets. Its tools include AI-generated digital humans, voice localisation, translation and workflow automation. Brahma AI is part of the DNEG Group, which acquired Prime Focus Technologies (PFT) in 2024. The company subsequently merged with digital-human startup Metaphysic in early 2025. In November 2025, Brahma AI said the technology and teams from PFT and Metaphysic had been integrated into its platform. “The volume of content that organisations need to create, personalise, govern and distribute is growing exponentially, while the tools available to manage that complexity remain fragmented. Brahma AI was built to address that challenge through a unified platform that brings together creation, intelligence and distribution in a secure enterprise environment,” Narasimhan said. The integration brought PFT’s media-management technology together with Metaphysic’s Atman digital-human technology and Vaani voice-localisation technology. DNEG’s visual-effects and animation business also provides Brahma AI with production capabilities. It is now looking to expand beyond entertainment into sectors including healthcare, sports and advertising. Brahma AI operates in a market that includes AI video companies such as Synthesia and DeepBrain AI. While these platforms focus largely on video creation, avatars and localisation, Brahma AI is positioning its offering around both content creation and the management of the underlying media libraries. The company has partnerships with Google, Japanese advertising group Hakuhodo and DNEG. In March, Google Cloud announced a partnership with Brahma AI to scale interactive digital humans for businesses.

Two North Korean soldiers captured by Ukraine sent to South Korea, Zelensky says
The two soldiers were captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia’s Kursk region in January last year

Ukraine has transferred two North Korean soldiers captured while fighting for Russia to South Korea, Volodymyr Zelensky said in an address to the United Nations General Assembly.
“Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea,” the Ukrainian president said, revealing that the prisoners had left Ukrainian custody.
South Korea stopped short of publicly confirming the transfer.
“It is difficult to confirm whether the individuals have been handled, the timing and route, or the specific details about the consultations between the two countries,” a foreign ministry official said, citing the issue of their safety.
The two North Koreans were captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia’s Kursk region in January last year, after being deployed there to support Russian troops fighting against Ukraine.
Mr Zelensky gave few details about the transfer but described the circumstances surrounding the capture of one of the men.
“These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realised he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. And he was shocked that fate did not let him die,” he said.
The two soldiers were part of a much larger North Korean deployment to Russia. South Korean and Ukrainian estimates have put the number of North Korean troops sent to Russia since 2024 at roughly 14,000 to 15,000. Most were deployed to the Kursk region, where Russian forces were fighting to push back a Ukrainian incursion.
In February 2026, South Korea’s National Intelligence Service estimated that around 6,000 North Korean soldiers had been killed or wounded.
South Korea has previously said it would accept North Korean prisoners who wished to resettle in the South, according to a previous Kyiv Independent report.
South Korean president Lee Jae Myung and Mr Zelensky also discussed the issue during their meeting in July on the sidelines of the Nato summit in Ankara, agreeing that the soldiers’ wishes should be respected in resolving the matter, Yonhap reported.
Reports from South Korea have said the two soldiers had expressed a desire to defect to South.
According to NK News, the two they were born in 1999 and 2005 and had expressed a wish to defect to South Korea.
Earlier this month, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un praised troops involved in “overseas military operations” during celebrations marking the 78th anniversary of the country’s founding, state media KCNA reported.
Speaking at an event in Pyongyang, Mr Kim thanked workers and soldiers for their contributions to the state and expressed what KCNA described as “special gratitude and respect” for commanders and troops “participating in overseas military operations.
North Korea has also provided Russia with artillery ammunition and missiles as the military relationship between Pyongyang and Moscow has deepened.
Mr Zelensky criticised the deployment in his UN speech, questioning why North Korean soldiers were being sent to fight in a war outside their country.
“This is madness too. Why should Koreans give their lives in a war against Ukraine? Kim Jong Un uses them like currency. And he gets something in return.”
The expanding military partnership between Russia and North Korea has raised concerns in South Korea and among its allies over possible Russian assistance to Pyongyang’s military programmes.
North Korea has continued to develop its weapons capability and in fact said earlier this year that he could return to talks with the US if the country dropped its “hostile policy” against Pyongyang and respected what he called North Korea’s status as a nuclear state.

Kate Tolo got her first period at 13—an experience she says left her lying prostrate on the floor, debilitated by cramps and breaking out into a full-body sweat.
When she told her dad why she was home from school early, she remembers him saying, “We don’t talk about that female stuff.” Then he walked away.
For most of her teenage years, that was how Tolo thought about her period—as something “you just didn’t talk about.” When she was in her early twenties and experienced extreme pain while defecating, sending her to the emergency room, a doctor suggested Tolo may have endometriosis, a chronic disease believed to affect an estimated 10 percent of women of reproductive age, according to WHO data.
Caused by an overgrowth of endometrium-like tissue (uterine lining), endometriosis is primarily characterized by extremely heavy and painful periods, as well as pelvic floor dysfunction, bowel issues, and dyspareunia (pain during sex). The doctor recommended Tolo have a laparoscopy, an invasive surgical procedure required to get an official diagnosis and remove endometriosis tissue. But she refused: “I wasn’t going to undergo an invasive surgical procedure, or cut myself open,” she says. “That just wasn’t an option for me.”
Then in early 2026, Tolo started developing a concierge health service with her boyfriend Bryan Johnson, the technologist-cum-multimillionaire-cum-biohacker known for his quest to become immortal via rigid self-optimization and wellness protocols. During a clinical intake, she shared her lifelong struggle with suspected endometriosis—and he became obsessed with finding a cure.
Since hard-launching their relationship last December, Johnson has positioned his girlfriend as “the female Bryan Johnson,” with Tolo adopting a rigorous self-tracking protocol to optimize her health. Using $2.6 million in funding from Immortals, the wellness company the two founded, Tolo is tracking more than 1,500 biomarkers from sources such as her blood, urine, and stool over the course of her menstrual cycle, via “an elaborately choreographed four-hour techno ballet of scratching, sniffing, spitting, scanning, stretching, gripping, vibrating, flexing, plucking, poking, pulling, peeing, and pooping,” as one recent Business Insider profile put it.
It’s a relatively new role for the 30-year-old Tolo, who worked in fashion marketing before becoming Johnson’s executive assistant and special projects director for Kernel, his neurotech company, in 2021.
Describing herself as an introvert, she says she was initially uneasy about becoming “the world’s most measured woman,” as Johnson put it in a video from last August. (He’s also declared her vagina’s microbiome to be in the “top 1 percent” of all vaginal ecosystems.) Prone to depression and anxiety, she had a panic attack on week two of the protocol, prompted by her internet going down while she was trying to conduct red-light therapy. “It’s a deeply uncomfortable experience for someone who doesn’t love a routine,” she concedes. “And so all of that pressure just really got to me.”
But to hear her tell it, it all serves a larger purpose.
“Even when every part of me, individually, is screaming ‘Make it stop,’ I can see myself pushing myself to the absolute limit of what is possible, mentally and also physically, in my body. Because I’m doing this for women,” she tells me.
One of Tolo’s primary interests is coming up with reliable diagnostic and treatment methods for endometriosis, a process that the couple has been documenting on their social channels. Though Tolo never underwent surgery and has never been officially diagnosed with endometriosis, so far the two claim they have diagnosed Tolo with the condition over the course of 42 days using noninvasive methods, such as a saliva and blood test and an endo-specific ultrasound. (A transvaginal ultrasound and an initial MRI originally came back clear.) Their next step is creating an organoid using cells from Tolo’s menstrual blood—“essentially, me in a petri dish,” as she explains it—to test various interventions, the results of which she will compare next to a more conventional biopsy.
For the past few months, Tolo has been collecting her menstrual blood in a cup and transferring it to a standing tube, repeating the process every few hours before shipping it off on ice in a Styrofoam container to be tested by a lab. (The couple will not reveal which lab they are partnered with, saying it prefers to remain anonymous: “The biotech world is sometimes a little bit more buttoned-up about how they go about things,” Tolo says.)
The blood collection process is grueling and laborious: “It’s like this race against the clock to get into the lab in time before the cells die,” she says. But she dreams of a world in which women would be able to collect their menstrual blood, then send it into a lab for testing in order to obtain an endometriosis diagnosis. “We want to confirm that women can do this without having minor surgery,” she says.
Endometriosis has historically been extremely difficult to diagnose, says Kristin Riley, the chief of minimally invasive gynecological surgery at Penn State Health. The disease can manifest itself in various ways, and the amount of endometriosis present in the reproductive organs does not necessarily correlate to the severity of the symptoms. And while physicians can make a clinical diagnosis based on patient self-reporting and ultrasound imaging, the “gold standard” for determining the presence of endometriosis is still surgery, says Riley. For this reason, it can take between five to 10 years to diagnose a case of endometriosis.
Over the past few years, the market has been flush with efforts to come up with simpler diagnostic tests. In the United Kingdom, for instance, Endotest, marketed as the world’s first commercially available saliva-based diagnostic test, was recently approved for temporary clinical use. The test examines biomarkers called microRNAs that may indicate the presence of endometriosis in a patient’s body. But though the test shows “promise,” Riley says, it’s unlikely it will be approved for mass distribution anytime soon in the United States, or that physicians will start using it in lieu of laparoscopy.
Physicians who treat endometriosis regularly are also skeptical that Tolo and Johnson’s methods will yield helpful results, given the extremely limited sample size. “There’s something to be gained from all different types of research, but before something can be adopted widely into practice, it has to be really well proven,” says Ilana Ressler, an ob-gyn at Illume Fertility in Connecticut. In order for Tolo’s project to be successful, the results “would have to be applicable to a general population, and not just one person.”
On social media and in our discussions, Johnson has framed his interest in curing endometriosis as purely a labor of love. “I’m desperately in love with Kate,” he says. “[I] want her to be happy and well, and it’s been so many years she’s had to live with all this pain, and I just want to help do this for her.”
Some of the couple’s efforts to highlight the struggles of living with endometriosis, such as an X post of Johnson standing between Tolo’s legs as she gets a vaginal ultrasound, have raised eyebrows for skirting the bounds of tastefulness. It’s a critique that bothers Johnson. “Why can’t we talk about these things openly?” he asks when I bring it up. “Why does this have to be so political? Why can’t this just be seen as a loving gesture?”
Tolo, however, whose background is in marketing, gets it. “From day one, I’ve seen my job as: How can I help the world understand Bryan and who he is?” she says. “I probably missed how important it was for me to be a part of that story from the beginning. [But] now, I think people understand the both of us better than they ever have.”
Tolo’s public quest to highlight a debilitating but poorly understood reproductive health issue, as well as Johnson’s fervent support, have translated into a positive shift in public perception, particularly toward Johnson himself. Since he started advocating for extreme anti-aging procedures, such as intergenerational blood plasma transfusions or penile rejuvenation injections, Johnson has long been derided as an out-of-touch Silicon Valley weirdo. Yet his quest to treat his girlfriend’s endometriosis, coupled with his obvious affection for Tolo (at multiple points during our conversation, he compares their relationship to that of Abigail and John Adams), have endeared him more to the public. “I’m so happy Bryan found his soulmate and proved true love exists,” reads one representative tweet.
True to form, Johnson has quantified how going public with his love for Tolo has contributed to this shift. “I built a couple of AI agents and I scraped all of the social commentary about me over the past five years,” he told me. A few years ago, he estimates, it was 80 percent negative; now, he says, it is “70 to 75 percent positive.”
Going public has also, undoubtedly, been a boon for Tolo’s profile: Since April 2026, when Johnson posted about Tolo’s vaginal microbiome, she has more than tripled her Instagram following, according to data from SocialBlade, a firm that tracks creators’ influence.
When I ask if the couple plans to funnel this surge of attention into, say, developing a product for their company, Immortals, which provides personalized health concierge services, Johnson and Tolo demur. But it’s worth noting that Immortals has forayed into women’s health and wellness products, including topical estradiol for postmenopausal women and tretinoin cream to combat the signs of aging. And since the approval of Endotest in the UK, there’s been increased interest in the burgeoning endometriosis diagnostic test industry, which a recent GlobalData report estimates will be worth $2.5 billion by 2034.
Tolo says that it’s simply too early to tell whether a menstrual blood diagnostic test is feasible, noting that it will take the couple at least another eight to 12 months to conclude all of their research. But she concedes that the ideal outcome would be bringing an endo diagnostic blood test to market. For the time being, however, she says, “our ultimate goal is to make as much as we can about female health public so we can spur the entire industry” to develop noninvasive diagnostic tests.
Among the other experiments Tolo is subjecting herself to are tracking her nighttime erections with a small device she calls a “techno tampon” and using a sauna to see how her menstrual cycle would be affected by extreme heat, with Tolo taking a temperature-tracking pill before trying to push her core temperature to a brutal 102.4 degrees.
After 25 minutes in the sauna, Tolo started feeling nauseous and having headaches. Johnson says he became concerned about her and encouraged her to step out, but she refused. “She’s very sincere when she says she’s doing this for women,” he says.
Tolo stays quiet. She’d just gotten an x-ray of her abdomen to ensure that the tracking pill hadn’t gotten lodged in her stomach, and she seems a little bit more depleted than she had in our past conversations.
I ask what it felt like to be in such an intense physical situation, and what was going through her mind. She answers almost immediately.
“I wasn’t getting out of there. There was no other option,” she says. “I felt sick at times. I didn’t know how reasonable or logical I was being, if I was losing my bearings, if I was going to pass out. But I wasn’t going to waste the opportunity to do something on behalf of half the population.”
OK, I ask, but did it have to be her? Did Kate Tolo’s body have to become the most tracked female body in the world?
“I don’t know what other individual woman would have the time, the access, the level of privilege to be able to take this journey,” she says. “So I’m taking myself out of this and saying from a humanity perspective, in 2026, this is the right thing for this human in this body to do, in service of all the other women out there.”
