ShinyHunters hackers claim to have 2-3TB of sensitive information about FBI employees
Financial extortion doesn’t seem to be the group’s goal this time.
Hacking group ShinyHunters has allegedly stolen extensive amounts of sensitive information from the US Federal Bureau of Investigation that includes details about its employees and job applicants. Reuters reports that it has seen a sample of the data obtained by the attack on the agency, and 404 Media also said it received confirmation of the action from a representative of ShinyHunters. The hackers also appeared responsible for an unauthorized takeover of the FBI website earlier this week.
"We hacked the FBI. We hold data on all FBI employees and applicants," the spokesperson told 404 Media. According to that source, ShinyHunters got the information by using a zero day exploit in the PeopleSoft program from Oracle to obtain access to Amazon Web Services' GovCloud servers.
A statement from the FBI shared with Reuters said that the agency was aware of "a cyber-criminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the FBIJobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information" and that it is "actively and aggressively investigating the matter."
The attackers claim to have 2-3TB of data, but the sample shared with the media appeared to contain names, addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, social security numbers and emergency contact details for 5,000 employees at the FBI. The group may also have gathered details about some work assignments for agents and about some FBI units that are working on intelligence, security and counter-espionage efforts, including operations focused on both China and Russia.
Many of ShinyHunters' previous hacks have been aimed at extortion, with actions against parties ranging from Ticketmaster to Rockstar Games in recent years. However, the rep who spoke with 404 Media claimed this move against the FBI was "not financially motivated" but rather aimed at coercing the government agency to remove or amend a previous statement made about ShinyHunters. In a report from May, the FBI said the hacking group "exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims."

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.

- In a recent Moore's Law is Dead Broken Silicon podcast, the leaker Tom claimed that Sony sent out a big survey to developers.
- Sony reportedly asked developers for feedback about its decision to end physical discs.
- The recent Marvel's Wolverine sales figure also revealed that there is a significant demand for physical discs among PS gamers.
The renowned hardware analyst and leaker Moore’s Law is Dead claims that Sony sent a survey to developers regarding the company’s plans to end PlayStation physical disc production. The company sought feedback from the developers on “whether there is an issue with not selling games physically.”
In the latest episode of the Broken Silicon podcast, Tom, the creator of Moore’s Law is Dead, claimed that his sources told him that Sony had sent its biggest developer survey yet. The company reportedly asked devs for feedback, albeit indirectly, on its plan to move away from physical game discs.
Tom also cited a report from Alinea Analytics on the recent sales of Marvel’s Wolverine. Although the latest title from Insomniac Games received mixed reviews from critics, the game has sold more than 1.9 million copies to date, with physical sales accounting for 22.9%. So, Tom believes there is still significant demand for physical discs that Sony should definitely pay attention to.
The new survey reportedly sent out by Sony could be seen as a positive sign. If developers can express their concerns about killing discs, the company could potentially reconsider its decision. However, keep in mind that these are all just speculations, and Sony has not officially announced any changes to its plans.
Earlier this year, Sony’s CFO doubled down on ending physical disc production. The CFO confirmed that the company is heading toward an all-digital future and said the company would cautiously move forward with its plan to end physical discs. Instead of traditional physical discs, Sony plans to sell codes in a box as part of its disc-free future.
In addition, Sony’s PS5 boxes now ship with a warning label about the end of physical support. As things stand, Sony is sticking to its disc-free future on the official side, but the latest survey rumors give hope to players that Sony may reconsider its approach.
Recently, Microsoft sent a survey to Xbox players via Xbox Insider Hub asking fans if they want Project Helix to support physical discs. Similarly, Sony should ask its fans directly whether they still want physical games.

Inside the confines of Manchester City's sophisticated data operation is a fundamental phrase its experts work towards: "What does it take to win?"
In practice, the motto is broken down into three sections: identifying players, evaluating them and assessing how the club could improve them, all with a view to enhancing the statistical probability of City winning the Premier League.
Last season, the club's data department projected they would be there or thereabouts when it came to the title race, but their metrics indicated Arsenal were favourites to be champions. They were accurate.
This time around, City prefer to keep their projections under wraps - but five wins from five Premier League games have prompted predictions from supporters and pundits they will again be the Gunners' closest challengers.
City's devotion to data is at the heart of their efforts to close the gap on Arsenal and BBC Sport has been given unprecedent access to the inner workings of the club's metrics machine as we uncover some of the secrets guiding their work - particularly regarding player recruitment and sales.
Their work is a sign of the times in the Premier League, with clubs across the top flight and beyond increasingly using data for transfers and monitoring their teams' performance.
At City, one of the fundamental aims is to reduce risk of any market transaction, be it a purchase or a sale.
City grade players based on:
- Ability;
- Overall characteristics;
- The system they play in at their current club and how the manager is asking him and the team to play.
Once those four aspects are observed, City's aim is to understand not just how good the player is but how good he could become at the Etihad.
Since winning the Treble in 2023, City's squad has undergone a vast overhaul using this approach. Only four players from that historic campaign remain.
It is crucial to stress, however, that while data has made an indefinite impact on how City operate in the transfer market, the work of traditional scouts continues to be the primary gauge of whether they decide to move for a player.
"Data plays a role in our decision-making, but it is just one part of the overall picture," City sporting director Hugo Viana told BBC Sport.
"We know data cannot tell us everything about a player. It cannot fully show a person's character, mentality or behaviour.
"That is why we study data insights but focus on the expertise of our scouts and other specialists."
The prominence of data, however, has grown significantly behind the scenes at the Etihad.
Here BBC Sport can take you to the core of some of City's key transfer calls from their extensive three-year squad revamp - including the £116m signing of Elliot Anderson.
From 650,000 players to the No 1 target
The starting point for any new signing is City's database of 650,000 footballers from around the world.
The next step is the brief: what sort of player is the club wanting to recruit.
This usually starts with a position, though that process isn't as simple as it sounds.
City, for example, categorise their full-backs into three types: those who are defensive, those who come inside, and those who play high and wide.
Once the club's data departments have the brief, filters that grade a player's overall ability are applied to whittle down the 650,000-man database to 20-50 names.
Juventus full-back Andrea Cambiaso is one player who has been on City's radar after the data highlighted him, particularly his ability to coming inside to build play in midfield.
That he is comfortable with both feet rated highly on the data, too.
In accordance with the data and the scouting reports it was decided the club would not proceed with their interest in Cambiaso in the previous window, but City's approach is likely to mean he will continue to be monitored.
The longlist of 20-50 names is cross-referenced with the scouting longlist. Generally there is a significant overlap between the players identified by data and the ones already on scouts' radar.
From there, further, more refined metrics are applied to rank and prioritise the longlist.
Scouts will then complete further diligence on the players to reduce the list to a maximum of about six players.
At this point, the club will complete deeper dives into the remaining players, including diligence on their injury record, athletic performance and behavioural habits.
The information is then collated into individual reports called acquisition packs which contain all the key metrics used to inform the decision on a player.
This includes a 'radar chart', which rates a range of specific on-field metrics.
For example, when Jeremy Doku was signed in 2023, then manager Pep Guardiola decided he wanted a winger who was direct, akin to Leroy Sane, because at the time they had Jack Grealish and Riyad Mahrez, who preferred to keep the ball and cut inside.
Among the criteria applied in City's brief were the following: making (running into) the box, pressure regains, take-on percentage and opposition-half pressure.
Doku's overall numbers ticked the boxes Guardiola was looking for, although the Belgian's 'making the box' score was among his lowest readings.
Since his arrival, Doku has improved this rating - an example City say shows how their data systems are helping to improve existing players.
There is also a 'utilisation chart' that records how often the player has been used over a three-year period, as well as a scouting grade that indicates how highly the traditional scouts rate the individual.
Each player is also awarded an overall "current impact score" - which predicts what impression he would be expected to make immediately on signing - and a "potential impact score" that projects the contribution the player could make in the future.
Perhaps the most intriguing reading on the acquisition packs is a player's "action value score". This positions them in a league table that includes City players and ones from rival clubs who play in a similar role.
Once the acquisition reports are evaluated, the list is further reduced to 2-3 players once City's valuation of the player has been factored in.
Data contributes heavily to the price range City believe a player falls in, and the valuation is never a single number.
A decision is then made on which player is the priority, though all players on the shortlist are worked on simultaneously in the event of changing circumstances, for example if a player becomes unavailable.
Indeed, being able to move according to the market is something the data team feel they have become adept at.
The sudden emergence of Yan Diomande last season led to City completing checks on him before he joined Real Madrid from RB Leipzig.
The club also paid close attention to Eduardo Camavinga's metrics in case Real decided to sell a midfielder.
Anderson - the signing that shows City's forensic approach
Anderson was an obvious signing for a top Premier League club.
The 23-year-old had developed into a key player for Nottingham Forest. An added appeal was the fact he is English, and had cemented his position in the national team.
City fought off other top clubs, including Manchester United, to sign him.
It would seem, on the face of it, a straightforward decision.
But the way City analysed it underlines their incredibly forensic approach even when, outwardly, it might be considered they did not need to be so comprehensive given Anderson's obvious talents.
The fact they still used their algorithm and went through all their normal steps says a lot about elite football in the modern day - and also the limitations of data alone.
That is because - perhaps surprisingly - Anderson's metrics didn't necessarily catch the eye.
At the start of last season, despite emerging uncertainty over Guardiola's future, the club knew they would be in the market for at least one central midfielder come the summer.
They knew Bernardo Silva was leaving while there were doubts over the futures of Rodri and Nico Gonzalez.
There was an acknowledgement that replacing Silva and Rodri like-for-like would be virtually impossible, so they looked for a player who was equally adept at building play from either deep or high central midfield.
As last season developed, doubt also emerged over the future of Tijjani Reijnders - but Enzo Fernandez was viewed as the favoured replacement for the Dutchman.
Anderson made the initial cut from the 650,000-man database to the longlist - but was not high in that group. However, his metric readings didn't immediately scream out the "no-brainer" he ultimately became.
As City took a closer look, there was an acknowledgement Anderson's case does highlight some of the limitations of data.
Anderson did not score lots of goals for Forest, or consistently provide assists. Because, generally speaking, Forest aren't a possession team like City, his general metrics in their algorithm did not grab the attention.
With that in mind, City's data analysts had to consider that, because Anderson was generally playing closer to his own goal than he would at City, he wasn't getting the opportunities to impress in the final third of the pitch.
So they paid close attention to what he was doing at Forest and modelled his potential role in a City team that generally plays closer to the opposition's goal, dominates possession and has more elite players.
Among the criteria graded on Anderson's 'radar chart' were defensive regains, duel success, line-breaking passes, aerial-duel success and defensive errors.
With his reading for defensive errors, it was acknowledged that, because Forest were a transitional side, some were a result of the area of the pitch in which he was asked to operate.
He may, for example, have regained possession deep inside his own half but lost the ball because he had to play a longer and a riskier pass after being asked to play forward quickly.
In the same scenario at City, it is anticipated Anderson would have options to play a shorter pass with a greater success rate.
"Just because a player doesn't have the opportunity to perform a particular action on a regular basis because of the team he is playing doesn't mean he can't do it," said a source.
Anderson's data readings improved significantly as the season developed, which compelled the club's scouts to watch him on a regular basis.
He stood up very favourably against City's existing midfielders - and a list of rival players the club had identified as possible signings in that area.
The results of the diligence completed by City's data team, scouts and other experts meant that even though Anderson's price increased beyond what City believed was his true valuation, they felt the risk was low.
"Elliot Anderson is a great example of how the process works," Viana said.
"The data was positive for Elliot and gave us real confidence in his profile, but it was the insight from our scouts and wider performance team that helped us understand the player and his attributes and this proved our belief that he was the right fit for the club."
The success of Alvarez and Khusanov
BBC Sport was also provided with fascinating insight into how data was used to sign Julian Alvarez from River Plate for £14m in 2022.
The initial recommendation came from scouts, and given Alvarez was not a player originally identified by his metrics, the data team had to take a closer look.
Because the Argentine league isn't recognised as one of the strongest globally, City's general data settings mean players will reach a natural ceiling with their readings in comparison to those playing in one of Europe's top five divisions.
So, City dug deeper into Alvarez's stats, and his impact on both the ball and River's scorelines.
The stats showed he was by far the best player in the Argentine top flight, and City believed they had enough evidence to say he would develop into a starter for a top-half club in one of Europe's top five leagues within two-and-half years.
The data model valued Alvarez between £26m and £40m. City signed him for £14m so believed they were signing an undervalued player.
Alvarez's projected value was £70m after three years. They eventually sold him to Atletico Madrid in 2024 for £81m.
The signing of Abdukodir Khusanov from Lens also provides intriguing insight into City's reliance on data.
The 22-year-old didn't initially make City's 50-man longlist, but on closer inspection they found while his output on the ball needed to improve, his physical data - for example his covering runs behind - was through the roof.
Khusanov's on-the-ball metrics, City say, have improved significantly since he signed in January 2025.
The impact of Guardiola leaving and squad building
The departure of Guardiola and the arrival of Enzo Maresca is not expected to alter the club's approach significantly.
The key metrics Maresca looks for in a player are understood to be very similar to Guardiola's, with the notable difference that the Italian prefers his full-backs to be more direct.
Rooted in City's coach recruitment process is a certain team philosophy and way of playing, with any new manager expected to produce a side that is possession dominant, can press high, regain possession high up the pitch, produce quality chances and entertain.
That philosophy was designed before Guardiola's appointment, and the Spaniard produced the purest form of City's footballing ideology.
With that in mind, the change in manager has not drastically altered the way City's data department approach their work.
Maresca will continue to work closely with them as he looks to build his own dynasty - but much of the hard work in building a squad to last is complete.
Before City's Treble-winning season, the internal data indicators were such that the club knew they would soon need to overhaul a squad that had reached its peak.
Selling players such as Kevin de Bruyne, Kyle Walker, Riyad Mahrez and Ilkay Gundogan wasn't easy given their illustrious service and the fact they were still performing at a very high level.
Data, though, allows the club to spot declining trends well in advance - often two or three years - before a player is offloaded.
Those particular metrics help City identify when the right time is to sell a player is - perhaps even before the buying club have spotted a drop in performance.
And when those trends are identified, the club can plan well in advance.
From there the club decide whether to start embedding a player from the academy or enter the market to replace.
Ayyoub Bouaddi's arrival from Lille this summer is a prime example. At 18, City realise he isn't necessarily going to have a profound impact this season - but the club believe the Moroccan will be able to make a bigger contribution within two years.
After the Treble season, the recruitment remit at City was to lower the average age of the squad and build a set of players that could deliver sustained success.
But doing that at City comes with a catch. Because at City, the team are always expected to compete for trophies.
Lowering the age of a squad is one thing; doing so while continuing to win is far more complicated.
In previous years, for example, City's data systems identified former Brighton trio Moises Caicedo, Marc Cucurella and Carlos Baleba, who have been lauded as data successes.
But there was a sense at City that the development of such signings would take too long for them to make an impact on a team that has the remit of winning titles or assets that could be developed and sold for a profit.
City have successfully lowered the average age of the squad to the extent they now have the third youngest set of players in the Premier League behind Newcastle and Chelsea.
But with the signings of goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, defender Marc Guehi, and Fernandez and Anderson they have added players who can not only grow with that new generation but also already have vast experience of top-level football.
City's data indicates their current squad will not peak for another two to three years - but also projects they are likely be among the title challengers this season.
Time will tell if they are right.

Trump’s push to acquire Greenland almost broke NATO. The winner of it all may be ... Greenland
In the end, it was all kisses and laughter as President Donald Trump hailed his “fantastic” relationship with Denmark and Greenland

In the end, it was all kisses and laughter as President Donald Trump hailed his “fantastic” relationship with Denmark and Greenland after signing a new security deal that America’s European allies hope will close one of the most dangerous chapters in transatlantic relations.
Trump’s territorial ambitions over Greenland almost broke the NATO military alliance and shattered trust with one of America’s oldest and closest partners. The new defense agreement puts an end to the standoff. But was it worth the cost?
While the new defense agreement is a bit broader, the United States already had extensive military access under an existing 1951 deal and all the gains laid out in the agreement signed on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday could, ostensibly, have been achieved by asking nicely a year ago. The trans-Atlantic distrust created since the end of 2024 seems a very high price to pay for what may ultimately be a fairly incremental gain.
Interestingly, one place may emerge from this standoff as the real winner: Greenland itself.
The promised investments and contracts may never fully materialize, but the episode marks a major step forward in its push for greater autonomy and a more influential seat at the table. Greenland is no longer merely the subject of foreign policy decided by its former colonial rulers. Increasingly, it is helping to shape it.
There's been progress toward self-determination
“A notable change is Greenland itself at the table today, signing this agreement," said Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen speaking to a room cram packed with journalists and officials at the UN to witness the signing of the deal.
That's an understatement. The world’s largest island, home to about 56,000 mostly Inuit people, was still considered a colony until the early 1950s. Progress towards greater self-determination has been slow and it wasn't until 2009 that Greenland became a self-governing country within the Kingdom of Denmark.
Even then, while the Self-Government Act recognized Greenland’s right to independence when requested by local voters in the future, Denmark retained control of defense and foreign affairs.
“I cannot stress it enough: This is the first time that we are venturing into a binding agreement as a country," Naaja Nathanielsen, one of Greenland’s two lawmakers in the Danish parliament and a former government minister in Nuuk, told The Associated Press. “That is a huge step forward in our quest for more self-autonomy.”
Denmark and Greenland confront their own troubled past
Like most former colonial powers that discover history keeps receipts, Denmark's ties with Greenland are complicated. Greenland's economy is heavily dependent on Denmark, families and students often live between the two territories and the cultural linguistic ties are strong. Yet underwriting modern relations are centuries of Danish policies that dehumanized Greenlanders and their families.
They included forced contraception, the removal of Inuit children for reeducation by Danish foster families, and controversial parental-competency tests that led to children being separated from their parents.
“For many, many years you believed that you were a good colonizer,” Múte Bourup Egede, then Greenland's prime minister and now its foreign minister, reminded Danish journalists early last year, shortly after a newly elected Trump made his first military threat against the island. “But time has also caught up with us, and ... cruel things have come to light.”
The abuses are not distant history; many victims remain alive. Hundreds of Inuit women have claimed compensation from Denmark, alleging that health authorities violated their rights by fitting them with intrauterine devices — often when they were teenagers and without their informed consent. Danish authorities estimate that as many as 4,500 women and girls received IUDs between the 1960s and mid-1970s.
While the first official apology for the historic mistreatment had long been coming it was finally delivered in the summer of 2025.
The standoff with the United States “has been applying pressure and focused some of the Danish attention” on reconciliation with Greenland said Ulrik Pram Gad, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, but “perhaps, some Greenlanders feel that it’s not as credible as it could have been without Trump.”
Trump's involvement changed the equation
While Denmark moved to address past grievances, anger with Trump's tactics also helped shore up support for its sovereignty and take the edge off calls by some in Greenland for quick moves to independence.
At the height of the crisis over Trump's ambitions in January, Nielsen said that “if we have to choose between the United States and Denmark here and now, we choose Denmark. We choose NATO."
For Denmark, the main victory is no doubt getting the US president off its back and succeeding in framing the crisis as a European security problem.
Danish and Greenlandic diplomats “have been working very hard to have European allies be part of this," Pram Gad said. "The result is an attempt to patch together the NATO alliance.”
And while Denmark has accepted some limitations to its sovereignty, investments by adversary countries such as Russia had long been off the table.
“The benefit of keeping the transatlantic alliance, or patching it together, or at least not allowing Greenland to be the occasion for Trump to blow it up, I think that counts heavily on both the Danish and the Greenlandic cost-benefit analysis here,” he said.
After Tuesday’s signing ceremony, relief was palpable. But while the Danish and Greenland delegations celebrated with a cold beer on a rooftop bar in Manhattan, the Greenland crisis has scarred a once undefiable bond. It leaves leaders in Copenhagen, Nuuk and other European capitals now assessing the reliability of the United States — and whether a signed agreement can repair trust once it has been broken.

England vs Spain: Anthony Gordon backs Thomas Tuchel's 'DNA' comments about possession and calls on Three Lions to focus on their strengths
Thomas Tuchel said control with possession is not in the DNA of England players after World Cup loss; Anthony Gordon agreed, explaining inbuilt ability for Spanish players; winger calls on England to focus on own strengths; Follow England vs Spain on Sky Sports website and App on Saturday
Thursday 24 September 2026 06:57, UK
Anthony Gordon has backed Thomas Tuchel's view that England's players have an inbuilt inability to control matches with possession - and has urged the team to embrace the country's traditional strengths.
Tuchel was criticised for England's defensive retreat after Gordon's goal gave them the lead against Argentina in the World Cup semi-finals, an approach which ultimately allowed their rivals to turn the match around in the final stages.
Tuchel responded by hitting out at the 'DNA' of English players. "I think ball possession plays a crucial role; it's maybe not in our DNA like it is in Spanish DNA or in Argentinian-Brazilian DNA, to take the ball and control the game with the ball," he said.
Tuchel made those comments despite leaving some of England's most technical players - Cole Palmer, Phil Foden, Trent Alexander-Arnold - out of his World Cup squad, and not giving midfielder Kobbie Mainoo a minute of game time during the tournament.
However, speaking ahead of England's Nations League opener with world champions Spain, Gordon has backed his manager's view.
"England, as a nation, we don't have that strength, like the Spanish, where we control games like they do," said Gordon in a press conference. "It's not in us."
- Analysis: Thomas Tuchel must win back trust
- England news and analysis | Follow our England blog
- Neville: I have a big problem with Tuchel's DNA comments
Gordon was speaking at St George's Park, a venue created to develop young English players in a technical style inspired by countries such as Spain, where former FA chief football officer Dan Ashworth outlined what became known as the 'England DNA' - an ironic backdrop given Tuchel's remarks.
Gordon, who now plays his club football in Spain for Barcelona, came through that system, starring in the country's successful youth teams, but said: "I'm not sure it's something that can be [taught].
"Playing in Spain, I can speak with an educated view on the way they keep the ball is different. It's much different than I've ever experienced playing in this country.
"I'm not sure we can ever get that but we can definitely get better, or maybe go the other way and really play to our strengths, which is play physical, play direct football, and on the counter-attack."
Speaking last week, Tuchel suggested England should perhaps "embrace the chaos" of that approach, and Gordon believes that could be the key lesson from the summer's World Cup disappointment.
"I think now that we've had that experience, probably the next time we're in that position, we'll go the other way," he said. "That scar doesn't have to be a negative one, because it might lead us to victory in the next tournaments."
'We're English and we have our own strengths'
Detailing the difference between Spanish and English players, Gordon said: "We, as English players, are educated the same way as the Spanish players. We know how to keep possession, but it's the decision-making of certain players in Spain which is just not a natural thing [for English players].
"I even look at some of the decisions they take on the ball sometimes and think, 'I'm not sure how you've seen that'. It's the way they're built.
"It's important for us that we can't keep looking at other countries and trying to be like them, because we're not them, we're English and we have our own strengths, which they don't have. So maybe we start playing to what we're good at."
Did iconic win in Mexico make England defensive?
Reflecting on the World Cup, Gordon also highlighted the impact of England's backs-to-the-wall, 10-man victory over Mexico at the Azteca, and how it subconsciously shaped their mentality for the subsequent matches against Norway and Argentina.
"The Mexico game was by far the best experience I've ever had in my life. But I think that probably set us up in a way," he said.
"The red card, it made us show a different side of us. We weren't so much the team that wanted to play anymore, we needed to really fight to get the victory, which we did. Then that probably became our MO a bit too much for the next two games, and ultimately didn't work for us in the semi-final."
Gordon, though, still backs the quality in the England squad - and is convinced they could have upset Spain in the final had they made it.
"I felt so confident," he said. "I felt like if we would have got to the final, I would have felt so confident playing Spain, that we would come out victorious, but we just didn't get there, so we'll never know."
It's not a World Cup final but England have the opportunity to show their level on Saturday at Wembley.
"If we can't be motivated to show what we can do at this level, then we're never going to be," said Gordon. "Spain are an incredible team.
"I spoke with the guys at Barca and said 'how would they have felt if we got to the final [instead of] Argentina?'
"They'd seen us as really competitive. It would have been a much more competitive game, because I felt Spain dominated the final. So maybe we can show that. We can show them how good we are.
"It won't replicate the final but playing against the best team in the world and winning and playing well, that'll do for now."

'This is our company': Nigerians show off oil wealth after share-buying frenzy
- Published
Every Nigerian is now an oil magnate.
At least that is what the social media memes would have you believe as investor fever hits the country.
Nigerians have been eager to have a piece of the energy business that was built up by the country's – and continent's – richest man: Aliko Dangote.
More than four billion shares in his giant oil refinery – representing just over 3% of the company - went on the market on Monday in Africa's biggest-ever sale of its kind.
The minimum purchase was 10 shares for about $4 (£3) and despite this only representing a miniscule portion of the firm, many are now celebrating and joking about their new-found (part-)owner status.
One popular social media video has a Nigerian narrating how he stopped a speeding Dangote company lorry driver, telling him not to be reckless with company property.
Other memes show investors trying to phone up Dangote to discuss business matters.
And the term "Yangote" – a pun in the Hausa language essentially meaning "we all have a share now" - has been trending on social media.
On the first day of the Initial Public Offering (IPO), investment apps crashed as they could not handle the high demand.
Bamboo, which runs one of the most popular investor tools here, later apologised, saying: "We know we let you down."
Public affairs analyst Jamil Ubah said he had rarely seen Nigerians as excited about something as this. He argued that it fed the dream that it could lead to greater riches for a population that is often battling to make ends meet.
"I think the hope for the common man is that his money will grow into something big, and don't forget this is coming at a time when many are struggling as the economy is not doing great," he told the BBC.
Dangote wanted this to be "the people's IPO" with drivers, cooks, cleaners and servants having the chance to be part of something big.
And they took him at his word.
Twenty-five-year-old clothes seller Idris Lawal Musa made his first-ever stock exchange purchase and told the BBC he was happy after investing 21,000 naira ($16; £12) in 40 shares.
"It is no longer Dangote but 'Yangote', the company belongs to us now," he said while laughing.
But he may make a quick sale.
"I am a trader by profession and when I see that the shares have increased in price I will sell," he noted.
The popularity also reflects a growing investment culture among younger Nigerians who have embraced mobile trading platforms, cryptocurrencies and digital savings products.
But fear of missing out may have also pushed some to get into the investment business.
In the build-up to the IPO, social media platforms were awash with financial conversations. People shared subscription guides, debated valuation metrics and encouraged friends and family to participate.
But amid the frenzy, experts have warned that there are risks – shares can go down in value, as well as up, meaning people could lose some, or all, of their investment.
Financial analyst Shuaib Uwais said prospective investors should avoid thinking of the IPO as a guaranteed route to wealth.
He urged people to consider a number of factors that could impact the refinery's future performance, including disruptions to crude oil supply, operational challenges, regulatory changes and fluctuations in demand for refined petroleum products.
"If for any reason the company experiences difficulty in sourcing its raw materials, there could be challenges," he told the BBC.
Nevertheless, the IPO has given people the chance to be part of this home-grown success story.
Dangote's sprawling refinery on the outskirts of Lagos, which began operating two years ago and now processes around 700,000 barrels of crude a day, has transformed the fortunes of Nigeria's oil sector.
Until recently, Africa's largest crude oil producer had no refining capacity and had to import the finished product. Now the Dangote refinery is feeding much of the domestic demand.
But for Dangote, the share offer is about raising cash to fund the growth of the business, something that the country's mini-magnates may now be able to get behind.

‘Proud to have Trump’s endorsement’ post gets MAGA rep slapped with community note
With the president’s favorability at record lows, a Republican gubernatorial candidate locked in a heated race wiped nearly all references to Trump from his campaign site — and then got called out for it

Rep. Byron Donalds was hit with a community note on X after attempting to un-distance himself from President Donald Trump, who gave him his endorsement in Florida’s nail-biter gubernatorial race.
Donalds, long a staunch proponent of Trump and MAGA, wrote on the platform that he was proud to celebrate Trump’s endorsement, and took a swing at journalists and political junkies alike for making a big deal out of his campaign’s decision to strip references to that endorsement from his website. “I am proud to have President Trump’s endorsement,” wrote Donalds. “While everyone is focused on our website, check out our policy proposals to make life more affordable for Floridians.”
But the X post quickly received a community note claiming that the Trump endorsement only reappeared after news sites reported it had been stripped from Donalds’ website, previously having been featured on the homepage on donation buttons, banners and other widgets. The site also previously featured a photo of Donalds and his wife Erika posing with Trump.
A third-term congressman, Donalds is now running against Democratic candidate David Jolly, a former member of the House, in the general election. Jolly’s bid would be an uphill battle for any Democrat in increasingly red Florida, but it has become a surprisingly competitive race as the Republican brand has suffered nationally in recent months at the hands of Trump, whose unpopular war with Iran continues to drag on and push prices for average Americans higher and higher. The state is also home to a Senate race this cycle which has Republicans sweating for the same reason.
Jolly and Donalds were in a dead heat in a poll released last week by Florida Politics, separated by just one percentage point. The close margin seen in the polling is part of a bigger picture this cycle where candidates in red-purple states like Texas, Florida, Iowa, Ohio and others are finding themselves in a rapidly worsening political environment for conservative candidates and particularly those closely aligned with the president.
With that in mind, more than half a dozen references urging users to “Chip in to Support Trump-Endorsed Byron Donalds” and labels calling him a “TRUMP-ENDORSED Proven Conservative Fighter”, or otherwise highlighting Trump’s endorsement were stripped from the website in the days following the Florida Republican primary in August. Trump’s sole references now appear on the endorsements landing page — far from hidden, but also a marked shift for a candidate who was previously running with close association with the president.
"Our campaign website reflects Byron's focus on the issues that matter most to Floridians -- affordability, insurance costs, and government transparency. He's running to be the next Governor of Florida, is proud to have President Trump's endorsement, and has real policy proposals to tackle those issues," a campaign spokesperson told ABC News.
The removal of multiple references to the president comes as Trump’s approval rating still hovers in the mid-thirties, and support for the war in Iran is plunging to new lows.
A CNN/SRSS poll this week found that three in four U.S. adults are opposed to the war, and polling has found for months that as many as seven in ten Americans do not believe Trump has a plan to get the U.S. out of the conflict.
Donalds won the August primary in a factional GOP contest that pitted him against a top ally of Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, Trump’s 2024 primary rival. Jay Collins has since endorsed Donalds’ bid for governor. Another candidate in the race was James Fishback, who ran an insurgent bid that was criticized by many for leaning heavily into overtly racist language against Donalds and his supporters.
A defeat of Donalds in November would be a massive blow to Republicans in Florida, who are highly organized and better funded than Democratic rivals in the state. It would also be a personal blow to the political capital of the president within the Republican Party, as Donalds’ opponents warned that he was a weak candidate for the general election and are generally looking for any opportunity to weaken Trump’s grip on the party.
n Florida, Trump’s adopted home, the president’s dominance in Republican Party politics is well-known; in 2024, he successfully won endorsements from the majority of the state’s congressional delegation, dealing a blow to DeSantis out of the gate.
Donalds is far from the most vocal Trump loyalist in D.C. but has not wavered from the president’s side publicly. He was previously floated as a candidate for speaker by a coalition of pro-Trump representatives during the ousting of Kevin McCarthy from the role in 2023.

UP trade show 2026 to open with ODOP, EVs and defence products on display
UPITS 2026 will showcase Uttar Pradesh's traditional products and emerging sectors to global buyers, with over 2,400 exhibitors and 550 international buyers expected. The fourth edition of the trade show will have Austria, Belarus, Japan, Russia, Singapore and Vietnam as partner countries.
Uttar Pradesh is set to showcase products ranging from its traditional One District One Product (ODOP) offerings to electric vehicles, electronics and defence equipment to global buyers as the fourth edition of the Uttar Pradesh International Trade Show (UPITS) 2026 begins in Greater Noida on Friday.
The five-day trade show, being held from September 25 to 29 at the India Expo Centre & Mart, is expected to bring together more than 2,400 exhibitors, international buyers, investors and business delegations as the state seeks to expand its export footprint. The 2026 edition will have Austria, Belarus, Japan, Russia, Singapore and Vietnam as partner countries.
The event is being held under the theme “UP for Global Growth: Innovation, Manufacturing and Exports”, with a focus on connecting businesses in the state with overseas buyers and investment opportunities.
FROM TRADITIONAL PRODUCTS TO NEW-AGE SECTORS
More than 27 sectors are expected to be represented at the trade show.
These include ODOP products and MSMEs, along with electronics and IT, defence and aerospace, pharmaceuticals, electric vehicles, agriculture, food processing, textiles, leather, renewable energy, tourism and startups.
The mix reflects the state's effort to showcase both its traditional manufacturing base and newer industries to international markets.
The trade show will also feature business-to-business meetings, country sessions and sector-specific discussions, allowing participating companies to explore sourcing, investment and technology partnerships.
SIX COUNTRIES TO PARTICIPATE
The international component of UPITS 2026 will feature six partner countries: Austria, Belarus, Japan, Russia, Singapore and Vietnam.
Foreign delegations are expected to include government officials, trade representatives and business leaders. The programme includes country pavilions and B2B interactions with businesses from Uttar Pradesh.
The participation of five countries, Austria, Japan, Russia, Singapore and Vietnam, is proposed to include 36 exhibitors and around 100 buyers, according to the state government's plans. Belarus is participating separately as a partner country.
OVER 550 INTERNATIONAL BUYERS EXPECTED
The Uttar Pradesh government expects more than 550 international buyers from 85 countries to attend the trade show. Overall, the event is expected to attract 1.5 lakh B2B buyers and 4.5 lakh B2C visitors, besides more than 2,400 exhibitors.
Interest from buyers has already been recorded ahead of the event. As of September 18, more than 45,000 domestic B2B buyers had registered, while around 1,500 international buyers had registered. More than 500 international buyers had been shortlisted and tickets for over 300 had been secured, according to government data.
The state is also targeting more than 4,000 MoUs, with proposed agreements worth over Rs 3,200 crore, while business enquiries are expected to cross Rs 13,500 crore.
BUILDING ON 2025 EDITION
The latest edition comes after a larger international turnout at UPITS 2025. The third edition had 2,228 exhibitors, 525 international buyers from 85 countries, 1,40,735 domestic B2B buyers and 3,66,364 B2C visitors.
It generated business enquiries exceeding Rs 11,200 crore, while more than 2,400 MoUs worth Rs 1,882 crore were signed.
With this year's event, the state is seeking to widen the reach of its products beyond domestic markets by using the trade show to connect local manufacturers, exporters and MSMEs with international buyers and potential investors.
The five-day event will run at the India Expo Centre & Mart in Greater Noida from September 25 to 29.

Meta Ray-Ban Display getting feature updates including holographic avatar support
The smart glasses are also arriving in five new markets this fall.

One of the notable changes coming to the device is support for a holographic avatar while taking calls. The Hologram feature will initially be available in early access later this fall for WhatsApp users in the US.
The glasses' heads-up navigation tools have also been expanded, allowing a wearer to ask for cycling or public transit directions with a voice command. Additionally, the navigation directions can now be based on the world around the person rather than solely relying on street signs for a more conversational experience. For example, you might be directed to "turn left at the yellow house" rather than to "turn left on Third Street."
When Karissa Bell reviewed the Ray-Ban Display smart glasses last year, one of the top issues she had with the Display was a lack of available apps. A new Explore app is coming to both the smart glasses and the Meta AI app that will help users to browse available programs that do work on the set.
The other features announced today include some incremental improvements to the user experience, such as bringing Dolby Atmos audio to its capture and playback tools, photo editing within the Display screen, a more detailed calendar, mirrored phone notifications and Threads for Community Feeds.
The Meta Ray-Ban Display is coming to five new markets: the UK, Canada, France, Italy and Germany. The glasses will be available to order online in those regions, as well as in the US. Display is available starting today in the UK starting at £749 and in Canada starting at CA$1,149. Pre-orders will begin today for the other three new markets for a base price of €899 before Display becomes available on October 13.

Noted conservationist and ornithologist Asad Rahmani’s latest book, Where Have the Birds Gone? Empty Nests. Quiet Skies. One Question (Indian Pitta, an imprint of Juggernaut Books), is dedicated to lost species: “the mountain quail, pink-headed duck and numerous other species that were exterminated, with an apology from humankind”. This sombre beginning sets the tone of his nuanced book.
Where Have the Birds Gone? illuminates “the scale of the crisis confronting birds today — a crisis unfolding not with a single dramatic blow, but through the steady erosion of safe skies, quiet habitats and the fragile continuity on which avian life depends,” writes the Lucknow-based Rahmani, former director of Bombay Natural History Society and author of 27 books and 150 peer-reviewed scientific papers.
The book begins by focusing on 14 of India’s most threatened birds, including the white-bellied heron, green munia, the Bengal florican and Jerdon’s courser, evaluating the factors that threaten their existence. These include habitat loss and fragmentation, alien species, wind farms, power lines, dams, illegal pet trade, pesticides, poaching, glass buildings, and free-ranging stray dogs, which have become apex predators in many ecosystems, according to the 76-year-old. “In India, dogs are reported to have attacked 80 wild species, including 31 threatened species, four of which are critically endangered,” he writes, throwing in a sobering statistic. “In Ladakh, for instance, free-ranging dogs kill nearly 60 per cent of the chicks of the black-necked crane, a species listed by the IUCN as ‘vulnerable’ to extinction.”
The book is full of more such dispiriting facts. For example, skylarks have declined by nearly 80% while Indian rollers have seen a 30% decline in 12 years; according to BirdLife International and the IUCN, 1,256 species — about 11.5% of all birds — are currently threatened with extinction, and fewer than 120 great Indian bustards persist, largely confined to two pockets in Rajasthan.
But it isn’t all doom and gloom. “I believe that I am an optimist (you cannot be a conservationist without being one),” he writes, citing success stories like the greater adjutant, painted stork, and spot-billed pelican, before offering conservation solutions rooted in “common sense rather than technological wizardry or cutting-edge science”.
Some of these solutions include expanding protected areas, conservation breeding, undergrounding power lines along major migratory routes and reducing free-ranging dog populations, states Rahmani, who firmly believes this. “If India truly aspires to be a Vishwaguru, a teacher to the world, then leadership must extend beyond economics and geopolitics. It must encompass sustainability, climate stability, environmental protection, equity, human rights and the rights of wildlife,” he says.
Edited excerpts from an interview:
Through birds you explore myriad facets of wildlife, from global biodiversity threats to Earth’s sixth mass extinction and climate change and human-wildlife interaction. What makes birds an effective entry point?
Birds and plants are almost the first things we see as children, which is why we feel connected to them. There are lots of positive stories about birds in our literature and culture, and birds like house sparrows and crows have become accustomed to us. Also, birds are not dangerous: no bird has killed a human being so far.
Another big reason why people like birds is that birdwatching is the second-most common (nature-related) hobby in the world, after gardening. Even if we live in small homes, we put flowers on our balconies as a symbolic gesture because we want to bring nature back into our lives. When we go birding, therefore, we aren’t just looking at birds, but at the whole environment. That’s why we end up getting concerned about other things, too.
One thing that came up in this book was that Project Tiger, while certainly offering conservation benefits, wasn’t enough to save many of our threatened birds because these birds don’t always live in protected areas. Could you tell us more?
Well, I wrote a book on India’s threatened birds in 2012. There, I analysed 156 species of threatened and near-threatened birds and where they are found. We found that 50% are not found in Project Tiger areas, or, even if they are, they don’t breed or spend much time there. For instance, the Sarus crane is found in Project Tiger areas, but it does not breed there because big cats like tigers and leopards can easily swim and eat it.
Of course, many birds have benefited from forest protection, but to say everything is protected by [flagship programmes such as] Project Tiger or Project Snow Leopard is not true. Once we accept this, we can think of other ways to protect them.
You’ve championed the Great Indian bustard for many years. The critically endangered bird nearly became India’s national bird before losing out to the peafowl. Is everything stacked against the bustards?
Everything is against them, starting with habitat change: these birds are long-lived and long-ranging. Even in areas where they are not killed, their population declines as their habitats shrink.
The biggest killer of the bustard, however, is high-tension wires. Bustards are largely terrestrial birds and only fly when disturbed by a predator, which is becoming more common because of free-ranging stray dogs in these areas.
This means that the chances of a bustard hitting a wire have increased tremendously. These birds fly at the level of these wires and have a visual blind spot: they see well to both sides but have narrow frontal vision, so they often miss what is directly in front of them. They don’t necessarily die of electrocution, but get injured and fall to the ground below, where the predator will be eagerly waiting for them.
Given that we live in a country where many underprivileged people, particularly pastoralists, fishers and indigenous people, share spaces with wildlife, how do we protect their homes and livelihoods as well as preserve what is left of our wilderness?
There is no single answer because the situation varies from species to species, culture to culture, area to area, and habitat to habitat. But we certainly have to listen to these people and try to protect these spaces through traditional methods.
Community conservation matters more than ever because population growth and shrinking available land have also reduced tolerance for wildlife. In general, if people are not harmed by an animal, they are more tolerant of it, which makes community conservation for animals like birds and reptiles much easier.
Wildlife, like leopards, for instance, become a bigger problem for understandable reasons: no one wants their child to be killed by an animal.
But India’s beauty is that, despite such a large population in such a small area, we have not lost any large animals. People in this country don’t always support conservation, but they never oppose it.

U.S. health regulators will review the scientific evidence on testosterone use in menopausal women on Thursday, including its benefits, risks, dosing and role in female health, as well as perspectives from doctors and patients.
The public meeting, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said could help guide future research and drug development, comes as a growing number of women are turning to testosterone to manage menopause symptoms.
There is no FDA-approved testosterone therapy for women, despite years of off-label use to treat low sexual desire, known as hypoactive sexual desire disorder, or HSDD.
Last year, the FDA removed the boxed warning about increased cardiovascular risk from testosterone products for men after reviewing post-marketing studies, though the products still carry warnings about increased blood pressure.
Physicians who prescribe testosterone to women typically rely on low doses of products approved for men, often dividing existing products such as AbbVie's AndroGel and Keenova Therapeutics' Testim, or on compounded formulations.
The lack of a female-specific product creates practical challenges for clinicians, said Diana Tordoff, an instructor in obstetrics and gynecology at Stanford, noting that an approved product could provide standardised dosing, labeling and safety-monitoring guidance and potentially improve insurance coverage.
Still, some experts say key questions remain unresolved. More long-term safety data are needed, said Stephanie Faubion, director of Mayo Clinic's Center for Women's Health.
The United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa have approved or licensed testosterone products specifically for women.
The FDA's request for public comments ahead of the meeting attracted hundreds of submissions, many from women describing improved libido, energy and quality of life while using testosterone.
Evidence and safety gaps
Interest in testosterone among menopausal women has grown alongside claims on social media that it can improve energy, muscle mass, bone health and cognition, though specialists say the evidence is strongest for HSDD.
"We do not have any evidence in women that it will improve muscle mass or bone density or mood or well-being or really any other metric," Faubion said.
Karen Adams, director of Stanford Medicine's Program in Menopause and Healthy Aging, said testosterone has been reviewed by the FDA four times for use in women but has never been approved because of a lack of long-term safety data and concerns about cardiovascular and breast cancer risks.
The FDA has approved non-testosterone options like Sprout Pharmaceuticals' Addyi and Cosette Pharmaceuticals' Vyleesi for certain patients with HSDD.
Testosterone is generally not recommended for women with a history of breast cancer because it can be converted to estrogen in the body that can drive some cancers.
Excessive testosterone exposure can cause acne and increased hair growth, physicians said, while rarer effects such as voice deepening and hair loss may be irreversible.
Studies show that testosterone therapy is generally considered safe for men with medically diagnosed low levels of the hormone when prescribed and monitored by a doctor.
Tordoff and Adams are leading Stanford's MIX-T pilot study examining how low-dose testosterone affects vaginal health and the vaginal microbiome in postmenopausal women. Results are expected within the next two years.

European football leader Aleksander Ceferin said Wednesday it is “our work” to repair the unity and trust broken by FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s failed World Cup sell-off plan.
The UEFA president, in rare public comments two months into the divisive global rift in football, did not cite Infantino by name but said “not everyone places the game above their own ambitions.”
“The project that shattered the unity of world football may be abolished, but the trust it broke has not returned, and repairing it is our work now,” Ceferin said in a video message to an audience of soccer and business executives in Lisbon.
ALSO READ | ‘New one’ Klopp promises fresh approach as Germany reign begins
Ceferin led UEFA’s backlash in July that helped stop Infantino’s plan to sell at least 20% of FIFA’s future commercial rights for USD 4.2 billion to investors led by Josh Kushner, the brother of U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
Though Infantino dropped the plan within days, UEFA said it would work toward removing him from office — before or at the FIFA presidential election in March — and preparing a criminal complaint against him in Switzerland for alleged financial mismanagement.
“Trust in our sport rests on three pillars: unity, transparency, and governance that serves the many, not the few,” Ceferin, a Slovenian lawyer, said Wednesday.
“In recent times, all three were disregarded by people who had sworn to protect them,” he said.
FIFA and Infantino have said the plan to create a FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) commercial spinoff was to accelerate development of soccer worldwide, outside the wealthy power base of Europe.
Ceferin has ruled out being a candidate in the FIFA election, where Infantino seeks a fourth and final term in office through 2031 to complete a 15-year presidency.
There were “many, many” potential candidates capable of challenging Infantino, Ceferin told reporters last week in Greece, after a UEFA executive committee meeting in Thessaloniki.
FIFA has a November 18 deadline to enter the election contest, four months before the vote by 211 member federations in Morocco — a key ally of Infantino, where the governing body has its African headquarters near Rabat.
FIFA’s 211 members effectively already own the Zurich-based not-for-profit soccer body which has at least $5 billion in cash reserves after the 2026 World Cup in North America.
Infantino planned to offer the 211 members $20 million each this year to approve the FFE project. It would have been a subsidiary controlling tens of billions of dollars of commercial rights for all future World Cups, Club World Cups and other tournaments.
UEFA and its continental allies, the North American soccer body CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation, have said FIFA can afford to spend USD 2.1 billion giving each member a USD 10 million one-off payment from the reserves without involving investors.
Infantino moved this week to calm critics of his hands-on executive presidency by offering to open an independent review of FIFA’s governance standards and decision-making. He is scheduled to chair a meeting of his 37-member FIFA Council, that includes Ceferin, on October 15 in Zurich.
UEFA asked last month for an independent review of the FFE project that was secretly developed over the past year without some FIFA senior management knowing.
Infantino has a checkered history with independent oversight of FIFA. In 2017, one year before the men’s World Cup in Russia, FIFA removed its most senior governance official who had enforced conflict-of-interest rules to stop Vitaly Mutko, who was a Russian deputy prime minister, from standing as an election candidate to retain his seat on FIFA’s ruling committee.
That removal of Portuguese academic Miguel Maduro prompted three of his independent colleagues on the FIFA governance panel — including former U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Navi Pillay, a South African judge — to resign in protest.

Trump winces as U.S. military jet carries out planned flyover for spectators, and looks out of place in gloves and winter coat next to placid Xi Jinping

Donald Trump raised a few eyebrows as a somewhat surreal red-carpet ceremony was put on for Chinese President Xi Jinping at a military base in Maryland on Wednesday for Xi’s arrival.
Video caught Chinese officials looking on as U.S. Marines smoothed out a red carpet for the Chinese president, who descended the stairs and was greeted by his U.S. counterpart, clad in a long winter coat and leather gloves in the 65-degree weather.
The pair, along with their spouses, then stood beside each other awkwardly as the national anthem was played, cannons fired in a salute, and a military jet soared loudly by overhead — causing Trump to visibly wince while Xi placidly watched the plane pass overhead.
“[I]t is 64 degrees at Joint Base Andrews right now and yet Trump is wearing gloves are he greets President Xi,” wrote journalist Aaron Rupar.
“Trump -- it’s YOUR airshow. How do you get scared?” asked Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who played video of Xi’s arrival for his viewers.
The ceremony was a major departure from the typically more reserved setting in which U.S. presidents meet leaders of major U.S. geopolitical rivals, like Russia and China. But Trump has broken protocol on that front before, including when he rolled out a red carpet for Russia’s Vladimir Putin when the latter visited Alaska in 2025.
Xi’s visit comes as the U.S. and China remain at odds over a number of trade issues including AI and semiconductors, and on both topics the U.S. president has been accused by his domestic critics of being too lax with Beijing. Ahead of Wednesday’s arrival ceremony, Trump faced criticism from a Republican senator typically closely aligned with the White House over putting on a “lavish” welcome for the Chinese president.
By comparison, Joe Biden waited to greet Xi until the Chinese president arrived at the site of their summit in San Francisco in 2024. Like Trump, Biden greeted Xi with a military guard and red carpet — though not one carted out to the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews.

The Eiffel Tower has reopened after a one-day strike was called in response to the landmark’s management ordering female staff to keep out of sight at the request of a visiting religious group.
City Hall, which operates the Paris landmark, has apologised for breaching France’s republican principle of equality and ordered a full inquiry.
Workers at the tower walked out on Monday, closing the landmark to visitors, after female colleagues were sidelined and replaced during a visit organised by a Hindu religious group at the weekend.
In a statement, staff said they objected to “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit.
“Some were asked to leave their posts and wait in separate rooms. In some posts, women were replaced by men. All female employees were instructed not to pass through or enter certain areas while the [Hindu] delegation was present,” they said in a statement.
Employees said they were shocked to find themselves in a situation that was “deeply contrary to the values of equality and nondiscrimination”.
“The Eiffel Tower is the symbol of France. We believe it must also be exemplary in the values it promotes and the way it treats staff,” the statement said.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement, whose members made the request in advance of a visit on Saturday, apologised.
“To our knowledge, nobody was refused access to the Eiffel Tower at any moment. Nevertheless, We offer our sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or offended by this situation,” it wrote in a statement.
BAPS is close to India’s ruling Hindu nationalist party, Bharatiya Janata, and was in France to consecrate its first major temple in the country on Sunday.
The public-owned Eiffel Tower operating company (SETE) acknowledged that BAPS had requested that “interactions with women” be limited, and said it should not have accepted these conditions. “They are not in keeping with SETE’s values or the principles of equality between women and men and the neutrality that must guide the organisation of visits to the monument,” it said.
Emmanuel Grégoire, the mayor of Paris, has promised an investigation to “get to the bottom of this as soon as possible”.
He said moving female staff out of sight was unacceptable.
“These are not my values nor those the Eiffel Tower must represent,” he wrote on X.
Ariel Weil, mayor of the Paris Centre district and president of SETE, said he was unaware of the “shocking and unacceptable” conditions afforded the visiting group.
“I confirm again the Eiffel Tower’s commitment to republican values and gender equality,” he said.

Eriksen leaves Wolfsburg by mutual consent
- Published
Christian Eriksen has left Wolfsburg by mutual consent, just over three months after collapsing during Denmark's friendly with Ukraine.
The former Manchester United midfielder's contract with the German second-tier side had been scheduled to run until June 2027.
Eriksen, 34, had previously suffered a cardiac arrest during Denmark's opening European Championship group match against Finland in Copenhagen in 2021.
"At the moment, it is important for me to be close to my family in Denmark. I'm pleased that we were able to find a solution together," Eriksen said.
"My time in Wolfsburg was marked by many highs and lows. I know that the club is now in good hands as it aims to make its way back to the Bundesliga, and I am convinced that a successful future lies ahead."
Eriksen, who has not played since June, joined Wolfsburg as a free agent a year ago after leaving Manchester United and made 34 appearances for the club.
The 151-cap international has previously played for Ajax, Tottenham, Inter Milan and Brentford.
In a statement, Wolfsburg's managing director for sport, Dieter Hecking, said: "It was clear that the decision about his future had to be Christian's.
"We wanted to give him that freedom in this particular situation and have now agreed to his request to terminate the contract.
"Despite his short time here, he has left a lasting impression on his team-mates, our staff and the fans."
