Meta's $1,300 VR Glasses look like the Vision Pro sequel Apple should be making
Finally, someone made lightweight VR specs.
After a few leaks, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg finally revealed the company's next-generation Meta VR Glasses at its Connect event tonight. Arriving in Spring 2027, they look like oversized sunglasses (similar to display frames from Xreal and other), paired with an external power and computing pod, like the Apple Vision Pro. The Meta VR Glasses also have onboard cameras to detect the wearer's hands for gesture-based controls. While they're not cheap at $1,300, they're a far cry from the Vision Pro's original $3,500 cost, or its current $3,700 price. And at first glance, they look exactly like how I'd imagine a true successor to the Vision Pro — a pair of unobtrusive and lightweight VR glasses at a more palatable price.
Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as an all-in-one entertainment and productivity device. Just like the Vision Pro, you can watch movies on enormous virtual screens, or connect to your computer to multitask with multiple windows floating in front of you. The VR Glasses are launching together with more than 75 hand-powered games, and you can also connect a pair of Touch Plus controllers to play existing Quest VR games.
The Meta VR Glasses are powered by Qualcomm's new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, the XR2 Gen 3, and feature a 5K (2,412 by 2,288 pixels) 120Hz micro-OLED display. It relies on six external cameras for color passthrough and motion tracking, and also has four internal eye-tracking cameras. With a 70-degree horizontal field of view, the Meta VR Glasses won't fill your eyes with VR as much as the Vision Pro's 100-degree FOV, but it's significantly higher than most display glasses. Meta's wired computing puck, which looks compact enough to slip in a pocket, holds 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage (along with a microSD card slot for more content).
On their own, the Meta VR Glasses weigh 100 grams, or about 0.2 pounds. That's only a tad heavier than Xreal's One Pro AR display glasses, and significantly lighter than the Vision Pro's headset, which weighs between 1.3 to 1.7 pounds. (Part of that weight is counter-balanced by the Vision Pro's head strap, to be fair.) Meta's compute puck weighs an additional 300 grams (0.6 pounds), slightly lighter than the Vision Pro's. Judging from the product photos, you won't be able to wear the Meta VR Glasses over your own spectacles, but as usual, you can order custom prescription frames.
Zuckerberg has never shied away from blatantly copying competitors, and it's pretty clear the company took plenty of inspiration from the Vision Pro for the Meta VR Glasses. Full-color pass-through lets you see the real world alongside VR experiences; the interface is entirely built around hand gestures; it's unlocked via biometric iris recognition; and you can virtually chat with friends using a digital "Hologram" recreation of yourself. It's like a checklist of the features that made the Vision Pro seem more thoughtful than a normal headset.
Meta appears to be aping the Vision Pro's approach to 3D movies as well: The Meta VR Glasses will have hundreds of 3D films available to buy or rent, and you'll also find 3D content in streaming apps like Disney+ and Peacock. Given the death of 3D TVs, the Vision Pro has ultimately become one of the few ways to enjoy 3D films like Avatar in their full glory, so it's nice to see Meta offering something similar. And since the Meta VR runs Quest OS, I'm hoping this 3D content storefront eventually heads to the Quest VR headsets.
Additionally, it sounds like the company is taking a cue from Apple's Immersive Video Format — Meta says National Geographic will be launching a new app next year with 180-degree 3D Video. A new "VR Enhanced Cinema" format will let you watch 3D movies with effects that bleed into your real-world space, similar to the way dynamic ambient lighting on TVs makes content more immersive. The company says Avenger's: Infinity War and Star Wars: Episode IV, A New Hope will be available in the VR format next year. (It's odd Disney didn't pick newer movies, though.)
Unlike the similarly-priced $1,050 Steam Frame, the Meta VR Glasses are, at the very least, evolving the idea of what a VR headset can be. It likely won't be as immersive as the Frame and other headsets that completely envelop your field of vision, but for most people, it's probably worth losing that to have a device that's just easier to wear. You won't look like a huge weirdo slipping them on while flying, and since you wear them like glasses, there's little chance they'll mess up your hair as badly as a typical VR headset.
The biggest downsides for the Meta VR Glasses are its $1,300 price — though I'm sure many VR diehards and Vision Pro fans would jump on it — and the fact they come from Meta, a company that not everyone is a huge fan of. Since these are obviously VR specs, I don't think they'd have the same privacy concerns as Meta's Ray-Ban and Display glasses, but the company has significantly poisoned the idea of wearing anything in public with cameras.
Apple's new CEO John Ternus isn't giving up on the Vision Pro just yet — "It's the early days of a long journey," he said in a recent interview with Clique TV (via MacRumors). But recent layoffs and the departure of the product's lead haven't been good signs for the headset. And now there's the Meta VR Glasses, which builds on the Vision Pro's innovations to deliver something that's lighter, cheaper and more consumer-friendly.

Vladimir Putin has arrived in India’s capital of Delhi ahead of an 11-member Brics summit set to be dominated by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as economic challenges.
The Russian president and his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, were due to hold talks with India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, while Chinese leader Xi Jinping was also expected to attend the two-day meeting.
Putin arrived at Palam air force Station in Delhi, where he was greeted by India’s minister of state for external affairs, Kirti Vardhan Singh, according to footage broadcast by Russia’s Ria Novosti news agency.
The summit will mark Xi’s first visit to India since 2019 and is seen as the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again recently, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
However, deep mistrust remains, with their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
On Friday posters of a beaming Modi lined streets in Delhi, along with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions in central districts. Delhi police have urged people to be patient and cooperative.
Brics was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by western powers.
It has since expanded and now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the US and Israel in February.
“The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the Brics summit,” said Harsh V Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation. “What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of Brics – today looks like a big constraint on Brics”.
It will be Pezeshkian’s first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.
“The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the [expanded] group’s cohesion,” said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the Brics foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important strategic partners and its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Putin last visited India in December 2025 but he also met Modi in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, this month.
India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, visited Kyiv this month, when the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he was “grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war”.

The Wedding Photographer of Darfur
Mohammed, a photographer from Darfur, was forced to flee the violence in el-Fasher and now lives in Tawila, a refuge for thousands displaced by the conflict in Sudan.

Pine Labs’ early backer Mastercard has exited the company by selling its entire 4.31% stake through a bulk deal on Tuesday. The investor offloaded 4.97 Cr shares at ₹187.75 apiece, fetching ₹933.6 Cr. The deal was executed at a 5% discount to Pine Labs’ closing price today. Mutual funds and foreign institutional investors emerged as key buyers, with ICICI Prudential Life Insurance Company picking up the largest chunk of 93.1 Lakh shares, according to BSE data. Societe Generale bought 87.7 Lakh shares, while Citi Group acquired 66.7 Lakh shares. BNP Paribas, Goldman Sachs, Franklin Templeton, Kotak Mahindra Mutual Fund, Morgan Stanley and Susquehanna Pacific were among the other buyers. This is Mastercard’s second major stake sale in Pine Labs since the company’s IPO in November 2025. The investor sold 59.2 Lakh shares in the IPO for ₹130.9 Cr, generating 1.7X returns on its initial investment. Mastercard first backed Pine Labs in 2020. Several of Pine Labs’ early institutional backers have pared their holdings since its listing. Actis, Invesco and Madison India have also offloaded shares in the company. The latest exit comes despite Pine Labs’ recent recovery on the bourses. The stock remains down more than 15% year-to-date but has gained over 25% in the past month, partly following the reintroduction of merchant discount rates (MDR) on UPI. Pine Labs shares closed Tuesday 2.07% higher at ₹197.55. The recent rally has also been supported by positive brokerage commentary. Motilal Oswal initiated coverage on Pine Labs on September 21 with a ‘Buy’ rating and a target price of ₹250, citing projected growth across its payments businesses. The brokerage expects Pine Labs’ digital infrastructure and transaction platform to grow revenue at a 24.5% CAGR through FY28, while its issuing and acquiring platform is projected to grow revenue at 23% CAGR. It expects overall revenue, adjusted EBITDA and PAT to grow at 24%, 46% and 129% CAGR, respectively, between FY26 and FY28, with adjusted EBITDA margins rising to 28.7% by FY28 from 9% in FY24. In the first quarter of FY27, Pine Labs net profit skyrocketed 4X YoY to ₹4.8 Cr while its operating revenue zoomed 20% YoY to ₹736.9.

Senior Judicial Officer, Yash Paul Bourney was sworn in as the Judge of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh at a solemn ceremony held in the Chief Justice’s Court at the Srinagar Wing of the High Court on Tuesday.
Dr. Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, administered the oath of office to Justice Yash Paul Bourney.
The Warrant of Appointment was read out by M. K. Sharma, Registrar General, High Court of J&K and Ladakh, who also conducted the proceedings of the ceremony.
The ceremony was graced by Justice Rajnesh Oswal, Justice Mohd. Akram Chowdhary, Justice Wasim Sadiq Nargal, Justice Rajesh Sekhri, Justice Mohd. Yousuf Wani and Justice Sanjay Parihar. Justice Sanjeev Kumar, Justice Sindhu Sharma, Justice Sanjay Dhar, Justice Rahul Bharti, Justice Moksha Khajuria Kazmi and Justice Shahzad Azeem joined the ceremony through virtual mode from Jammu wing of the High Court.
The family members, close relatives and friends of Justice Yash Paul Bourney were also present on the occasion, lending special significance to the ceremony.
Among other dignitaries present were Mir Syed Latif, Judicial Member (HOD) of the Central Administrative Tribunal, Srinagar Bench, Shaleen Kabra, Additional Chief Secretary, M.K. Sinha, ADGP CID, Achal Sethi, Commissioner Secretary Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs; Divisional Commissioner, Kashmir, IGP Kashmir, IGP Security, Senior Advocates; Executive Members of the Kashmir Advocates’ Association and the J&K High Court Bar Association, Jammu; Law Officers; Judicial Officers; and officers of the High Court Registry.
The Ministry of Law and Justice, Government of India, issued the notification appointing Justice Yash Paul Bourney as the Judge of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh on September 19, 2026.
Born on August 25, 1967, Justice Yash Paul Bourney hails from village Dadwara, Bhaddu, Billawar, District Kathua. During his distinguished judicial career, he has held several important judicial and administrative assignments. He served as Principal District & Sessions Judge at Leh, Baramulla, Udhampur and Jammu, besides serving as Special Judge, Anti-Corruption, Srinagar and Special Judge, Anti-Corruption, Jammu.
Justice Bourney also served in key institutional positions as Member Secretary, J&K Legal Services Authority; Registrar Vigilance, High Court of J&K and Ladakh; and Director, J&K Judicial Academy.
After serving as Principal District & Sessions Judge, Jammu, Justice Bourney was appointed on deputation as Member, J&K Special Tribunal, Jammu. He was serving in the said capacity immediately prior to his elevation as a Judge of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.

'Make women feel seen': Why the Dutch have a new word for labia
- Published
Can you imagine seeing the words "shame lips" on your medical notes? The term, which can also be translated as "pubic lips", is the Dutch word for a women's body part. But, for some, it's just one of countless examples that are outdated and loaded with stigma.
Last month, leading Dutch dictionary Dikke van Dale said it would include a new term for the labia, "vulvalippen" - in its upcoming online addition - alongside the traditional term "schaamlippen".
European campaigners have long been calling for a rewrite of terms used to discuss women's bodies, sexuality and health. What unites them is the desire to move away from terms that are often seen as misogynistic or judgmental.
"Language shapes how we see ourselves," says Shari Klein, one of the founders of the Schaamteloos campaign, which targets words that use "schaam" or "shame".
"It's crucial people have a more neutral, anatomically correct word - not a word that links to shame, whether consciously or sub-consciously," she says.
'Sex positivity'
Calls to use vulvalippen aren't new but campaigners say inclusion in the dictionary may be a sign society is "finally ready for change".
Esther Van der Valk, part of prominent Dutch feminist group Dolle Mina, says it's also about sex positivity and reducing body shaming.
The campaign's next steps are to convince doctors and officials to use vulvalippen in leaflets and consultations.
Ton den Boon, editor of the dictionary, says adding vulvalippen is justified because it is becoming more established in the language and is being used more in the media, biology text books, medical leaflets and is even seen in veterinary medicine.
But whether it will be adopted widely is yet to be seen.
Other Dutch words, relevant to both men and women, could carry similar connotations - from "schaam haar" (pubic or shame hair) or "schaam been" (pubic or shame bone) to even "schaam lice" for pubic lice.
However, critics say changing a word will not necessarily change people's lives.
- Language around birth should be less judgemental 
  - Published15 June 2022
The campaign mirrors attempts in Germany, where in 2018 journalists Gunda Windmüller and Mithu Sanyal started a petition to change "Shamlippen" to "Vulvalippen".
Windmüller says she was compelled to after a gynaecologist told her of the shame some women carry when discussing their bodies and having medical examinations.
When writing her article, she realised she couldn't even mention anatomy without including the word shame.
"Vulvalippen" has not yet been adopted by a German dictionary, but Windmüller has spotted it in conversations, school textbooks and women's magazines.
Her hope is the Dutch move will ignite support closer to home.
'Virginity membrane'
Similarly, in Sweden a new word for "hymen" was added in the academic dictionary after a 2009 campaign.
The association for sexuality education (RFSU) felt traditional term "mödomshinna", which translates as maidenhood skin or virginity membrane, was anatomically inaccurate and did nothing to dispel myths around hymens and virginity.
The new term "slidkrans" translates as vaginal corona - reflecting the fact the hymen is often folds of tissue in a ring, rather than a seal that breaks once.
"With a new word we can challenge the myths that seek to control women's sexuality and freedom," Sonja Ghaderi of the RFSU says.
Ghaderi says slidkrans is used particularly by healthcare professionals and in youth clinics but adds misinformation still exists emphasising the "need to change social constructs".
In the UK, feminist podcast host Nicola Denson-Elliott started a petition to replace the word "hysterectomy" (surgical removal of the womb) with "uterectomy".
She argues, as others have, that hysterectomy has linguistic links with hysteria, external - once seen as a disease of emotional excess in women - and wants a more "anatomically correct term" not one "associated with emotion."
The petition describes it as "medical misogyny", adding: "Women deserve terminology that respects them."
'Judgmental words'
Linguistics researcher Dr Beth Malory says any changes need to be researched first.
"Will people understand uterectomy? Is simply saying removal of the womb better?"
New words cannot be ambiguous, she says, it's important to look at the whole system so there is no confusion.
Malory also studies language around pregnancy and loss.
One phrase highlighted in her research is "incompetent cervix" used to describe the shortening of the cervix that can increase risks of pregnancy loss and early birth. Women told her it made them feel blamed for the medical issue.
"Why do we need judgmental words like failure or incompetence?" says obstetrician Dr Brooke Vandermolen, external.
Even though they appear in medical textbooks, she tells me she's moved away from certain terms, including "failure to progress" - which describes labour not moving forward as expected.
"Language is incredibly important and the words we choose can show recognition and make people feel validated and seen."
In 2022, the Royal College of Midwives produced guidance offering alternative phrases.
But Vandermolen says some traditional terms are still being used and still cause distress.
"I hope this change in the Netherlands sparks more conversations here about how we speak about women's bodies. What we say can have a lasting impact."

Alzheimer’s blood tests are advancing diagnosis. What can they really tell us?
Blood tests such as p-tau217 and p-tau181 can help identify changes linked to Alzheimer’s disease. Neurologists explain what these tests can detect, how they aid diagnosis and what the results can and cannot tell patients
For now, the important question is not simply whether a blood test is positive or negative, but what the result means in the context of the person’s symptoms, clinical assessment and the specific test used.
| Photo Credit: AFP
Changes in the brain linked to Alzheimer’s disease can begin years before memory and other cognitive symptoms appear. Blood-based biomarkers offer a less invasive way to detect some of these biological changes. These include phosphorylated tau (p-tau), such as p-tau217 and p-tau181, and amyloid-beta measures such as the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio. However, these tests do not directly measure memory loss, brain-cell loss or the severity of cognitive impairment.
Tau is a protein found in nerve cells. In Alzheimer’s disease, abnormal tau is linked to the formation of neurofibrillary tangles. The build-up of amyloid-beta is another biological change associated with the disease.

US-Iran War News Live: The war between the US and Iran entered its 208th day on Thursday as the two sides continue to claim that they are ready for talks. Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian has said that Tehran is “ready for dialogue, diplomacy, and negotiations but insisted that the Islamic Republic won’t accept the “language of force”. US President Donald Trump, in his UNGA address, said that he may "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal isn't reached soon to end the nearly seven-month war. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a deal with Iran would involve hard work and that Trump “has a number of options available, including military options”.
US sanctions hit Iranian flights
The US has also said it will impose so-called secondary sanctions against any country that allows Iranian flights after Wednesday. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state TV that Iran would ensure neighbouring countries' airports could not function if they stop Iranian flights.
US, Iran hold first talks since July
Iranian and US officials held their first known indirect talks on Tuesday since a ceasefire collapsed in July, with Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner communicating through mediators.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Tehran had conveyed conditions during a two-hour exchange of messages with Washington via a Qatari mediator. These included an end to the war on all fronts, a halt to US "acts of aggression" and the release of frozen Iranian assets.
Indian seafarer killed off Oman
The Indian Embassy in Oman said on Wednesday that an Indian national was killed in an attack on merchant vessel MV Cape Dao while it was transiting towards India. The victim has been identified as Wiper Suraj Yadav, from Deoria in Uttar Pradesh. A total of 19 people were rescued from the vessel MV Cape Dao, which came under attack on Wednesday while sailing towards India.
Forward Seamen's Union of India (FSUI) is the largest trade union representing merchant navy seamen and seafarers in India, has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi following yet another fatal attack on a ship that killed an Indian national.
“Suraj Yadav was a civilian seafarer, not a combatant. This death is not justified. Indian seafarers keep being killed and reported missing in Hormuz, Gulf of Oman, Red Sea and Black Sea,” the FSUI said in its letter.
FSUI has also demanded the repatriation of his remains and compensation to his family.
Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, has said that Iran’s conditions were completely different from those of the past and that Tehran would not return to previous arrangements.
“Until our conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened and we will not negotiate,” Rezaei said, according to state-run IRNA news agency.
He said Iran wanted the United States to take action first to restore the trust of the Iranian people, stressing that Washington would have to act before Tehran would consider entering negotiations.
Iranian airlines were forced to cancel some international flights on Wednesday after the United States tightened sanctions on Iran's aviation industry in a new effort to cripple its economy.
Georgia and Azerbaijan have officially confirmed suspending flights, and a travel agent in Tehran told AFP that flights to Baghdad, Muscat and Qatar were also halted, though routes to other destinations remained available, including China.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the new measures on Monday as part of an earlier threat to impose "economic D-Day" on Iran, an attempt to force it into submission following nearly seven months of war.

Following the seizure of counterfeit drugs, especially those used to treat cancer, Health Department officials are now tracking patients to check the current status of their health.
Licences of 16 retail and wholesale pharmaceutical firms were cancelled and eight licenses were suspended.
Speaking to The Hindu, U.T. Khader, Minister for Health and Family Welfare, said, “Officials will track records of cancer patients from various private hospitals across the State. We will call them up and check the status of their health. They may have unknowingly bought these counterfeit drugs.”
“We don’t sell fake drugs at government hospitals, hence there is no question of tracking patients to know their status,” he added.
Mr. Khader stated that in order to make it easy for laboratories, doctors, and pharmaceutical firms to differentiate between fake and original drugs, the department has written to the headquarters of Pfizer to release their reference standards.
“When the fake drugs are sent to labs for testing, we need to have the company’s reference standards. It will make the process of drug testing easier for our department. However, the company hasn’t replied to our email so far. Hence, we have written to the Union government to take a note of the increasing number of fake drugs and medicines in the market, measures to identify them, and stop them from being sold in medical shops. State governments have a minor role to play in giving permissions to drug manufacturers and what is brought into the market for selling,” he said.
He added that the investigation of counterfeit drugs is ongoing, while the department is contemplating booking fake drug manufacturers, distributors, pharmaceutical firms, and medical store owners under Section 105 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), according to which if the act is done with the intent to cause death or bodily injury likely to cause death, the punishment is either life imprisonment or imprisonment for five to 10 years and penalty depending on the nature of offence.
An all-India health conclave will be hosted in Bengaluru in the third week of October, said Health Minister U.T. Khader. “Health Ministers from across all the States, FSDA officials from State governments, FSSAI officials and other stakeholders will be part of the conclave. We will not only discuss and debate but take some strong decisions to tackle issues like counterfeit drugs across the country,” he said.

Digital lender Moneyview’s ₹1,092 Cr IPO was subscribed 65% by 12:48 IST on the first day of bidding today. The public issue received bids for 15.19 Cr shares against 23.25 Cr shares on offer, according to BSE data. Retail investors led the demand, placing bids for 10.89 Cr shares against the 11.72 Cr shares reserved for them. This translated into a subscription of 93%. The portion reserved for non-institutional investors (NIIs) was subscribed 85%, receiving bids for 4.29 Cr shares against 5.02 Cr shares on offer. Within the category, the portion reserved for investors bidding between ₹2 Lakh and ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 1.33 times. Meanwhile, the portion for bids exceeding ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 62%. The qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) portion received bids for only 41,895 shares against the 6.51 Cr shares reserved for the category. Moneyview has fixed the IPO price band at ₹32-₹34 per share. At the upper end of the price band, the IPO values the company at around ₹5,985 Cr ($624 Mn). The public issue comprises a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹750 Cr and an OFS of up to 10.05 Cr shares, amounting to around ₹341.7 Cr at the upper end of the price band. The IPO will close on September 28 (Monday), while the company’s shares are scheduled to list on the stock exchanges on October 1 (Thursday). Ahead of the IPO, Moneyview raised ₹327.5 Cr from anchor investors by allotting 9.63 Cr equity shares at ₹34 apiece. Seven domestic mutual funds subscribed to 6.96 Cr shares worth around ₹236.7 Cr. Other anchor investors included Goldman Sachs, Amundi Funds, 360 ONE, HDFC Life Insurance Company, and India Acorn Fund. Cofounders and promoters Puneet Agarwal and Sanjay Aggarwal, along with investors such as Accel, Tiger Global Management, Ribbit Capital, and DI Investment, are selling shares through the OFS. Moneyview intends to use ₹325 Cr of the fresh issue proceeds to support loan disbursals under default loss guarantee arrangements. Another ₹250 Cr will be infused into its NBFC subsidiary Whizdm Finance to augment its capital base, while the remaining proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes. The lending tech company offers personal loans, payments, investments, and insurance through its digital platform. On the financial front, Moneyview’s consolidated net profit jumped 2.6X to ₹173.8 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹67.2 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Its operating revenue rose 50.2% to ₹1,041.1 Cr from ₹693 Cr during the period. For FY26, Moneyview’s operating revenue grew to ₹3,351.2 Cr from ₹2,339.1 Cr in FY25. Its consolidated profit increased marginally to ₹242.7 Cr from ₹240.3 Cr due to exceptional losses of ₹206.7 Cr.

You can build an Android app with Google Antigravity by designing the UI in Google Stitch, generating the app with Gemini using Expo React Native, previewing it through Expo Go, and creating an APK with Expo EAS. You can also connect Supabase for cloud sync.
Building apps on software is now everyone’s cup of tea, thanks to AI. Even if you have never written a single line of code before, you can just go to any AI tool and build the app you want. However, the real complexity lies in making those apps useful instead of AI slop. To help you out, we have created this series where we help you learn how to build fully functional and reliable apps using AI tools.
To start with beginners, in this guide you will learn how to create an Android app using Google Antigravity.
There are multiple ways to create an app. However, this guide explains how you can create Android apps using Expo, a cross-platform builder that lets you easily build apps and share them between Android and iPhone, and you can also run Expo apps on the web. In the future, you will learn how to create Flutter apps, which offer more flexibility.
Table of Contents
Prerequisites
To create Android apps, you need:
- A Google AI Pro subscription
- Antigravity installed on your Mac or Windows
- An Android phone
- Download the Expo Go app. You can install it for free from the Google Play Store
- An Expo account (which you can sign up here for free)
How to Create Android apps Using AntiGravity
Step 1: Get Google Gemini AI Pro
First, opt for Google Gemini AI Pro. This subscription gives access to the Google Gemini models inside Antigravity. If you are looking for a totally free way with a generous limit to create Android apps, you can view our tutorial on how to create Android apps using Google AI Studio for free.
If you already have a Google One AI Premium subscription, you can directly install the Google Antigravity application and get started.
Although Google isn’t the best at its coding models, it offers very generous free terms compared to other models. Moreover, Google’s recently launched Gemini 3.8 Flash is also reliable for building apps if you guide it in the right way.
Step 2: Create the app UI using Google Stitch
Once you have opted for a Google AI Pro subscription, go to this website: stitch.withgoogle.com to design the UI of the app you are building. It is a free tool, and if you have a Google AI Pro subscription, you get better rate limits.
Stitch is a UI design website similar to Figma, but it relies more on an AI approach, which lets you generate UI for apps and websites just by prompting.
In my experience, Google Stitch, in most cases, produces generic UI designs, but it’s a great start for someone to get started with the app UI.
You can also skip this step if you have reference images. Most AI models are very good at replicating designs and understanding the structure. However, if you want a structured approach and a little customization, you can follow this process: Generate your initial designs using Stitch, then edit and modify them. Finally, use those references in tools like Google Antigravity to generate apps with the best UI, exactly the way you need.
To create a UI design, you can view our full, detailed tutorial on how to create UI designs using Google Stitch.
Step 1: First, open Google Stitch and enter the prompt for the app you want to create.
In this case, let’s create a to-do list app because that is a very good starting point, even for beginners. Remember to select “app” as an option while creating, because Google Stitch supports both app and website designs.
Step 2: Now, enter a prompt to generate the UI of the app. Then tap on Enter
Step 3: Now wait until Google Stitch provides a full UI design of the app.
Step 4: You can tap on any element or use AI to describe the changes you want, or you can just use the built-in basic tools to edit sections, text, and much more.
Step 5: If you dont like the design, you can click on the plus icon and tap on upload files, and then you can upload the reference files.
Step 6: To preview how the app works, you can tap on the prototype option to preview how the full app works
Step 7: And once you have the design, tap on Export, and you can export directly to Google Antigravity or save it as a ZIP file.
I recommend downloading it as a ZIP file because sharing to Google Antigravity doesn’t work in most cases.
Step 3: Open Google Antigravity
Now open Antigravity and set it up as a CLI. You can also use it as an agent for UI; Antigravity supports both, but I prefer the CLI experience. Now tap on Open Folder and create a new app, or you can select an existing folder. For those who are unaware, all app files will be stored in this folder.
Now open the CLI, and on the right, you can see the chat interface. Now, in the chat, you can tap on the model’s name and select Google 3.8 Flash High. For your information, Google 3.8 Flash is better than the Pro series. It is the latest model and very good at AI generation, especially if you have reference images.
Step 4: Add your UI reference images
Now, click on the plus icon and attach the images. You can attach up to five images at a time.
Now enter this prompt to ask Google Antigravity to create an app.
Please build an Expo React Native app in TypeScript based on the attached UI designs.
Requirements:
Replicate the layout, typography, colors, and components from the attached screenshots as closely as possible.
Use standard Expo packages (@expo/vector-icons, @react-native-async-storage/async-storage, expo-linear-gradient, react-native-safe-area-context).
Implement full client-side state with local persistence using AsyncStorage so added tasks and items persist across app reloads.
Keep the code modular with clean components in a src/ folder.
Ensure there are zero TypeScript compile errors.
Step 5: Create the app using Gemini
Once you are done, wait for some time until Google Gemini 3.8 Flash creates an app.
Since it runs on Expo, you can preview the build on your Android phone. Simply enter this prompt, and it will generate your QR code in the terminal. If you want to make any changes, you can ask Google Gemini to do that for you.
Step 6: Preview the app on your Android phone
Now, open your Android phone and install the Expo app. Open the Expo app on your Android phone and tap on “Scan QR code,” and the app will be installed on your device. Now you can preview all the changes that you have made.
If you want to make any changes, you can enter the prompt with the required changes. Maybe also include better UI references to help the Google Gemini model understand better. In my experience, Google models hallucinate a lot. Once everything is finished and you are happy with the output.
Step 7: Create an Expo account
Now, before that, you need to go to Expo.io and create a free account. If you have already created one, you can just sign in. Now, Expo EAS will use your Expo account to create the build.
Now, once the account is created, there are two ways to connect Expo Go with your Google Antigravity. First is using a local authentication session, which is stored in your home folder. You can run login in Terminal at any time to connect.
To do that, open Terminal in Antigravity and then run this command
Command: npx eas-cli login
Now enter the username and password you created for your Expo account. Google Antigravity will remember these credentials for all future builds. So this is a one-time process; you don’t need to do this for every new app build.
If you don’t want to submit your credentials, you can create an Expo access token (perhaps for one-time use, or if you are sharing with a friend). You don’t need this if you are using it personally on your device.
However, if you want to connect your Expo account through an access token:
- Go to expo.dev/settings/access-tokens.
- Create a token, name it “Antigravity”, and generate the new token.
- Open the terminal and run this command:
Commad: export EXPO_TOKEN="your_copied_token_here"
Step 8: Build the Android app
You can simply enter the prompt and wait for some time until Google Antigravity starts an Expo build in the Expo build app. Once it finishes, it will give you a direct download link for the app.
Prompt:

Rogue OpenAI agent 'infiltrated' Australian government website in world first
- Published
A rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June and accessed private data in what experts say is the first known case of its kind in the world.
The agent "infiltrated" a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in New York on Wednesday, local time.
He had a "very frank discussion" with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for taking "too long" to disclose the breach and said there would be "legal consequences".
OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.
Five days later, that government agency, Services Australia, escalated the email to Australia's cybersecurity centre before a government minister was notified and the prime minister alerted.
Albanese said he spoke to Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident" as well as his "disappointment" that the company had taken months to reveal the breach and "the nature of the way" it did so.
The Australian leader said Altman had acknowledged there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.
A "forensic investigation" led by the country's cybersecurity agency would aim to find out if other government systems were affected, Albanese said.
The probe would also assess if the matter needed to be dealt with by police, he said, noting there "will obviously be legal consequences".
Detailing the breach, Albanese said it had involved "public and non-public files" on the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal, home to "non-sensitive" data and statistics.
Three other government systems "may" also have been affected: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare and two state-based agencies - the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and the Victorian Department of Health.
"No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage, but investigations are ongoing," Albanese said.
"Nonetheless this situation is obviously unacceptable," he said.
OpenAI, in a statement, said it had "identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation".
"In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend," the statement said.
Albanese declined to answer whether he raised the matter with US President Donald Trump during their face-to-face meeting on Tuesday night in New York, where world leaders have gathered for the UN General Assembly.
Australia was one of 22 countries that earlier this week signed a joint statement calling for global oversight and guardrails for the development of AI.
Cybersecurity experts told the BBC the incident is a wake up call for regulators, given that AI agents are becoming more widely available for individual and commercial use.
Dr Hammond Pearce, senior lecturer at the University of NSW Institute for Cyber Security, told the BBC that though this is the first known incident where AI agents have chosen to breach a government body of their own volition, there'll be more to come.
"I expect that these kinds of attacks will keep occurring," he said, adding that they would likely "grow in severity and in frequency".
"I do hope that this incident does start ringing alarm bells in governments around the world."
Earlier this year, OpenAI revealed a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls and secretly worked together to hack another tech firm named Hugging Face.
And a string of other rogue AI incidents have also been made public this year, including a case where a digital assistant - without instruction - booted someone off a pilates class waiting list in a bid to get an Australian man in.
Several AI firm leaders themselves - including Altman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, and Elon Musk - have said the speed at which AI is developing is dangerous to humanity and needs to be reined in.
But the US and China, who are vying for AI supremacy, are roadblocks. Both are hostile to greater regulation, wanting the economic and technological spoils of AI, and have downplayed safety concerns.

As Canada deepens ties with Europe, could it leave U.S. banks and dollars behind?
Some see U.S. financial dominance as a threat — and are taking action
Canadians know how it feels to be hit by U.S. tariffs. But Canada hasn't been subjected to Washington's more aggressive tactics such as trade sanctions and asset freezes.
Or rather, most Canadians haven't.
Judge Kimberly Prost, a Canadian jurist who serves on the International Criminal Court, is the exception. She found her credit cards cancelled, her Google accounts closed and was effectively "de-banked" after U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared the court "an instrument for lawfare against the United States and our close ally Israel."
Prost is a living example of the dangers of digital and financial interdependence with the United States — and a warning of what would happen if such financial controls were turned against this whole country.
Until now, Trump's main tool of coercion for most countries has been tariffs, said Fen Osler Hampson, chancellor of Carleton University and co-chair of the Expert Group on Canada-U.S. Relations.
Trump has responded to court defeats by bringing the same tariffs back under new legal justifications. But he is running out of pretexts.
"There's concern that he may shift to using various forms of financial pressure," he said.
"What may happen is that, as the tariff lever becomes harder to pull, the president decides to pressure key trading partners — including Canada — by for example issuing executive orders barring U.S. financial institutions from processing Canadian transactions, or attaching conditions on access to dollar clearing. And those financial tools sit squarely within presidential authority."
Dollar clearing is the process of ensuring that real funds have been received from one party before releasing to the other.
The most drastic tool a U.S. president could use might amount to a "kill switch" on a large part of Canadian commerce, says Vass Bednar, managing director of the Canadian Shield Institute think-tank.
"If Visa or Mastercard were to be compelled by the Trump administration to turn off our access or geographically restrict service so that the province of Ontario just can't process transactions anymore, it would effectively halt a huge part of our economy," Bednar said.
"It would be unfathomable, but it's not impossible. And that's what happens when you grow too reliant and allow fragility like that to be introduced."
'This amazing weapon'
Karl Schamotta is chief market strategist at Corpay, one of the world's largest corporate payments companies. He says the U.S. has always sat at the centre of the world's transactions, but started to realize the power it had when it effectively iced North Korea out of the U.S. financial system.
Schamotta said a small number of banks in New York validate most international U.S. dollar transactions — creating the opportunity for vast "secondary sanctions" against any financial institution connected to those banks.

- Incoming ambassador says Canada won't pay directly into EU budget
"Not only did they have control of banks within the U.S., but they had secondary control over any bank that touches those banks," he said.
"[The U.S.] realized, wait a second, we have this amazing weapon that we can use … so that escalated fairly rapidly over the years."
Incoming Canadian system has its limits
Canada is expected to launch its new payment system, called Real-Time Rail, later this year. But Bednar says it was conceived at a time when the priority was greater efficiency, not sovereignty, and offers little protection from outside threats.
Visa and Mastercard are central to the U.S. government's ability to shut down other countries' economies, handling about $32 trillion US of transactions annually — 90 per cent of all card transactions outside China.
In Britain, where Visa and Mastercard control about 95 per cent of card transactions, banks are co-operating with the government to create DeliveryCo, a system that can handle payments if the credit card companies ever hit the kill switch.
One country that has succeeded remarkably in freeing itself from Visa and Mastercard is Brazil, with a government system called Pix, originally set up by Brazil's central bank in 2020 to allow people without bank accounts to transfer money and make payments.
"Pix has been phenomenally successful, beyond anyone's expectations," said Schamotta. "There was no expectation that we would see it essentially go viral and displace basically everything else in the Brazilian system."
But the Trump administration accused Brazil of reducing market opportunities for Visa and Mastercard, and cited it as one justification for 25 per cent tariffs.
"They are targeting and bullying another jurisdiction, and saying that your pursuit of a form of digital sovereignty is unacceptable to us," said Bedmar. "This is all the more reason to keep building up sovereign systems like this."
American banks and American dollars
But Pix, like Canada's Interac system, only avoids the U.S. banking system for domestic transactions, said Schamotta.
Still, he said some countries are setting up "swap lines" that go around the U.S.
Cryptocurrencies — including some that are pegged to currencies such as the U.S. dollar — are also gradually replacing dollars in international transfers.
The biggest non-U.S. system is China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), which works with a digital currency interchange developed by China and other partners called mBridge. When the U.A.E. and Saudi Arabia sell oil to China, the payments clear without touching U.S. banks.
Canada and Europe similarly have the technical ability to design a way for their parallel systems to "talk to each other in a smooth fashion, and clear between one another in a smooth fashion without much difficulty," said Schamotta.
A new lane on an existing highway
Just as Canada seeks to protect its trade with Europe, it should also seek to do the same with other like-minded partners, Bednar said.
"It would be smart for Canada and the middle power alliance to be building up this payment infrastructure … in a way that can maintain that neutrality we expect, instead of a superiority and control that can be weaponized," she said.
The goal, says Hampson, is not to stop dealing with U.S. banks entirely, but rather "adding a lane to a highway."
And if the U.S. were to block or toll international transactions as a form of leverage, he said, the rest of the world will be looking for such a lane.
Coercion is a double-edged sword
In an interview with Bloomberg days before heading to Europe last week, Carney referred to financial transactions as an example of "those interconnections, that integration [that] can be used as leverage against you."
And speaking to the European Parliament, he listed payments as one of several areas where Canada and the EU can "secure our strategic autonomy through deep co-operation."
Hampson says countries are increasingly seeing their ties to the U.S. as vulnerabilities, rather than advantages.
"Once you start weaponizing the bonds of economic or financial interdependence, it cuts both ways. Just as you know, tariffs impose a real cost on American consumers … the same is true when it comes to government intervention in financial markets, which depend heavily on trust, on stability."
Continued U.S. control of the world financial system depends on the U.S. not abusing its position, he said. Such abuse, he said, would "run the risk of losing it."
With most international credit and currency reserves being held in U.S. dollars, Schamotta said breaking free of that dominance is unlikely to happen fast.
But in the meantime, Bednar says Canada can do a lot to reduce its vulnerabilities to reckless behaviour from the U.S.
"We used to smoke cigarettes in the hospital, and that used to be a norm of our society that we didn't question. We moved away from that for very good reasons," Bednar said.
"Right now, when it comes to digital sovereignty and our own payment sovereignty, I would say we're smoking cigars in the hospital, and we can't do that anymore."

Australia has faced a series of hacking attempts on corporations and government-linked firms over the past four years.
Defence Minister Richard Marles said the Medicare portal that was breached did not contain individual medical claims, benefit payments, personal banking details, or patient medical histories of Australia's 27 million people.
Instead, the website holds only aggregated data on healthcare use across the country, he said. However Australia considered the breach serious.
"There were blocks clearly which were coming back telling the AI agent 'no'. The AI agent found a way around those blocks — didn't accept no for an answer," Albanese told reporters.
The incident is the latest of several recent incidents in which ChatGPT maker OpenAI has disclosed hacks or unauthorized activity involving its AI agents well after they occurred.
Rivals Anthropic, Google's Gemini, and Meta have also disclosed incidents of their agents accessing external systems.
Maurice Chiodo, an Australian mathematician who works at Cambridge University's Centre for the Study of Existential Risk, said the breach appeared to be "a significant escalation in seriousness from similar incidents we have seen in recent months."
He added that while there was a lot of talk of new laws around AI, policymakers needed to first consider enforcing existing ones, like those that criminalize unauthorized intrusions into computer systems.

The man who died following a Sunday shootout with police outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., alluded to killing Jewish people using a slur and railed against immigrants in interactions with a friend in the weeks leading up to the fatal attack, CBC News visual investigation team has learned.
According to a childhood friend CBC News spoke to, Sean Ward — a former member of the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) — tried using a slur for Jewish people combined with the word "killer" as a username for an online game, but settled on "kitekiller" after it was censored. The friend was with Ward online on Sept. 2 while they waited to play the video game Once Human when Ward attempted to use the username.
"There was that one game we played … he tried to name himself the k--e killer, and it changed to 'kitekiller' because you can't obviously have that on there," said his friend.
The word is a deeply offensive term used against Jews.

- Suspect in Belleville, Ont., shooting is dead, SIU says
CBC News is not naming the friend due to his fear that he will lose his job because of his association with the suspect.
Using text messages, online usernames and social media accounts, and an interview with the childhood friend, CBC News was able to put together a partial profile of Ward — a person who not only routinely engaged in antisemitic speech, but who more recently espoused anti-immigrant sentiments, blaming them for his lack of employment.
"He said he was depressed," said his friend, recounting a conversation with Ward earlier this month. "He was saying, 'F--k the immigrants', like … 'I can't find work.' "
"I just didn't think he would do anything to that extreme."
A spokesperson with the Special Investigations Unit, the civilian agency that investigates police conduct during shootings and other serious incidents in Ontario, said Ward, 29, died from injuries sustained during the exchange of gunfire outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville on Sunday night, where congregants gathered for Yom Kippur services.
According to the SIU, Ward is alleged to have fired at Belleville Police Const. Jeff Smith with a shotgun, then Smith and a second officer on scene returned fire, with dozens of shots exchanged.
Smith was injured in the confrontation.
Both were taken to hospital, where Ward died on Monday night.
So far, police have not released any information about the suspect's potential motivation for the attack.
'Don't do anything stupid'
The friend CBC spoke to said he noticed a change in Ward over a period of months this summer. His appearance changed, the friend said, noting Ward went from bulky to slim, with long, greasy hair.
"He just looked different. Felt different. I could feel a different vibe on him," the friend said. "Usually we talk more. So that's why I felt odd because, like, he wasn't shooting the shit like we usually did. Like, he was like, in his head kind of thing."
The friend said the last time he saw Ward in person was Sept. 2, roughly three weeks before the shooting.
"When he was leaving … I was like, 'Don't do anything stupid, bro.' I was like, 'I know times are tough, but don't do anything stupid.' "
Following news of the shooting Sunday, the friend messaged Ward.
"I immediately texted Sean," he said. "And the message never sent. So that kind of clicked to my brain that he probably did do it."
The friend said Ward always had his phone on. "Like always. He'd always answer pretty quick."
CAF confirmed Tuesday that Ward had served in the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry from 2017 to 2022. CAF did not comment on the reasons for Ward's release, but multiple people CBC News spoke to, including the friend, said Ward refused to be vaccinated.

'Alarming' - does WSL have a homegrown problem?
- Published
When London City Lionesses beat Manchester United on the opening night of the 2025-26 season, it suggested times were changing in the English women's game.
For some, that had become clear about an hour before kick-off in Bromley when the team news revealed a starting XI without any English players - the first time a Women's Super League side had done so on the first day of the season.
Two days later it happened again, when Scotland striker Kirsty Hanson was the only British player to start for Tottenham in their win over West Ham.
Both instances speak to the increasing ability of WSL clubs to attract top talents from across the globe, creating a league many now view as the world's best.
But, with the Women's Champions League returning this week, is what's good for the WSL good for homegrown players, and by extension the home nations?
Or is it, as The Guardian's Tom Garry puts it, "alarming" for the hopes of the home nations?
Arsenal v HB Koge, Women's Champions League
Tuesday, 22 September, 20:00 BST
Listen to BBC Radio 5 Live commentary and follow text updates of the matches featuring English teams on the BBC Sport website as the Women's Champions League returns
The changing make-up of the WSL
Ten years ago when current champions Manchester City last won the WSL title, they did so with an all-British starting line-up.
Much has changed since.
In 2018, the WSL went fully professional, the subsequent success of the Lionesses in the 2020s rapidly grew the game's audience and revenues have increased accordingly.
As a result, clubs have expanded their scouting pool and been able to attract players from a wider variety of nationalities - with transfer fees exploding since the turn of the decade.
Over recent windows, WSL clubs have recruited heavily from Germany and Sweden, while two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas exchanged the trophies of Barcelona for big-spending London City this summer.
The proliferation of players from Japan and Australia also highlights the WSL's attractiveness for those at the top of the game as those clubs with the deepest pockets pack their squads with players from across the globe.
"Our league has grown significantly and attracted world class athletes from all over the world," says Birmingham City manager Amy Merricks. "Unfortunately that blocks some of the pathways for the youngsters coming through.
"We need [this] talent in our league because our league is growing, but at the same time we have got to try and address this issue."
Looking at the proportion of homegrown players (English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish) to start 11 or more matches, half of a WSL season, the data shows a steady decline over the past three seasons to under a third.
The first three weeks of 2026-27 have offered a bump on last season, but that can partly be attributed to the WSL's expansion from 12 teams to 14 teams and the greater proportion of homegrown talent in the promoted trio of Birmingham City, Crystal Palace and Charlton Athletic.
It is a downward trend that is not mirrored across other major European leagues.
For 2025-26, 61% of those to start half or more of Premiere Ligue matches in France were French, 63% of those in Frauen Bundesliga games were German, and 69% of Liga F players in Spain were Spanish.
And, while WSL managers say they appreciate the importance of cultivating homegrown talent, the reality of the job ensures it is not their first priority.
"The club has a responsibility to raise young players, give our own talents possibilities to be in the squad and compete every week," says Manchester City boss Andree Jeglertz.
"But when it comes to team selection, I always need to pick the team that gives us the best chance of winning the game. If that contains eight young and promising English players or zero, I don't care. I just want to win the game."
What is the potential impact on the national team?
1 of 4
It feels like a crossroads has been reached between clubs wanting to be competitive, the WSL continuing to grow, and the need to regenerate an England squad that has not changed much over the past three major tournaments.
After all, England are the two-time European champions but seven of the team that started against Spain in June also played in the Euro 2022 final against Germany - while two of the remaining starters in this year's game were on the bench four years ago.
Sarina Wiegman's side were outclassed in Majorca, losing 4-0 to miss out on automatic qualification for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil. They must now navigate two rounds of play-off matches, starting against Greece next month.
Discussions on England's future is pertinent given the biennial Women's Under-20s World Cup is ongoing in Poland.
Last Thursday, Lydia Bedford's young side were dismissed 3-0 from the last 16 by Nigeria, albeit with the caveat a number of players such as US-based Erica Meg Parkinson and Laila Harbert were not released by their clubs to play.
Nevertheless, in 2022 and 2024, like the other home nations, they did not even qualify.
It is a far cry from the class of 2018 where the likes of Alessia Russo, Lauren Hemp and Georgia Stanway led the Lionesses to third place in the Under-20s World Cup, setting the tone for the incredible subsequent success.
Wiegman has handed debuts to 21 players since her arrival in September 2021, but only Lauren James, Hannah Hampton and Lucia Kendall have become established starters.
When England kick off in Crete on Friday, 5 October (20:00 BST), it is likely to be the same faces once again.

To try and facilitate the pathway to top level football for young academy players, Football Association rules require WSL sides to include eight homegrown players in their squad lists.
The quota for WSL 2 clubs is higher and works on a sliding scale depending on squad size.
Former England striker Ellen White told the Women's Football Weekly podcast this was insufficient, saying: "We should be updating that quota of eight players, tweaking it to best help and complement our international structure, our homegrown talent."
"I would love to see them go much further - something mandated, a minimum on the pitch at any one time," the Guardian's Garry told BBC Women's Football Weekly. "London City's line-up was alarming.
"It's great for the product over here, but will we see pain in 15 years' time if England are struggling to go deep in major tournaments because we're not developing players?"
Last month, the FA approved a controversial plan to allow some WSL academy sides to play in the National League from 2027-28, saying it would "strengthen the women's football pyramid, raise standards across the league, and improve the development pathway for young players".
The FA believes this reform will address the relative lack of competitive minutes young English players receive.
Chelsea have already confirmed they plan to enter an academy side in the third tier and Manchester City women's managing director Charlotte O'Neill has previously said she would want to enter a team too.
