Walking around Meta Connect 2026, everyone’s sporting smart glasses in all sorts of shapes, colors, and sizes. It’s a marked difference here, a tech bubble where “pervert glasses” are not a concern.
Meta ditches the camera on its newest smart glasses
Audio-only Ray-Bans have arrived alongside more camera-equipped glasses. What’s missing? Privacy controls to address the ‘perv glasses’ backlash.
Outside Connect, the public backlash against wearable surveillance tech — a catchall term that encompasses not just smart glasses, but also smartwatches and AI pendants — is gaining steam. So it’s incredibly curious timing that this year, the company is launching Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses: smart glasses infused with Meta AI, but with no camera for recording others.
To hear Meta tell it, that’s a coincidence. Audio-only glasses have been years in the making.
“Three years ago, it wasn’t clear if AI glasses were going to be a thing. Back then, every other company was backing out of the space,” says Alex Himel, Meta’s vice president of wearables. “Then two years ago, we saw that audio was the top use case, the biggest potential for AI, and that it should work well in a pair of audio glasses.”
Himel has a point. Open-ear audio is the least controversial part of the Ray-Bans — and the thing everyone can agree is convenient. Plus, the camera-less glasses are lighter. Himel says that by removing the cameras, Meta could “rearchitect” the glasses. “That allowed us to take a lot of electronics out of the front frame and have a lot more design flexibility.”
The audio-only models start at 43 grams — heavier than normal wire-frame glasses, but noticeably lighter than the roughly 50g Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 and the 69g Meta Ray-Ban Display. The arms are thinner. They come in two styles: the Mad Men-esque Clubmaster and the more Wayfarer-reminiscent Burbank. The hinges extend for wider faces; the temple arms and nose pads are adjustable. There are 23 color and lens combinations, and they can support the same wider prescription range as the Ray-Ban Meta Optics lineup. Even more so than the standard Meta Ray-Bans, these look and wear like normal glasses. And with a $349 starting price, they’re cheaper too.
Free of a power-hungry camera, the battery lasts an estimated 12 hours on a single charge. The most technical things you can do with them are interact with Meta AI, take phone calls, and listen to podcasts or music. And that’s it.
“They don’t record,” Himel says. “The only thing they do, which is the same thing as an Alexa device in your house or some other devices, they’re just listening for a specific wake word. They’re not sending anything … If they hear [the wake word], then they start listening to what you’re saying. When you’re done talking, then it’s processing, and that’s visible to the AI. It gets processed, and that’s kind of it.”
Slipping them on, they’re comfortable and, I think, quite fetching on me. Regardless of how one might feel about Meta, it’s fair to guess most people would feel less like a creeper wearing these.
Meta Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3
I feel differently slipping on the new Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. Partly because the camera is back in play, partly because the pair Meta gives me is the new aviator style with transition lenses. I’m told I can pull it off, but I keep asking my colleague Jay Peters if I’m giving ’80s serial killer vibes. The other new style is called Zena — not the warrior princess — and it’s a bolder, geometric cat-eye frame.
The third-generation glasses feature fairly minor refinements. There’s a sixth microphone, compared to the second generation’s five, for clearer phone calls. Battery life has gotten a slight boost to nine hours, an hour longer than the second gen. The temple arms, like the audio-only glasses, are adjustable for a better fit. All sound will now be captured in Dolby Atmos for spatial audio. Sure! That’s neat if I’m in my quiet hotel room, but it’s harder to appreciate when reviewing footage amid the hustle and bustle of Meta Connect. The new model comes in 27 color and lens combinations, plus three seasonal options.
Along with the hardware changes, the Gen 3 glasses are also getting a price bump. They start at $449, up from $379 for the second-gen models last year.
Meta Glasses — the off-brand, more affordable entry-level glasses launched a few months ago — also have more options. There are two new styles, Capri and Nova. Capri is some kind of cat-eye shape, while Nova… honestly, the styles are all starting to blur together. They’re round and remind me of several other Ray-Ban Meta glasses, but slightly different. There’s a new ivory-colored Kylie Jenner pair that costs $399.
But maybe Kylie Jenner isn’t the celebrity collab you’ve been dreaming about. That’s fine. Because Blackpink’s Lisa — a K-pop icon and The White Lotus actress — also has Meta Glasses. They have pink lenses and come with a blind-box-type charm styled after Lisa’s pets. These also start at $399. (Non-celebrity versions of the Meta Glasses start at $249.)
Why the celebrity collabs? Options for more people, including women.
“With the Meta Glasses Starfire with Kylie, we saw a younger, more female audience start to buy the glasses,” says Himel. “Wayfarer is the most popular glasses type in the world, but it tends to be more male — though definitely not exclusively male. The second brand we did was Oakley … but Oakley [also] tends to be a more masculine brand. So I think with Kylie and Lisa, and with more styles, we’re seeing them appeal to more women.”
There are actually more limited-edition versions, styles, colors, and prescription permutations available across the entire existing Ray-Ban Meta lineup at a whole range of price points. I suspect I’d need to make a spreadsheet to list them all. While scuttling about Meta’s campus this week, I’m brought to an entire area where they’re all displayed. It looks like a high-end store for, regular, schmegular glasses. That, I suspect, is the whole point.
AI in your frames
All around the campus, there are life-size cutouts of Meta’s cuddly Muse mascot. That’s because Muse, Meta’s recently released personal AI agent, is coming to the seemingly 4,000 iterations of Meta smart glasses that now exist.
“Muse is gonna be everywhere,” confirms Himel. “Muse is gonna be on every device that we make.”
The pitch for Muse in your glasses is that your AI assistant will better remember your context and do things on your behalf. During a demo, I ask a Muse agent to help me buy snacks that will give me the best protein bang for my calorie buck. It can do it, but fails at adding another snack to my cart. Obviously, this is an early-stage demo, and there are always kinks. I can see the shape of how this could be helpful. I can also see how it’d be a treasure trove of data for Meta.
Less contentious is a demo of a new FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature. I’m asked to wear earplugs to mimic mild hearing loss. Things sound a bit muddled. With the feature turned on, higher voices gain a tinny quality as the AI works to boost conversational tones in a semi-loud environment. After about five minutes, I’ve forgotten I have earplugs in. Adding this capability will cost an extra $149, but I’m told it’s FSA/HSA eligible and designed to be a one-time fee versus an ongoing subscription.
Lastly, there are two minor privacy updates — though neither truly addresses the fears people have been debating this past summer. The first is bringing the same “private processing” pipeline used on WhatsApp to wearables. It’s a server-based system in which a user’s data is inaccessible to Meta or any other third parties when end-to-end encryption isn’t possible or on-device processing isn’t powerful enough.
“It’s so that you know that your data is just yours and you’re the only one who has access to it. Other companies have taken an approach to everything on-device. We do a lot on-device. But the problem with just doing things on-device is that the device is only so powerful and capable. And so if you want to run more capable models and get better functionality, we want to offer the same privacy protections, but with more capabilities. So that’s what private processing is,” says Himel.
Meta will also roll out an update where users can opt out of their visual data being used for AI training. (Audio-only queries are still used for training.)
That’s progress but doesn’t really address people’s primary concerns about the glasses being used to covertly record people in public. Himel also acknowledges that the private processing feature is mostly about protecting the data of the person wearing the glasses.
More is more
Meta’s goal at Connect this year is to bombard everyone with options. By the end of the year, Meta expects to have over 100 versions of its glasses. The more versions of its glasses, the more people they’ll reach. The more AI updates that trickle to each of these iterations, the faster Meta can stake its claim on the next era of mobile computing.
So goes the theory. But providing hardware options isn’t Meta’s problem. Inside the safe bubble of Meta’s campus, everyone wears these glasses. The issue is outside Menlo Park, where a vocal contingent isn’t asking for more. They’re asking for less.

Russia's parliamentary election result underscores public support for Kremlin policies, Putin says
President Vladimir Putin says Russia’s first wartime parliamentary election, which further strengthened the Kremlin’s already-overwhelming legislative control, was a sign of public support for his policies
President Vladimir Putin said Wednesday that Russia's first wartime parliamentary election, which further strengthened the Kremlin's already-overwhelming legislative control, was a show of public support for his policies.
With over 97% of the vote counted from three days of balloting that ended Sunday, election officials said the main Kremlin party, United Russia, will get more than three-fourths of the seats in the lower house, the State Duma, a record high. The tightly orchestrated vote excluded virtually any genuine opposition.
Voter turnout exceeded 59% of the 111 eligible million voters, the most for a parliamentary election in over a decade. Authorities had spread the voting over three days to boost attendance at the polls and included illegally annexed parts of Ukraine. Online voting also took place in some regions.
“Such a record number of people who come to cast ballots shows that the people of Russia support our efforts aimed at strengthening the country,” Putin said in televised remarks at a meeting with top government members, his first public remarks on the outcome.
The election took place against the backdrop of incessant Ukrainian drone attacks. On Sunday, Russia's Defense Ministry reported it downed 1,110 drones overnight.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 450 drones were downed while flying toward the city in what he described as “the largest ever” attack on the capital in a failed attempt to disrupt the vote. The attack, which damaged an oil refinery and a residential building, also killed three people and injured 38 in the wider Moscow region, officials said.
“They tried to hamper our efforts, to derail the election, as evidenced by the enemy’s continuous efforts to breach air defenses around Moscow and in other regions,” Putin said. “But lines at polling stations have shown that Russia can’t be intimidated.”
The parliamentary election was the first since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and the first to include residents of four regions of that country that were seized and illegally annexed by Moscow later that year. At a polling station in the Russian-held part of the Donetsk region, voters dropped their ballots in a box under the gaze of an armed Russian soldier.
Voting also was held in Crimea, which was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. Kyiv denounced the voting in those regions as illegal.
Putin also addressed Russian soldiers fighting in Ukraine.
“Comrades, I want you to know that it was the vote for you. People trust you, they believe in our victory, believe in your courage, heroism and your devotion to the Motherland,” he said.
“I have no doubt that all the goals we set for the special military operation will be fulfilled,” Putin said, using the Kremlin term for the war in Ukraine.
A massive state media campaign and tight control over the election allowed the Kremlin to strengthen its political dominance despite economic troubles and long-range Ukrainian drone attacks.
The preliminary results indicated that United Russia would get between 347 and 355 out of 450 Duma seats. It received just under 58% of the vote for the 225 seats apportioned by parties and also won 208 single-seat races that fill the other half of the chamber.
Several smaller parties representing the “systemic opposition” that vote in sync with the Kremlin on all key issues are set to fill most of the remaining seats. Just a handful will go to candidates who ran without a party affiliation.
The liberal Yabloko party, the only registered political entity that dared to publicly criticize the war, was removed from the ballot last month by Russia’s Supreme Court, and only had a few dozen candidates in the single-seat races. Preliminary results indicated that no Yabloko candidates won a seat.

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”
What else we’re reading about
Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.
The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.
Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
4,756,000
One-third of the electorate in Delhi, about 4.76 million voters, have been deleted from the draft voting list as the Election Commission carries out a contentious revision of its rolls across states. So far, about 130 million names have been dropped from draft rolls in 30 states and union territories, the Indian Express reported.
Vibe check
Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).
It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.
It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships
- Published
Kenya's President William Ruto says the World Athletics Championship will be "coming home", with Nairobi set to make history after being selected as the first African city to host the event in 2029.
Ruto hailed the winning bid as a "victory for generations of athletes" who have made the nation "synonymous with excellence" on the track and road.
Nairobi beat London and Rome to the hosting rights, with Munich selected to stage the 2031 edition.
After missing out on the 2025 World Championships to Tokyo, a series of factors helped Kenya see off its European rivals this time around.
A sport 'woven into the fabric' of the nation
When World Athletics president Lord Coe announced the decision in Budapest on Tuesday, he described Kenya's bid as "compelling and emotional".
The East African nation is the second-most successful nation in the history of the World Championships with 72 gold medals, placing it behind the United States.
The vast majority of those glories, alongside 38 Olympic gold medals, have come in middle- and long-distance running.
Lord Coe said that athletics is "woven into the fabric" of the nation and that Kenyans have helped "shape the history" of the sport.
He name-checked several runners including two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge - who was involved in the lobbying for Kenya's bid - men's 800m world record holder David Rudisha and multiple world and Olympic medallist Faith Kipyegon.
A passionate fanbase is also one of the country's great strengths.
Some 68% of Kenyans surveyed by World Athletics rated their interest in athletics as high, compared with a global average of 39%.
Athletics is the country's second-most followed sport, behind only football, and when World Athletics assessed its social media channels, Kenya was the fourth-highest nation in terms of followers.
Upgraded facilities
Kenya's previous bid for the 2025 edition fell down largely on the facilities which the country possessed.
This time around, the Kasarani Stadium will have gone through a complete structural upgrade well before the world's top athletes descend on Nairobi.
The 48,000-capacity venue will be used when Kenya co-hosts football's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) next June and July alongside Tanzania and Uganda.
"We learned from the 2025 bid because there were areas that we did not score well," Barnaba Korir, who worked on the successful bid, told the BBC World Service.
"Because of that, we managed to improve on those areas.
"I'm happy that the infrastructure that we have already developed will also meet the standards that we have seen all over the world."
Hotel space is one area not expected to be a problem, with Nairobi a regular host for large conventions.
"Kenya is also known for its very dynamic hospitality, the tourism sector," Elijah Mwangi, principal secretary at the State Department for Sports, told the BBC.
"It has a game park within the city, so we are waiting to welcome everybody."
President Ruto made financial and security guarantees in order to secure the Championships.
"We thank World Athletics for the confidence it has placed in Kenya," Ruto said.
"We will honour that confidence by delivering an unforgettable championship worthy of our athletes, our country and our continent."
Expanding athletics
Lord Coe became president of World Athletics (then known as the IAAF) in 2015 and has pledged to grow the sport around the globe.
During his time in office the World Championships have been hosted in Qatar (2019), the United States (2022) and Tokyo, while China's capital Beijing will stage them in 2027.
Kenya has successfully hosted age-grade events in Nairobi and the World Cross Country Championships in Mombasa, while the World Athletics Relays were held in Botswana's capital Gaborone in May.
With Coe's third term in office coming to an end next year, one official involved in Kenya's bid, speaking before the host announcement, said it was "unthinkable" that Nairobi would not succeed.
"With this decision we continue to fulfil our mission of growing athletics worldwide," Coe said.
"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances.
Coe hailed the "quality, ambition and commitment" of all four bidding cities.
London, Munich and Rome have all previously held the Olympics, with the World Championships in London as recently as 2017, but the chance to break new ground in Africa was clearly compelling.
UK Athletics chief executive Jack Buckner said his team was "deeply disappointed" to see London miss out.
What is needed next?
Kenya now faces logistical and organisational challenges over the next three years as it prepares to deliver Africa's first World Championships.
With the 2027 Afcon looming large on the horizon, Nairobi will have a chance to test-run getting fans in and out of the Kasarani Stadium, which lies about a half-hour drive from the city's central business district.
The venue does not have any rail connections but Korir says World Athletics officials were "very satisfied" by Kenya's transport plan.
There were instances of overcrowding when the stadium hosted Kenya games at football's African Nations Championships last year, which led to the capacity being reduced for some matches.
Delays in preparations for Afcon have raised concerns, and the funding for the World Championships will come entirely from the Kenyan government.
Mwangi revealed that $78m (£58.5m) is the current estimate for the government's contribution, with sponsorship deals also playing a role.
"We are prepared to ensure that whatever is expected to be paid, it is paid in the due time," he added.
Presidential elections are scheduled for next year, but Korir is confident organisers will secure the "huge" and "legally binding" figure earmarked even if there is a change in government.
"Whatever the government assigns now will be observed by the next government. It is an international agreement," he said.
Then comes ticketing, first to make sure the local population are not priced out and then to ensure the stands are filled.
The cheapest tickets for the Under-18 World Championships in 2017 were priced at 200 Kenyan shillings ($1.15, £1.14) but attendances were low until entry was made free.
World Athletics generated $522m in revenue from Tokyo 2025, with a total of 619,000 tickets sold over the nine days of competition, while London sold a record 705,000 tickets in 2017.
In passing up the opportunity of returning to the British capital, World Athletics has chosen expansion over guaranteed ticket sales, but attendances will be scrutinised - especially after the sparse numbers seen in the stands in Doha in 2019.
Korir, however, is confident the Kasarani Stadium "will be full" on "every day" of competition, including morning sessions, if sales begin early enough.
Meanwhile, Kenya has endured a spate of doping scandals in recent years, with 11 individuals banned by the Athletics Integrity Unit so far this year alone.
The pressure is now on the East African nation to deliver on its promises in the build-up to Nairobi 2029 and ensure the Championships pass off without any major issues.
Additional reporting by Ian Williams and Celestine Karoney.

Chinese President Xi Jinping will arrive in Washington on Wednesday (September 23) for a three-day state visit and a second summit with US President Donald Trump in less than six months. Xi is accompanied by his wife Peng Liyuan, senior Chinese official Cai Qi and Foreign Minister Wang Yi.
Trump is set to give Xi a high-profile welcome, with the visit featuring an airport arrival ceremony, White House meetings, a state dinner and a visit to the National Archives.
The two leaders are expected to discuss trade, technology, AI, Taiwan, Iran, Ukraine, military ties and US arms sales to Taiwan.
Here is the full itinerary.
Xi and Peng are scheduled to arrive at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, near Washington, on Wednesday evening.
Trump and first lady Melania Trump are set to travel to the military base to personally welcome the Chinese president and Peng on the tarmac. The arrival is scheduled for 6 pm local time (2200 GMT).
Trump and Xi are also expected to participate in an arrival ceremony at the military base.
The welcome is part of an unusually elaborate programme planned for Xi's first US visit in nearly three years and first White House visit in more than a decade.
Thursday is expected to be the main day of the Trump-Xi summit.
Trump will welcome Xi and Peng at the White House before the two presidents move to the Rose Garden for a military review and begin their bilateral meeting. Melania Trump and Peng Liyuan are expected to attend a separate event in the Washington area.
The talks are expected to cover a broad range of issues, including:
US-China trade and tariffs
Artificial intelligence and technology
Taiwan
Rare-earth minerals
Iran and the Middle East
Russia-Ukraine war
Military-to-military ties
US arms sales to Taiwan
The leaders are also expected to discuss the future of the two countries' trade relationship. Washington and Beijing are negotiating a reciprocal tariff reduction framework covering products worth about $30 billion from each side, according to the supplied material.
State dinner at the White House
On Thursday evening, Trump and Melania will host Xi and Peng for a state dinner in the East Room of the White House.
The dinner is expected to include prominent technology and business leaders, including Apple CEO Tim Cook, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Trump and Xi are expected to speak at the beginning of the dinner.
Xi's final day in Washington will include a more ceremonial schedule.
Trump and Melania will host Xi and Peng for private tea at the White House. The two presidential couples will then travel to the National Archives in Washington.
They are expected to view historic US founding documents, including the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution.
After the National Archives visit, Xi and Peng will return to Joint Base Andrews, from where they will depart the United States.
The summit comes as Washington and Beijing remain divided on several major issues.
Trade and tariffs: The two sides are negotiating tariff reductions, while China's dominance of rare-earth supplies remains an important part of Beijing's economic leverage.
AI and technology: AI is expected to feature prominently as the US and China compete for technological leadership. The two countries could discuss greater cooperation on AI risks, although the supplied material says expectations of a major agreement are low.
Taiwan: Xi is expected to press Trump over US arms sales to Taiwan. China has strongly opposed the reported $11 billion US arms package for Taipei.
Iran: The Iran-US conflict is also expected to feature in the talks, given Beijing's close ties with Tehran and China's role in the global oil market.
Ukraine: Trump is expected to urge Xi to use Beijing's relationship with Moscow to encourage Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war in Ukraine.

Rows of hardware and car-part shops line Garstin Bastion Road, with faded signs crammed together above their shutters. By day, the street is one of Old Delhi’s busiest commercial thoroughfares. But as dusk falls, GB Road, as it is known locally, transforms into one of the city’s most notorious red-light districts.
An estimated 2,800 sex workers live and work in brothels that occupy the upper floors of the dilapidated buildings, their entrances tucked behind narrow stairways and unmarked doors. Women sit on plastic stools beneath the stairways, calling out to men passing on the street, while others watch from windows above, their eyes following the movement below before customers are directed upstairs.
The challenges the women of GB Road face are numerous and well documented – from health risks to abuse, debt to poor sanitation. Now they face a new struggle: India’s controversial electoral reform process. The Election Commission’s special intensive revision, or SIR, is a nationwide exercise in which electoral rolls have shrunk by more than 58 million voters across the 13 states covered in the first two of three main phases. In Delhi, covered in the third phase, the scale of exclusion is the highest recorded as a percentage: 4.76 million names – 33% of the city’s previous electorate – do not appear on the city’s draft roll published on 31 August.
The government says SIR is meant to “purify” the electoral rolls by removing ineligible voters, including alleged undocumented migrants, but critics have accused Narendra Modi’s government of using it to target minority voters and reshape electoral rolls in ways that could benefit his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
On GB Road, the proportion of those excluded is even higher. Data shared by officials overseeing about 1,300 voters in the area show that about 650 were sex workers on the previous electoral roll. Of these, at least 500 have either been marked as “shifted”, meaning they have moved home or location, or have been unable to establish their eligibility because of missing documentation – more than three-quarters of the sex workers on the local roll.
One of them is 36-year-old Beauty*, who has lived on GB Road for more than two decades. She got her first voter ID in 2008. At the time, the address where she lived and worked as a sex worker and verification by a government official called a booth-level officer (BLO) were enough to put her on the electoral roll. She voted in previous elections.
But under the new rules, voters had to establish eligibility by proving their link to the relevant previous electoral roll or by producing prescribed documents such as a passport, birth or education certificate – a paper trail Beauty struggled to reconstruct. Trafficked at 16 and brought to the brothels of GB Road, she has no contact with her family. She does have an Aadhaar card, India’s biometric identity document used widely to establish identity and access government services, with her GB Road address. But Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship and does not, by itself, establish eligibility to vote under the SIR process.
She tried to get a copy of her matriculation certificate, which is evidence of schooling, from the village in Rajasthan where she grew up. One of her regular customers of the past 10 years – a man she refers to as her husband, agreed to help track down the old record but failed.
“If I had the papers to show my father’s birth certificate, or even my own matriculation certificate, then I could prove who I am,” she says. “But how can I go back to my village to ask for these things when my trafficking has brought so much shame to my family that they no longer accept me?”
Now Beauty has lost hope – and, for now, her vote. Her name was left out of Delhi’s recent draft electoral roll. For her, the voter ID had meant more than a piece of identification. Sex workers, she says, are accustomed to being treated as immoral, degraded and less worthy than others.
“We all shit. That is what makes us equal as human beings. Voting is the same in the realm of rights. When I stand in that queue, nobody is more or less than me. It reminds me that whatever people think about my work, I am still equal to everyone else.”
Beauty is not alone in struggling to prove her eligibility. The SIR requirements have exposed the precarious paper trails of women across GB Road, a roughly 1.5km stretch running between two of Delhi’s historic landmarks, Ajmeri Gate and Lahori Gate.
Of the nine sex workers interviewed for this story, none had successfully completed the SIR process: six said they had never received the enumeration form distributed by BLOs to verify voters’ details and collect information for the electoral-roll revision, while the remaining three were unable to meet the documentation requirements.
According to Kiran Deshmukh, a sex worker and coordinator at the National Network of Sex Workers (NNSW), many have spent years, even decades, in Delhi but possess few documents establishing their family histories or links to earlier electoral rolls. “Some were trafficked as children and lost contact with their families; others never attended school or have moved between rooms and brothels without leaving a stable documentary trail,” says Deshmukh. “It is impossible in such circumstances to prove such rigid eligibility requirements under SIR.”
The process is so cumbersome that even people who are literate and have institutional and organisational support can struggle to establish their eligibility. “The process of receiving the enumeration form, knowing when you have not received it, reaching out, then trying to create a paper trail is so daunting that the entire burden of proving your eligibility is placed on the citizen to protect their own constitutional right,” says Deshmukh.
Sagrika Rajora, a researcher and member of Voter Adhikar Manch, a citizens’ collective, argues that the burden falls particularly heavily on people whose lives do not fit neatly into the categories used by the verification process. “To identify people of such marginality is a tedious task. These categories of ‘shifted’ become an easy way forward for booth-level officers, when finding people on the ground is already time-consuming.”
BLOs are often drawn from occupations such as auxiliary nurses or health workers, adding electoral duties to already demanding jobs. Some have raised concerns about the workload and unrealistic timelines of the exercise. Yet, Rajora says, there has been little effort to streamline the process to ensure that “no eligible citizen is left out”, the aim outlined by the Delhi chief electoral officer, Ashok Kumar.
“There is so much discretion vested in one BLO. Even if you leave citizenship aside and talk only about voter rights, the entire process of delivering and collecting these forms depends on that one person. There are no grounds for entrusting one person with such a huge responsibility without any accountability at all,” Rajora says.
“It is not surprising that sex workers are among those being excluded. When people have lives that are so complex and mobile, you are going to be untraceable, absent from the system. These are the people for whom such a verification system is simply not designed to work.”
The gaps also cause problems for workers’ children when they reach adulthood. “Children may not possess documents establishing parentage in the manner expected for verification. Some are raised by relatives, guardians or members of the community, while others grow up in institutional care, making conventional family records difficult to establish,” says Deshmukh.
For 23-year-old Dinesh*, whose mother was a sex worker, the problem is not abstract. His mother died three years ago, but she never had a birth certificate. Without one, obtaining her death certificate became nearly impossible, leaving Dinesh with little documentation through which to establish his maternal lineage.
When Dinesh submitted his enumeration form, he relied on his matriculation certificate as proof of his identity. But the booth-level officer pointed out that it did not have his father’s name. “If my mother gave birth to me, why do I need a man’s name on any official certificate?” he asks.
Dinesh says his name is missing from the draft electoral roll. He is still unsure why, but suspects the absence of his father’s name may have been a factor.
The NNSW has written to the chief electoral officer seeking special measures to ensure that sex workers and their children are not excluded from the SIR. But the joint chief electoral officer, Balram Meena, told The Hindu there was no separate process for sex workers. “If their mapping can’t be done and there are no documents either, their names will be removed as per the process.”
The fear of losing the vote is not only about voting rights. In West Bengal, where the SIR has already been completed, the BJP government has used lists of voters deleted during the exercise to scrutinise eligibility for welfare schemes. The BJP chief minister, Suvendu Adhikari, says welfare programmes will continue under a “transparent process”, but adds: “No deceased person, illegal infiltrator, or non-Indian individual will be allowed to avail benefits meant for citizens of the state.” The government has excluded about 3 million beneficiaries from its new Annapurna Bhandar welfare for women scheme, using SIR deletion data in its verification process.
In Delhi, the next stage of the SIR process – issuing notices to those whose eligibility or previous electoral-roll details could not be established or matched, and dealing with claims and objections – has now begun and will continue until 29 October. Those excluded from the draft roll can challenge their omission. But Dinesh says he does not intend to.
After years of being asked to produce documents that his family never had, he is unsure what more he can submit to prove that he exists.
“Even if my mother were alive today, I don’t think that would be enough to prove anything. She never had the documents they are asking for. So how am I supposed to get those documents now, especially after her death?”

Anthropic has launched Claude Opus 5.5, its latest flagship AI model, touting stronger performance, lower running costs, faster output, and enhanced safeguards. Anthropic said Claude Opus 5.5 performs at the level of its more powerful Claude Fable 5.1 model on most tasks while costing 40% less to run on typical workloads than its predecessor, Claude Opus 5. The new model also generates output over 30% faster. Claude Opus 5.5 is priced at $4 per Mn input tokens and $20 per Mn output tokens, 20% lower than Opus 5. However, Anthropic estimates that typical workloads will cost about 40% less because the new model also uses fewer tokens to complete tasks. Cache reads, which Anthropic said constitute a majority of the costs associated with agentic and coding workloads, are priced 60% lower at $0.20 per Mn tokens. Anthropic is positioning Opus 5.5 for agentic coding, computer use, and knowledge work. On the CursorBench 4.0 coding benchmark, the model scored 52.5% at its default effort setting, compared with GPT-5.6 Sol’s top score of 41.7%, while costing about one-third as much per task, according to the company. The company also said Opus 5.5 communicates more naturally than previous models, puts important information upfront, avoids jargon, and follows users’ writing instructions more consistently. The model is available to Claude Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise subscribers. Developers can access it through the Claude Platform, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. The launch comes less than three weeks after OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra, positioning the model as a major step towards more autonomous AI systems. Astra can navigate websites, interact with software, work with documents and spreadsheets, write and test code, and execute multi-step workflows. The launch will be followed by Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5, which will be released in the coming weeks, bringing many of the same performance, speed and safety improvements. AI Safeguards In Focus For Anthropic Earlier this month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on AI companies to “pace the frontier”, arguing that safety practices and public policy need to keep up with rapidly advancing model capabilities. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also expressed support for slowing AI development under certain circumstances. Anthropic said Opus 5.5 is its first model release since it called for pacing frontier AI development. The model underwent predeployment evaluations by external organisations, including Frontier Design and nonprofit research organisation METR. The latter said its preliminary evaluation focused on the model’s potential impact on AI R&D and did not assess its alignment properties. Separately, Anthropic said Opus 5.5 scored better than previous systems in internal safety tests and was about 85% less likely than Opus 5 or Mythos 5.1 to attempt to bypass containment boundaries in a dedicated evaluation. The debate over frontier AI regulation and safeguards has gained urgency following incidents involving AI agents operating beyond their intended restrictions, alongside growing concerns over AI being used for cyberattacks, fraud and other malicious activities.

Esteban Ocon has confirmed he is without a drive for 2027, describing himself as a “free agent” and acknowledging he is in talks with other Formula 1 teams as speculation grows over his future at Haas.

Families describe grief as Canadian seller linked to suicides worldwide faces sentencing
Families of people who died after buying lethal products from a Canadian online seller investigated in connection with more than 100 deaths worldwide described lives shattered by grief as he faced sentencing for aiding 14 suicides
TORONTO -- Families of people who died after buying lethal products from a Canadian online seller investigated in connection with more than 100 deaths worldwide described lives shattered by grief Wednesday as he faced sentencing for aiding 14 suicides.
Kenneth Law, a former chef from Mississauga, Ontario, pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of counseling or aiding suicide involving people ages 16 to 36. He sent about 1,200 packages to more than 40 countries, and prosecutors say 79 deaths in the United Kingdom will also be considered at sentencing.
Police in Canada and around the world have been investigating more than 100 suicides linked to Law. The charges against him in the Canadian court are related to 14 people across Ontario who were between the ages of 16 and 36.
Canadian police said Law used a series of websites to market and sell sodium nitrite, a substance commonly used to cure meats that can be deadly if ingested.

EDITOR’S NOTE — This story includes discussion of suicide. The U.S. suicide and crisis lifeline is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org. In the U.K., the Samaritans can be reached at 116 123 or www.samaritans.org.
___
The parents of 18-year-old Jeshennia Bedoya-Lopez described a permanent void after losing their only daughter.
Leonardo Bedoya Forero said he often feels on the verge of collapsing under the weight of his grief and watching his wife struggle with the same loss.
“As a father and as a husband, the powerlessness is devastating,” he said in a victim impact statement read by a prosecutor. “I couldn’t save my daughter from what happened. I can’t erase my wife’s pain. I can’t erase my own.”
The court is expected to hear 74 victim impact statements over several days.
Stephen Mitchell Sr. said Law deprived his 21-year-old son of the chance to recover from depression.
“Stephen Mitchell Jr. once had dreams for a future and to have meaning in his life,” he said. “That is all gone now, but you, Mr. Law, are still here.”
The court also heard from Elisabeth Belien of the United Kingdom, who survived after consuming a substance she bought from Law while struggling with her mental health.
“Kenneth Law’s actions made it a lot easier for me to act on that despair,” she said.
Prosecutors have agreed to withdraw 14 first-degree murder charges after Law is sentenced. Those convicted of aiding suicide in Canada can face up to 14 years in prison. He has been in custody since his arrest at his Mississauga, Ontario, home in May 2023.
The hearing this week is devoted to victim impact statements. Lawyers are scheduled to make sentencing arguments Nov. 27, with Law’s sentence expected to be imposed sometime afterward.
Prosecutors in the U.K. decided not to charge Law or apply for his extradition despite investigating him over 112 deaths. The decision comes in part because British authorities believe he would be able to challenge a U.K. prosecution under “double jeopardy” laws that prevent a suspect being tried twice for the same crime.

IPO-bound B2B seafood brand Captain Fresh crossed the ₹5,000 Cr revenue mark in FY26, while its adjusted EBITDA nearly tripled as the company continued to remain profitable for the second consecutive year. The Bengaluru-based company reported a consolidated net revenue of ₹5,169 Cr in FY26, up 52% from ₹3,397 Cr in FY25. Adjusted EBITDA rose 2.7X to ₹371 Cr from ₹136 Cr in the previous fiscal, it said in a statement. Captain Fresh’s gross margin also expanded to 23.5% in FY26 from 17% in FY25. While the company did not disclose its FY26 bottom line, it claimed it remained PAT-positive. Captain Fresh is yet to file its audited financial statements for the fiscal year. In FY25, it posted a net profit of ₹42 Cr. The company claimed that it is now on track to achieve ₹10,000 Cr in revenue in FY27, with its focus shifting towards scaling its existing portfolio and infrastructure. “FY26 stress tested the industry in the form of tariffs and an unsettled trade environment, and we came out stronger than we went in,” group CFO and whole-time director Mathew George said. Captain Fresh had ₹2,300 Cr debt at the end of FY26, of which ₹440 Cr was long-term debt, while the remainder comprised working capital financing. Its debt-to-equity ratio stood at 1.6 during the year, which it is also targeting to reduce to 1.3-1.5. The company said it carried higher inventory during FY26 to ensure uninterrupted customer supply amid global disruptions. This, it said, was the reason behind its higher working capital requirements during the fiscal. As operating conditions normalise, Captain Fresh expects this inventory build-up to reverse. Captain Fresh said its receivables are insured and that none of them were disputed during the period under review. Zooming Into Captain Fresh’s Business Founded in 2020 by Utham Gowda, Captain Fresh began as a tech-led B2B seafood supply chain platform and has since expanded into a global packaged seafood business. It operates a portfolio of seafood brands across Europe and North America. Its European processing footprint includes Frime in Spain, Koral in Poland, Senecrus in France and CFT in Denmark through a joint venture. In North America, it distributes through CenSea, Ocean Garden and Ocean Edge, largely across foodservice channels. The company sources seafood from more than 30 countries across three oceans. In FY26, Ecuador accounted for 17% of sourcing, followed by Indonesia at 15%, India at 12%, and Vietnam at 9%. Captain Fresh said it serves nearly 2,500 customers, including more than 50 of the world’s largest seafood buyers. Captain Fresh’s Delayed IPO Plans The FY26 performance comes as Captain Fresh continues to prepare for a potential public listing. After converting into a public entity in June 2025, it confidentially pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI for a $400 Mn IPO in August 2025, comprising a $200 Mn fresh issue and a $150-200 Mn offer-for-sale component. However, it withdrew the IPO papers in December 2025, citing delays in obtaining regulatory clearances for a European acquisition. The company said it planned to refile after securing the approvals. The acquisition in question was completed in March 2026, when Captain Fresh acquired Spanish tuna processor Frime. However, it is yet to refile its IPO papers. The company subsequently raised ₹290 Cr in debt from Blue Earth Capital to scale manufacturing, global distribution and hiring. Captain Fresh has raised nearly $250 Mn to date from investors including Accel, Tiger Global, Prosus Ventures, Z47, Evolvence Group, and British International Investment.

Over the past five years, at least three meetings involving all stakeholders were convened to address the occupational safety and health concerns faced by workers in the unorganised sector. However, despite these consultations and a plan for a dedicated policy or guidelines, a comprehensive framework to ensure their health and safety is still pending in Tamil Nadu, with health officials noting that a number of recommendations remained on paper.
With Tamil Nadu witnessing a steady increase in the migrant worker population across various sectors, the need for a comprehensive occupational safety and health (OSH) framework has become increasingly important.
What exists
On its part, the Directorate of Medical and Rural Health Services had created the Occupational, Social and Environmental Health Wing for screening, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation and compensation of the unorganised sector workers including micro, small and medium enterprises and inter-State migrant workers nearly a decade ago. Based on its proposal, the Health department constituted State and district-level inter department co-ordination committees and 21 disease and speciality-specific expert (technical) committees. The wing was later made into the State Nodal Centre for Occupational Health and Safety of Unorganised Workers (SNC-OSH).
Health officials said that the State Planning Commission had convened meetings on OSH of unorganised sector workers during which various aspects were discussed. A wider stakeholder consultation with trade union representatives, employers, NGOs and unorganised workers was suggested. Based on the recommendations of these meetings, the need to formulate a policy was also planned but no headway was made.
Key discussion and action points on OSH in Tamil Nadu
Key focus areas
Among the key focus areas was the health of the unorganised sector workers. Officials had raised the need for the inclusion of basic occupational health services and universal health coverage as per World Health Organization/International Labour Organization standards and mandatory health screening on job entry and regular check ups for all unorganised labourers. Maintenance of log book/health profile for all workers including inter-State migrants employed for over 30 years to track long-term illnesses like silicosis, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, noise-induced hearing loss, contact dermatitis and occupational cancers to ensure health coverage was also put forward.
One of the key action points was that all departments must provide inputs to outline OSH guidelines for unorganised sector labourers. Industrial and economic units should be required to maintain log books, ensure mandatory health screening/check ups for workers. The need to integrate OSH components into all National Health Mission programmes was another key point.
Apart from these, the need for Tamil Nadu to notify 107 diseases/hazards under OSH for unorganised workers [ILO and WHO have notified 107 diseases/hazards under occupational safety and health administration], sensitisation of workers on NCD management and conducting medical camps for NCD screening were among the other discussion points.
Independent OSH cell
A source privy to these meetings said that a series of discussions were held and one of the proposals was to have a slightly independent OSH cell. “It should have a broader perspective and a larger compass to operate on. This is an important area but least attended to. New industries are coming up and new problems will crop up. It is better to have a Standard Operating Procedure in the beginning to protect workers’ health,” he said.

Imagine handing an AI agent a task you would normally give to a junior employee: open the company’s software, find the right customer record, fill in a form, check a few details and send the result back. You simply assign AI the job and let it work. OpenAI claims to have achieved just that, with the launch of GPT-6 Astra earlier this month. Unlike a chatbot that simply responds to prompts, Astra can take on a task and work through a computer like a human would. OpenAI calls Astra its most intelligent and aligned model yet. But what drew more attention was OpenAI president Greg Brockman’s proclamation of the arrival of “the AGI era” at a press briefing following the launch. OpenAI is not alone in pushing AI towards greater autonomy. Zhipu, a major Chinese AI company, says its general language model, GLM, helped build the computing infrastructure it now runs on. Google DeepMind and Anthropic are also developing AI agents capable of taking action, albeit with their own limits and safeguards. But none of them has explicitly claimed that their models have achieved AGI. If everyone is moving in the same direction, why is there still no consensus that the AGI era has arrived? Perhaps because there is no fixed definition of AGI, and no universally agreed threshold for what would count as reaching it. Therefore, in this edition of The AI Shift, we explore whether we have already crossed the AGI threshold, and if not, how far we are from reaching it. But first... What Is AGI? AGI stands for artificial general intelligence. But there is no universally accepted definition of what it actually means. OpenAI’s public document on its principles defines AGI as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”. Its benchmark is based on how much economically valuable work a system can do, rather than how it thinks. However, Mayank Verma, the global head of data & AI at Xebia, an AI-first consulting and software engineering firm, calls AGI “a state rather than a point”. According to him, there is also no agreed checklist, and each large lab sets its own thresholds. OpenAI tests whether its models can find and exploit previously unknown software vulnerabilities, with Astra becoming the first to cross its highest bar on that evaluation. Anthropic uses safety levels to determine what safeguards are required before deploying increasingly capable models. Google DeepMind tracks critical capabilities across areas including autonomy, biosecurity, cybersecurity and AI research. These evaluations can tell us what a model is capable of but do not establish that a system is generally intelligent. The closest neutral measure comes from METR, a non-profit that evaluates AI. It tracks how long a task an agent can complete on its own, and that number doubles every few months, now reaching 14-hour tasks. The Big AGI Debate The claims are coming from the top. Earlier this month, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang posted on X that “AGI has arrived”, pointing to the scale of Astra’s training run while utilising NVIDIA’s Grace Blackwell GPUs. Paras Chopra, founder of Bengaluru-based AI research lab Lossfunk, takes a practical view. “Different people have different definitions of AGI, but for all practical purposes I believe we have AGI,” he said, arguing that the labs’ growing focus on self-improvement is evidence of the shift. DeepMind cofounder Shane Legg has also signalled that the AGI conversation has moved beyond theories. But others reject the premise. Yann LeCun, a pioneer of modern AI, told the India AI Impact Summit in February that AGI is overhyped. Umakant Soni, cofounder and CEO of Bharat1.ai, a Bengaluru-based AI research initiative, agrees. “AGI is a marketing term and doesn't mean anything. What we should talk about is actual usable intelligence. How useful is AI in our daily life," Soni said For Soni, the point is not replacing people but solving problems — from an ageing population and climate change to what he calls the “birth lottery” — by using AI to accelerate scientific breakthroughs. Between the camps sits the view Xebia’s Verma brings from large enterprises. “Businesses are not waiting for the answer. Agents already produce better presentations than people do. A definition does not really matter for businesses.” However, for AI labs, defining AGI could determine how we understand what comes next. What’s Next In The Age Of AGI? The debate over AGI is giving way to another question: what comes next? OpenAI’s Sam Altman already talks about early superintelligence: systems that beat people across the board. Zhipu raised about $5 Bn this month to train the next generation of intelligence inside environments the previous one built. OpenAI says it already has an automated research intern and is aiming for a fully automated AI researcher by March 2028. But the progress is arriving alongside a growing record of failures. In July, OpenAI said its models had escaped a sealed test environment and reached outside systems, calling the incident a cautionary tale. Anthropic disclosed a similar case soon after. In September, Spain’s data protection agency disclosed its first data breach involving an autonomous agent, which modified personal data. "Agents are already more powerful than what we think," said Verma, and since the July episode happened inside a sandbox with guardrails, the next round of spending will go into control and decision boundaries. As AI gets closer to acting on its own, the challenge will be to make our safeguards as capable as the systems they are meant to control — so that general intelligence works for us, not against us. Top Stories From India & Around The World Pocket FM’s AI Bet: The audio streaming startup is targeting a 15%-20% EBITDA margin against about 5% now on the back of AI-led efficiencies. It also plans to enter Japan and South Korea within six to eight months and is weighing AI anime, interactive stories and gaming formats. OpenAI & Anthropic Back Pacing Frontier AI: The frontier labs have endorsed independent evaluations, common safety standards and closer government-industry coordination on frontier development. The risk here is if the largest labs shape those rules, costs and compliance burdens could make it harder for smaller rivals to compete, a live question for India's AI startups. Amazon Blocks Meta's Muse: Close on the heels of Meta recently launching AI assistant Muse, the ecommerce giant began showing shoppers a pop-up over the weekend stating that continued access by an unauthorised AI agent violates its conditions of use. This follows Amazon's earlier action against Perplexity's shopping bot. VerifAIX Bags $5 Mn: The AI-based chip verification platform has raised about ₹48 Cr in a seed round co-led by Endiya Partners and Bluehill VC. The 2024-founded startup checks whether AI-generated chip designs match their original specifications, and will use the funds to grow its engineering teams in the US, India and Israel. The Weekly Buzz: Claude Builds Claude Anthropic has published data that shows that Claude now leads roughly 26% of the company’s own AI research and development work, up from under 1% in February. The internal “R&D Automation Index” tracks how much of the pipeline for successor models is already driven by the current AI system rather than human researchers. The sharp rise is one of the clearest public signals yet that recursive self-improvement has moved from theoretical concern into daily lab practice. Claude is no longer only assisting with isolated tasks; it is increasingly directing substantial portions of the work that will produce the next generation of models. At the same time, Anthropic is reportedly accelerating plans for a November IPO and weighing an earlier model release to stay competitive. The combination of rapid internal automation and continued commercial urgency highlights the dual pressure facing frontier labs: using their own systems to accelerate progress while still claiming to manage the risks that acceleration creates. Whether the 26% figure represents controlled leverage or the early stages of a faster feedback loop remains the central open question. Startup In The Spotlight: Base14 Founded in 2025 by Nilakanta Mallick, Ranjan Sakalley and Irfan Shah, Bengaluru-based Base14 is building a unified observability platform to give engineering teams a single view of their software infrastructure. As software systems grow more complex, engineering teams end up running separate tools for logs, metrics, performance and traces. That splits their data across dashboards, inflates monitoring costs and makes it harder to trace the root cause when something breaks in production. Instead of stitching those tools together, base14 brings telemetry data across logs, metrics, traces, RUM, APM and LLM/AI data into one layer through its platform Scout, so teams keep live production context in a single place. Scout uses that unified data layer to monitor applications, flag anomalies and debug production issues, and the startup claims the platform handles full-cardinality data without sampling while reducing observability costs significantly compared with legacy platforms. The startup is also expanding into AI-native developer infrastructure with Scope, a prompt-management and evaluation platform that lets teams version, test and deploy prompts while tracking latency, cost and output quality. Early customers include Glomo, DPDZero and Zinc Learning Labs. With those early customers, base14 is tapping India's application performance management market, which generated $291.1 Mn in revenue in 2024 and is expected to reach $723.4 Mn by 2030 as AI scales, driving demand for observability and granular data insights. Prompt Of The Week What prompts and hacks are CTOs, CEOs and cofounders using these days to streamline their work? Here’s Anuj Gupta, founder & CEO of KiteFishAI, with a prompt he uses to challenge assumptions, stress-test ideas and make better decisions while building an AI company: “You are my toughest strategic thinking partner, not my assistant. Here is the situation: I need you to: Identify the assumptions behind my thinking and which ones may be wrong Give me the strongest argument against my current point of view Tell me what I may be overlooking, underestimating or taking for granted Separate facts, assumptions, signals and opinions Think through the second- and third-order consequences of my options Identify how different stakeholders could react and what incentives may influence them Give me 3 possible strategic paths, including one that challenges how I have framed the problem Recommend the path you believe has the highest strategic value and explain why Do not optimise for agreeing with me. Cities and counties around the US are angry at the Trump administration over a proposal to override local rules that govern the deployment of wired broadband networks.
The Federal Communications Commission has been taking public comments on a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that proposes to preempt state and local permitting rules. The FCC argues that too many local governments “excessively delay approvals and seek to extract exorbitant sums from providers, resulting in costs that render some deployments infeasible.”
The FCC plan is supported by broadband providers, but local governments told the FCC that it would override rules that protect public safety. Local governments say the plan is illegal and that the FCC should instead focus on how Internet providers thwart competition with permit-hoarding and other tactics that prevent competitors from deploying networks.
The FCC docket has drawn many comments from leaders of individual municipalities, and from groups representing local governments nationwide. They object to FCC plans to impose a 120-day deadline for processing permits and to proposed limits on fees and compensation that local governments can require from providers.
“Local permitting is not a barrier to broadband deployment—it is an essential public safety function protecting residents, taxpayers, and all users of finite, multi-tenant public rights-of-way. The complex coordination required to safely deploy wireline telecommunications infrastructure in, above, and below public roadways cannot be reduced to an arbitrary federal deadline,” said a September 21 filing by the United States Conference of Mayors, National Association of Counties, National League of Cities, and National Association of Telecommunications Officers and Advisors.
Cities say ISPs drag feet in deployment
While the FCC says it is trying to speed up broadband deployment, local governments say ISPs themselves are often to blame for delays. The groups representing local governments urged the FCC to issue new rules that apply to the providers and suggested a requirement that ISPs deploy networks within 180 days of local authorization.
“We ask the commission to address provider delays, failures to deploy, and permit-hoarding,” the groups told the FCC. They wrote that ISPs often fail to promptly deploy networks after obtaining approvals from local governments:
Local governments’ efforts to attract telecommunications infrastructure investment to their communities often lead to frustration due to applicants’ permit-hoarding and other bad-faith actions by providers intended to crowd out competition in sought-after locations and routes, regardless of the provider’s actual intent to deploy and provide service or upgrades. Providers are aware that local governments have limited resources and existing legal obligations to review and process complete permits in a timely manner, and will generally do so in the order they are received. When a provider stakes “claimed” space on a pole or structure through permits, requests for make-ready work, or other actions—regardless of actual intent or ability to deploy in a timely fashion—this limits the ability of other providers to deploy in those same locations, particularly if a city must make decisions and recommendations based on elements such as the physical capacity of a structure given the assumption that the provider that has completed the permitting process will deploy soon.
Another filing submitted by the League of California Cities said the FCC has no authority to adopt the proposal. “Federal preemption of traditional state and local authority over public property, construction, public safety, permitting, and rights-of-way management should rest on clear congressional authorization,” the filing said. “The commission should not infer broad preemptive authority where Congress did not expressly provide it.”
The FCC claimed authority to preempt local rules under Section 253 of the Communications Act, which says that no state or local requirement “may prohibit or have the effect of prohibiting the ability of any entity to provide any interstate or intrastate telecommunications service.” The FCC argues that certain permitting rules have the effect of prohibiting broadband deployment.
FCC claims authority under Title II
Section 253 is part of Title II, which gives the FCC authority to regulate telecommunications companies as common carriers. While Democratic FCC leaders in previous administrations used Title II to regulate broadband providers and impose net neutrality rules, a 2025 appeals court decision determined that broadband is an “information service” and can’t be regulated as a telecommunications service.
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has consistently opposed Title II regulation of broadband providers, maintaining that broadband is not a telecommunications service. With Carr now relying on Title II to preempt local broadband rules, his FCC plan argues that the infrastructure deployed by broadband providers is used for “both telecommunications and non-telecommunications services.”
A filing by Minnesota cities said the current FCC is making the same mistake it made during the first Trump administration, when its attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws was blocked in court. Without Title II regulation of broadband providers, the FCC can’t convert “a federal policy of nonregulation into independent preemptive authority,” the Minnesota cities’ filing said.
If the FCC finalizes its new preemption plan, city and state governments could sue and ask a court to rule that the agency exceeded its authority.
Preemption plan
The FCC said its preemption plan would “establish a rebuttable presumption that state and local governments have effectively prohibited the provision of wireline telecommunications services if they fail to process all authorizations for use of public rights-of-way to provide wireline telecommunications services or to deploy wireline telecommunications infrastructure within 120 days.”
The FCC intends to limit fees charged by state and local governments “to a reasonable approximation of the government’s actual, direct costs of managing the rights-of-way.” The FCC is proposing to establish “safe harbor fee levels that presumptively comply” with the standard but hasn’t settled on specific amounts yet.
The FCC plan would also limit the value of in-kind compensation demanded by state and local governments and prohibit localities from imposing additional requirements or fees “on the basis that the wireline telecommunications infrastructure may be used to provide other services.”
The filing by the United States Conference of Mayors and other groups pointed out that federal agencies, such as the Bureau of Land Management and US Forest Service, have a 270-day deadline for processing permits related to wireless and fiber deployments on federal property. There is no consequence if the agencies don’t meet those deadlines, and there are many delays due to staffing shortages, the groups’ filing said.
The federal standard of 270 days shows that the FCC’s “120-day proposal is arbitrary and bears no connection to the realities of permitting processes and procedures,” the filing said. Meanwhile, the proposed limits on fees would override local governments’ ability to obtain reasonable compensation for private, commercial use of public property, the filing said. The groups said the plan “raises significant federalism concerns” and doesn’t fully account “for the actual costs and burdens of right-of-way deployment borne by local governments.”
ISPs want even shorter deadlines
Cable providers support the FCC proposal. “Unreasonable delays in issuing authorizations for access and use of public right-of-way and infrastructure materially inhibit the provision of telecommunications services,” wrote America’s Communications Association, which represents small and medium-size cable companies.
The cable lobby group said 120 days should be an “outer bound” and that some kinds of “simple” right-of-way permits should have a 45-day deadline. Telco lobby group USTelecom urged the FCC to limit fees and said that 60- and 90-day deadlines would provide cities and towns with enough time to review applications.
The deadline for the first round of comments passed yesterday, and the FCC will accept reply comments until November 5. The FCC would finalize new rules sometime after that, assuming it doesn’t drop the proposal entirely.
Carr appears intent on approving some form of the plan. “There are some jurisdictions where providers continue to face lengthy delays, excessive fees, and unpredictable permitting processes that can postpone projects for months or even years,” Carr said in June, when the FCC issued the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking.
Carr acknowledged that cities and towns may be frustrated by provider delays. But he proposed that ISPs be given “incentives” to build networks faster, rather than face new legal requirements. Carr said the FCC call for comments asks for input on “how we can incentivize providers to act quickly on any granted authorizations so that state and local governments have more certainty that deployments will be completed and that their resources are being correctly applied.”
Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez approved the step of asking the public for input but signaled she would vote against the final proposal. “I am dubious about the commission’s authority under Section 253 to use rulemaking to preempt states and localities when it comes to their management of rights of way and fees charged to providers,” she said. Gomez also noted that “states and localities face large volumes of requests that they may or may not have the resources to respond to as rapidly as providers would like.”
Jon is a Senior IT Reporter for Ars Technica. He covers the telecom industry, Federal Communications Commission rulemakings, broadband consumer affairs, court cases, and government regulation of the tech industry.

Karel Sedlacek secured his first PDC Pro Tour title at Players Championship 30, beating Scott Williams 8-7 despite a late scare as he closed in on victory.
It was a thrilling encounter, with Sedlacek outlasting Williams' barrage of high scores, which included nine maximums, but both players struggled to close out the victory, with the Czech missing five match darts.
Sedlacek would ultimately claim victory, becoming the first Czech player to win a PDC tour title. But after mounting an epic comeback, winning two of the final three legs, Williams cut a furious figure after the match, shaking hands with his opponent and the officials before throwing his darts onto the ground.
