West Bengal govt to roll out new industrial policy before Durga Puja: CM Adhikari
West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari said the new industrial policy will cover incentives, land policy and single-window clearances to attract investments.
West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Wednesday said the state government will roll out its new industrial policy before Durga Puja, which begins on October 10, as he outlined incentives and measures aimed at attracting investments and said the state was facing an “insolvent-like situation”.
“The state cabinet set up a Group of Ministers (GoM) headed by Tapas Roy, state industry and commerce minister. They have already submitted a draft of the industrial policy to the state chief secretary. The state government’s new industrial policy will be rolled out before the Durga Puja,” Adhikari said, speaking at a government programme in Kolkata where land was allotted to 33 industries and entrepreneurs to set up various projects.
Adhikari also said that he would hold one-to-one meetings with industrialists at least twice every month while giving a broad outline of the upcoming policy.
“The new policy will cover all aspects starting from incentives, land policy and single-window system for getting clearances, land pooling and development among others. Industrialists who will invest more than ₹100 crore, need not approach the civic bodies or panchayats to get their licenses and plans sanctioned. We know they are ready to harass you. The state government will provide everything,” he added.
Slamming the previous Left Front government and the Trinamool Congress administration, Adhikari said that the two regimes had a very negative approach to industries. He alleged that more than 54,000 industrial units, including jute mills and ancillary industries, were closed down during the 34 years of the Left Front regime and the 15 years of the TMC rule.
“The CPIM-government destroyed everything. The Mamata Banerjee-government washed her hands off and asked the industrialists to purchase land on their own. This can’t be an industrial policy of a government. Because of the government’s negative policy, the Tata had to leave Singur. We are positive. We will not misuse our power and police against farmers and land-owners. The government is directly purchasing land for industrialists,” he said.
Mass movements in Nandigram and Singur against land acquisition during 2006-08 paved the way for Banerjee’s political resurrection and helped her come to power in 2011.
“The financial condition of West Bengal is very poor. The state is an insolvent-like situation. We have allocated a budget of ₹5,000 crore to give incentives to industries based on the employment they would generate,” he added.

- After French President Emmanuel Macron said France was providing two-thirds of all intelligence to Ukraine on Jan. 15, 2026, a rumor gained traction that this was because Ukraine had given false intelligence to the U.S., which the United States then leaked to Russia, revealing the U.S. as an unreliable intelligence partner for Ukraine. The rumor continued to circulate in September 2026.
- Snopes could find no evidence confirming the rumor Ukraine had shared false information with the U.S. Instead, this part of the claim came from an apparent misunderstanding of a Jan. 16, 2026, interview on a French news television channel.
- In that interview, Vincent Crouzet — a former intelligence officer at the Directorate General for External Security (DGSE), France's foreign intelligence agency — said, without citing any sources, that Ukrainian intelligence officials suspected the U.S. had leaked information to Russia, causing Ukraine to stop sharing intelligence with the United States. In an X post two days later, Crouzet appeared to deny the claim that those leaks involved intentionally false information.
- Snopes first contacted Crouzet in January 2026 and reached out to him again in late September to ask about his evidence for these alleged leaks and whether there was any indication they involved Ukraine intentionally feeding the U.S. false information. We had not received a reply before publication but will update this story if we learn more.
In September 2026, a claim recirculated online that Ukraine had allegedly given the U.S. false intelligence that the United States then leaked to Russia, which revealed the U.S. as an unreliable intelligence partner.
Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, starting a war that is ongoing as of this writing.
For example, one X user, whose post had been viewed more than 8 million times at the time of publication, wrote (archived), "France and Ukraine fed Trump false intelligence to test whether he would leak it to Putin—and he did."
An Instagram user then posted a screenshot of that X post (archived). The caption said the claim fueled "speculation that Trump or people around his administration were leaking intelligence to Moscow," but added that it "has not been proven."
(X)
The rumor first spread at the start of 2026, shortly after French President Emmanuel Macron said France was providing two-thirds of Ukraine's intelligence on Jan. 15. Social media users then suggested the reasoning behind the French-Ukrainian intelligence partnership was the alleged leak of false Ukrainian intelligence from the U.S. to Russia. Posts making the claim featured on X, Substack, Medium, Bluesky and Reddit.
Several posts, including one on Facebook (archived), featured a screenshot of a since-deleted X post by user Luc Rombout, which read:
Interesting message on French newschannel LCI:
"Ukrainian intell services sent false strategic info to US intell services... and observed that the information had been relayed to RUS and was used by RUS forces."
=> total replacement of US as Intell partner with FRA, GBR, DEU [France, the U.K., Germany]
"Trump is leaking intelligence about our allies to Russia," the Facebook post's caption read.
Snopes could find no evidence confirming the rumor Ukraine had shared false information with the U.S. Instead, this claim appeared to stem from a misunderstanding of an interview that aired on Jan. 16, 2026, on the French news television channel LCI.
The interview subject was Vincent Crouzet, who formerly worked at the Directorate General for External Security (DGSE), France's foreign intelligence agency. He said in the interview, without citing his sources, that Ukrainian intelligence officials suspected the U.S. had leaked information to Russia, causing Ukraine to stop sharing intelligence with the United States.
Asked to clarify his assertion that the U.S. had leaked Ukrainian intelligence to Russia, Crouzet said in a Jan. 18, 2026, X post (archived), which in English reads, "No, I did not say that: I said Ukrainians suspected risks of information leaks from the U.S. to the Russians."
Snopes first contacted Crouzet in January 2026 and then reached out to him again in September to ask him what evidence he could provide that Ukrainians suspected intelligence leaks from the U.S. to Russia and whether there was any reason to believe Ukraine had fed the U.S. false information. We also contacted the White House for a comment on the rumor. We will update this report if we receive any responses.
Due to the fact that we could not verify or disprove these details independently, we did not give this report a rating.
The interview that sparked the rumor
The rumor spread, in part, via the screenshot of the X post by Rombout, who identified himself on his LinkedIn page as the head of a crisis management center in Belgium.
Rombout's post appeared to reshare a video clip posted on the 24H Pujadas account. 24H Pujadas is a program on LCI, considered reputable in France.
The clip itself was genuine and not created or altered using an artificial intelligence tool. Snopes identified an X post by the TV program 24H Pujadas with the video clip (archived) and a full video of the segment on the day it aired, Jan. 16, 2026. The presenter on that day was French journalist Yves Calvi.
Rombout seemingly deleted his original X post that made the claim. In a later post, he said in French that he was quoting the discussion in the French news program, implying that the claim did not originate with him.
A review of the televised interview showed Crouzet saying, in the context of discussing Macron's speech announcing France was now providing two-thirds of Ukraine's intelligence, that two Ukrainian intelligence officials had decided to stop sharing intelligence with the U.S. due to a lack of trust (emphasis ours):
So this announcement went a bit under the radar, yet it is essential. It is essential in two ways. First because it marks the divorce between Ukrainian intelligence and U.S. intelligence, because if we [France] supply two-thirds of Ukraine's intelligence, I can well imagine that the last third is supplies by other European partners — in this case, Germany and the U.K.
When did this divorce happen? It happened on Feb. 28, 2025, during the famous session in the Oval Office, which created a break in the trust between Ukrainian intelligence and U.S. intelligence, to the point where the two leaders of Ukrainian intelligence — so, Vasyl Malyuk for the SBU [Security Service of Ukraine] and Kyrylo Budanov ... you can see them on the screen ... for the GUR [Main Directorate of Intelligence, military intelligence] — decided to no longer share effective intelligence they had with their U.S. partner due to U.S. leaks to Moscow.
Rombout's X post seemingly misinterpreted some details. At no point did Crouzet say Ukraine had fed the U.S. false information and then tracked that information to Russia. We first reached out to Rombout in January and then contacted him again in September for his response to our findings about the possible translation error. We will update this report if we receive a response.

India is moving closer to introducing regulations that could restrict the sale of foods high in fat, salt and sugar within 50 metres of schools, as authorities step up efforts to curb rising junk-food consumption and childhood obesity, Reuters reported.
The proposed rules are likely to affect family-run shops, restaurants and food stalls selling high-fat, salt and sugar (HFSS) products near the country’s roughly 1.5 million schools. The move could also create challenges for global food and beverage companies, including PepsiCo, Coca-Cola, Mondelez and Nestle.
According to the Reuters report, India is separately considering warning labels for products high in fat, salt and sugar, potentially bringing its regulations closer to those adopted by countries such as Chile and Mexico.
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is driving the proposed changes as part of a broader push to encourage healthier food choices around schools.
FSSAI chief executive Rajit Punhani said the objective is to prevent children from developing unhealthy eating habits at an early age, Reuters reported.
“We have to discourage children from having these. We have to inculcate this habit,” Punhani told Reuters.
He said the proposed restrictions would not have a major impact on businesses because shopkeepers could continue selling foods that do not fall under the high-fat, salt and sugar category.
The regulations are also intended to encourage food companies to reformulate products and make them healthier, Punhani said.
According to Punhani, there is currently no fixed timeline for the regulations, which were first proposed in 2020.
The authority has invited public feedback on the proposal until 6 October.
India has seen a sharp rise in the number of children and adolescents classified as overweight or obese.
According to World Obesity Federation data cited by Reuters, the number of Indians aged 5-19 considered overweight or obese increased from 28 million in 2015 to 41 million in 2025. The figure is projected to reach 56 million by 2040.
The rise comes as processed and packaged foods have become increasingly popular in India. Products such as chips, chocolates and instant noodles are widely available in the market.
While the proposed federal rules aim to restrict the sale and advertising of HFSS products to schoolchildren, Maharashtra has adopted a broader approach.
Maharashtra has said shops within 50 metres of schools should not stock such products, state food safety commissioner Tukaram Mundhe told Reuters.
Mundhe said enforcing a rule based on whether a product was actually being sold to schoolchildren would be difficult, given the large number of shops located near schools.
Researchers at the University of North Carolina say five countries have proposed or implemented restrictions on the sale of junk food around schools, while 48 countries have rules limiting such sales inside schools.
Chile introduced warning-label requirements in 2016 and also prohibited the sale and promotion of junk food in schools.
A Lancet study published this year found that after 18 months of exposure to the Chilean regulations, the probability of excess weight was 2.85% lower among girls and 2.4% lower among boys.
The regulations also encouraged manufacturers in Chile to reformulate several food products.
(With inputs from Reuters)

It was at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona when the mutterings about a new "secret weapon" started.
Dozens of Great Britain athletes had been taking a new product that increased muscle mass and improved athletic performance – a "wonder pill" that didn't fall foul of any doping rules.
They were talking about creatine.
Now found in tubs and bags on many supermarket shelves and tagged in your social feeds, it is the supplement of choice for millions of people and one of the most scientifically researched.
But back then, when it came on the scene at the very top of British elite sport, there were suspicions and stigma around the use of any substance described as 'performance enhancing' – even if it was legal.
From the minute an athlete wakes, to the moment they go to bed, they are thinking about how they can optimise their performance and recovery.
Today, creatine is just one of a long list of supplements taken by elite athletes in this pursuit of marginal gains. Some help with muscle size and strength, while others correct deficiencies in the diet.
"There are various reports in the literature of some studies that say maybe up to 90% of athletes take supplements. I often jokingly say that means 10% are lying," says Prof Graeme Close, professor of human physiology at Liverpool John Moores University.
"The sports teams that I've worked in, I think that's probably closer to 100% of athletes will be taking some form of supplementation."
So, what do supplements actually do and why do athletes take them? And in the world of strict liability, where elite athletes are solely responsible for what they put in their bodies, how do they make sure they stay clean?
While experts like Close advocate for seeking to meet nutritional needs through food in the first instance, it may not always be possible or practical to do this - and that is where supplements come in.
Take, for example, creatine, which is found naturally in meat and fish.
"You would need the best part of a kilogram of raw chicken a day to get the amount of creatine you need," says Close. But it is unsafe to eat raw poultry because of the food poisoning risk from harmful bacteria.
Creatine is a natural compound in the body produced in the kidneys, liver and pancreas. It is a quick source of energy for muscles, which is especially important for short-duration, high intensity activities such as sprinting.
Its big break as a supplement came in the 1990s when two scientists who had been researching it for two decades shared their findings with Steve Jennings, whose Maxim sports nutrition company supplied products to the British Olympic team.
During the 1992 Barcelona Games, investigative reporter Doug Gillon had learned of a 'secret trial' involving British athletes and seen a box of their Ergomax C150 – effervescent creatine tablets. He wrote that if the scientists' claims - that creatine could improve explosive athletic performance by 1-3% - were true, then "sport may never be the same again".
In terms of sport supplements and nutrition, he was right. By the time of the next Olympics in 1996, an estimated 80% of athletes were taking creatine, and since then it has become mainstream, with research suggesting there may be cognitive benefits as well as physical.
According to the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, the creatine breakthrough of the 1990s had "launched a new era in sports nutrition" and "sparked exploration into other supplements".
The global dietary supplements market size was valued at $209.5bn (£154bn) in 2025 and is projected to grow to $431.7bn (£317.4bn) by 2033, according to Grand View Research., external
Close, who oversaw nutrition for last year's British and Irish Lions rugby union tour, sees supplements as the "final piece of the jigsaw" rather than a starting point.
"What we're talking about is small margins of benefit, where actually these athletes who focus on the food, I think what you often find is that they've got the big-ticket items right," he says.
"So they're seeing great performance benefits because their overall diet is immaculate.
"They might be missing out on the one per-centers, but they've really nailed the 99 per-centers. And they often do better than those who chase the one per-centers but have not given enough attention to the 99 per-centers."
Australian cyclist Nicole Frain agrees, adding: "I'm a pretty big believer that they are called sport supplements. They are there to supplement the things you already do right.
"I don't think supplements are the answer to fix my problems.
"You need to be eating a balanced diet, training well, sleeping right, recovering well, hydrating – all of those things – before we add in all of the extras."
Close puts protein powders top of the list of supplements taken by athletes he works with, followed by creatine and vitamin D.
Protein powders maximise muscle repair and contribute to muscle growth, while creatine is a quick source of energy for muscles and important in short-duration, high-intensity activities like sprinting. Vitamin D, meanwhile, is essential for bone health and supports muscle function.
Other popular supplements include carbohydrate gels, which Close says were key in the first sub-two hour marathon run earlier this year by Kenyan long-distance runner Sabastian Sawe.
"As sport nutritionists we were all fascinated at what the fuelling programme was, and it was the sports drinks and gels that played a huge part of that fuelling," Close says.
"There was a calculation done of what it would take to break the two-hour marathon, and that did involve making sure that over 100 grams of supplemental carbohydrate were ingested per hour.
"And the reports coming out of the recent sub-two-hour marathon was that it was 110 grams of carbohydrate per hour that was achieved."
Supplements can improve performance, but there is an uneasy ring to describing them as 'performance enhancing' because of the association with banned substances and anti-doping rule violations.
So what determines whether something is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's (Wada) banned list?
"For Wada to put anything on the list, it's got to hit two out of three criteria: dangerous to health, performance enhancing, and against the spirit of sport," Close explains.
"So just because something enhances performance, if it's not dangerous to health and not against the spirit of sport, Wada will not touch it.
"So creatine is a good example.
"Though something like an anabolic steroid, where it's against the spirit of sport to be injecting yourself for a performance benefit, it's dangerous to health and it's performance enhancing - that hits all three."
But taking a supplement still carries anti-doping risks.
"No guarantee can be given that any particular supplement is free from prohibited substances," UK Anti-Doping advice states, urging athletes to "be vigilant" in using them.
And if you test positive for a prohibited substance, consuming it unintentionally can result in the same four-year ban as if you deliberately took it.
There are supplement-testing programmes which batch test products before they are sold to make sure they do not contain any Wada-prohibited substances.
One of those is Informed Sport, which says as many as one in 10 supplements is contaminated with ingredients and compounds prohibited in sport and points to a study carried out by the Anti-Doping Knowledge Centre that showed product contamination was responsible for 8% of all anti-doping violations between 2005 and 2022.
While Informed Sport is a very well used system among athletes, Wada makes it clear that quality assurance schemes can reduce but do not eliminate the risk of an anti-doping infringement.
If you do accept the risk, you need to be organised to keep track.
In the case of Great Britain rower Heidi Long, it takes a spreadsheet.
"I've recorded the batch number of every product that I've taken and its expiry date because if you take it after the expiry date the Informed Sport [certification] is no longer viable," she says.
Close says he has also done site visits to factories to see where the supplements are made to check the manufacturing processes because "the risk of failing a drugs test is huge".
There are risks to the general population too, he adds, saying: "You can be buying supplements off the internet that are made in somebody's garage and you've got no idea of the manufacturing processes."
He points to studies on creatine products which have found there is no creatine in them and so "you're completely wasting your money" and that in the worst case scenario it may contain substances that are dangerous to your health.
"So it is really important that the message is that while they can play a small role, the safety considerations are the key factor," he says.
There is, however, more than one way for an elite athlete to chase a competitive edge – and some are going back to basics.
For every trending supplement, there is an unprocessed, wholefood alternative – from the anti-inflammatory benefits of turmeric, staving off cramp with pickle juice or consumption of high-nitrate foods like beetroot before competition.
It is what Close calls a "food-first" or "food-only" approach and something he says every athlete should use as a starting point.
The latest to have its moment in the spotlight is an ancient Ethiopian grain called teff.
Used for thousands of years in traditional east African diets, teff is now making its mark globally in performance nutrition.
In comparison to other popular grains like wheat, rice and quinoa, teff has a high mineral content and is rich in calcium, iron and vitamin C. Naturally gluten-free and good for the gut, it is also unique for being a 'complete' protein, meaning it provides all nine essential amino acids required for human nutrition.
These superfood credentials have caught the attention of some of the world's best athletes over the years, from Olympic champion marathon runner Haile Gebrselassie to seven-time Grand Slam singles champion Venus Williams, and it is now becoming a more common sight on UK supermarket shelves.
British boxer Fran Hennessy was introduced to teff by her nutritionist and it is now part of her daily routine.
"I've never looked back," she says. "What I'm putting in my body is good fuel and energy and teff has so much. It energises you so much before a workout and it gives you the fibre you need."
As well as boosting her performances, Hennessy credits teff with being key to recovery.
She says: "Each meal I'm having there's a reason behind and everything that's in it there's a reason behind... I know what I'm putting in my body is fuelling me, recovering me, energising me."
Cost is another consideration when athletes are deciding on supplements.
"The supplement industry is really expensive," says Long. "And we're definitely not made of money. So I think it's really picking and choosing when you want to put that investment in."
She says it makes sense to have more supplements around racing time "when the performance is super critical and very time dependent".
"[But] on a daily basis if I can get the protein intake from my dinner and a glass of milk or yoghurt and breakfast then actually I was going to be eating that food anyway so it's not as expensive."
And then there is taste.
"I would much rather enjoy a coffee in the morning with friends or while I'm working rather than have one of the gels," she says. "Some of the gels ... you'll end up holding your nose when you take it.
"I guess it's just like the enjoyment of what you're taking, you know, it's nicer to eat food than it is to take supplements."

Aftermarket devices that can boost or augment a vehicle’s native advanced driver assistance systems are the target of a new federal investigation this week. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation says it knows of five crashes in which drivers using devices from comma.ai crashed into stopped or slow-moving cars. Two of the crashes resulted in three deaths, and 11 people were injured in four of the five crashes, some seriously.
Comma.ai was the brainchild of George Hotz, who rose to prominence at the start of the last decade by jailbreaking iOS and hacking Sony PlayStations. In 2015, Hotz turned his attention to partially automated driver assists, which were gaining attention following Tesla’s exploits with its Autopilot system. Hotz first modified his own Acura to give it a more advanced driver assist that let him take his hands off the wheel, with the goal of selling his system to Tesla and replacing Mobileye as the company’s supplier.
(Mobileye dropped Tesla as a customer the following year after becoming unhappy with the way the car company was using Mobileye products in unintended ways.)
Comma’s first attempts to sell devices that owners could plug into their cars’ ODB port evaporated once NHTSA began asking questions in 2016. Instead, Comma decided to post its openpilot software, as well as its plans for hardware, to GitHub, allowing anyone to make the devices themselves. At first, the Comma Neo and OpenPilot supported a single Acura and single Honda model, but by 2020, the company’s software and $999 device were rated more highly by Consumer Reports than any OEM system.

Mumbai: IIT Bombay has postponed its mid-semester examinations scheduled for September 26 and 27, days after the death by suicide of second-year BTech student Sahil Wakode triggered protests on the campus.
Exams Shifted To Next Month
The exams have now been shifted to October 10 and 11, reported NDTV. The institute said the decision was taken after consultations with student representatives and other stakeholders. The postponement is also intended to give a newly constituted committee time to prepare a student-friendly Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for invigilators dealing with suspected cases of academic misconduct.
According to the institute, the revised SOP will lay down clearer procedures for handling alleged academic misconduct and is aimed at ensuring that examination-related cases are dealt with fairly and consistently. Faculty members have also sought detailed, step-by-step guidelines covering the various stages of such cases. The proposed SOP and revised rules will later be placed before the Senate for formal approval before being implemented.
The development comes amid continuing protests at IIT Bombay following the death of 22-year-old Sahil Wakode on September 18. Wakode, a second-year student, was allegedly caught using a mobile phone during a mid-semester examination shortly before he was found dead in his hostel room.
CCTV Allegedly Shows Wakode Caught Cheating
CCTV footage from the examination hall shows Wakode seated in a front-row seat when an invigilator, Professor Suryanarayana Doolla, approaches him. The footage reportedly shows Wakode handing over his mobile phone to the professor before gathering his belongings and appearing to leave the examination hall.
Wakode's family has alleged that he faced caste-based harassment and had spoken to them about the issue. Police then registered an FIR alleging abetment to suicide and invoked provisions of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.
Professor Doolla, who has been named in the FIR, was sent on leave amid the investigation. He was also removed from his administrative responsibilities following protests by students. IIT Bombay and its faculty forum have defended Doolla, maintaining that he was performing his duty as an invigilator and had followed the prescribed procedure after allegedly detecting misconduct.
The institute has said Wakode was counselled after the examination incident and assured that it would not affect his academic career. On Wednesday, IIT Bombay also constituted a 10-member high-level committee to examine the circumstances surrounding Wakode's death.

Bushra Bano cleared the Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission examination in 2017 with Rank 6, becoming a PCS Officer and later a sub-divisional magistrate. She studied on her own, without coaching, while working full-time and raising two children with her engineer husband. She sat for the UPSC exam twice — in 2019 and 2021 — before securing Rank 234 and clearing the Indian Police Service.
On September 14, 2026, she was transferred from her post as additional SP of Kharagpur in West Bengal’s Paschim Medinipur district, a day after propaganda news channels and Right-wing accounts targeted her for using the Arabic words, ‘Assalamu Alaikum’, ‘Jazakallah’, and ‘Inshallah’, in a video.
In the clip, Bushara is heard commending a government-aided residential coaching academy for minorities, women and SC/ST students at Aligarh Muslim University. While she spoke, she said the three phrases in Arabic. She said, “Assalamu Alaikum. My name is Bushra Bano… ” at first. Towards the end, she said, “…If they (the students) stay and study through the RCA then Inshallah many more people will move forward like me and get the opportunity to serve their country.” At the end she ended her video by saying, “Thank you, Jazakallah”.
“Assalamu Alaikum” is a common greeting which means “Peace be upon you”; “Inshallah” translates to “God willing”, and the phrase “Jazakallah” means “May God Reward You”. The reader might note that these are not religious phrases but greetings and wishes.
A simple video, made by a Muslim IPS officer who used a few Arabic phrases, sent ripples across the Right-wing ecosystem. On September 13, propaganda outlet Sudarshan News, which has its own national TV channel, shared the video on X and said, “Starting with ‘Assalamualaikum,’ slipping in ‘Inshallah’ midway, and wrapping up with ‘Jazakallah’, Bushra Bano… shared how she came from Saudi Arabia and became an IPS officer in India… She made full use of the scheme being run by the government at Aligarh Muslim University.”
“अस्सलाम वाले कुम” से शुरू कर बीच में “इंशाल्लाह” कहते हुए “जज़ाकल्लाह” पर किया खत्म,
खड़गपुर में एडिशनल एसपी के तौर पर तैनात बुशरा बानो ने बताया कि सऊदी अरब से आ कर वो कैसे भारत में बनीं IPS..
सरकार द्वारा अलीगढ़ मुस्लिम यूनिवर्सिटी में चलाई जा रही स्कीम का उठाया भरपूर फायदा.… pic.twitter.com/foYKjihMV2
— Sudarshan News (@SudarshanNewsTV) September 13, 2026
Soon, a barrage of online trolls started targeting Bano. An X handle called @HinduLegalFund posted on X that a complaint had been filed with the West Bengal home secretary regarding the video. “She began with Assalamualaikum, used Inshallah, ended with Jazakallah — and did not use Vande Mataram or Jai Hind…” the post read. Additionally, it stated that a serving officer should maintain “neutrality and national expressions in public communication”.
Complaint filed with West Bengal Home Secretary regarding IPS Bushra Bano’s official video statement.
She began with Assalamualaikum, used Inshallah, ended with Jazakallah — and did not use Vande Mataram or Jai Hind.
A serving officer representing the Indian state should…
— Hindu Legal Fund (@HinduLegalFund) September 13, 2026
Several Right-wing accounts, including @JaipurDialogues and @MeghUpdates, also shared the video and complained that no ‘Vande Mataram’ or ‘Jai Hind’ had been used by the IPS officer.
A notification issued by the government of West Bengal on Monday stated that Bano, alongside two other WBPS officers, was being transferred to a different posting “in public interest”. She has been made the deputy commandant of the state armed police 4th battalion. The notification does not state any reason behind the transfer.

Subhendu Mandal posted as Addl DC, Chandannagar
Dr. Bushara Bano, transferred as Dy. CO, SAP 4th Bn. pic.twitter.com/MHu5WK4De1
— ANI (@ANI) September 14, 2026
It should be common knowledge that Arabic is a language and Islam is a religion. Muslims use Arabic extensively for religious purposes, but Arabic is not synonymous with Islam. In other words, none of these expressions is simply a ‘Muslim word’ in the narrow linguistic sense. They are Arabic phrases whose meanings and histories intersect with Islamic religious usage, but they are not exclusive to Islam. The tradition of greeting a person with ‘Peace be upon you’, for example, exists in other languages and religious traditions — the Hebrew expression ‘shalom aleichem’, for example, literally means ‘peace be upon you’ and is common in Jewish religious literature. None of this, however, came in the way of pro-BJP handles slamming the officer for her alleged religion posturing.
Sudarshan News editor Suresh Chavhanke, whose history of peddling misinformation and communal propaganda is well documented, called Bano’s case ‘UPSC Jihad’.
Even if one were to accept this as an instance of religious posturing, it would hardly be the first time a police officer has done so. What stands out, however, is how differently such conduct is received depending on the community to which the officer belongs.
In May 2026, IPS officer C V Anand invited priests to perform a puja in his office on the day he took charge as director general of police of Telangana.
Senior IPS officer CV Anand taking charge as Telangana DGP. pic.twitter.com/5ZSSAT6K3w
— Piyush Rai (@Benarasiyaa) May 2, 2026
He himself posted about this on X. No one batted an eyelid. Anand is still serving as the DGP of Telangana.
Anand wrote, “As per the muhurtham , I reached the DGP office at Lakdikapul with my family , took the salute and followed the pujari into the dgp chambers where the puja and blessings were done.”
It was a very busy and perhaps the biggest day for me and my family . As per the muhurtham , I reached the DGP office at Lakdikapul with my family , took the salute and followed the pujari into the dgp chambers where the puja and blessings were done.
Then at 11:05 AM , signed… pic.twitter.com/wlkJX8hszp
— CV Anand IPS (@CVAnandIPS) May 1, 2026
More such instances are not difficult to find.
In Uttar Pradesh’s Sambhal, a circle officer named Anuj Chaudhary, who was an accused of firing during the violence at the Shahi Jama Masjid in November 2024, was pictured joining a Hindu religious procession in January 2025. He was accused of participating in religious rituals while on duty and violating service conduct rules. A complaint was filed by retired IPS officer and Azad Adhikar Sena president Amitabh Thakur, following which a probe was launched.
The same year, on Holi, Chaudhary had stated: “Holi comes once a year, Jumma comes 52 times. If you want to serve sevai, you must also eat gujiya.” Again, an investigation was initiated, and Chaudhary was eventually given a clean chit.
In May 2025, he was transferred from Sambhal to Chandausi, some 30 km away. Three months later, in August, Chaudhary was promoted to the role of additional superintendent of police (ASP). His colleagues and senior officers, including SP K K Bishnoi and ASP Rajesh Kumar Srivastava, marked the occasion with a felicitation ceremony.
Was there no outrage when Anuj Chaudhary carried a mace and marched in a religious procession in uniform? There was, from one section, but he went on to be promoted. Bano’s case panned out differently. The principle, presumably, is that the same rules apply to everyone. In practice, however, some seem to be considerably more equal than others. And if Bushra Bano’s transfer was, as the government put it, “in public interest”, one is left wondering exactly which ‘public’ that interest was meant to serve.
Bano’s transfer set off a series of critical reactions from the Opposition. Several politicians alleged that the transfer was a direct fallout of her use of Arabic phrases. Comparing the incident with Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s inauguration of the Parliament “with sengol & bare chested sadhus”, Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra remarked, “…We are a nation gone mad, poisoned with hate & bigotry. God Save India”.
For a country whose Prime Minister inaugurated new Parliament with sengol & bare chested sadhus, transferring a Muslim IPS officer for saying Assalamalaikum & Inshallah is ridiculous. We are a nation gone mad, poisoned with hate & bigotry. God Save India.
— Mahua Moitra (@MahuaMoitra) September 15, 2026
Former Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Mehbooba Mufti also criticised the move, saying the transfer, which was followed by the West Bengal CM “calling an election a ‘test’ of Muslim loyalty”, was “a veiled threat to the community”. “…First our food, clothes and marriages , now even our vocabulary and our votes are being policed”, she added.
Congress MP Imran Pratapgarhi took to X to condemn the move. “A hate-mongering TV channel first sensationalized that video by posting it and incited online trolling against the female IPS officer, and instead of standing by her, the state government transferred her the very next day. What kind of India are you building, @narendramodi ji? @IPS_Association, are you watching this?”, he wrote.

Meta's new holographic avatars are here and they're surprisingly real
They're a notable improvement over the company's earlier attempts at digital likeness.
I'm almost embarrassed to admit that the first time I saw one of Meta's new holographic avatars today, during a WhatsApp call with a Meta rep I had just met a few minutes before, I didn't immediately clock that I was speaking to an avatar. That's how far the company's avatar technology has come in the last couple years.
Meta announced at Connect that it's bringing its holographic avatars to its new VR glasses and to the Meta Ray-Ban Display frames. I got the chance to experience both ahead of the keynote and was surprised at how far the tech has come since the first time I experienced it on Meta's Orion prototype.
Setting up an avatar is a bit different depending on which device you're using. With the display-enabled glasses, you create an avatar in the Meta AI app through a process similar to creating a Vision Pro "persona." Using your phone's camera, you're prompted to turn your head to show different angles of your face. It then asks you a series of questions that are meant to capture how your voice sounds in different interactions.
In my demo, it asked me things like "what does your perfect day look like from start to finish" and "what's one of your hobbies, and why do you like it." This part of the demo actually glitched. The Meta AI app kept skipping through the questions as if it couldn't detect my voice, but the hiccup didn't seem to affect the process. I was then prompted to "smile and show your teeth" and repeat a phrase as if I was surprised.
In all, creating a holographic avatar for the display glasses should only take about 5 minutes from start to finish. Once set up, you can use it on a video call while wearing your display-enabled glasses, whether you're chatting via WhatsApp or Zoom.
The avatars are powered by Meta's new Muse Realtime Avatar model, and it uses that brief training period to approximate your actual facial expressions while you speak. Watching my avatar speak was a strange experience. While I was wearing the glasses and speaking as my avatar, I could see a small preview of myself in the bottom corner of the display. It looked exactly like me, but my brain was also able to immediately recognize that it wasn't me.
But when I tried the experience from the other side, holding the phone and chatting with an avatar, I was fooled at first. It might be because I had only just met the person I was speaking to. So I wasn't familiar with his mannerisms or expressions, but it looked very similar to how I would have expected him to appear on a typical video call. It was only when looking more closely at his background that I could detect the video wasn't quite normal. Meta is also adding a transparent watermark to all video calls with an avatar. In my first viewing, I mistook this for a logo on his shirt, but if you know what to look for, it is a clear identifier.
Meta's plan for holographic avatars in its new VR glasses is even more ambitious. Because the cameras and sensors on that device are much more advanced, you can create a full-body avatar and you don't need to "teach" it your expressions. It instead relies on the inward facing cameras and sensors to understand your facial expressions.
I was able to chat with a full-size hologram of a Meta product manager while wearing the VR glasses. And it felt less weird than I expected. It was definitely much more natural looking than Apple's "persona" avatars, which have always looked weirdly smooth and alien-like to me. (Those also don't show lower bodies or arms, which doesn't help.)
But the VR avatar I spoke with looked pretty close to the person I had just met, and didn't feel creepy either. There was some distortion toward her feet, especially if I moved around the room, and I could see some blurring towards the edges of her head. The avatars aren't fully 3D. They only show a frontal view of a person, so there are some limitations. But I was surprised at how much more realistic it felt than any other interaction I've ever had with a VR avatar (a low bar, to be fair).
Holographic avatars are still in an "early preview" stage, and there's clearly some bugs to be worked out. Availability is also limited to the device you're using, so someone with Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses can call someone else as their avatar but only when wearing the glasses. And someone on display glasses can't call someone wearing VR Glasses. VR avatars are limited to glasses to glasses interactions for now.
Meta has said these avatars could help people feel more of a sense of presence when on a video call, and I definitely felt that in my demo. There's still something about calling a close friend or family member as my avatar that would feel weird and inauthentic, but I could see how some might feel otherwise. The Meta reps I spoke with told me they often call into work meetings as their avatar, which might be a nice alternative when you're not quite camera-ready.
Holograms will be available to Meta Ray-Ban Display in early access this fall.

Adani Group Chairman Gautam Adani on Thursday announced an investment of more than ₹4,000 crore for the proposed Adani Arogya Mandir in West Bengal, a healthcare initiative that is expected to generate over 10,000 employment opportunities. Adani made the announcement at the foundation stone ceremony for the project in New Town. He also said the Adani Group intends to invest more than ₹1 lakh crore in West Bengal by 2035, with investments spanning multiple sectors such as ports, logistics, power generation, transmission and distribution, roads, bridges, ropeways, green cement and hyperscale data centres. The Adani Arogya Mandir is planned as a 2,000-bed not-for-profit healthcare facility. Half of the beds will reportedly be allocated to economically weaker patients covered by state or central government health insurance programmes. The project will also feature a medical college and facilities focused on advanced healthcare and research, according to ANI. Adani, accompanied by his wife Priti Adani and son Karan Adani, performed the ‘bhumi pujan’ and formally laid the foundation stone for the proposed project. Describing the project as part of the Adani Group’s broader investment plans for the state, Adani noted, “While healthcare can transform individual lives, infrastructure can transform the opportunities available to millions and this is where our larger commitment to Bengal begins." The Adani Arogya Mandir will be developed across 51.75 acres as an academic medical centre and integrated healthcare facility, according to a statement, further noting that the the centre is expected to treat more than 2 lakh in-patients and over 20 lakh out-patients every year. The project will establish a research network covering areas such as genomics, precision medicine, biomedical informatics, artificial intelligence, clinical trials, molecular sciences and other fields of applied biomedical research, as per PTI. The facility will focus on converting scientific advances into better methods of diagnosis, treatment and disease prevention, the statement said. The Adani Foundation has partnered with Mayo Clinic Global Consulting in the US and Singapore-based SingHealth to bring international expertise in clinical services, academic medicine, digital healthcare, quality standards, workforce development and innovation, it added. Describing West Bengal as a key maritime and logistics link connecting Northeast India with Southeast Asia, Adani said the state could develop into “one of Asia's greatest integrated industrial and economic platforms”. Adani also announced that the group would back the restoration of the Writers' Building, the redevelopment of Kumartuli Ghat and efforts to take Kolkata’s Durga Puja to a global audience. Referring to Mundra Port in Gujarat as the Adani Group’s first ‘karmabhoomi’ (land where one works), he expressed hope that West Bengal would become the conglomerate’s second ‘karmabhoomi’. Adani said he visited the Kalighat Temple earlier on Thursday, where he prayed for the strength to lead, the determination to dream and the energy to turn those dreams into action. Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has celebrated a “historic” meeting with Donald Trump in New York, posing for a smiley photo with the US president less than nine months after he ordered the abduction of her boss, Nicolás Maduro.
The former foes met at a five-star hotel in Manhattan a few blocks from Trump Tower late on Tuesday, on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly. The hotel is about 7 miles from the Brooklyn prison where Maduro has been held since he was snatched during a special forces raid on Caracas.
On the eve of Tuesday’s encounter, an American reporter asked Rodríguez if she would be visiting Maduro, under whom she served as vice-president, during her stay in New York. She did not reply.
But Venezuela’s interim leader did find time to meet Trump at the luxury Lotte New York Palace hotel, with the get-together seen as a key part of Rodríguez’s push for international legitimacy after years of diplomatic isolation under Maduro’s dictatorship. On Wednesday she is expected to address the annual UN assembly.
“We held a historic meeting with … Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, security and other matters of common interest,” Rodríguez wrote on Instagram, in a 133-word statement that made no mention of her incarcerated ally.
Oliver Blanco, one of Rodríguez’s top diplomats, claimed the meeting marked “a new stage of dialogue and understanding between both countries” and was “an important step toward new opportunities for our country and our people”. Blanco also posted a cheery photo in which both he and Trump smiled and gave the thumbs up to the camera.
A White House aide said the meeting was also attended by top US officials including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and the deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller.
Hours earlier, Rodríguez had sat in the general assembly hall watching Trump celebrate the “massive military operation” during which Maduro – whom he called an “outlaw dictator” and “a real criminal” – was captured. “It was a war … [and] to the victor belong the spoils,” Trump bragged of the recent oil deal between the US and Venezuela, as she appeared to wince.
Some observers also detected signs of discomfort in the body language captured in the photo of Trump and Rodríguez, who appears to be clenching her left fist as she poses beside the grinning US president.
Some of Rodríguez’s critics in Venezuela called her treatment by Trump an unmitigated humiliation for a socialist party politician who has spent years railing against Yankee imperialism.
After Maduro’s capture, Trump warned that Rodríguez would “pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro” if she did not toe the US line. Since then, Rodríguez has made a series of major concessions, including ceding control of Venezuela’s oil revenues to Washington and agreeing to a controversial 65bn-barrel oil deal that Trump on Tuesday called “the largest oil deal in history”.
One opposition figure denounced the Rodríguez/Trump meeting as an encounter between a “shameless puppet and her unscrupulous puppeteer”.
But Rodríguez has succeeded in consolidating power, with Trump seemingly more focused on gaining access to Venezuela’s natural resources than pushing for a fresh presidential election that would move the South American country back towards democracy.
Trump has repeatedly praised Rodríguez’s “fantastic” and “terrific” leadership while sidelining her main rival, the opposition leader María Corina Machado. Machado, who left Venezuela late last year to receive her Nobel peace prize in Oslo, has been unable to return and is exiled in Panama. She reportedly made three attempts to return to Venezuela this week, but failed.
Before Tuesday’s tête-à-tête, the presidents of the US and Venezuela had last met in 2015, when Barack Obama and Maduro spoke briefly during a regional summit in Panama. In the decade that followed, Maduro became an international pariah as he led his country into economic chaos and increasingly authoritarian rule, and Venezuela was hit by punishing international sanctions.
At the 2015 summit, Obama conceded that the days in which “the US could meddle with impunity” in Latin America were over. But Trump has dramatically different ideas and has been forging ahead with attempts to reassert US dominance in a region it has long considered its back yard.
As well as capturing Venezuela’s government and trying to topple Cuba’s communist government by strangling its economy, Trump’s push for hegemony has also seen the US accused of trying to swing Brazil’s presidential election in favour of the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro through diplomatic and economic pressure.
Addressing the UN assembly on Tuesday, the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, hit back at such efforts, without directly citing the US. “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians,” said Lula who is facing a tough battle to win re-election in October’s vote.
“Brazil doesn’t fit into anyone’s back yard,” added Lula, who also called for fresh elections in Venezuela. He did not meet Rodríguez during her visit to New York but said the “people of Venezuela deserve to decide their own future”.

What to know about the agreement signed by President Trump and the leaders of Denmark and Greenland
U.S. President Donald Trump and the leaders of Denmark and Greenland have signed an agreement about Greenland's status
U.S. President Donald Trump and the leaders of Denmark and Greenland signed an agreement about the status of the Arctic island after months of threats by Trump to seize the semiautonomous territory of a NATO ally.
The deal was officially signed Tuesday in New York, after U.S., Greenlandic and Danish officials had quietly negotiated for months behind the scenes — searching both for solutions to address some of Trump’s security concerns about the territory, as well as alleviating Danish and Greenlandic fears of being taken over by the U.S.
The three parties expressed satisfaction with the deal at the signing ceremony — but what exactly does it say?
Washington is allowed to “modernize and expand” its activities at the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest, according to the agreement.
The U.S. can also set up “defense areas” at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east, and “may establish additional defense areas in Greenland and strengthen its military operations or facilities.”
The accord calls for wide U.S. military mobility on Greenland’s territory, including “undersea access," noting that “ the security situation in the Arctic is changing and that more efforts are needed to ensure security there in the future.”
The agreement reaffirms “the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark,” and recognizes the Greenlanders' "right to self-determination.”
The agreement says all three parties “support a stronger NATO engagement in the Arctic, including as regards planning, presence, exercises, and joint intelligence gathering.”
It allows U.S. military access to Greenland to defend the NATO area, Greenland itself and the American continent — including through a “Golden Dome defense system."
The deal spells out that “no state that is not a member of NATO shall be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland nor shall they be allowed a persistent presence of military forces in Greenland."
In the preamble, the signatories recognize “the need to protect the pristine environment of Greenland.” It also stresses “the economic, social, and cultural rights of the people of Greenland, including with respect to their lands and their way of life, including hunting, fishing, and other traditional, cultural, historical, future activities.”
The accord “does not have an end date” and, if Greenland chooses to become independent, it will agree to remain in NATO and take on Denmark’s rights and obligations under the deal.
The deal will only “enter into force” once the “necessary parliamentary processes of the Kingdom of Denmark, in conjunction with Greenland, have been completed.”

Cooking likely to get cheaper as Centre cuts customs duty on edible oils
Duty on crude soybean and palm oils has been cut from 10% to 5%, while that on refined varieties has been reduced from 32.5% to 27.5%.
Cooking oil is likely to become cheaper after the Centre reduced the basic customs duty (BCD) on several edible oils.
The duty cuts will be effective from September 24, the finance ministry said in a notification, according to ANI.
The duty on crude soybean oil and crude palm oil has reportedly been cut from 10% to 5%, while the duty on refined soybean oil and refined palm oil has been reduced from 32.5% to 27.5% .

The government has also reportedly abolished the duty on crude sunflower oil, reducing it from 10% to nil. The duty on refined sunflower oil has been lowered from 32.5% to 22.5%.
The duty cuts are expected to reduce the import cost of edible oils, potentially easing prices for consumers, depending on how the reduction is passed through the supply chain.
Vegetable oil prices in India have risen by nearly 20% over the past year, and a measure to lower prices could boost consumption during the September-November festive season, when demand for sweets, snacks and fried foods typically increases, Reuters reported.
The increase in Indian demand could also support benchmark Malaysian palm oil and US soyoil futures, analysts said.

Landslides, major flooding and other damage in the Kanto region caused by Typhoon Dujuan earlier this week have left local residents struggling to deal with the aftermath — some for the second time in weeks after heavy rain caused flooding in August.
At least 10 people have died in Chiba and Kanagawa prefectures after the typhoon ravaged the area from late Sunday through Tuesday morning, many in landslides that engulfed houses. One man was found dead after he became trapped in an inundated car.
A levee at Lake Inba in northeastern Chiba Prefecture was breached in four places, causing houses and stores to be inundated. The water level at the lake reached a record 5.04 meters at one point on Tuesday morning, far higher than its maximum safe level of 4.25 m.
Some 17,000 houses were still without electricity as of noon Thursday.
About 560 houses have been flooded in the prefecture. In the city of Sakura, Kazuyoshi Sugo, who also experienced flooding due to heavy rain last month, found the ground floor of his home filled with muddy floodwater.
“It was just after I was cleaning things up” from last month, said Sugo, 59, as he swept away water and mud that had collected in the entrance area. “There’s no point in dwelling on it.”
At an izakaya (Japanese tavern), where floodwater had reached as high as waist level, three regular customers were helping to carry bottles of alcohol and food packages out of the building on Wednesday.
“It could have been better if we had used sandbags to stop the water beforehand,” said one of the customers.
At Tani Fish Farm in the city of Narita, about 100,000 koi carp either died in muddy water or swam out of the premises during the floods. This, along with damage to machinery, caused losses of about ¥1 billion ($6.3 million), Kansai Television reported Wednesday.
The facility is part of a recreational park that also houses a putter golf course, a fishing pond and a restaurant, all of which were inundated.
“We can’t do anything until the floodwater recedes,” Kenji Tani, CEO of the fish farm, told the broadcaster.
Typhoon Dujuan came closest to the Tokyo metropolitan area on Monday and caused heavy rain in the region during the Silver Week holidays.
Train services were suspended and many events were cancelled. Kamogawa Seaworld, an aquarium in Chiba, and Ueno Zoo in Tokyo were among the many facilities that closed Monday due to the typhoon.
According to a survey by private forecaster Weathernews, 60.8% of respondents in Kanto said they had to change their plans due to the storm.

Three Maoists surrender in Bankura with AK-47, INSAS rifles: West Bengal Police
Three CPI (Maoist) cadres surrendered in Bankura with AK-47 and INSAS rifles; police said around 80 cases are pending against them in West Bengal and Jharkhand.
Three members of the CPI (Maoist) surrendered before the West Bengal Police with AK-47 and INSAS rifles in Bankura district on Wednesday, police said.
“Three Maoist cadres who were active since 2006-2007 surrendered before the police in Bankura district. At least 80 cases were pending against them in various police stations in West Bengal and Jharkhand. All of them were carrying rewards announced by the Jharkhand government,” said a senior officer of the West Bengal Police.
The trio was identified as Jaba Mahato, Nayantara Sahu and Ramprasad Mandi. While Mahato and Sahu were members of the zonal committee, Mandi was a regional committee member.
The surrender comes days after the Special Task Force (STF) of the Kolkata Police arrested Asim Mandal, a top-level Maoist leader and the last central committee member of the banned CPI (Maoist).
Mandal had been absconding after Misir Besra, a politburo member of the outlawed group, was arrested. Besra was arrested from Dhanbad on July 28 during a joint operation by Cobra-9, the Intelligence Bureau and Jharkhand Police. Officials said that after Besra was held, the arrest of Mandal was only a matter of time.
“The three surrendered their arms which include AK-47 and INSAS rifles. This reveals how prominent and active they were in the outfit. The arms were looted from the police. The criminal proceedings against them will continue,” said an officer.

Hunting hidden gems - is there anywhere in the world left to scout?
- Published
The world's biggest clubs were all aware of the teenage sensation turning heads for Universidad de Chile, the one dubbed his generation's Alexis Sanchez.
"When we signed Dario Osorio, it was not because no-one knew about him," Kristian Kjaer, technical director at Midtjylland, tells BBC Sport.
Osorio was on the radar of AC Milan, RB Leipzig, Salzburg and a number of other English and German clubs before he left Santiago for Denmark at the age of 19.
It was a carefully considered pathway. After three seasons in Scandinavia, the winger joined Crystal Palace on loan this summer with a £24m option to buy which would make him the most expensive sale in Danish Superliga history.
Midtjylland, where Brentford owner Matthew Benham was a majority stakeholder between 2014 and 2023, are renowned as one of the most innovative clubs in Europe for their use of analytics - from set-pieces to smart recruitment.
"We work on both pathways," explains Kjaer. "We have subjective scouting, more classic video scouting, live scouting, a network, people we trust in the club and also our partners. And then we have the data scouting.
"And Dario Osorio, we were aware of him long before we signed him."
From feet-on-the-ground to the increasing availability of footage, data analytics and artificial intelligence, Premier League clubs - whether buying direct from source or tracking players like Osorio's progress - have a large proportion of the world's emerging talent covered.
"That hidden gem kind of thing almost does not exist any more in football," says Kjaer. "Sometimes it does, but it's rare."
'Find me a player like Ashley Cole...'
"You would put this period as one of the most transformational in talent ID and recruitment," explains Sam Turner, head of operations at scouting and development platform Eyeball.
Clubs can now obtain an incredible level of detail on players across the globe before they have even made a senior appearance. Eyeball, for example, was founded five years ago to focus on those predominantly aged 13 to 21.
It is used by more than 60% of clubs in Europe's top five leagues, and a majority of Premier League sides, for access to more than 400,000 young players across 42 global markets from Europe to Africa and Latin America.
Winger Malick Yalcouye, a new 20-year-old star at Brighton, was tracked on the system since developing at Ivorian side ASEC Mimosas, likewise Bazoumana Toure, who is now at Newcastle.
The breadth of coverage is highlighted by other recent moves - Josue Caicedo left Ecuador's LDU Quito for Barcelona, Mustapha Nyassi swapped Gambia's Real de Banjul for Copenhagen and Nour Ashraf joined Leipzig from Egypt's ENPPI.
"The availability of data and footage has prompted a change in methodology," says Turner. "That has brought a load of benefits in terms of data-led recruitment, time saving, cost saving."
Eyeball takes north of 2,000 data points every match, typically from leading amateur clubs and elite academies who film and upload their fixtures.
The result is a huge database allowing analysts to watch all of a player's progressive passes, for example, discover who covered the most distance or simply ask 'find me a player like Ashley Cole'.
"There is always this human feel that can never be lost," adds Turner. "I like to think we have aided scouts and recruitment teams, supplemented them with the tools, data, information to be able to make more informed decisions on a more consistent basis."
Data, says Midtjylland's Kjaer, is "extremely important because it gives you an objective tool you can lean towards" when complemented by years of decision-making experience.
"We cannot just turn on the computer and it tell us who to sign and then we go sign them," he says. "We also need to know about the cultural background, the family background, to make sure they fit into our football club.
"Of course, data has given us opportunities. We sign young. So the sample size will simply be smaller for us because if we are waiting until it's big enough, Brighton and Liverpool and Brentford and other guys, they will sign the player in front of us."
Where are the emerging markets?
"We can find interesting players all around the world," explains Kjaer.
"I like us to be open-minded. We are particular in the way we play and the way we sell. And therefore, we need to find these players who fit that style of play.
"When you have done your due diligence and you feel certain, pull the trigger. The pace in decision-making is also a hidden gem."
One country regularly mentioned is Uzbekistan, who played in their first World Cup this summer, while Turner says Azerbaijan is pioneering a national talent network and "very forward-thinking and motivated to progress the game domestically".
Then there is Japan, which Turner calls a "guiding star" in youth development for a system which takes players from grassroots, to school and college football and then the professional game. Think Kaoru Mitoma's thesis on dribbling techniques.
For European clubs, it makes identifying young Japanese prospects more complex.
Latin America, too, remains a hotbed of talent.
As former Midtjylland chairman Rasmus Ankersen, who has since worked for Brentford and Southampton, wrote in his book The Gold Mine Effect, a club such as Cruzeiro will reject 4,000 players under the age of 15 for every one they take in.
Brazilian clubs are naturally protective of their assets.
"They know eventually players will leave," says Turner. "But it is allowing them to leave at the right age where those clubs can benefit locally. And we are very invested in that."
Much of the region, however, remains "untapped" but recording games creates opportunities.
"It's just a visibility piece for a lot of these players that means they don't get picked up," says Turner.
"We have gone a long way in solving that for a lot of markets, but there are many more that can be picked up with brilliant players everywhere."
One of those markets continues to be Africa.
"There'll be thousands," says Thomas Randolph, founder of Delphlyx, when asked whether talented African players may have missed out on big moves in the past.
Delphlyx works with Premier League clubs and ownership groups, and others across Europe, the United States and Mexico, to provide information on the best - and most relevant - 14 to 21-year-olds in West Africa, often through data, live scouting and private tournaments.
"We have over 19,000 players in Africa on our platform that you could just sit right here in London and watch, then pick up the phone, call one of them and organise a trial or a transfer. That just wasn't happening before," adds Randolph.
With a projected average age of just over 18, Randolph says the region is a "young, growing, developing space" - a "sporting mecca". Football remains the main passion, though NFL and NBA are starting to invest in certain countries.
But Randolph disputes the idea African scouting is now saturated, citing a number of areas that remain relatively undiscovered, often because of conflict or logistics, with scouts drawn to the region's biggest cities.
"Zadok Yohanna is a good example," explains Randolph. "He moved to Brighton recently. He comes from Ikon Allah, which is a tiny and relatively unknown academy in northern Nigeria.
"The southern bit of Senegal is where Sadio Mane is from, where [Lamine] Camara is from, who Chelsea tried to sign, and there's only one team down there. So within all these big countries, there are certain regions that are less scouted."
Historically, it was agents who brought players out of Africa rather than scouts discovering them, whereas Delphlyx aims to help clubs identify and analyse certain talent first so scouts can visit specific tournaments or showcases to watch targets.
Randolph mentions eastern Mali, Togo, Guinea-Bissau and Burkina Faso but Benin, situated between Nigeria and Togo, is of particular interest for the way the country has invested federation grants in football infrastructure and pitches.
"One place they've used the Fifa money very well is Benin," says Randolph. "It's now produced probably a future female Ballon d'Or winner - Romaine Gandonou, who's 15, just played at the Under-20 World Cup, and got the likes of PSG, Barcelona, everyone after her.
"Benin is going to be a country that over the next few years will become very interesting."
Some Premier League clubs are buying directly from Africa. At 18, Senegalese defender Mor Talla Ndiaye has already been on the bench for Liverpool after arriving from Amitie, owned by ex-Newcastle and Chelsea striker Demba Ba.
Ndiaye was spotted at last year's Under-17 World Cup, where Burkina Faso midfielder Mohamed Zongo also impressed. He will join Chelsea and Strasbourg owners BlueCo's project when he turns 18 in two years' time.
"The Under-17 World Cup is a big one," says Randolph. "If your African nation plays there and you do well, you're going to get a good move."
Scouts have also been at the recent Under-17 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying and Delphlyx has helped organise trials for players from Senegal and Gambia at Premier League clubs.
The pool is narrowed, however, because players must obtain a Governing Body Endorsement to be granted a work permit or - most likely - take one of a club's four Elite Significant Contribution spots, which essentially comes down to how many youth or senior internationals they have played.
It's part of the reason young players initially move to European countries where regulations are less stringent and why Randolph believes Scottish clubs, where the same criteria does not apply, should be looking into the African market the way Scandinavians do.
Nordsjaelland are unique in that the Right to Dream academy - founded in Ghana in 1999 by former Manchester United scout Tom Vernon - bought the Danish club seven years ago to provide a pathway for its biggest prospects, which have included Mohammed Kudus, Simon Adingra and Kamaldeen Sulemana.
Brighton's Yalcouye and Newcastle's Toure made their first moves to Swedish clubs IFK Goteborg and Hammarby, while Midtjylland have a partner club in Nigeria, FC Ebedei. Coventry's Frank Onyeka played for both on his way to the Premier League, as did Paul Onuachu, now at Trabzonspor.
Like with Osorio, and others such as Guinea-Bissau forward Franculino, who left this summer for Trabzonspor, or Ivory Coast defender Ousmane Diomande, now at Nottingham Forest via Sporting, Midtjylland can highlight a track record of developing young players before selling them on.
"I see Midtjylland a bit like Silicon Valley for tech companies - we have produced so much talent over the years," explains Kjaer.
"We can focus only on the development. Of course, we need to win, but it's a bit more of a secure environment.
"What we say is, if you want to focus on your career as a football player, you have to come here because that is the only thing we do. That is what we are experts in."
Undiscovered talent on the doorstep?
There remains, however, undiscovered talent close to home. France, particularly Paris, boasts an incredibly rich talent pool.
A unique national youth league system, where amateur sides face professional academies - and regularly beat them - offers clubs the chance to witness unsigned prospects competing against the most gifted players in their age group.
"Scouts from all over the world come to Ile-de-France to look at players in our leagues," said Jamel Sandjak, president of the Ligue de Paris Ile-de-France, which boasts more than 1,000 clubs and 270,000 players.
"Most of the France national youth teams are full of our players. So our regional teams are playing at national level."
Last season, amateur side ES Nanterre, from the outskirts of Paris, won Championnat National Group B ahead of Champions League outfits Lens and Lille and second-tier clubs Reims, Bastia and Red Star.
Forward Exauce Luyindula was the division's top scorer for renowned amateurs AAS Sarcelles - where Riyad Mahrez played until he was 18 - and has since joined Ligue 2 Guingamp.
Other Eyeball partners enjoyed memorable victories, too. AFC Creil beat Lens at under-15 level, Olympique Rovenain's under-19s beat Nice and CS Bretigny's under-17s edged Paris St-Germain.
"Until recently, the vast majority of clubs were relying on the fact the best players are in the best academies or national talent systems, when actually a lot of those players were chosen by 12 or 13," explains Turner.
"A lot of the time that can be right, but also statistically the best players at 12 aren't always the best players at 18.
"There is such a high concentration of players in that region, there is not enough space. The best players aren't necessarily in the national systems."

More than 170,000 respiratory cases recorded in haze-choked Indonesia
- Published
Some 175,000 people in Indonesia have suffered from respiratory illness since August, its health ministry said, as it continues to battle wildfires that have raged for weeks.
More than 40,000 cases – which range from coughs to bronchitis and more serious conditions like pneumonia – involve toddlers.
Forest fires have blanketed parts of the country as well as neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore in toxic smog, pushing air quality indices into "unhealthy" territory.
Indonesia has deployed more than 54,000 officials and dozens of jets to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra for water bombing, but the vast territory and challenging peatland conditions make it hard to put out the fires, authorities say.
"From the air to the ground, all forces continue to move," Indonesia's Cabinet Secretary Teddy Indra Wijaya said on Monday.
"Everything is being done to extinguish the fires, reduce the impact of the smoke, and, most importantly, protect the public from the threat of forest and land fires."
Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during its annual dry season, which usually runs from July through October.
This year, however, the fires and haze have been turbocharged by a so-called "Godzilla" El Nino, which has fuelled extremely dry conditions.
The independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas has detected around 734,000 hotspots across the country as of Wednesday - a figure that is more than 30% higher than that of 2019, one of Indonesia's worst wildfire seasons.
Since January, at least 895,657 hectares of land – nearly six times the size of Greater London – have been burned.
The wildfires have led to school closures and a surge in hospital admissions across Indonesia.
The number of people suffering wildfire-related respiratory illnesses had more than doubled to 113,336 by 9 September, up from 50,891 on 1 September, according to figures from the health ministry.
The toxic smog has also taken a toll on wildlife, including critically endangered orangutans.
Late last month, an Indonesia-based wildlife foundation shared footage showing an orangutan writhing on the ground on a palm oil plantation in West Kalimantan, one of Indonesia's hardest-hit provinces. The great ape, which was discovered by a farmer, was rescued and given emergency treatment for hypoxia, but later died.
Indigenous and civil society groups in West Kalimantan filed a class action suit last week against the central government and local administrations, accusing them of deliberate negligence for failing to properly tackle the wildfires scorching the province.
"This is a disaster that occurs every year. This recurring pattern proves our view that the defendants knew about the potential haze disaster and the risks of disaster from forest and land fires," the group's lawyer Glorio Sanen said in a statement at the time.
Indonesia has carried out several rounds of cloud-seeding operations in recent weeks, some conducted together with members of Japan's Self-Defense Forces who arrived in Borneo earlier this month to help with firefighting efforts.
Cloud seeding involves manipulating existing clouds, such as by dropping salt crystals or silver iodide into them, to help produce more rain. Meteorologists, however, are divided over the effectiveness of the practice.
In the Malaysian state of Sarawak, one of the worst-affected areas outside Indonesia, authorities launched a five-day cloud-seeding operation earlier this month.
Apart from tackling the ongoing haze, this exercise was aimed at boosting declining water levels at several hydropower dams ahead of a severe dry spell forecast for October.
"October might be hotter and drier," Sarawak's Deputy Premier Douglas Uggah Embas told reporters. "We want to increase the water levels as much as possible while we still can."
The haze has reached as far as parts of the Philippines, where local officials have urged residents to stay indoors as much as possible, and Singapore, where authorities have begun issuing daily haze advisories.
