UK survivor of Canadian poison seller says he exploited her despair
- Published
A British woman, one of the survivors of Canadian poison seller Kenneth Law, faced him in court on Wednesday to describe how he had exploited her vulnerability.
Elisabeth Belien told the four-day sentencing hearing of Law in Ontario, Canada she had been at her lowest ebb when he sold her toxic chemicals when she was just 23.
Belien, who until Wednesday had not been known as one of his customers, said she had physically recovered after being successfully given an antidote by medics.
But as she faced him as he sat in the glass-panelled dock, she revealed she had suffered "survivor's guilt" after learning from police others had died.
Law has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada after meeting people in suicide forums online. But there are almost 80 deaths in the UK that have also been linked to him.
As part of a plea deal with Canadian authorities, Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths.
But impact statements from their families are being read during the sentencing hearing this week.
Belien told the court: "I had struggled with my mental health for a long time before this. Kenneth Law made it a lot easier to act on that despair.
"I continue to struggle with intrusive thoughts and flashbacks of that day.
"I made a full recovery. However, emotionally and psychologically, the effects are far more long lasting.
"I feel guilty for surviving. Although I survived It has also impacted my loved ones. I feel like my vulnerability was exploited. I still feel a lot of shame about what happened.
"I felt like the purchasing from Kenneth Law, I enabled him to continue his business, supplying his products, to other people who might have been vulnerable, like I was. I felt guilty for surviving."
Belien, who said she took the poison in January 2023, said being in court reminded her "how easily" it could have been her own parents there talking about her.
"I'm learning that things can get better," she said.
"I'm learning to be excited to see what the future holds for me. But the gratitude I'm feeling for being alive today doesn't take away from the trauma of the experience."
Authorities say Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients he met in online suicide forums in 40 countries. Roughly a quarter of the packages were sent to the UK.
He was arrested in May 2023, following a complex investigation by at least 11 law-enforcement agencies that involved investigators from around a dozen countries, including the UK, Italy and the US.
David Parfett, whose son Tom died in October 2021, said in a victim impact statement: "Since Tom died, I've struggled with my mental health.
"Initially, in the months after he died, I didn't properly mourn him, because my focus was on understanding, and then exposing the harm caused by the internet platforms that allowed Law to trade suicide to kids.
"I'm still, after five years, unable to fully process Tom's death. I'm a very different person to who I was before Tom took his own life, having previously been gregarious, outgoing. I find it difficult to enjoy life."
A statement was also read from the parents of Henry Tucker, a 14-year-old British boy who died in October 2021.
Kate and Henry Tucker said Henry had been diagnosed with autism but actually had a neurological condition that could have been treated with antibiotics.
"The realisation that his suffering and his death could have been prevented is a weight that is impossible to bear," they said.
"The death of a children under these circumstance is a heavy burden to carry for the rest of our lives.
"We will carry it however with Henry's blessings until we meet again. We love you Henry."
Norson Harris, the father of British victim Ashleigh Harris, read a statement in person on the agony of losing his daughter.
He said: "The circumstances of Ashleigh's death have been incredibly tough to bear.
"We all feel we should have been able to prevent Ashleigh's death.
"Rather than offer the help needed that individual Kenneth Law sold her a chemical that Ashleigh took to end her life.
"I still hope over time Mr Law will recognise the answer to Ashleigh and the myriad of others who reached out to him should have been that they were loved and there was help available to them."
Earlier Stephen Mitchell Sr, the father of Canadian Stephen Mitchell Jr, told of the aftermath of his death on March 25 2023.
"He was ill, he needed help, and I tried my best to bring him that help," he said.
"Mr Law robbed my son of that chance to be well."
Mr Mitchel Sr, addressing Law in court, said: "I'm willing to accept that during Mr Law's time in incarceration, he might have had brief moments of regret, or even despair and helplessness.
"Perhaps he may have even thought during those moments: my life is meaningless, what is the point of living.
"That was the same thoughts that my son Stephen had before he took the chemicals that Mr Law sold him.
"When my son was well, he would have gladly helped Mr Law work out his depressive thoughts, if asked, because he believed in the value of people."
Sandra Scott, whose daughter, Amara Scott, died on February 9 2022 aged 25, said she and her family were trying to help her through a mental health crisis.
"Our efforts were cut short when, in her most vulnerable state, she made contact with the accused, she said.
"The day I and her friends found Amara, and the way that she died – it broke my heart.
"It was a blessing and an honour to be Amara's mother."
The hearing continues.

Microsoft's new Surface Pro 12 and Surface Laptop 13 feature Snapdragon X2 Plus chips
There's also a new haptic Surface Mouse on the way.
Microsoft's hardware business seems to be in disarray on all fronts, especially Xbox, but it's still trucking along with refreshed versions of its smaller Surface Pro 12 and Surface Laptop 13. The big change is the new Snapdragon X2 Plus chip, which aims to be a solid update from the slower Qualcomm chips powering those devices last year. As Microsoft's smallest PCs, the key for both the Surface Pro 12 and Laptop 13 is portability over raw power. These were also ostensibly low-cost devices last year, with launch prices below $1,000, but as with everything else, the RAMaggedon has bumped the Surface Pro 12-inch up to $1,150 and the Surface Laptop 13 to $1,199.
Design-wise, nothing has changed with either device. The Surface Pro 12-inch is still a small 12-inch tablet with a kickstand, and it can transform into a pseudo-laptop with the $150 Surface Pro keyboard (sold separately, as always, because Microsoft seems to hate smart consumer choices). The Surface Laptop 13, meanwhile, is the company's basic notebook design shrunk down to a 13-inch screen and 2.7-pound frame. Both systems also feature new 500-nit displays, which are 25 percent brighter than before.
I thought the 12-inch tablet was absolutely adorable when I reviewed it last year, and I'm hoping the new internals alleviate my performance concerns. Microsoft claims the Snapdragon X2 Plus chips deliver 60 percent better graphics than the last generation, as well as 95 percent faster on-device AI and 18 percent better battery efficiency. As for basic Office productivity work, the company says the new chip is 18 percent faster. The upgrades sound compelling for anyone who was interested in these smaller Surface devices, but couldn't stomach the major speed downgrade of the previous Snapdragon X chips. If you picked up one of these systems last year, though, it's probably worth waiting a bit longer to upgrade. And if you need more power, the larger 13-inch Surface Pro and Surface Laptop 13.8-inch are also available with newer Snapdragon X2 chips (and much higher pricing of their own).
The Surface Pro 12-inch is also launching together with Microsoft Ink Canvas, an "AI-powered, pen-first experience for sketching, annotating, generating images and summarizing text directly on the canvas," as the company describes. That doesn't sound particularly unique, but at least it's something to do with the Surface Slim Pen. The app will also be available on the Microsoft Store on October 13th for other Surface devices.
Alongside the PC hardware, Microsoft is launching a new $80 Surface Mouse, an ambidextrous mouse with haptic functionality. The company says you'll be able to feel certain Windows 11 interactions, like snapping a window or aligning objects. That's similar to what we've seen with the Logitech MX Master 4. It's an evolution of the previous Surface Mouse, which was notable for evoking Microsoft's classic Intellimouse design.
All of Microsoft's new Surface hardware will be available on October 13.

President Droupadi Murmu on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) urged popular film artists not to endorse products harmful to people's health, saying a “true star” spreads light, not darkness, highlighting the impact of words and actions of celebrities on young minds.
Ms. Murmu distributed the 72nd National Film Awards for 2024 in various categories of cinema at Ekta Nagar (Kevadia), near the Statue of Unity, in a glittering ceremony attended by top talents of the film industry.
"When successful artists speak about the benefits of a disciplined lifestyle, millions of children and young people emulate them. I urge popular artists not to endorse products that are harmful to people's health. A true star is the one who spreads light, not darkness," Ms. Murmu said.
The President also called for greater participation of women on juries selecting films for the National Film Awards.
"I would like to see women's participation ensured in every regional jury," she said, noting that many women had received awards at the ceremony.
She said women should also be represented on the juries, noting that "incorporating the female perspective in any field makes it possible to form a holistic human outlook".
She appealed to the film industry to ensure respect and social security for workers, small-scale artists, assistants and others who contribute to the creative economy while struggling to make their mark.
"Please ensure that the workers, small-scale artists, assistants, and those struggling to make their mark, who contribute to this economy, receive both respect and social security," President Murmu added.
Ms. Murmu recalled that at the previous National Film Awards ceremony, she had urged the industry to make respect and sensitivity towards every member of the film crew an integral part of its work culture.
"I hope you are paying heed to these requests," she said.
Describing film artists as key representatives of the creative economy, the President said highly popular artists possessed immense potential to influence citizens, especially the youth.
She also praised the quality of films being produced in the country, saying it strengthened her conviction that Indian films would set world-class benchmarks for quality.
"Learning about the quality films being produced in the country strengthens my conviction that our films will set world-class benchmarks for quality. I wish you all and the film industry a golden future," Ms. Murmu said.
Veteran Kannada actor Anant Nag received the prestigious Dadasaheb Phalke award, the highest honour in cinema. Yami Gautam, Mammootty and Kartik Aaryan were conferred with awards for best actors in male and female categories.
Hindi feature film 'Article 370', directed by Aditya Suhas Jambhale, received the Best Feature Film award.

Government hospitals across Tamil Nadu are facing a shortage of surfactant medicines, a critical and life-saving medicine for pre-term babies.
The shortage has been persisting for the past few months, and several Special Newborn Care Units (SNCUs) at government hospitals have been flagging it up for the Health Department.
Doctors said surfactant medicines are essential to inflate the lungs of pre-term babies in need of the therapy. They utilised external bovine or porcine surfactants (intratracheal) in pre-term babies. These surfactants were part of the speciality drug rate contract purchases of the Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation (TNMSC).
Inquiries with a number of hospitals and doctors revealed that a number of centres were facing short supply of surfactants in the past few months. Official sources confirmed that government hospitals, among them medical college hospitals in Theni, Dharmapuri, Tiruppur, Cuddalore, Tiruvannamalai, Vellore and Karur districts and in Chennai, reported surfactant vial shortage, while some hospitals said they had uninterrupted supply.
A doctor, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the shortage prevailed in the past three to four months owing to a number of factors. “First, we got no allotment. Secondly, some centres miscalculated their requirement, which is based on the average number of pre-term babies delivered, and thirdly, there was higher utilisation. This is a life-saving medicine essential to inflate the lungs of pre-term babies who are otherwise solid,” he said.
A doctor at another hospital said continuous supply was not assured, and shortage occurred frequently. “Currently, we are borrowing from other sub-centres which are referring babies to us. It is very difficult for us to manage newborn units without surfactants. Sometimes, we purchase them privately using SNCU funds to save the babies,” another doctor said.
A senior paediatrician said that after 34 weeks of gestation, the foetal lungs are generally mature enough to support exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide after birth. “However, in very pre-term babies, the alveoli, which are the tiny air sacs in the lungs, may not be sufficiently mature to function effectively on their own. Surfactant, a substance produced in the lungs, helps keep the alveoli open. But in babies born very prematurely, not enough surfactant may be produced, making it difficult for them to maintain adequate oxygen levels. Depending on the baby’s condition, doctors may use respiratory support such as CPAP or a mechanical ventilator. Surfactant is delivered directly into the lungs through the endotracheal tube to prevent hyaline membrane disease.”
Lung maturity in a newborn is critical as decreased oxygen could cause hypoxia and conditions such as retinopathy of prematurity and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, he said.
A Health Department source denied that there was any shortage. “There was no procurement delay. Some centres may have miscalculated their requirement, resulting in shortage, or may have utilised more vials. In such circumstances, they have obtained the required supply from neighbouring facilities. A six-month purchase order, worth nearly ₹9 crore, has been issued. Additionally, operational costs are provided for paediatricians to make local purchases whenever required,” he said.
Another official said the TNMSC has issued purchase orders and it will be supplied within two days. Officials said Cuddalore faced shortage and arrangements were made to send supplies from Coimbatore. The situation was being closely monitored, they said.

Pune: On Wednesday evening, music lovers experienced a deeply devotional concert featuring unique devotional and laudatory compositions highlighting the power and greatness of Devadhidev Mahadev (Lord Shiva). The blend of vocal music with traditional Indian instruments doubled the charm of the performance.
Organised as part of the Pune Festival, the program 'Namami Shambho' was presented on Wednesday at the Yashwantrao Chavan Natyagruha. Paramount Spiritual Guru P. P. Dighe Mavashi and Mr. Sanjeev Dighe graced the occasion with their presence.
Devotional compositions celebrate Shiva
Beginning with the invocatory Nandi (tribute) "Panchatunda Nararundamaladhara Parvatisha Adhi Namito", the musical worship kept the audience spellbound right up to the concluding Bilvashtakam. The program was structured specifically to depict the glory, nobility, and majesty of Lord Shiva. The hallmark of Namami Shambho was its rich variety of devotional compositions—spanning Sanskrit songs, verses (shlokas), rhythm patterns (parans), hymns (stotram), theatrical songs (natyapada), invocations (nandi), and film songs. The rhythmic arrangement was rendered equally rich through instruments such as the conch (shankha), pakhawaj, tabla, flute, and damru.
The inspiration behind the program was P. P. Dighe Mavashi, while the concept was developed by Sanjeev Dighe. Vocalists Shekhar Kendale, Chandarani Kendale, Ashwini Ausekar, Manish Tupe, and Sumit Jadhav rendered the devotional praises with deep dedication. They were accompanied by musicians Pratik Gujar (pakhawaj), Anil Bhujbal (tabla), Hritik Gujar (percussions), Shailesh Deshpande (flute), and Prakash Sutar (keyboard), whose harmonious support elevated the performances. Harshal Bhandare hosted the event.
Soul-stirring performances enthral audience
The atmosphere became immersed in divine devotion through powerful renditions of compositions including the Shiv-stuti Nandi, Karpura Gauram, Shadja Shiva Hai (Shivmahimna Stotram), Aadidev Mahadev, Shiva Raksha Stotra, Lingashtakam, Shiva Kailaso Ke Vasi, Shiva Swarnamala, Sadashivashtakam, Shambho Shankara, Parvati Vallabhashtakam, Mano Bhootnatham Namo Devdevam, Rudrashtakam, Shankarabharanam, Namami Shambho, the song Satyam Shivam Sundaram, the theatrical song Soham Hara Damaru Baje, a prayer by P. P. Mavashi, Shiva Tandava Stotram, and Bilvashtakam.
The strong backing of traditional Indian instruments alongside the recitation of parans and stotrams made the performance exceptionally soul-stirring. The Shiva and Ganesh Parans received immense applause due to the powerful pakhawaj accompaniment. Featuring distinct compositions beyond the usual repertoire created a fine blend of freshness, uniqueness, and variety.
Artists felicitated at event
At the beginning of the program, Krishnakumar Goyal (President, Pune Festival), Dr. Satish Desai (Chief Coordinator of Cultural Programs), and Mohan Tillu (Trustee) felicitated the singers, artists, instrumentalists, host, and organisers. Organising committee members Atul Gonjari, Shrikant Kamble, Sachin Adekar, Namdev, and others were also present on the occasion.

A video showing a group of people removing and breaking metal barricades near a water body is being widely shared with a claim that it shows people in Karnataka vandalising barricades after authorities restricted Ganesh idol immersion (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: A video shows devotees in Karnataka vandalising barricades after authorities restricted Ganesh idol immersion.
Fact: The video is from Hyderabad. It shows members of the Bhagyanagar Ganesh Utsav Samithi removing barricades at Tank Bund while protesting restrictions on Ganesh idol immersion. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to an Instagram post by South Matters featuring the same visuals. According to the post, the visuals show tension at Tank Bund in Hyderabad, where representatives of the Bhagyanagar Ganesh Utsav Samithi staged a protest against restrictions on Ganesh idol immersion. We also found a post by the BNN channel on X stating the same.
Based on this, we conducted a relevant keyword search and found multiple media reports about the incident (here, here, here). According to these reports, the barricades were installed to prevent devotees from immersing Ganesh idols along the Tank Bund stretch. Members of the Bhagyanagar Ganesh Utsav Samithi (BGUS) protested against the restrictions and demanded that devotees be allowed to continue idol immersion at Tank Bund.
The comparison between the viral visuals and the visuals reported by the media can be seen below.
To sum up, this viral video of devotees removing barricades is from Hyderabad, not Karnataka.

ICC convicts former Central African Republic militia commander of torture
Judges at the International Criminal Court have convicted former Seleka rebel commander Mahamat Said Abdel Kani of persecution and torture as crimes against humanity committed while he ran a prison in Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- Judges at the International Criminal Court on Wednesday convicted rebel commander Mahamat Said Abdel Kani of persecution and torture as crimes against humanity committed while he ran a prison in the Central African Republic.
Said, 56, wore jeans and a blue sweater and remained expressionless for most of the hourlong hearing as presiding Judge Miatta Maria Samba described the conditions prisoners endured at the facility in the capital, Bangui.
During the trial, witnesses described cramped cells with walls marked by “bullet holes and blood” and said they were whipped “until they soiled themselves,” Samba said. Other victims testified that they were confined in a windowless room under the floorboards of Said’s office.
The charges stemmed from fighting more than a decade ago between the predominantly Muslim Seleka rebels, who had seized power from then-President Francois Bozize, and a mainly Christian militia called the anti-Balaka.
Said pleaded not guilty to all charges when the proceedings began in 2021. His sentence, which could be as long as life in prison, will be decided at a later date.

It's sleek, Swedish, relatively affordable, and designed for efficiency. Oh, and the color scheme? Yellow and blue.
No, it's not Ikea. It's Neko Health — the three-year-old healthcare brainchild of Spotify cofounder Daniel Ek — a new annual go-to longevity checkup for skin cancer, heart health, and more.
Up and running in Stockholm since 2023 and London since 2024, the clinic is opening its doors in the US this week, with a first location in New York City's SoHo.
Already, 25,000 people have joined a waitlist in New York, and Neko plans to open more US locations soon, with their second set for Miami this fall.
Business Insider got a complimentary sneak preview of the Neko scan ahead of the launch on Thursday.
It's slick and high-tech, includes at least 20-30 minutes of quality time with a doctor, and comes with a transparent $499 out-of-pocket price tag.
Was it cool? Yes. Was it quick? Sure. Do I have notes? A few.
What Neko delivers is not that different from what's covered at a free, preventive annual doctor's exam. It's the engaging, tech-forward experience that makes Neko a product over 100,000 Europeans have already decided is worth the extra expense.
A fancy, tech-forward way to check on your heart, skin, and body shape
When I stepped into Neko's New York clinic, I felt like I was entering some kind of high-end boutique for your body — complete with a soft yellow robe, satin hair tie, and foamy blue slippers.
The check-up started with Neko's flagship body scan, which collects thousands of pictures of your naked body to survey for skin cancer and provides some information on your body fat distribution.
After you're back in your robe and lying down on a very comfy exam table, a technician takes blood pressure readings, cuffing not just one arm, but all four of your limbs, to assess how well blood is flowing through your arteries.
Then there's some rapid bloodwork for cholesterol, blood sugar, and more, a grip strength test, EKG measurements for heart health, and an eye pressure exam.
Most of these are diagnostics you could have had done at a decent primary care office, and they would not have cost anything close to $499. (Under the Affordable Care Act, annual preventive checkups are free, as long as you stay in-network.)
The key difference is that Neko promises your results will be delivered in under an hour and presented to you in an unrushed, data-heavy, easy-to-digest conversation with a doctor after you've been examined.
No need for prior authorization to order labs, or doctors' offices chasing down patients to discuss concerning results. It's one-stop shopping for health.
That consumer-focused approach is critical, said Zen Chu, the faculty director of MIT's healthcare ventures course, who is not affiliated with Neko Health. It can make patients more receptive to a doctor's advice and more engaged with their own health.
"That's what we've been teaching for 15 years," Chu said. "We need to redesign these experiences in healthcare, and those are enormous, multibillion-dollar opportunities, even when you're not changing the underlying technologies."
The visit summary includes charts forecasting your future health, and (what I considered) horrifying, aggressively accurate mockups of your current body shape, showing every curve and ripple on your frame. It's all meant to compel people into lifestyle changes that can prevent some of the most common chronic health issues later in life, including heart disease and diabetes.
As someone with a family history of melanoma, the skin scan may have been the most valuable part of my Neko visit. Skin scanning for cancer is important, and it can be hard to keep track of how your own moles are evolving over time.
About a week and a half after my scan, a representative from Neko called to say that one of the moles on my torso warranted further investigation by a dermatologist. Fewer than 1 in 10 Neko customers are referred out to an external provider for some follow-up, and apparently, I'm one of those few.
If it turns out that Neko can more easily connect me with a dermatology appointment and cut the typical monthslong wait for a time slot, that's arguably worth it for me, though it's a pricey way to get skin cancer screening, which typically ranges from free to under $100 with insurance.
The Neko scan is way more fun than going to the doctor
Neko gets a few simple things right that "normal" primary care could learn from. First and foremost: the clear focus on a beautifully designed product that can propel people into meaningful action.
According to Neko's recent "year three" report, based on results from 80,000 people, members who scan themselves annually at Neko tend to make meaningful improvements to their heart health, lowering blood pressure, improving cholesterol, and stabilizing blood sugar.
The check isn't meant to replace traditional hospital care — only 1% of Neko customers identify something life-threatening like a serious heart issue or late-stage skin cancer hiding out in their body.
My Neko provider's biggest concern was my "elevated blood pressure" — I don't normally have high blood pressure, so he said it was probably just "white coat syndrome," or doctor's-office nerves, and that I should redo my reading later.
My verdict: I could find better ways to spend $500 on my health
If I had $500 extra to spend on my health, I'd probably skip Neko and get a gym membership first, then consider a DEXA scan (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) to track my body composition in finer detail.
If I was worried about cancer, I'd go for a full-body MRI to get a better picture of what's going on inside me.
"Cash pay care is one of the biggest trends coming in American healthcare over the next decade, and Neko is one of many examples of that," Chu said.
Neko's scan is a lot of fun, but for anyone who's already somewhat aware of their health and wellness, it remains a little too basic.

Throughout 2026, people shared a rumor alleging Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix responded to U.S. President Donald Trump calling a reporter a pig. According to social media users' posts, the NFL quarterback publicly rebuked Trump, saying that "staying silent makes me part of the problem."
For example, on Sept. 20, a Facebook post (archived) read, "BREAKING NFL NEWS: Broncos star Bo Nix breaks his silence in shocking video response after 'Little Pig' comment to a female reporter shocks T.r.u.m.p — NFL superstar condemns disrespect towards women and sparks nationwide outrage."
The post featured a meme showing side-by-side images of Nix and Trump, with a purported Nix quote reading as follows:
When I watched that clip, something in me snapped. I play this game with fire and pride, but I was raised to respect every woman who cheers, works, and sacrifices behind the scenes. If a man with that much power can mock and demean them in front of the world, then staying silent makes me part of the problem. And I refuse to be part of that.
Other examples of the claim appeared on Facebook, Instagram and Threads. Snopes readers also searched this website in September 2026, specifically asking, "Did Bo Nix stand up for a female reporter?"
We first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo to locate possible evidence from credible sources about Nix publicly commenting on Trump. If the story was true, journalists with reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or Reuters — or sports blogs — would have widely reported on it. That was not the case.
The rumor about Bo Nix responding to Trump was fictional, and as a result we've rated the claim false.
The claim appeared to take inspiration from a real remark Trump made in November 2025 while aboard Air Force One, when he told a female reporter asking a question, "Quiet. Quiet, piggy." 
People.com, citing a journalist's X post, reported the female journalist Trump addressed as "piggy" was Bloomberg reporter Catherine Lucey. The subject matter of Lucey's question pertained to asking Trump about his past relationship with deceased convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
We emailed the Denver Broncos to ask if the organization would like to address the fake Nix quote and will update this article if we receive further details.
Digging into the rumor
In addition to social media posts, the untrue rumor about Nix publicly rebuking Trump appeared on a handful of generic-looking WordPress blogs. Those blogs lacked author names and credible information about their founding. An examination of the blogs found they were not reputable outlets, for example such as well-known newspapers or established news websites, or websites for local or national TV channels.
A scan of the text in one blog article with the artificial intelligence detection tool Pangram displayed the results, "We believe that this entire text is AI," as well as, "100% of this text is AI."
Snopes doesn't depend solely on AI detection tools, which vary in reliability, and instead considers the tools' results as one of several data points toward judging an image's authenticity. For Pangram, we bear in mind the platform's strong performance in third-party and internal evaluations, as well as criticisms of the tool.
Creators of content like the fabricated Nix quote capitalize on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up stories, profiting from advertising revenue on external websites to which the posts link. (Snopes has previously reported on the business strategy.)
The fictional story about Nix standing up for women resembled glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental."
For further reading, we previously reported about whether Broncos head coach Sean Payton fired two players for refusing to stand for the U.S. national anthem.

Barcelona exploring two new sources of financing to complete Camp Nou renovation
MADRID, Sept 24 : Spanish champions Barcelona are exploring two new sources of funding to cover the mounting costs of renovating their Camp Nou stadium, which will come in the form debt placements.
Last Saturday during a general assembly club members approved €510 million ($580,02 million) in additional financing to complete work on Camp Nou and cover revenue shortfalls.
The Catalan club will divide that financing into two distinct elements.
A source told Reuters on Thursday the first €300 million will take the form of project finance debt, structured through the securitisation fund that is financing the stadium.
It will be repaid from future Camp Nou revenues, in particular the new VIP hospitality areas being added, and has a maturity of 30 years.
This money can only be allocated to complete the works and is secured against stadium revenue rather than the club's assets. The source added that talks with potential investors had already taken place and were handled by Goldman Sachs.
Goldman Sachs declined to comment and Barcelona have yet to respond to a request for comment.
Separately, the club has arranged up to €210 million in senior debt secured against future television rights from LaLiga and UEFA competitions. This will be issued as media notes and has a maturity of 10 years.
This financing is specifically aimed at covering a cash-flow gap caused by delays to the stadium project, which have impacted Barcelona's projected revenues.
It will be split into two €105 million issues, one of which was placed in July and the other expected before the end of 2026.
Barcelona began work on Camp Nou in 2023, which was due to be completed in 2026. The renovated stadium will extend the roof, which previously covered only the main stand, around the whole stadium and increase the capacity to 105,000.
During Barca's general assembly, vice-president Ferran Olive said work on the stadium would not be completed until the 2028-29 season.
During the first half of the 2027-28 campaign, Barcelona will play at the Olympic Stadium in Montjuic while construction of the roof is completed. Olive said they were budgeting for a return to Camp Nou in January 2028, though it could be earlier.
Olive and Barcelona President Joan Laporta blamed the conflict in Ukraine and global economic trends for rising costs and supply chain issues that contributed towards the delays.

- Snopes found that the interview was originally conducted by Brooke Shirley (the mother of the conservative social media personality Nick Shirley, who is herself a conservative social media personality) in August 2024, while the Democratic National Convention was happening in Chicago.
- The woman interviewed in the video made several claims that closely resembled major Republican talking points at the time. Some of those claims referenced policies that have become outdated, while others were misleading or exaggerated. As a result, we have not rated the claim.
- We contacted Smith for comment on the fact that his posts sharing the video never mentioned that the interview took place in 2024, and will update this story if we learn more. We also reached out to the Illinois Housing Development Authority to confirm that a program that provided up to 6 months or $15,000 in renter's assistance for asylum seekers was no longer active; it said that program stopped processing applications in June 2024.
In September 2026, a video posted by the conservative pundit Rob Smith appeared online claiming that Democrats were giving $20,000 in benefits to "illegals" in Chicago.
Snopes readers asked us to verify or disprove the claims made in the video, the latest in a long stretch of Republican-promoted rumors suggesting Democrats give large amounts of money or other benefits to immigrants living in the country without authorization. (Snopes fact-checked a version of that claim from the White House here).
Oftentimes, as is the case here, such claims are accompanied by the idea that these payments are the first step in a Democratic-led plot to permanently control the federal government.
The video presents its narrative without providing any additional evidence to support any of its claims, which are as follows:
Immigrants living in the country illegally receive $15,000 in food stamps from the government; - These immigrants receive $5,000 in cash from the government;
- These immigrants receive free, government subsidized Wi-Fi;
- The government covers these immigrants' rent for two years;
- Democrats give immigrants living in the country illegally these benefits as a sort of "bribe," with the later goal of granting them the right to vote. The immigrants would then repay the favor by voting for Democrats in large numbers, effectively diluting the voting power of non-immigrant Americans and giving the party long-term control.
We have refrained from rating this article because of the complexity of the claims in the video. Our research indicated that the first two claims were unfounded at best, while the third and fourth are exaggerated, though the fourth might have been the source behind the $15,000 figure. (The fifth claim is also unfounded, since it depends on the other four being true.)
We also noted that much of the rhetoric resembled common claims made during the last two years of President Joe Biden's administration, when Texas Gov. Greg Abbott made a show of busing migrants entering the U.S. to cities like Chicago. Much of the reporting around these issues also came from that time, leading us to suspect that the interview took place in the lead-up to the 2024 election, rather than in 2026.
We were able to confirm the theory using a reverse image search. The original video first appeared on the Instagram (archived) and TikTok accounts of conservative social media personality Brooke Shirley in late August 2024. Shirley, the mother of conservative social media personality Nick Shirley, originally posted the video in the days following the 2024 Democratic National Convention, which was held in Chicago. She has reposted the video at least twice since then.
As part of reporting this story, we contacted the Illinois Housing Development Authority, which ran a program that paid some rent costs for immigrants legally seeking asylum, though not to the extent suggested in the video
We also contacted Smith seeking clarification on the time discrepancy, since his September 2026 video never mentioned that the interview originally took place two years prior. We also asked whether Smith believed the policies described in the interview were active in 2026, but had not heard back.
Wealso attempted to confirm that the interview featured in the video, conducted with a woman who said she lived on Chicago's south side, was real — if it was instead generated using AI tools, for instance, the person who generated it 
Immigrants did not get $15,000 in food stamps
Immigrants who are in the country without authorization have never been eligible for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, and the video's assertion otherwise is not based on concrete evidence.
SNAP eligibility is extended to some non-citizens, but there are strict requirements, which were made even more strict after the passage of the Trump administration's much-touted "One Big Beautiful Bill" budget act in July 2025.
The principal requirement is that an immigrant must have a permanent residency card and have lived in the U.S. for at least five years, or be under the age of 18. Prior to July 2025, however, there were exceptions for refugees and individuals granted asylum. Even before these exceptions were eliminated, however, the claim would still have been untrue. SNAP benefits are calculated using the number of individuals in a household (in 2024, for instance, a family of four could receive a maximum of $973 each month, or just over $11,500 per year, with money subtracted based on an individual's household income. Immigration status does not factor into the calculation at all.
Immigrants are not getting $5,000 in cash
This claim also spread significantly around the time the video was originally shared.. It, too, is not based on any evidence. Snopes disproved a claim that immigrants got roughly $3,800 in 2017, and many prominent fact-checking organizations have disproved the claim that immigrants are getting $5,000 in cash or gift cards.
Furthermore, although exposing and cutting alleged wasteful government spending has been a major policy platform of the second Trump administration, there was no evidence the administration has identified or targeted programs matching the claims in the video.
Chicago has a free WiFi program ... for families of students

However, we found that the city does offer a free home internet program that immigrants can access. The program is eligible for families of students enrolled in Chicago Public Schools who receive free or reduced meals, and there are no eligibility requirements based on immigration status.
According to a city fact-sheet about the program, the internet access is valued at $10 per month — a drop in the bucket compared to the alleged $20,000 in benefits each immigrant allegedly receives.
Chicago did pay some immigrants' rent ... for up to 6 months, or $15,000
Snopes found that in the fall of 2022, months after Greg Abbott's busing program began, the state of Illinois did implement a program through the Illinois Housing Development Authority to cover the housing costs for the influx of migrants seeking asylum entering Chicago. (It should be noted that migrants are legally entitled to claim asylum, and therefore the description of these individuals as "illegal immigrants" is suspect at best).  
However, contrary to the claim, this program did not cover rent for two years. Several outlets have separately investigated a similar claim about the government of Michigan, too.
Instead, it covered a security deposit and rent for three months, with an optional extension for another three months, making six months in total. Applicants could receive a maximum of $15,000, which we suspect may have been the source of the food stamps figure.
According to an IHDA document detailing the program's accomplishments, it gave $3.7 million in grants to 681 families by the beginning of 2023, and another $1.4 million went toward additional three-month extensions. The authority claimed households received an average of $6,369, which is significant, but still below the fictitious $15,000 in food stamps described previously.
The program provided $53 million in rental assistance to 6,623 asylum seekers and families over the course of its lifespan, meaning that each successfully applicant received an average of just over $8,000.
One last note on this program: the IDHA's program paid landlords directly wherever possible — the money for rental assistance offered through the program was not given to immigrants.

In sum, the claims were a combination of 
It is true that immigrants were eligible for some welfare programs in Chicago during the later years of Joe Biden's presidency. However, the emergency housing program ended in 2024, while the additional restrictions on SNAP implemented by the Trump administration specifically bars refugees and asylum seekers — the individuals generally being incorrectly described as "illegal immigrants."

Cristiano Ronaldo walked into a packed room, claimed to be nervous, then did what he has done for more than two decades: taking centre stage, swatting away critics and insisting the final whistle is not yet in sight.
The 41-year-old Portugal captain, speaking on Wednesday at the Portugal Football Summit main stage before Thursday’s UEFA Nations League match against Wales, said he still had plenty to offer his country as Jorge Jesus prepares for his first game as national team coach.
Jesus replaced Roberto Martinez after Portugal’s disappointing World Cup campaign ended in the round of 16 against eventual champion Spain.
Ronaldo, now on 979 career goals — 833 for clubs and 146 for Portugal — is 21 short of the 1,000-goal landmark he has openly targeted. Asked whether winning the Nations League or reaching four figures mattered more, he grinned and chose both.
“One goal is to achieve both – reaching 1,000 goals and the national team trying to win this Nations League,” Ronaldo said.
“It’s a new era with manager Jorge Jesus, whom we all know well; I just hope things go well for him.”
Ronaldo said reaching 1,000 in Portugal colours would be “the icing on the cake”.
“Scoring my 1,000th goal for the national team would be the culmination of something – a beautiful story,” he said. “It wouldn’t be the end of it, but it would be a beautiful story.”
Ronaldo insisted, however, that he was not consumed by the chase.
“I’ve already admitted that I want to get there, and I will get there,” he said. “An obsession? No ... The rest is about enjoying it, enjoying every day.”
PRODUCTIVE TALKS
Ronaldo acknowledged he had considered his international future after Portugal’s World Cup exit, but said talks with the Portuguese FA and Jesus convinced him to continue.
“They count on me. I still believe that I’m able to help the national team,” he said. “The most important point is to be able, inside the pitch, to score goals and help the team to win games.
“If the manager doesn’t count on me, I can leave today – no problem at all... When I feel that I’m not doing anything here, that I’m not contributing on the pitch, not scoring goals, creating a bad atmosphere, or that they don’t want me here, I’ll be the first to pack my bags.”
Pressed on retirement, Ronaldo refused to draw a clear line under his career.
“I learnt something from my late 30s onwards, which is to live in the moment, don’t think about tomorrow,” he said.
“Is it possible? Yes. Highly likely? Yes. But will it happen? No, I don’t know.”
Ronaldo also bristled at criticism, saying media outlets had been trying to “kill” him for years.
“That’s not going to happen under any circumstances – not even with a shotgun,” he said. “And even so, I still manage to dodge the bullet.”
Ronaldo may be 21 goals from four figures and perhaps closer to the exit than he cares to admit, but for now he remains exactly where he likes to be: in Portugal’s shirt, in front of the cameras, and dodging bullets with a smile.

Trump set to greet Xi for high-stakes state visit
BEIJING/WASHINGTON — Chinese leader Xi Jinping is set to arrive in the United States on Wednesday evening for his first state visit in 11 years, opening high-stakes talks with President Trump at a pivotal moment for both men.
It is the second time the leaders are meeting this year after the Beijing summit in May, when they agreed to build a more stable bilateral relationship.
Both leaders are trying to shore up power at home. For Trump, the visit comes just over a month before the midterm elections, and for Xi, preparations for an all-important Party Congress start when he returns to Beijing.
But despite both countries projecting a willingness to build what China has dubbed a relationship of "constructive strategic stability," fierce negotiations over weighty subjects such as AI and trade are underway.
"Under the water, the Chinese seem to have done a lot of kicking lately. And you know, if we have to, we'll kick back," U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a Fox News interview in July.
A "fragile" detente
Trump has frequently spoken warmly about how he was treated during his recent visit to China, which included pageantry and a state banquet at Beijing's Great Hall of the People.
One of the banquet attendees, Wu Xinbo, who directs the American Studies center at Shanghai's Fudan University, said it was the warmest he had seen in the U.S.-China relations in years.
But since then, Wu said, things have been more "fragile."
"In the last several months, the U.S. has continued to contain and pressure China in economic, technological [and] people-to-people exchanges," he said.
For example, the U.S. imposed extra tariffs on Chinese exports over forced labor claims, and the Pentagon added Chinese tech giants on a military blacklist. The Federal Communications Commission banned new imports of Chinese humanoid robots and robot dogs over national security concerns.
Ups and downs are to be expected in a relationship as complicated as the U.S. and China's, said international studies professor Zhang Yun at Nanjing University.
The key is to build high-level channels to deal with problems as they emerge and "mitigate the negative impacts," he said.
Zhang said Taiwan, tech and trade are high on Xi's agenda this trip. Discussions on the wars in Iran and Ukraine, plus tensions along the Korean peninsula, are also expected.
The U.S. is expected to reciprocate the high level of pomp and circumstance for Xi regardless of the tough negotiations expected — and Trump has publicly held Xi in high regard.
Rare earths and AI
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said this week that the two countries are still negotiating the potential extension of a rare earths truce that would ensure continued flow of Chinese rare earth products for the U.S.
China dominates the refining of rare earths and other critical minerals that are important to manufacture a range of products, from cellphones to weapons.
However, American officials have complained that China has not upheld its end of the bargain. NPR reporting shows that mutual distrust scuppered an offer from Beijing to extend the rare earths truce to the end of Trump's term, in January 2029.
The NPR Politics Podcast
Trump takes the world stage
Trump and Xi are also expected to talk about AI governance.
China has "been trying to figure out, in talking to the United States, what kind of so-called guardrails or controls can be put on artificial intelligence," said Rose Gottemoeller, a former NATO official who attends regular dialogues on nuclear proliferation with retired Chinese military officials.
"So it's a combination nowadays of the older issues related to nuclear stability and new issues related to new technology," she said.
China is interested in imposing safety measures, according to Zhang, but he said there is a lot of "mistrust" between the U.S. and China on the proposed solutions.
Taiwan on the table
In their previous meetings, Xi has repeatedly emphasized to Trump that Taiwan, a self-governing island Beijing claims as its own, is a red line and if mishandled could put the U.S.-China relations in "jeopardy." Trump told reporters later that he was not interested in a war thousands of miles away.
"Let's see if the United States can make [a] clearer statement opposing Taiwan independence," said Zhang.
This spring, the Trump administration paused a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan. Experts say Xi is expected to press Trump to maintain this momentum when he sits down with Trump on Thursday.
On Wednesday, as Xi departed for the U.S., China's state news agency published a statement from the country's cabinet-like State Council excoriating Taiwan's president, Lai Ching-te. Lai is despised by Beijing, which suspects he is trying to lead Taiwan to declare formal independence.
"The most important issue that the Chinese always raise in preparation for these high-level visits is the topic of Taiwan," says William Klein, acting deputy chief of mission at the U.S. Embassy in Beijing until 2021.
Trade discussions underway
Trump and Xi also agreed to create trade and investment boards back in May. Among the discussions is a reciprocal tariff reduction framework on products worth $30 billion or more.
China is expected to announce purchases of American agricultural products, and the U.S. is expected to announce tariff reductions on what are called 4A consumer goods, which include footwear and apparel, according to two people in the U.S.-China business community who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
However, no details of who will be on either trade or investment boards have been announced yet.
During Trump's visit to China this spring, the U.S. said China agreed to purchase American beef, soybeans and 200 Boeing jets.
But data shows China is already behind schedule on its promises to buy American agricultural goods.
Jasmine Ling contributed to this reporting.

Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda
- Published
Teenage brothers Olly and Seb Fisher are closing in on their dream of international recognition - but it won't come from their homeland of Scotland.
Instead, the Partick Thistle duo are in line to play for Uganda.
They believe they would become the first white players ever to represent the African nation, thanks to their mother Kate being born there.
"My gran and grandad lived out here for, I think, four or five years," Olly, 18, tells BBC Sport Scotland. "My grandfather came out here to teach in a school then my mum was born here. So, it's a bit of a strange one."
The siblings became aware of interest from Uganda about six months ago, following a chance conversation some time before between their father and a football consultant at a game in Nigeria.
And, at the start of August, they were invited to attend under-20 and under-17s training camps.
They spent last week in Jinja in the country's eastern region and will stay on for one more week, with the pair saying they're "shocked" and "honoured" at the call-ups.
"I couldn't believe it," 16-year-old striker Seb said. "It's one of those things you look at and you're shocked. You can't believe it. Most other people couldn't as well."
Goalkeeper Olly had a similar reaction. "A real mixture of emotions," he said. "I was quite shocked. I didn't really think that this was a possibility but I was honoured to be asked to represent Uganda. I thought it was a real big opportunity."
Mum Kate is "ecstatic" and "thinks it'd be a great experience for us", adds Seb.
'The other boys have been brand new'
There is another Scottish link with Uganda, with former Hearts and Ghana midfielder Laryea Kingston currently coach of Uganda's under-20s.
And he is the one who believes the Fisher brothers are on the verge of making history.
"Coach Kingston was saying we'd be the first white boys to play for Uganda, which would be history in the making," Seb explained. "It is very special."
And Olly added: "It's never been done before, so definitely it is very special."
The pair feel like they're making connections with the African nation, having been reared on stories about Uganda from their grandparents.
And even though they have been training in oppressively warm conditions, they are embracing the opportunity.
"Everyone has been brilliant, welcoming, really great," Seb said. "The other boys have been brand new with us. Some of the boys actually come from the same area where my mum was born. So, they were all talking about that."
The boys will return to Scotland soon, combining training and playing with Thistle with university and school, but are planning to rejoin their new international team-mates in the near future.
Olly hopes to be part of his squad if they qualify for the Under-20's Africa Cup of Nations early next year, and Seb could be in the Under-17 squad for November's World Cup in Qatar.
"That's what you want as a footballer, being in an international environment," Seb said. "It makes you a better player and hopefully it does for the two of us, and I think it will, and benefit us very much going back to Scotland playing at Thistle."

The 51st episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu explores what constitutes a healthy diet amid the growing focus on protein, along with recent developments in osteoarthritis research, corneal donation and rabies prevention.
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss nutrition, weight management, osteoarthritis, corneal donation and transplantation, and rabies prevention.
Protein has become a major focus of nutrition advice, particularly on social media. The episode discusses the role of protein in the diet and why a healthy diet needs to be considered as a whole rather than through the lens of a single nutrient or product.
The conversation also looks at what happens to protein consumed in excess of the body’s requirements. Unlike carbohydrates and fat, protein is not stored in the body as a dedicated reserve. Amino acids from protein are used for functions including tissue repair, muscle maintenance and the production of enzymes and hormones, while excess intake can be used for energy or other metabolic processes.
The episode examines the role of diet and exercise in weight management, including research suggesting that combining dietary changes with physical activity can help support sustained weight loss. It also discusses why overall dietary patterns matter when assessing healthy eating.
Another segment looks at new research into osteoarthritis and cartilage regeneration. The research involves stromal-cell extracellular vesicles derived from menstrual blood and their potential role in cartilage repair. The findings are preliminary and are discussed in the context of ongoing research into new approaches to osteoarthritis care.
The episode also examines challenges in corneal donation and transplantation. Despite the potential of donated corneas to restore vision, some donated tissue does not reach patients who need it. The discussion looks at gaps in the process and the need to improve the use of donated corneal tissue.
Rabies prevention is another focus of the episode. The discussion looks at dog vaccination as an important part of preventing human rabies, given the role of dogs in transmission of the disease.

The Manipur Police arrested two persons, including a 40-year-old woman, from Thoubal district’s Lilong on September 14 in connection with the seizure of addiction-causing pharmaceutical drugs. The police found in their possession 50 boxes containing 15,000 capsules of “Tramadol Hydrochloride Tramanil”, weighing about 7 kg.
Also Read: Highest prevalence of opioid use disorders in eastern parts of India: UNODC report
The consignment, allegedly for illegal distribution to specific clients, was seized almost a month after a youth died at a drug rehabilitation centre in the State’s capital, Imphal. He had reportedly been injecting crushed tablets of Tapentadol, an opioid analgesic thrice as potent as Tramadol.
These incidents and the admission of another Tapentadol user at the drug rehabilitation centre with a serious infection due to injections confirmed what anti-narcotic officials and counsellors suspected — drug addicts were shifting to opioid analgesics available as prescription pain management medication from heroin and other narcotic substances made costlier by the ongoing ethnic conflict in Manipur.
“We are investigating to ascertain the source and intended destination of the Tramadol capsules and to determine the extent of involvement of the arrested duo in the possession or distribution of the pharmaceutical drug,” a Manipur police officer said.
The police and drug enforcement agencies in Manipur said data on seizures of opioid analgesics sold or ferried illegally in the State were not immediately available. They, however, said the price factor could have dictated the shift from methamphetamine and heroin, locally known as No. 4.
High prices
The prices of narcotic substances increased sharply after Manipur spiralled into seemingly unending violence in May 2023. According to reports in the local media, a vial of heroin, for instance, costs almost ₹5,000. A strip of Tramadol or Tapentadol costs between ₹40 and ₹400 depending on strength, brand, and manufacturer.
“Tramadol and Tapentadol are painkilling compounds derived from opium alkaloids. Taken for pain relief, they cause a sense of well-being, but can develop dependence if these are taken continuously for a few weeks,” Krishanu Krori, a Guwahati-based medicine specialist, told The Hindu.
“Addicts increase the dosage through injections after typically starting with 50-100 mg. Apart from a sense of euphoria, they develop disinterest in daily activities, withdrawal from family and society, and a craving for violence,” he said.
Counsellors in Manipur said pharmacists should strictly observe prescription requirements and health authorities should monitor emerging patterns of Tramadol and Tapentadol misuse. Hospitals and rehabilitation centres also need updated guidance on dependence, withdrawal, and complications associated with its misuse and injection, they said.
Opioid analgesics have become a worry for enforcement agencies beyond India’s northeastern region too. In August, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) unearthed an organised network involved in the clandestine manufacture, concealment, and illegal export of such drugs, a scheduled psychotropic substance, to African countries.
The seized items included 1 lakh Tramadol Hydrochloride tablets, 1 lakh Tapentadol tablets, machinery, and raw materials. The DRI sleuths arrested three key members of the syndicate during the operation at the Mumbai Air Cargo Complex.

In Summary
- Google recently unveiled the first batch of Googlebooks, its new kind of notebook, with devices from Lenovo, Dell, Asus, Acer and HP.
- The first batch of Googlebooks comes packed with top-of-the-line hardware and premium design, and has premium prices beginning at USD 899.
- While we wait for them to hit the market (they go on sale on October 4 and 5), we take a look at eleven features of Google’s new notebook concept.
Is it a rejigged Chromebook? Or is it a new attempt by Google to get Android into the notebook space? Google took the wraps off its much-talked-about Googlebook notebook recently, with Googlebooks from five leading brands: HP, Asus. Acer, Lenovo and Dell. What exactly is so special about them, and should you be interested in one? Here are eleven things that we think you need to know about the new Googlebook that might help you make up your mind about them, even as the first batch of Googlebooks gets set to arrive in early October:
Table of Contents
Built on Android, designed to work in sync with your (Android) phone
“If you use an Android phone, your laptop shouldn’t treat it like a stranger,” says Google, so it is hardly surprising that one of the USPs of the Googlebook is the fact that it works seamlessly with your phone, provided it is an Android phone. Googlebooks are built on what Google calls a “share Android foundation,” so you can log in to them with your Android username and password, and access apps and files on your phone on the Googlebook, and do much more, effortlessly. We have no news on compatibility with iPhones at the time of writing.
Comes with a touchscreen
While touchscreens were broadly optional with Chromebooks, as of now, all Googlebooks come with a touchscreen display of up to 2.8K resolution. The touch interface is an integral part of the Googlebook experience. As of now, there is no talk of Googlebook tablets, but given the touch UI, we expect to see them at some stage.
Premium innards (Top-of-the-line chips, lots of RAM)
Unlike Android and ChromeOS, which were both optimized to run even on relatively modest specs, the Googlebook is clearly a high-end beast. All Googlebooks have to come with Intel Core Ultra Series 3 or Snapdragon X Elite with dedicated NPUs capable of over 45 TOPS. They also come with a minimum of 16 GB RAM. The Googlebook at this point seems clearly to be designed for high-end work.
…and outards too
It is not just their hardware; the Googlebook itself also has to be made of premium materials, such as carbon fiber, magnesium and aluminum. Trackpads also have to be made of glass, and the keyboards have to be backlit.
A bar that glows!
They might be sleekly designed and made of premium materials, but perhaps the most striking feature of the Googlebooks is the thin glowing bar on their lids. This Glow Bar lights up in different shades when one starts up the Googlebook, shows battery level, and also “supports other playful patterns” on different occasions, such as when one is using Gemini.
Keyboards that are slightly different
While the keyboards on Googlebooks are broadly similar to those seen on Windows notebooks, there are some subtle differences. Keyboards on the Googlebook come with two special keys – a special key labeled G to invoke Gemini. The capslock key on a Googlebook also acts as a Quick Insert key. Pressing it gives you access to a number of features such as clipboard history, instant translation, emojis, and local search tools. There is also a dedicated shortcut key for Rambler, Google’s voice dictation app that’s making waves these days. Don’t get fooled by those classic keys – there’s a lot under the surface of a Googlebook keyboard!
Runs on Googlebook OS
The operating system of the Googlebooks is – well – Googlebook OS. It is a blend of Android and ChromeOS, and was codenamed Aluminum. It is built on Android and has the same security architecture as ChromeOS. Yes, not many prizes for innovative nomenclature, but then this is the tech world which has operating systems called One and Nothing, so who are we to judge?
Gemini is literally a cursor wriggle away
Every Googlebook comes packed with AI and AI tools, and a super special way of summoning Gemini, Google’s AI assistant. You do not need to hit a button; just wriggle the cursor, and Gemini will pop up! Google calls it the Magic Pointer, and it certainly adds a new dimension to accessing AI on notebooks.
All of Android’s apps and a “desktop Chrome” experience
At the time of writing and based on what has been made public, the Googlebook’s main source of apps is the Google Play Store for Android. What’s more. Android apps and games run natively rather than in a special environment (as on Chromebooks), delivering smooth performance. You also get a proper “desktop” Chrome experience, so all extensions will work, and there is also support for Office 365. What’s more, Android apps and games on a connected Android phone will also work smoothly on a Googlebook. Many of the apps are optimized to run on the large screen and come with support for keyboard and mouse. We do not know if APK files can be installed or if apps can be “sideloaded” onto Googlebooks at this time, though.
PC games can be played…but on the cloud!
But what about PC games? After all, the Googlebooks do boast some seriously powerful hardware, including high-resolution displays, flagship chips, and stacks of RAM. Well, at the time of writing, PC games cannot be directly installed on the, but one can stream PC games via GeForce NOW. We hope that changes in the coming days, given Google’s specs and price tags.
10 years software support
Impressed by the seven years of software support on the Pixel phones? Well, the Googlebooks come with a massive ten years of software support. And given that the hardware inside is top-notch and the frame is made of premium materials, there is every chance that these notebooks will stand the test of time.
And one more thing: They are going to be premium devices as of now!
The current set of Googlebooks unveiled by Google starts at USD 899, with some even starting at prices in excess of USD 1000. Given the current hardware and material requirements laid down for them and the trend of rising component prices, it is likely that Googlebooks will remain premium devices for a while. Of course, we would love it if they became more affordable. Premium tech is wonderful, but affordable tech is love.

The death of an Anna University student at Government Kilpauk Medical College Hospital (KMCH) on Friday (September 18, 2026), due to scrub typhus, has once again brought this bacterial infection to the fore. University authorities have said they have started screening students for scrub typhus as well, along with dengue and leptospirosis
What is scrub typhus?
Scrub typhus is a bacterial infection caused by the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi. It is spread by the bite of infected larval mites or chiggers -- it is not a mosquito-borne disease.
Scrub typhus is a major public health burden in South and Southeast Asia. A 2021 systematic review noted that scrub typhus, a common acute febrile illness, is “a grossly under-recognised public health problem in India.” It stated that the proportion of scrub typhus among acute undifferentiated febrile illness (AUFI) studies was 25.3%, and community seroprevalence was 34.2%. The review also noted that the disease causes severe morbidity and accounts for a large number of deaths, with its bueden “underappreciated.”
A 2025 multi-centre study of 587 children with acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) from Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu revealed that scrub typhus is now the most common infectious cause of AES in southern India.
What are the symptoms?
Symptoms usually begin within 10 days of infection. The United States Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) lists symptoms of scrub typhus as: fever and chills, headache, body aches and muscle pain, a dark, scab-like region at the site of the chigger bite (also known as eschar), mental changes ranging from confusion to coma, enlarged lymph nodes and a rash.
Timely treatment is critical. If left untreated, severe illness from scrub typhus infection can lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), shock, meningitis and kidney failure, which can be fatal, notes a research paper, Incidence of Scrub Typhus in Rural South India published in The New England Journal of Medicine last year.
In India, there is a high mortality of scrub typhus, primarily due to late diagnosis and treatment.
How is it diagnosed and treated?
Since the symptoms of scrub typhus are common to those of several other diseases, diagnosis is often delayed. A blood test (IgM ELISA or PCR) can help confirm the diagnosis.
Scrub typhus should be treated with the antibiotics doxycycline or azithromycin. If the treatment is begun in time, it is effective. Results of a trial carried out in seven centres in India, published in 2023, in which patients were randomly assigned to receive a combination therapy of doxycycline and azithromycin, showed faster resolution of complications compared with two other arms where patients were given monotherapy with either doxycycline or azithromycin. The frequencies of respiratory, renal, hepatic, and central nervous system complications were lower in the combination-therapy group than in either of the monotherapy groups.
How can it be prevented?
There is no vaccine as yet for scrub typhus. The infection is not contagious.
Chiggers live in areas with lots of grass, thick vegetation, agricultural fields, plant litter and bare soil across rural areas of Asia, and usually feed on small mammals such as rats and shrews.
Keeping oneself safe from bites through protective clothing, covered footwear and the use of insect repellent may help. Ensuring surroundings are clean and well maintained can also go some way towards reducing mite habitats.
“Early diagnosis and prompt treatment can significantly reduce complications and mortality. Establishing good surveillance and instituting appropriate control measures are urgently needed,” the 2021 review notes.

Here is a story that on the face of it seems so wildly unlikely it can only be true. Indeed, the very concept of a romantic documentary sounds almost oxymoronic, an indication of how much nonfiction films have become synonymous with grim histories full of suffering and injustice. Let’s hope this sweet work, directed by Orlando von Einsiedel (who’s made his share of hardcore, suffering-intensive docs including Oscar-winning short The White Helmets) launches a new trend in nonfiction film-making for stuff that makes you happy-cry.
The basic meet-cute happened in 1975, when PK (played by Chirag Lobo in the film’s extensive re-enactments) met Lotta (Mina Dale) in Delhi. He was a poor street artist, a Dalit, the lowest possible caste, once called Untouchables. The real PK Mahanandia appears on screen to explain how he had left his rural village for Delhi in order to get away from all that caste hierarchy. When he met Lotta he pretty much knew he’d met the woman of his dreams because he’d been carrying a horoscope his father had commissioned for him when he was a baby that prophesised he’d fall in love with a woman whose family owned a jungle. Lotta, a backpacker from Sweden, hailed from a clan back home that owned a forest, so that was good enough for PK to believe he’d met his fate. After a chaste holiday romance bloomed between these two crazy kids, she went back to Sweden and he decided to bicycle the 6,000 miles all the way there from India to prove his love.
As we hear the now elderly young lovers describe what they were thinking at the time, we watch Lobo and Dale act out the journey, with poor PK getting into a few scrapes that set him back a few steps as he plods his way westward. Some of the most touching interludes are the interactions he has with strangers along the way that seem incredibly naturalistic and semi-improvised. Cynics might quibble that one can’t help wondering what darker parts of the story have been left out, and note that the actors chosen to play the lovers are a few notches more conventionally beautiful than the actual people – but every love story has its soft focus, flaw-concealing fudges so we’ll let it slide here.

'Tragic but avoidable' - how serious is heat-death risk in sport?
- Published
On Monday, 3 August, Fijian rugby player Saimoni Vunilagi set off from home to train with his team-mates.
After the session, he was taken to hospital. A few days later, the 26-year-old was dead.
In a statement announcing his death, Japanese second division club Kyuden Voltex said Vunilagi "displayed symptoms consistent with severe heatstroke" during the training session, adding "despite the best efforts of the medical team, he sadly passed away".
Japan, like the UK, Europe and many other parts of the world, suffered severe heatwaves this summer.
By noon on the day Vunilagi became ill, the temperature in Fukuoka - where Kyuden Voltex are based - had risen to 35C. The humidity was more than 75%.
In the weeks before, the daily high was between 32 and 37C. It had been a month since the daily high was below 30C.
No formal cause of death has been publicly released, but the link suggested by the club between training in heat and Vunilagi's death has caused alarm, given the increase in global temperatures and the rising frequency of extremely hot days.
So, how serious a threat is extreme heat to athletes, what measures could help and do perceptions within sport need to change?
'Extreme heat should be treated like lightning'
There have been a variety of heat-related medical incidents during sports events in 2026.
Tennis players Jakub Mensik and Ekaterina Alexandrova collapsed during matches played at more than 30C, and eight runners had to be taken to hospital during a marathon in South Korea in April at which temperatures reached 29C.
Tour de France winner Tadej Pogacar called this year's heat "dangerous" during the event, while Matthew Brennan asked "what are we doing?" after the temperature topped 40C at the Vuelta a Espana, in which he won five stages.
This summer's World Cup also featured controversial hydration breaks at every match, which Fifa insisted were introduced to aid player welfare.
Many sports - including tennis, athletics and cycling - monitor potentially dangerous levels of extreme heat using the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT), which produces a measure for heat stress levels by assessing air temperature, humidity, wind speed, sun angle and solar radiation.
But some experts believe athletes need greater protection, or the risk of further fatalities will increase.
"We have seen an increase in the number of heat illness events in rugby and many other sports around the world in recent years," says Dr Madeleine Orr - assistant professor of sport ecology at the University of Toronto.
"People assume we've seen such extreme heat before and think, 'it was fine, we pushed through, we can do it again'.
"That's not necessarily true - the heatwaves we're experiencing today are hotter than the ones in your childhood, because heatwaves are relative to the local normal, and 'normal' levels have risen."
Though the requirements of each sport mean the impact of high temperatures can differ, there are growing calls for blanket rules to be implemented across sports which offer more cast-iron protection when things become really extreme.
"Different leagues have different policies - there needs to be more of a standardised approach so that everyone just knows what to do," says Orr.
"It's similar to lightning - most people are familiar with the idea that when there's lightning near a sports event, we take a break for 30 minutes and start once it has gone away.
"We need a similar policy on heat and we need it to apply everywhere - it's easier for people to get behind if it's universal that once we get to a certain threshold, we know what happens."
'Players need protecting from themselves'
One of the big challenges with heat-related illnesses in sport is convincing athletes and their coaches to do what is best for their health.
"I've got no doubt that a lot of coaches think that heat regulation is a hindrance," says Christian Day - general secretary of the Rugby Players' Association.
"And it's a tough one for the player, isn't it? Because you don't want to be the player who puts their hand up and says they're not feeling well, or that it's too hot to train on a certain day. Players need protecting from themselves sometimes.
"It's important for team staff to have a regulatory number that they know if it hits it, there's no discussion, you just stop playing.
"It's also about educating players as to what signs to look for to identify one of their team-mates who is struggling in training."
World Rugby updated its heat and air-quality guidelines in 2025, including use of a heat stress index - a measure from 0 to 250 used to determine how dangerous hot conditions are for players, with provisions for water breaks and extended half-time periods at low levels of danger, and potentially suspending or postponing matches at the higher end of the scale.
But players spend far more time training than they do playing matches.
"If this level of heat is going to become the norm, then we need central regulation and governance as to how we help clubs manage their players and how they should react to these kind of temperatures," says Day.
"Maybe there are cases where perhaps training needs to be limited in time, or doesn't take place at all that day outdoors.
"It's not a matter of trying to call people out or produce problems. It's trying to ensure the safest possible training environment."
Pre-season can be an especially dangerous time for athletes across sports.
On 5 June 2026, the Japan Rugby Football Union (JRFU) warned clubs heatstroke was an increasing concern during the summer, and told teams safety should be the overriding priority when planning summer training camps.
'Every single death is one too many'
Heatstroke is a sudden, dangerous health condition which occurs when the body overheats and can no longer cool itself.
This can damage the organs, cause the intestines to release toxins and potentially be fatal within little more than an hour.
Symptoms include dizziness, nausea, headache, confusion and slurring.
"Heatstroke is 100% preventable, so every single death is one too many," says Orr.
"It's not the case that athletes can handle heat better because of their fitness.
"And the bigger the body the faster it heats up, so bigger bodies are more vulnerable as well. Moving that mass around takes a lot of energy.
"So while yes, professional athletes are extraordinarily fit, that doesn't save them when the issue of concern is cooling off the body."
Amateur athletes playing for the love of the game can be at risk too.
"Whatever the elite level does, we'll see it trickle down into grassroots," says Day.
"And that's why it's crucial that the elite level of every sport sets the right example because the kids, the players of tomorrow, will absolutely copy whatever they see their heroes doing."
