So far, AI in the inbox has so far meant assistance in drafting. Microsoft has pushed Copilot deeper into Outlook, Google has embedded Gemini across Workspace, to provide AI assistants designed to organise inbox, draft replies in your specific tone, and capture meeting notes directly. Almost all of them still wait for the final go-ahead. Sol, a proactive AI assistant, wants to flip that order. Founded in 2025 by three former Cred executives, Anish Karan, Prateek Srivastava and Ranjith Nair, the startup emerged from stealth today with $4 Mn (over ₹38 Cr) from General Catalyst, Nexus Venture Partners, DeVC, Peercheque and Kunal Shah. The offering: if a user has already written "I'll send the deck" or "I'll set up time", an AI automatically begins working without waiting for a prompt. The product scans a user's Gmail (Google Mail) for commitments and then produces the work those promises imply, from research and documents to slide decks, calendar coordination and reply drafts assembled from several threads. The user retains final approval. Sol runs in its own computer environment, can browse the web and draws on a library of more than 100 specialist skills, running on OpenAI’s model under-the-hood. Some of the use cases include: Creating or reviewing a document in Word or Notion, or building and reviewing slides Finding and shortlisting time slots across internal and external calendars Running research ahead of a reply or a decision Drafting replies that pull context from scattered email threads The idea surfaced during the cofounders stint at Cred. While Karan worked in the product of the fintech major, Nair was in the design and product team, and Srivastava was the engineering lead. After identifying the problem, Karan spoke to around 55 enterprise teams from the US, South Korea and Australia to check whether the problem was local for companies in India. It was not. "People whose work runs through email often have to repeat themselves: first in email, then again when they ask an AI tool to act," Karan told Inc42. "We shouldn't have to become experts in AI to benefit from it." Commercially, Sol is pre-revenue with no pricing tiers fixed yet. Karan says the pricing model will be usage or outcome-based with a fixed component to start, since the work varies in volume and complexity per user. Pricing will be in US dollars with no India currency pricing plan yet. He declined to commit to a gross margin target, arguing that model costs are falling and adoption matters more, for now. The go-to-market motion is “prosumer” first: anyone can sign up (waitlist at the moment), and an enterprise sales motion follows once enough people in one organisation use it. Integrations begin with Google Workspace, covering Gmail, Docs and Slides, while Outlook is open to a small group of testers. The stack is model-agnostic, using OpenAI models today with routers that switch between them, and runs on AWS in the US. Karan argues Sol has no direct competitor, only the workflow it replaces, and that reliability plus a simple interface are the moats a challenger must cross. That claim faces incumbents bundling agents into the inbox for free, and the trust problem every email agent inherits: an unapproved draft is harmless, but an approved one carries the user's name. Karan explains that the fresh capital is earmarked mainly for R&D, including talent, model costs and customer time. Sol plans to widen access beyond the waitlist soon. Whether proactive assistants become the default layer of work email, or get absorbed into Gmail and Outlook as features, only time will tell.

Burnham brands ban on football fans drinking alcohol in stands as 'discrimination'
- Published
Andy Burnham has branded a ban on fans being allowed to drink alcohol in the stands during men's football matches as "discrimination".
The prime minister told reporters that "I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out", as he suggested a change could be trialled.
Laws have been in place since 1985 which have prevented drinking in view of the pitch at stadiums for clubs in the top five tiers of men's football in England. Other sports do not face such a restriction.
The Football Supporters' Association (FSA) said the "outdated" legislation should be reviewed, but police chiefs have warned against relaxing the law and would like to meet the PM to "explain the challenges".
The legislation was introduced in 1985 by Margaret Thatcher's government for English and Welsh football grounds. At the time, then-Home Secretary Leon Brittan said that alcohol was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behaviour" in football grounds.
Burnham is a keen football fan and a season-ticket holder at Premier League team Everton.
Shortly before he became prime minister, he criticised the restriction on football fans as he attended a rugby league game at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium where it was possible for supporters to have a drink in the stands.
Speaking to reporters on his trip to the United Nations in New York, Burnham was asked if it was still his view now he is in Downing Street.
Burnham replied: "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different.
"And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis.
"But I'm not going to back away from what's been a long held view of mine. I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently."
A trial or pilot scheme to look at whether a change would be possible is not being ruled out by government sources.
But any wider move would require extensive consultation involving football clubs, fans and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport - none of which is currently planned.
'Incredibly rash'
A UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) spokesman warned that changes to the law would pose "challenges" to policing and the "safety of staff and fans at football games".
He said: "Other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour.
"It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games."
He added it would be "incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area".
FSA chairman Tom Greatrex said it was "unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match - especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league".
He said "many clubs" were in favour of a change, adding: "We welcome the prime minister's comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed."
A fan-led review of football governance in 2021 called for the law to be re-examined.
The rules have been relaxed this season with all Women's Super League (WSL) clubs allowed to offer alcohol to supporters in the stands following two seasons of successful trials.
The law is more restrictive in Scotland, where the general sale of alcohol has been prohibited in Scottish football stadiums since 1981, but trial sales have been taking place recently and fans can now buy alcohol at Hampden Park games.

The 2013 sci-fi blockbuster film Gravity, starring Sandra Bullock and George Clooney, popularized the notion of the Kessler syndrome. In the movie, Russia shoots down a defunct satellite and creates a cloud of debris, leading to serious tension in orbit.
The movie is fantastic, a true thriller, and while some liberties were taken with the depiction of outer space, the basic premise of a cascading series of collisions rendering orbits too cluttered with debris to be usable is valid. The idea was first proposed by NASA scientists Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais nearly half a century ago.
Still, the movie was science fiction, right?
Well, a lot has changed since Gravity‘s release. At the time that theatergoers were sitting on the edges of their seats and watching Bullock dodge debris, there were only about 1,000 active satellites in orbit. Today, that number is closer to 17,000, according to CelesTrak.
The preponderance of this growth has been driven by SpaceX’s Starlink constellation, which now has approximately 11,000 satellites in orbit, with many thousands more on the way. And SpaceX is not alone in the race to provide Internet from space. Amazon has launched hundreds of satellites, with thousands more to follow. Multiple Chinese Internet constellations are likewise in progress.
We’ve written a lot about these constellations, and they have generated a bunch of questions. Most prominent among them: Just how sustainable is all of this? Will we see the Kessler syndrome play out in real time? Here are some answers.
How bad is the situation?
It depends on who you ask, so let’s start with the glass-half-empty and glass-half-full outlooks.
Starting with the pessimists: A few years ago, one of the world’s experts in orbital debris, University of Texas at Austin professor Moriba Jah, told Ars that he worries a lot about the consequences of satellites and debris in low-Earth orbit.
“I think we are going to lose the ability to use certain orbits because the carrying capacity is going to get saturated by objects and junk,” Jah said. ” I also predict that we will see a loss of human life by (1) school bus-sized objects reentering and surviving reentry and hitting a populated area, or (2) people riding on this wave of civil and commercial astronauts basically having their vehicle getting scwhacked by an unpredicted piece of junk. I predict that both those things are going to happen in the next decade.”
At the other end of the spectrum is the person almost solely responsible for the remarkable growth in satellites over the last decade, SpaceX founder Elon Musk. His attitude has largely been that space is big, and things will probably be just fine. For example, during a SpaceX-produced interview this summer at the company’s Starlink terminal factory in Bastrop, Texas, Musk said, “Space is really big. It’s not like space is gonna get crowded. Space is enormous. If you actually look at it relative to the Earth, the satellites are so tiny you can’t even see them.”
So in one way of thinking, very, very bad things are coming. In another, everything’s fine. Where does the truth actually lie?
What’s really happening?
One of the most credible sources for this kind of information is the European Space Agency, which has long studied space debris and its impacts on various orbits.
Fortunately, it just released its annual Space Environment Report a week ago. The European agency has produced such a report over the last decade to provide a transparent overview of global space activities and assess the quality of efforts to preserve the sustainability of spaceflight.
There are some striking—and concerning—changes this year. For example, the European report has dramatically increased its projections of future satellites in this year’s report after reassessing the current trajectory of large constellations.
“The notable increase in the index this year is primarily driven by the substantially larger future population resulting from the current extrapolation scenario,” the report states. “In particular, the growing influence of large constellations highlights the limitations of traditional mitigation approaches when applied to future traffic at unprecedented scales. At the same time, the results are affected by the limited availability of detailed and verifiable information on future deployment plans, operational practices, and end-of-life strategies of these systems.”
The projection for objects in orbit in this year’s report has gone up dramatically.

More satellites mean an increasing probability of collisions, which helps to push us toward a Kessler-like scenario.
As part of the report, the European scientists modeled a number of different scenarios. Assuming that satellite launches continue to increase—by far the most likely trend—even if operators continue to follow best practices in terms of disposing of older satellites and avoiding collisions, the orbital environment will still become significantly more cluttered.
“The extrapolation of our current behavior, which assumes the continuation of explosion in orbits at current rates, adherence by constellations to at least the minimum desirable post-mission disposal success rates, and continuation of the currently estimated post-mission disposal success rates for all other objects, leads to an unstable environment with collision rates increasing exponentially,” the report states.
In its technically precise language, the European Space Agency is essentially saying we’re on a road that could ultimately lead to something like the Kessler syndrome. Such a scenario, with a dramatic growth in constellations using best practices for satellite disposal, looks like this in terms of collisions in orbit.

It does indeed start to look pretty dicey by mid-century.
Also worth noting: The projections in ESA’s 2026 report do not include the new category of orbital data centers, as they exclude projects “still being prepared” for launch. It remains unclear whether these mega-megaconstellations of data centers in space will prove to be economically viable, but if they do, they could be the ultimate tipping point for orbital sustainability.
What is happening up there now?
The European Space Agency talks a lot about the need for responsible behavior, and in managing its massive Starlink constellation, SpaceX has been responsible. The company has been effective at deorbiting satellites that lose functionality and at managing a constellation of thousands of satellites. It’s an unprecedented task that the company has learned, on the fly, to carry out at a scale no government or company has attempted before.
We know from mandatory reporting to the Federal Communications Commission that SpaceX is frequently moving satellites around in orbit, making small but precise maneuvers to avoid collisions. Five years ago, its (much smaller) constellation made about 500 such maneuvers a month. During the most recent reporting period, through May 2026, that number had jumped to nearly 35,000 per month. That comes to one maneuver every 75 seconds.
It is important to characterize these properly. Each maneuver is not a “near miss.” Rather, SpaceX has significantly lowered the probability threshold to trigger a collision avoidance maneuver. The NASA standard for maneuver is 1-in-10,000. At the outset of Starlink, though, SpaceX used a 1-in-100,000 threshold and has since become even more conservative, with a threshold of 3-in-10 million, according to a 2025 letter to the FCC.
So it’s clear that SpaceX is not operating its Starlink constellation in a cavalier manner. But it’s also clear that the company’s constellation, and those like it, are cause for significant concern going forward.
What should we be worried about?
No credible experts are saying that the Kessler syndrome could happen imminently—a single collision won’t set off a Gravity-style cascade.
But space is getting more crowded, and some orbits, particularly from 520 km to 1,000 km above Earth. A 2025 paper by Hugh Lewis and Kessler (yes, that Kessler) found that some orbital bands in this region have already reached what is known as a “collisional-runaway threshold,” which is to say that any serious collisions there may create new debris faster over time than debris would be naturally removed by the pull of gravity, down into Earth’s atmosphere.
Another concern comes from spent “rocket bodies,” upper stages from rockets that were not properly disposed of after launch. This was more common in decades past, but some launches today still do not reserve enough propellant to properly deorbit a second or third stage. These school bus-sized stages are particularly problematic at altitudes of 840 and 975 km, said LeoLabs space debris expert Darren McKnight. They are winging around uncontrolled, of course. And the higher the altitude, the longer the debris hangs around, from decades to centuries.
Finally, because there is so much stuff flying around orbit, it would be relatively easy for bad actors to start shooting missiles at satellites in low-Earth orbit, creating debris fields that could potentially wipe out communications and cause massive financial damage. The probability of Kessler syndrome becomes much higher if humans start deliberately blowing things up in space. Did we mention that Iran recently became the ninth country to put a domestically built satellite into orbit?
What’s the bottom line?
In the near term, it seems unlikely that space will become unusable. But it will likely become more and more expensive to operate there when considering avoidance technology, people to manage all of this, and propellant for maneuvers. And finding launch windows that avoid known debris will become more difficult.
Longer term, perhaps as early as 15 years from now but more likely longer, a Kessler-syndrome type outcome may start to become increasingly plausible.
Eric Berger is the senior space editor at Ars Technica, covering everything from astronomy to private space to NASA policy, and author of two books: Liftoff, about the rise of SpaceX; and Reentry, on the development of the Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon. A certified meteorologist, Eric lives in Houston.

Sanjana Sanghi at UNGA: Actor calls for investment in education, healthcare and greater role for youth
Sanjana Sanghi addressed a UNGA engagement, calling for greater investment in education and healthcare and a bigger role for young people
Actor and UNDP India Youth Champion Sanjana Sanghi addressed a high-level engagement at the United Nations in New York, calling for greater investment in education and healthcare and a bigger role for young people in shaping policy decisions.
“Are we preparing our generations in a way that they deserve to be prepared?” she asked, reflecting on India's large youth population and her own work in youth-led development.
She said she believes that education can be a starting point for wider social change and drew from her personal experience of engaging vividly in youth-led work during her teens.
Addressing the UN General Assembly, Sanghi lay emphasis on the capacities of today's systems to give youth adequate resources and opportunities to shape their accelerated growth. The UNDP India Youth Champion also pointed out to the global military spending and deliberated over divergence of how even a fraction of this expenditure, if directed towards better healthcare facilities, education, vocational training and art centres could allow communities the means to tackle some of these challenges themselves.
Also Read | UNGA 2026 highlights: Trump seeks Iran's ‘economic isolation’, calls for Ukraine peace
‘Acute poverty of trust’
At the heart of her argument, she spoke about trust. Her message ultimately came down to the fact that young people cannot remain mere beneficiaries of decisions made for them when they are the ones who will have to live with what those decisions leave behind.
“The real thing it comes down to is an acute poverty of trust,” Sanghi said, adding that she would rather see fundamental problems in education and healthcare addressed through collective action before young people reach a point where they have to take to the streets.
Sanghi’s journey on the global youth stage began well before this latest appearance. In 2024, she opened the Action Days of the Summit of the Future, making the case for young voices to be heard where the decisions shaping tomorrow are taken. Through her work with UNDP India, she has continued to champion youth inclusion, digital access and the Sustainable Development Goals.
Also Read | NYC bomb scare update: Chrysler Building in Manhattan evacuated after suspicious suitcase found amid UNGA
Her international work is not merely limited to individual UN appearances. Sanghi has served as a UNDP India Youth Champion and was named to the Millennium Campus Network’s Board of Advisors. She was also part of the United Nations’ Distinguished Judges Panel for the 2025 Young Leaders for the SDGs cohort.
What Sanghi carried to the UN was ultimately larger than a single set of demands. It was a vision of young people moving from the margins of policy conversations to their centre, equipped not merely to inherit the future, but to participate in building it.

A fungus that can cause severe pneumonia in people with weaker or weakened immune systems appears to have become resistant to a drug that never intended to kill it, according to the findings of a study by researchers from around the world published in Science Translational Medicine.
The study focused on mycophenolic acid (MPA), an immunosuppressive drug used with people who have received solid-organ transplants. MPA helps keep the immune system from rejecting the organ — but it was also found to affect Pneumocystis jirovecii fungi.
The team analysed 163 P. jirovecii samples from China, Denmark, Germany, Japan, Switzerland, and the U.S., of which 96 came from recipients of transplanted organs, most of whom were also involved in pneumocystis pneumonia outbreaks from 2005 to 2019. The remaining samples were controls.
MPA works by inhibiting an enzyme called IMPDH in human immune cells. The fungus possesses a similar enzyme, and the researchers believe this could be the link. The team found six relatively common mutations in the fungal gene that produces IMPDH. Some 86% of samples from transplant recipients contained a mutation in that gene, versus 13% in the non-transplant samples.
The researchers also produced normal and mutated versions of the fungal IMPDH enzyme in the lab and exposed them to MPA. Depending on the mutation, considerably more MPA was required to inhibit the mutated enzymes than the normal enzyme.
The mutations also appeared in at least 11 fungal strains and varied between countries and over time. That is, rather than resistance arising once and spreading from that source, P. jirovecii seem to have evolved similar adaptations as different populations encountered the same selective pressure.
The researchers have acknowledged that they have only established resistance at the enzyme level, rather than in infected patients, and that their cohort sizes and clinical data were limited.
Nonetheless, researchers understand antimicrobial resistance as microorganisms evolving to resist antibiotics, antifungals or other medicines. But in the study, a drug intended to act on the human body was found unintentionally exerting pressure on a pathogen as well. And mutant fungi that could better tolerate MPA may have enjoyed an advantage among transplant recipients taking the drug, allowing them to survive and spread.
The “results challenge the current status quo on P. jirovecii’s unknown resistance,” the study authors wrote, “calling for reevaluating immunosuppressive strategies and infection control measures and highlighting the broader potential for other pathogens to evolve under selective pressures imposed by human-targeted therapies.”

Jammu, Sep 23: The 17-year-old son of BJP Hiranagar MLA Vijay Kumar was traced to Delhi early Wednesday, a day after he was reported missing from his hometown in Kathua district of Jammu and Kashmir, officials said.

Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault
- Published
Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a criminal sexual act against a former assistant.
In a victim-impact statement in court, Miriam Haley said the assault had had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away".
Appearing in court in a wheelchair, Weinstein denied the allegations but apologised to "anyone I may have hurt by my actions".
Weinstein has already spent several years jailed in New York, where he has faced three trials over rape and abuse allegations. He was convicted in a separate sex-crime case in Los Angeles.
This is the second time he has been given a prison sentence in the Miriam Haley case. Weinstein was first convicted and sentenced in 2020, but New York's highest court overturned the conviction in 2024, along with another involving actress Jessica Mann. The court ruled that Weinstein did not get a fair trial.
He was retried and convicted again last year on a single charge of a criminal sexual act against Haley.
Weinstein, 74, is currently being held in a prison ward at New York's Bellevue Hospital for a series of ailments reported during his incarceration.
Once the high-flying producer behind Miramax, the studio that produced hits like Shakespeare in Love, Weinstein fell from grace in 2017 after the New York Times and the New Yorker revealed multiple women's allegations of sexual assault stretching back decades.
The accusations against him sparked the #MeToo movement, but New York prosecutors have had to navigate a twisting path in securing convictions and sentences.
In the 2020 trial, Haley testified that Weinstein had assaulted her in a bedroom in his Manhattan apartment in 2006. Haley was a production assistant on the Project Runway television series at the time.
On charges related to Mann, juries could not reach a verdict, and he was found not guilty in another charge involving model Kaja Sokola.
After testifying in the retrial last year, Haley told the BBC she felt compelled to take the stand.
"I just thought, I have to stand up for myself. I have to stand up for the truth," she said.
Weinstein is still awaiting sentencing in California, where he was convicted in 2022 of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in a hotel room in 2013.
An appeals court ordered he be re-sentenced in the case after the New York convictions were overturned.
Weinstein has consistently denied the allegations against him, and said he believes he will be proven innocent.
On Wednesday, Judge Curtis Farber criticised the former Hollywood mogul as he announced the 15-year sentence.
"You took what you wanted by force and you have never accepted responsibility," Farber said.

US criticises Australia's proposed algorithm opt-out laws as 'censorship'
- Published
The US has criticised Australia's proposal to give users the ability to opt out of social media algorithms, saying it amounts to "censorship of protected speech".
Under Australia's draft digital duty of care laws, tech firms risk hefty fines if they fail to give users the option to turn off algorithms in a bid to protect them from harmful content.
In a rare submission to the proposed laws, the US embassy in Canberra said it had "serious concerns" and allowing the government to "enforce vague definitions of 'harm'" would lead to "viewpoint-based censorship".
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the legislation was not about giving governments control but giving it back to individuals.
"We ask that Australia clarify how exactly 'harm' and 'risks' shall be determined... ensuring these definitions do not encroach on protected speech," the US said in its submission.
The US also claimed that the proposed laws may risk "reducing the reach of independent journalists or other voices whose content touches on sensitive or controversial topics" if tech firms had to "pre-emptively demote" them.
An opt-out option would "allow regulators to impose rigid, one-size-fits-all platform design requirements" on tech firms and this could affect users outside of Australia, it said.
"Mandated platform design features, especially when applied to algorithms, may affect what users see, say, and hear not just in or from Australia, but globally."
The US also called on Australia to address industry concerns that the "biases and preferences" of government officials do not "disadvantage independent or minority-viewpoint speech".
Another worry was that the proposed laws could affect Australia's "reputation as a jurisdiction that enables innovation," the submission said.
The criticism comes during Albanese's visit to the US to speak at the UN's General Assembly about his government's tech policies.
On Tuesday, local time in New York, Albanese responded to the criticism and claims of the proposed laws being government overreach.
"It's not about giving government control," he told the media in New York.
"It's about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices."
US President Donald Trump meanwhile used his speech at the UN to play down fears about AI, rejecting proposals for guardrails on it and arguing it should be renamed "super intelligence" as "the use of the word artificial makes it sound fake".
This latest move by Australia to protect its online users from harm comes less than a year after the country introduced a social media ban for children under 16 last December.

Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region.
Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.
The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”.
Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño:
‘Climate risk maps’ in China
In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees.
Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat.
In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.
Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.
Taiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke.
The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces.
Sri Lanka plans to process salterwater
El Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts of India there has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families.
The Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”.
In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets.
But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is in Sri Lanka, where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry.
Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water.
The country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable.
Tackling an agriculture crisis in south-east Asia
In south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs, disproportionately hitting the region. At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees.
During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%.
“We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore.
The Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.
“In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.”
With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says.
To prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers.
“We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” say Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.”
South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert system
South Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoes as being “boiled” in the ground.
The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours.
Officials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away.
Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoons
Japan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating.
El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised.
Japan recorded its first official “cruelly hot day” – or kokushobi – in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C.
Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons.
The public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm.
This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drowned during record-breaking rain in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo.

The festive season has officially arrived, and Indian kitchens are once again coming alive with preparations of laddus, payasam, halwa, burfis, and other traditional sweets. With the rising awareness about the impact of sugar, however, some ingredients in popular sweets are being changed. Refined sugar is increasingly being replaced with jaggery, while some consumers are also experimenting with artificial sweeteners such as stevia, and of late, monk fruit sweetener.
The intention is understandable: enjoy festive food while reducing sugar use. The science behind these sweeteners however, is more nuanced. Not every alternative to sugar is nutritionally equivalent, and ‘natural’ does not automatically mean low-sugar. The important question is not simply what sweetener is being used, but how much sweetness and sugars a person consumes overall.
Jaggery counts as sugar
Jaggery has long been associated with traditional Indian cooking and is often perceived as a healthier alternative to refined sugar because it undergoes less refining and may retain small amounts of minerals. However, it remains a concentrated source of sugar.
This distinction becomes particularly important during festivals, when sweets are rarely eaten in isolation. A person may have a laddu, a serving of payasam/kheer, sweetened beverages and several savoury foods in the same day, or worse in a single meal.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that free sugars contribute less than 10% of total daily energy intake, with a further reduction to below 5% providing additional health benefits. For a person consuming around 2,000 calories a day, 5% is roughly 20 to 25 grams, or 4 to 5 teaspoons of sugar.
Therefore, replacing sugar with jaggery does not make a sweet sugar-free. From a doctor’s perspective, portion size and the total amount of free sugar consumed during the day remain far more important than whether the sweetener is brown or white.
Artificial sweeteners
Across the country, many people are now using low-calorie or no-calorie sweeteners. These include artificial sweeteners such as sucralose, saccharin and aspartame, as well as naturally derived sweeteners such as steviol glycosides and monk fruit extract.
Monk fruit extract, the newest addition to sweeteners in the mass market, is particularly interesting because its sweetness comes from compounds called mogrosides. Monk fruit extracts can be approximately 100 to 250 times sweeter than sugar, depending on their mogroside content. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has noted that the use of monk fruit extract is ‘generally recognised as safe’ under its intended conditions of use.
Artificial sweeteners work differently. They provide intense sweetness with little or no calories and are commonly used in products marketed as ‘sugar-free’, ‘light’ or ‘diet’. Approved high-intensity sweeteners are considered safe within their specified conditions of use, and several have established acceptable daily intake levels.
However, a ‘safe’ label does not necessarily mean beneficial. The World Health Organization currently advises against relying on non-sugar sweeteners as a strategy for long-term weight control. Its recommendation is conditional and is based on evidence that replacing free sugars with non-sugar sweeteners does not provide a clear long-term benefit for reducing body fat.
This is an important distinction for consumers. A sweetener can be safe to consume and still not be a reason to increase the amount of sweet food in the diet.
A better approach
The biggest misconception is that changing the sweetener automatically changes the nutritional quality of the sweet.
A jaggery laddu is still sweet. A sugar-free dessert can be calorie-dense if it contains large amounts of ghee, nuts, cream or other ingredients. Similarly, replacing sugar with monk fruit does not make an otherwise highly processed dessert a health food.
The more useful approach is for us to look at our entire festive eating pattern. One traditional sweet enjoyed occasionally is very different from consuming several servings every day throughout the season. The goal is not to find a sweetener that allows unlimited sweetness; it should be to reduce excessive sweets while retaining the cultural and social pleasure associated with festivals.
So, if a festival sweet is made with sugar, moderation matters. If it is made with jaggery, moderation still matters. Monk fruit essence or other non-sugar sweeteners do not automatically bestow a license to eat more.
The aim should be not to move from sugar to jaggery or from jaggery to monk fruit. It should be to simply learn to enjoy our favourite sweets alittle less sweet, and a little less often. This also aligns with broader dietary recommendations from the WHO that advise building diets on minimally and unprocessed foods, and restricting free sugars.
There is no need to cut out every single sweet, but do practice portion control and choose wisely. Instead of five laddus, have one and enjoy it mindfully. Keep the overall diet rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains and fibre, and let sweets remain a small part of the meal.
(Suparna Mukherjee is a dietician with Narayana Health City, Bengaluru. suparna.mukherjee@narayanahealth.org)

India’s Roshibina Devi finished her Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026 campaign with a silver medal after losing to China’s Xiaoyu Zhang in the women’s 60kg final in wushu on Thursday.
The 25-year-old Roshibina, who also won a bronze in 2018 and a silver in 2023 at the Asian Games, lost 0-2 to Zhang in the final. She is the first Indian Wushu player to win medals in three back-to-back editions of the Games.
All five judges gave unanimous 5-0 decisions in favour of the Chinese player in both the rounds of two minute each at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall.
Zhang dominated the first round with the scores of five judges reading 6-2, 6-3, 6-2, 6-2, 8-2 in her favour. The relentless Chinese player was even better in the second and final round with 10-2, 8-3, 7-3, 7-3, 6-1 scores in her favour from the five judges.
Roshibina comes from a farming family in Kwasiphai, Bishnupur district, Manipur. Before her foray into the seniors, she won gold in the Asian Junior Championships in 2017. Her achievements have been recognised with the Arjuna Award, India’s second-highest sporting honour, in 2023. She was also named the IWUF Female Wushu Athlete of the Year (Sanda), the same year.
“I have won silver earlier and this time also, I could win only silver. I could not give the gold medal to the Indian people. I could not give what everyone wanted,” Roshibina said after the bout.
“There was a lot of disturbance when I came here for the Asian Games. I did not get much time to prepare. But, my coach (Amit Pal) supported me a lot to reach here. I will try my best in the upcoming Games, learn from my mistakes and come back,” said the Manipuri.
“I came to know of my inclusion in the team around September 10 and straightway came here from home (from Manipur) without training much,” she said.
Roshibina was a late inclusion in the Indian squad after original choice Divyanshi Choudhary had to be withdrawn due to an anterior cruciate ligament injury.
Talking about her opponent, she said, “She (Chinese player) is a new player, I have not fought against her. She was good in her side kicks. I also tried to defend. I tried to throw her, but she did better. I will do my best for India in the upcoming Games.”
Roshibina’s coach Amit Pal also talked about her lack of preparation ahead of the Games.
“The Chinese fighter was very good, something lacking (in Roshibina). But also, Roshibina did not get much time to prepare. She was out of the national camp for one and half months.
“After trials in June in Srinagar, she left for her home since she lost. After Divyanshi’s ACL injury, Roshibina was named in the team on September 10. She had little training (in between) and straightaway came here,” he said.
At the ongoing edition of the continental showpiece, India has won 14 medals so far - one gold, six silver and seven bronze.

Australia-A slumped on either side of a Jason Sangha spin counterattack and folded for 171, a massive 163 short of India-A’s 334, on the second day of the first unofficial Test at the Siechem Cricket Stadium in Puducherry on Wednesday.
Sangha produced a 64-ball 46 after walking in at 37 for three and late recovery appeared to be the theme for the second day in a row.
He began with consecutive sweep shots against Shams Mulani (4/68) after Tea before riding the bounce against Tushar Deshpande and punching him through point twice.

Liam Scott took a leaf out of this playbook and ransacked 14 runs off Tanush Kotian in three deliveries. He bookended a hit down the ground with a cut past point and a slog sweep through midwicket.
He was approaching Mulani in the same vein when he hopped out and wafted him into the sightscreen. But the left-arm orthodox had the last laugh as he floated a delivery full, got it to turn and had Scott caught behind.
Two overs later, Sangha threw his wicket away in an attempt to clear the point fielder with a reverse sweep.
Kotian and Mulani wrapped up the tail, giving India-A the option of imposing a follow-on when play resumes on the third day.

How Ceuta, football and Israel are shaping Morocco's election
- Published
Disillusioned young voters in Morocco were courted with viral football slogans, promises of one million jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls ahead of Wednesday's parliamentary elections.
Yet, for many young Moroccans, politics remains deeply disconnected from reality.
"I have no hope for this election. I'm ashamed of our political scene. It's a complete circus," Siham Azeroual, 32, an environmental activist who lives in the Atlas region, tells the BBC.
The outcome of the vote will decide the make-up of the next government, just weeks after 60,000 people risked their lives to cross from the North African country to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - a sign of the lack of opportunities many young people feel they have at home.
Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy where political parties compete for 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the legislative chamber.
Yet executive power remains closely tied to the crown. King Mohammed VI, the 63-year-old monarch, appoints the prime minister from the political party that comes first in the election, but also presides over the Council of Ministers - the country's most important policy-making body.
The current campaign also follows a wave of Gen Z protests that erupted in September 2025 over unemployment, healthcare and living costs.
Demonstrators chanted slogans like "freedom, dignity, and social justice" which escalated to "get out Akhannouch", a reference to current Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
More than 2,400 people faced prosecution following the unrest. Despite the crackdown, some young activists are choosing to enter the political arena.
Hamza El Kharroubi, 29, was briefly arrested during the protests. He is now running for parliament with the little-known Environment and Sustainable Development Party, which has a green agenda.
"As a young person, I don't have much hope. I joined this party because they wanted more Gen Z faces and they are allowing us to speak freely about our demands," El Kharroubi tells the BBC.
He comes from Tetouan, just 34km (21 miles) from Fnideq beach, where the migration wave to Ceuta started in late July.
Some 60,000 people crossed, both Moroccans and other nationalities. At least 100 people died in the largest migration surge to the enclave in recent history.
"We want justice for the families of those who died crossing to Ceuta. We want compensation for their families," El Kharroubi says.
He argues that the crossing was widely linked to economic hardship and unemployment.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates overall unemployment stood at 13% last year, while youth unemployment - between the ages of 15 and 24 - reached 37.3%.
El Kharroubi says his goal is not to compete with established heavyweights - but securing a voice in parliament to build toward 2031.
"As young people, we have to enter the parliament so by 2031 we have strong young politicians who can compete for a seat in the government."
Fouzi Lekjaa, head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a senior politician who works in the finance ministry, has emerged as the kingdom's newest political sensation - and a definite heavyweight.
Credited with helping the Atlas Lions - as the national men's football team is known - become global contenders, Lekjaa joined the centrist Party of Authenticity and Modernity (Pam) in July.
Videos of his campaign rallies have gone viral in the football-mad nation that is jointly hosting the next World Cup along with Spain and Portugal.
The clips show crowds chanting "Sir" which means "Go" in Moroccan Arabic - the iconic catchphrase from Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup run, when it became the first Arab and African side to make it to the semi-finals.
Lekjaa has promised to make Morocco sixth in the world in education and healthcare, to match the Fifa ranking of the men's football team.
Pam is competing against 26 other parties, including Prime Minister Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI). In its bid for a second term, RNI has renewed a pledge to create one million job opportunities by 2031.
Political expert Rachid Aourraz, from the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis (MIPA), remains sceptical about this promise.
"The slogan 'one million jobs' has become an overused electoral slogan. There is also talk of raising the minimum wage, but what is proposed cannot withstand a structural inability to create stable net jobs," Aourraz tells the BBC.
He adds that major parties "do not compete over an alternative model", but rather over how to implement public policies set by a royal vision.
Also seeking a political comeback is the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) - using anti-Israeli sentiments to woo voters.
Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 along with several other Arab countries, under the US-brokered Abraham Accords.
Led by populist former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, the PJD is campaigning heavily on a promise to end diplomatic ties with Israel. He says the normalisation was a "mistake" made by his party which led the government between 2016 and 2021.
Bilateral ties were hit during the Gaza war with weekly protests taking place in the capital, Rabat, against the Israeli diplomatic presence.
During the conflict the Israeli liaison office was closed and direct flights between the two countries were suspended.
Yet despite an outpouring of pro-Palestinian protests, with tens of thousands taking to the streets and setting ablaze the Israeli flag at the height of the war, it was announced earlier this month that Israel and Morocco had agreed to open full embassies in their respective countries.
This followed a meeting between their top diplomats and the US ambassador to the United Nations.
"We have to speak up," Benkirane told supporters at a campaign rally in Marrakesh.
"If we work hard, the king will close the Israeli embassy. The king does not like going against his own people," he added, warning of "the dangers of Israel and Zionism in Morocco".
I think young people should focus on the microscale: rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top"
More than half of Morocco's total population of roughly 38.8 million is under the age of 35 - though only 4% of the more than 15.8 million registered voters are aged between 18 and 24.
"I am not keeping up much with the campaigns - but I noticed the same faces as usual," says Hiba, a 27-year-old Moroccan living in Canada who preferred not to use her last name.
She lives in Montreal which has a large Moroccan diaspora of about 104,000 people, according to the 2016 census.
Many of last year's Gen Z protests were more vocal outside the country, where young Moroccans were able to express their anger without fear of repercussions.
Hiba, who co-organised several Gen Z protests in Montreal, says she would have considered voting had she been able to find a proxy in Morocco - which is how those in the diaspora can cast their ballot.
"Gen Z protests didn't go in vain. We achieved something. At least now we see more debates with young people on state TV," she says.
Azeroual, the environmental activist, agrees.
But having lived through both the 20 February movement in 2011 that changed the constitution and the recent Gen Z movement, she believes change must come from a multi-faceted approach.
"I think young people should focus on the microscale - rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top," she says.
Despite not being fully convinced by any political campaign, she says she will be heading to her local polling station to cast her ballot.

In September 2026, some Facebook accounts shared a rumor of a chimpanzee saving a person's life by pulling them from a faulty electrical cabinet.
For example, one Facebook page claimed (archived) a chimpanzee left its enclosure to pull a zookeeper away from an electrical cabinet that shocked him and knocked him to the ground. The post included an image of what appeared to be two security camera screenshots showing the chimpanzee pulling the zookeeper away from the cabinet and a rescue team running towards the zookeeper while the chimpanzee watched.
The story as shared by the page read in full:
A chimpanzee pulled a zookeeper away from a faulty electrical cabinet, then sat nearby until the rescue team arrived.
The keeper had entered a service area beside the chimpanzee habitat to inspect a control box that had stopped working. Moments after he opened it, an electrical fault knocked him to the ground.
He was still conscious, but badly disoriented and unable to move away from the cabinet.
A chimpanzee watching from the nearby access doorway immediately became agitated. Instead of retreating, it entered the service yard, grabbed the back of the keeper's jacket and began pulling.
The chimpanzee dragged him several feet across the concrete until they were safely away from the loose cable. Then it released his clothing and moved back toward the habitat entrance.
Other zoo workers noticed the emergency on a security monitor and called the rescue team. Less than a minute later, three responders came running through the service gate with medical equipment.
By then, the keeper had regained enough strength to sit upright. The chimpanzee remained beside the habitat doorway, quietly watching as help approached.
Staff later said the animal had never been trained to perform a rescue. It simply saw someone it knew lying in danger—and did the only thing it could think of.
The rescue team treated the keeper, but the chimpanzee was the one who first pulled him out of harm's way.
The tale was posted to Facebook groups (archived) and also appeared on YouTube (archived). A reader sent Snopes an email asking if the claim was true.
There is no credible evidence supporting the story of the chimpanzee's rescue. The image included in the post was generated using artificial intelligence, and it is likely the story is AI-generated, too. Therefore, we've rated this claim false.
Snopes first looked for evidence supporting the story on various search engines.
We searched for "chimpanzee pulled zookeeper from electrical cabinet" (archived) and "zookeeper saved by chimpanzee" (archived) on Google, and made similar searches (archived) on DuckDuckGo (archived), Bing (archived) and Yahoo (archived). None of the searches yielded any reporting of the incident by credible news organizations, press releases, blog posts from a zoo or any other type of primary evidence of the incident, such as the security footage that allegedly captured it.
Reverse image searches through Google (archived) and TinEye (archived) did not yield any such results either. The few instances of the image the search engines found online were all from Facebook posts retelling the story.
If the story was real, it's very unlikely there would be no reporting, discussion or firsthand accounts available online. The Facebook posts do not identify the people involved, the name of the zoo or the location of the zoo; many fabricated stories are intentionally vague on such details to make it more difficult to debunk them.
The post embedded above, posted by the Facebook page Animal Rescue Stories, appeared to be the original source of the claim. Snopes reached out to the Animal Rescue Stories page over Facebook Messenger to ask whether the page was the source of the story and to request credible evidence supporting the story if it had any. We'll update this story if and when we receive a reply answering our questions.
Evidence of AI generation
The Animal Rescue Stories post also included an "AI content" label. Facebook will automatically apply the "AI content" label when the content was created or modified by Meta AI, or when it detects AI signals within the content (such as hidden watermarks). Facebook users can also add the "AI content" label to their posts themselves.
In this particular case, the label could mean the attached image, the written story or both were generated by artificial intelligence tools.
This label aligns with the about section on Animal Rescue Stories' Facebook page. The about reads:
Emotional stories of animal rescue and hope.
Spreading kindness, protecting wildlife and nature
The stories you are watching are recreated with AI, but the video aims to spread values of compassion, education, and animal protection.
That disclaimer reads as if it only applies to video content, and not to the images or the written stories. Due to this uncertainty, Snopes also asked the Animal Rescue Stories page via Messenger if it generated the story itself using AI. The page didn't reply prior to publishing.
The two screenshots from the security footage have easily identifiable inconsistencies that wouldn't be possible in reality. Although the visible timestamps suggests the screenshots were taken less than a minute apart, there are significantly more objects lining the left wall in the second screenshot than there are in the first. The first screenshot depicts enough space between the right wall and the fence to fit a dumpster and a small vehicle, while the second screenshot depicts significantly less space and different objects in the same area. Even the size of the entrance to the chimpanzee exhibit differs between the two screenshots.
Pangram, a reputable AI text detection tool, determined that the text of the story was 100% AI-generated.
Let us note here: These types of AI detection tools are fallible. Snopes cautions people against using them for definitive answers on media's authenticity without supporting evidence.
The fictional story about the chimpanzee helping the zookeeper resembled glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental."
This particular story is similar to other AI-generated stories of chimpanzees purportedly saving zookeepers' lives.
For further reading, Snopes fact-checked a similar AI-generated story and image claiming a gorilla cried out for help when its favorite caretaker collapsed.

Kalyan District and Sessions Court Judge Santosh Aage on Wednesday (September 23, 2026) acquitted Uddhav Thackeray, Deputy CM Eknath Shinde, Anand Paranjape and Rajendra Devlekar in a case of defamation that Vasant Davkhare filed 17 years ago. The court cited lack of evidence.
The court held that records, testimony and statements did not support the charges. It noted gaps in the investigation and in sequence of events, as per the proceedings and advocates.
Vasant Davkhare was the NCP candidate from the Kalyan Lok Sabha seat in 2009. Anand Paranjape was the Shiv Sena candidate. Mr. Paranjape won. During the campaign, a meeting took place. Uddhav Thackeray, Eknath Shinde and Anand Paranjape showed recordings of sound and images about Davkhare to people through television, as per a complaint.
Rajendra Devlekar organised the meeting. Mr. Devlekar was a corporator from Kalyan with the Shiv Sena. He died. After the election, Mr. Davkhare filed a suit against Mr. Thackeray, Mr. Shinde, Mr. Paranjape and Mr. Devlekar. He said the meeting defamed him.
The case remained in Kalyan court for 17 years. It came up for hearing before judgment on Wednesday. Anand Paranjape attended. Advocate Jayesh Wani argued for Uddhav Thackeray. Wani is the spokesperson of Shiv Sena Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray.
Testimony of witnesses, twenty in number, was recorded. These included party workers, office bearers, police officers at the venue, police, organisers and officers who investigated. The process under Section 313 against leaders was completed. A month before, Eknath Shinde and Uddhav Thackeray recorded statements before the court through the system for conferencing by video. Thackeray denied allegations.
During the hearing, the side for the accused raised questions about the recording, printout, lab report and investigation. It said the accused had no connection with case of CD and that evidence was not available. The court examined the aspects and acquitted the accused because evidence was not there and because the sequence had gaps and additions, according to the defence.
Adv. Jayesh Wani said the case of defamation was filed with vendetta in politics. The purpose was to gain in elections. Witnesses in this case did not speak to facts. Records showed testimony was taken before the incident. The sequence of events in this crime did not match records and had no basis. Therefore, the court acquitted Mr. Thackeray. Truth has won.
Anand Paranjape said Vasant Davkhare filed this case of defamation on charges related to politics. We have always respected Vasant Davkhare. We will continue to do so. Mr. Davkhare filed a criminal case in this matter after his defeat. There were no facts in this case. We have now got justice.

Trump loses big in Iowa court after trying to sue pollster for wrong election call
A judge on Wednesday dismissed Donald Trump’s lawsuit accusing The Des Moines Register and its former pollster of misrepresenting the state of the 2024 presidential race

A state judge on Wednesday dismissed a legal challenge Donald Trump brought against The Des Moines Register and its former pollster, rejecting claims that media coverage of a pre-election survey violated Iowa’s consumer fraud law and ruling that press reporting on political contests is fully protected under the Constitution.
Describing the lawsuit as extraordinary, Iowa District Judge Scott J. Beattie cautioned that letting the case and its "faulty" legal claims move forward in court could have a severe chilling effect that "can discourage others from reporting on and debating public affairs."
Judge Beattie ruled in favor of pollster J. Ann Selzer and the newspaper, affirming that political polling and news coverage detailing survey results constitute constitutionally protected political speech rather than a commercial product governed by state consumer protection statutes.
Wednesday's court ruling came just hours after a separate judge held a hearing but did not issue an immediate decision in a legal challenge over Trump’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds. Trump barred journalists from the three media organizations last Friday from accessing White House grounds, assailing their news coverage as "fake news."
Following the court ruling in Iowa on Wednesday, a spokesperson representing Trump’s legal team confirmed that the president will take his case forward by appealing the dismissal directly to the Iowa Supreme Court.
Trump originally initiated the lawsuit against Selzer, The Des Moines Register and its parent publishing company in December 2024. The lawsuit accused the defendants of fraudulently publishing deceptive polling data to damage his presidential campaign and aid Democratic candidates, asserting that news coverage of public opinion polls does not constitute protected speech under the First Amendment.
The legal battle in Iowa is part of a broader series of lawsuits filed by Trump and his legal advisers against various media organizations accusing them of political bias. These legal actions have repeatedly called into question the legal boundaries of free speech protections for press organizations, though some of those cases have previously resulted in out-of-court settlements.
The free speech advocacy group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression took on Selzer's legal defense. Speaking on Wednesday, Selzer said she was grateful for the ruling, which she noted "reaffirms the fundamental freedom to pursue and publish the truth without political interference."
"Polling is a social science, not clairvoyance, and no responsible pollster can guarantee an election outcome," Selzer added in a written statement.
Attorneys representing Selzer at FIRE and her fellow co-defendants also celebrated the favorable court ruling.
"Today is a victory for the First Amendment — and for the essential role of a free press in American democracy," Polly Grunfeld Sack, chief legal counsel for USA Today Co., said in a statement celebrating the outcome. USA Today Co., formerly known as Gannett, is the parent company that owns The Register.
In his decision dismissing the legal challenge, Beattie wrote that Trump’s lawsuit attempted to "stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability." After hearing the legal arguments, the judge concluded that constitutional protection "is too great and the reach is too far. The case must therefore be dismissed."
Beattie said the lawsuit would still have to be dismissed even if, solely to decide the pending defense motions, he accepted the Trump team’s claims that the poll was deliberately skewed and its results fabricated. "Even with this assumption, each of the three counts still fails," the judge wrote, explaining that the lawsuit failed to meet the legal requirements for fraud or consumer deception.
The disputed survey, conducted by Selzer’s firm in the final days of October and published just days before Election Day 2024, showed then-Vice President Kamala Harris, the Democratic presidential nominee, capturing 47% support among likely Iowa voters to Trump’s 44%. Trump ultimately won Iowa by securing 56% of the nearly 2 million votes cast.
Republican U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and former Iowa state Sen. Brad Zaun had joined Trump as co-plaintiffs in the lawsuit.
Trump, Miller-Meeks and Zaun had alleged in their legal filing that the misleading poll coverage harmed their public reputations, consumed valuable time in the final days of the campaign, and depleted significant campaign funds and resources.

Donald Johnson said he works delivering luggage because nowhere else will hire him

Online donors are rallying around an 81-year-old Texas man who has taken on difficult work — the only job he could land — to help pay for his wife's healthcare needs.
Donald Johnson works as an independent contractor delivering lost luggage to people's homes, and he was doing the grueling work when Erin Howell of The Colony, a suburb near Dallas, saw him struggling with some of the heavier bags.
"The other day, I looked out my door cam and saw an 81-year-old man slowly and painstakingly carrying my heavy luggage that had been lost on a recent flight up a steep flight of stairs," Howell wrote in a GoFundMe entry. "He looked absolutely exhausted, and his steps were heavy with effort."
After talking to him, she learned that Johnson started doing his luggage job three years ago to help pay for his wife, Josephine, who is battling cancer. The couple has been together for 57 years.
Howell asked Johnson why he picked such a physically demanding job, and he reportedly told her that it was the "only job that will hire me."
"The staggering medical bills, continuous treatments, expensive prescription medications, and everyday costs of living have completely overwhelmed them," Howell wrote of Johnson's situation. "At an age when he should be resting and spending every precious single moment by his wife's side, he is out on the road lifting heavy bags just to keep her alive and cared for."
To make matters worse, since Johnson is an independent contractor, he has to use his own car for deliveries. He reportedly has put more than 200,000 miles on his car delivering luggage, and the miles have taken their toll on the vehicle's condition.
Moved by Johnson's struggle and dedication to fight for his wife, Howell started a GoFundMe to help Johnson retire without having to give up on paying for his wife's cancer treatments.
Howell said that all of the money raised will go toward paying for Josephine's medical bills, which will allow Johnson to stop working and focus solely on caring for his wife.
As of Wednesday morning, the fundraiser has raised an impressive $87,000 of its $150,000 goal.
Howell said that she knew Johnson was unlikely to ask for help, so she started to fundraise on her own.
"He is a deeply proud, selfless, and dedicated husband who would never ask for charity himself, which is exactly why I am stepping in as to start this GoFundMe campaign," Howell wrote. "He shouldn't have to carry this crushing financial and physical weight all by himself anymore."
